title: Robust Bichromatic Classification in 3D Using Planes and Slices
summary: Given two sets of points in 3-dimensional space $R$ and $B$, we want to separate these two sets of points using a classifier based on linear constraints, while ensuring robustness against outliers. The problem was studied in $\mathbb{R}^2$ by Glazenburg et al. We follow their approach and present various algorithms for many types of classifiers under various definitions of outliers. Our algorithms rely mainly on the duality of points and planes in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

AI.tldr: Extends 2D robust linear separability to 3D using point–plane duality; proposes multiple robust algorithms for separating two point sets with linear constraints under different outlier models.
AI.motivation: Robustly separating two classes of points in 3D with linear separators while mitigating outliers; builds on Glazenburg et al.’s 2D work and leverages the point–plane duality in R3 to design algorithms.
AI.method: Translate points to planes via duality and exploit geometric duality to formulate robust linear classifiers in 3D. Develop multiple algorithms accommodating various definitions of outliers and different classifier types, paralleling the 2D approach of Glazenburg et al., but in three dimensions.
AI.result: A set of algorithms for robust linear separation in R3 under several outlier models; demonstration of the approach’s viability and adaptability to different classifier families.
AI.conclusion: Extends robust 2D separability results to 3D using point–plane duality; provides a flexible framework for designing robust linear classifiers in 3D with multiple outlier models.

title: Covering Planar Lattices with Interior-Disjoint Unit Disks
summary: We study an infinite variant of the coin-covering problem for periodic point sets in the plane. Given a point set of spacing $d$, we ask whether all of its points can be covered by pairwise non-overlapping unit disks. We consider the triangular lattice, the square lattice, and the honeycomb point set, and construct periodic motif patterns that certify several intervals of coverable spacings. For the triangular lattice, our constructions include single-family patterns with vertex, face, and off-lattice realizing centers, as well as multi-family patterns. For the honeycomb point set, additional native motifs fill gaps left by the triangular-lattice constructions. For the square lattice, we revisit the constructions of Alm et al., identify an unintended overlap in one motif realization, and give new patterns that recover part of the affected interval and establish an additional coverability interval.

AI.tldr: Develops motif-based periodic coverings to certify intervals of spacings for unit-disk cover of infinite periodic point sets (triangular, square, honeycomb) in the plane; provides multiple motif families, fixes a square-lattice overlap, and expands known coverability intervals.
AI.motivation: Generalize the coin-covering problem to infinite periodic point sets and determine which spacings allow all points to be covered by non-overlapping unit disks using periodic motifs.
AI.method: Construct periodic motif patterns with realizations at vertex, face, and off-lattice centers (for triangular lattice); develop multi-family patterns; extend native motifs for honeycomb; revisit Alm et al. results for square lattice and identify/repair an overlap, yielding new patterns and an additional interval.
AI.result: Certifies several intervals of coverable spacings across the three lattices via explicit motif constructions; resolves an unintended overlap in square-lattice realization and adds an extra coverability interval; enriches the set of known configurations for infinite coverage.
AI.conclusion: A motif-based framework can systematically certify coverability intervals for periodic point sets in the plane, highlighting lattice-specific constructions and fixes; the approach yields extensible designs and potentially more intervals with further motifs.

title: Removing Online Exponential Net Search from Solovay-Kitaev
summary: The Solovay-Kitaev algorithm describes how to approximate, to arbitrary precision, a matrix in the special unitary group SU(d) using any fixed universal gate set. Although the algorithm scales as O(poly(log(1/$ε$))), where $ε$ is the maximum targeted approximation error, its running time depends exponentially on the qudit dimension d. This bad dependence can be traced to its explicit use of an $ε$_0-net of size 2 $Ω$(d^2) , which is queried O(poly(log(1/$ε$))) times throughout the execution. For this reason, the standard Solovay-Kitaev theorem is usually stated for fixed d, with the base net and its lookup cost absorbed into the constants. We study the algorithmic problem in the variabledimension regime and show how to avoid searching an exponentially large precomputed net for each target unitary. In particular, we introduce the notion of a good exponential basis and show that such a basis can replace the usual depth-zero net-search routine. This yields a modification of the algorithm in which the use of an explicit net is fully moved to a preprocessing step. For instruction sets that already contain, or allow the efficient construction of, a good exponential basis, the resulting online synthesis algorithm is polynomial in d and polylogarithmic in 1/$ε$. For arbitrary universal instruction sets, the exponential dependence on d^2 is not removed, but is isolated into a one-time additive preprocessing cost. Our technique uses differential-geometric methods to devise an integerized version of trotterization that replaces the depth-zero net query by a constructive local synthesis routine. The same framework also suggests possible extensions based on other discretized numerical integration schemes.

AI.tldr: For the Solovay-Kitaev problem in variable dimension, the authors introduce a good exponential basis to replace the depth-zero net search, moving the net-search cost to preprocessing. This yields online polynomial scaling in the dimension d and polylogarithmic scaling in 1/ε for instruction sets containing such a basis; for general universal sets, the exponential in d^2 remains but is confined to preprocessing.
AI.motivation: The conventional Solovay-Kitaev construction uses an ε0-net of size exponential in d^2, causing the algorithm’s running time to scale exponentially with the qudit dimension. In the variable-d regime, this dependence hinders scalability; the goal is to achieve scalable online synthesis without incurring a prohibitive per-instance net search cost.
AI.method: Introduce the concept of a good exponential basis and replace the depth-zero net-search with a constructive local synthesis routine. The approach shifts the net-based preprocessing into a preprocessing step, using differential-geometric ideas to derive an integerized version of trotterization. This yields a framework that can leverage discretized numerical integration schemes and allows a preprocessing-only net cost.
AI.result: For instruction sets that already contain or allow efficient construction of a good exponential basis, the online synthesis algorithm becomes polynomial in d and polylogarithmic in 1/ε. For arbitrary universal instruction sets, the exponential dependence on d^2 is not removed but is isolated to a one-time additive preprocessing cost.
AI.conclusion: The framework shifts the heavy net-search cost to preprocessing via a good exponential basis and local synthesis, enabling scalable online synthesis in the variable-dim regime for suitable instruction sets, with potential extensions to other discretization schemes.

title: FineServe: A Fine-Grained Dataset and Characterization of Global LLM Serving Workloads
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as always-on online services, making efficient LLM serving a critical systems challenge. Achieving low latency and high throughput under volatile demand requires deep understanding of real-world serving workloads, yet existing studies often rely on proxy traces or coarse-grained characterizations that fail to capture the heterogeneity of modern multi-model LLM platforms. We present FineServe, an in-the-wild, multi-model LLM serving workload dataset collected from a global commercial marketplace, enabling fine-grained characterization of real-world serving dynamics across heterogeneous models and tasks. Leveraging FineServe, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of arrival dynamics and token behavior, revealing fundamentally different fluctuation regimes across model architectures, scales and task intents. Building on these insights, we develop the FineServe workload generator, which composes fine-grained model-aware workloads into configurable mixtures tailored for benchmarking multi-model serving platforms. By exposing these fine-grained workload dynamics, FineServe provides a realistic foundation for evaluating routing, scheduling, and capacity-planning strategies in LLM serving systems. FineServe is available at https://github.com/hihiztc1/FineServe.

AI.tldr: Introduces FineServe: a real-world, multi-model LLM serving workload dataset and a workload generator for benchmarking routing, scheduling, and capacity planning.
AI.motivation: Addresses the need for realistic, fine-grained workloads to capture heterogeneity across models, tasks, and scales in modern LLM serving, as existing studies rely on proxy traces.
AI.method: Collect a real-world dataset (FineServe) from a global marketplace; perform fine-grained analysis of arrival dynamics and token behavior across models and intents; develop a model-aware workload generator to compose configurable mixtures.
AI.result: Reveals distinct fluctuation regimes across architectures, scales, and tasks; provides a generator to synthesize realistic, fine-grained workloads for benchmarking; makes the dataset available publicly (GitHub).
AI.conclusion: FineServe offers a realistic foundation for evaluating routing, scheduling, and capacity-planning strategies in multi-model LLM serving and enables realistic benchmarking across heterogeneous models and tasks.

title: Stack and Queue Layouts with Defects
summary: Linear layouts of graphs -- particularly \emph{stack} and \emph{queue} layouts -- are well-established types of representations in graph drawing, thanks to their connection with numerous theoretical and practical problems. In such layouts, all vertices are linearly ordered and the edges are partitioned into sets that avoid specific forbidden configurations: in a stack layout no two independent edges within the same set cross, whereas in a queue layout no two independent edges within the same set are nested. A central problem in this context is to determine, for a given graph $G$, its \emph{stack number} or \emph{queue number}, that is, the minimum number of sets into which the edges can be partitioned so that a corresponding stack or queue layout of $G$ exists. In this work, we introduce a relaxation of stack and queue layouts, which allows some forbidden patterns for the edges in the same set. Namely, for a given integer $k > 0$, a \emph{$k$-defective stack layout} (resp. a \emph{$k$-defective queue layout}) allows an edge to be in a crossing (resp. nesting) relationship with at most~$k$ edges within the same set. Our motivation is to extend the classes of graphs that admit linear layouts using a limited number of edge-partition sets, at the cost of allowing some defects. We study defective linear layouts both from a combinatorial and from an algorithmic perspective, providing an array of results across different graph classes and parameters.

AI.tldr: Introduces k-defective stack/queue layouts: a relaxation allowing up to k crossings/nestings per edge within a same set; studies combinatorial and algorithmic aspects across graph classes.
AI.motivation: To extend the reach of linear layouts by tolerating a bounded number of edge defects, enabling more graphs to admit stack/queue-like representations with limited violations.
AI.method: Define k-defective variants of stack and queue layouts and perform combinatorial and algorithmic analysis across various graph classes and parameters, deriving a spectrum of results.
AI.result: The abstract states an array of results across different graph classes and parameters but does not provide specific theorems or bounds.
AI.conclusion: Defective layouts extend the range of graphs that admit linear layouts with bounded defects, suggesting rich directions for both theory and algorithms.

title: Hybrid LSTM-Graph Neural Framework for Robust Financial Fraud Detection and Adversarial Resilience
summary: Financial institutions face significant challenges in detecting sophisticated money laundering patterns, such as smurfing and layering, due to extreme data imbalance (0.13% fraud rate) and evolving adversarial evasion tactics. This paper proposes FraudShield AI, a hybrid framework that integrates Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks with hand-crafted Graph Topological Features to capture both temporal sequences and structural relational context. By engineering network-centric features including PageRank Centrality, In-Degree dynamics, and a custom Flow Ratio, the system shifts the detection paradigm from isolated transaction analysis to network-level forensics. A Focal Loss objective is used to address class imbalance, and a dynamic thresholding mechanism is introduced to improve resilience against low-value smurfing attacks. Experimental evaluation on the PaySim dataset shows that the proposed hybrid model substantially outperforms Logistic Regression and XGBoost baselines in Precision, Recall, and F1-Score, particularly on hard-to-detect micro-transaction fraud patterns. An ablation study confirms the complementary contribution of both the temporal and topological components.

AI.tldr: Hybrid LSTM with graph-topology features and adaptive thresholds for fraud detection under extreme class imbalance, outperforming baselines on micro-transaction fraud in PaySim.
AI.motivation: Address evolving money laundering patterns (smurfing, layering) under severe data imbalance (0.13% fraud) by incorporating network context and robust training objectives.
AI.method: Combine LSTM for temporal sequences with hand-crafted network features (PageRank Centrality, In-Degree dynamics, Flow Ratio); use Focal Loss to handle imbalance; apply dynamic thresholding; evaluate on PaySim; ablation to assess temporal vs topological contributions.
AI.result: Significant gains in precision, recall, and F1-score over Logistic Regression and XGBoost, especially for hard-to-detect micro-patterns; ablation confirms complementary benefits of temporal and topological components.
AI.conclusion: Network-level forensics with a hybrid temporal-topological model and imbalance-aware training yields improved detection of sophisticated money laundering patterns; both components are necessary for strong performance.

title: Detect Early, Escalate Rarely: Anytime Detection of AI-Generated Video from the Compressed Bitstream
summary: Detectors for AI-generated video are evaluated offline. A clip is decoded to pixels and scored once, increasingly by a large vision-language model. Detection, however, is deployed online. We recast the task as streaming perception and score the motion field the codec already wrote into the bitstream. Reading that field is a parse, not a pixel-domain forward pass. Because the running aggregate is monotone, one end-calibrated threshold is anytime-valid at the data-dependent decision time. Recalibrating at each prefix is not. Escalation is priced in closed form. A compute budget maps to a deferral window, on a frontier monotone exactly where the deferral condition holds. On matched GenVidBench the codec stage reaches full-length AUC 0.64 at five orders of magnitude less compute than a pixel CNN, on CPU. Its gate holds the stopping-time false-positive rate at target while the real data match its calibration, and drifts above it under distribution shift. Deferring 15% of clips lifts accuracy from 0.75 to 0.78 at $7\times$ less compute (paired: McNemar $p<10^{-6}$). The stage-1 ordering replicates on AIGVDBench. We introduce no new detector. The contribution is the reframing, two guarantees, and the measured frontiers. Code, configurations, and evaluation splits: https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/streamdet.

AI.tldr: Streaming-perception framing for online AI-generated video detection. Uses the codec-embedded motion field as a parseable score, enabling a monotone, anytime-valid threshold and a deferral-based compute budget. On GenVidBench, achieves 0.64 AUC with 5x10^? less compute than a pixel CNN on CPU; deferring 15% of clips raises accuracy from 0.75 to 0.78 at ~7x compute savings; stage-1 ordering replicates on AIGVDBench; no new detector, but reframing and frontiers with two guarantees. Code provided.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between offline detector evaluation and online deployment; enable accurate detection with low compute while maintaining calibration under distribution shifts.
AI.method: Frame detection as streaming perception by reading the motion field encoded in the bitstream (a parse) rather than performing a pixel-domain forward pass. Use a monotone running aggregate to yield an anytime-valid threshold; calibrate once at data-dependent decision time and use a deferral window mapped from compute budget via a frontier monotone condition. Apply stage-1 ordering and validate on GenVidBench and AIGVDBench; report frontiers and guarantees.
AI.result: GenVidBench: codec-stage AUC 0.64 with CPUs at 5 orders of magnitude less compute than a pixel CNN. Stopping-time gate maintains target FPR and calibrates to data, but drifts under distribution shift. Deferring 15% of clips increases accuracy from 0.75 to 0.78 with ~7x compute savings. Stage-1 ordering replicates on AIGVDBench.
AI.conclusion: Main contribution is reframing to streaming/perception with two guarantees (anytime validity and monotone deferral frontier) and measured frontiers rather than new detectors; code and configurations are provided.

title: Native Multi-Dimensional Subquadratic Operators via Input Dependent Long Convolutions
summary: Subquadratic alternatives to attention require compromises when applied to multi-dimensional data: standard convolutions lack global receptive fields and input dependency, while recurrent models require rasterizing data such as images, volumes, and partial differential equation (PDE) into an ad-hoc $1\rm D$ scan order that violates their spatial structure. We introduce \textit{HyenaND}, a subquadratic, global, input-dependent operator that acts directly on the native geometry of multidimensional data through convolutions with implicitly parametrized global, input-dependent multi-dimensional convolutional kernels. Our CUDA implementation, \texttt{nSubQ}, fuses the FFT-convolution path to turn HyenaND's $\mathcal{O}(L \log L)$ scaling into wall-clock speedups. Across long-context genomics, computer vision, medical imaging, and PDE modeling, pure HyenaND stacks match the accuracy of strong attention baselines, while hybrid configurations that interleave HyenaND and attention layers outperform both pure attention and strong recurrence-based hybrids.

AI.tldr: HyenaND provides subquadratic, global, input-dependent multidimensional convolution to process data in native geometry; CUDA implementation nSubQ uses FFT-convolution to achieve O(L log L) scaling; pure HyenaND matches strong attention baselines, while HyenaND–attention hybrids outperform pure attention and recurrence-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Standard attention is costly and limited in multi-dimensional data: convolutions lack global receptive fields and input dependency, while recurrent models require rasterizing data into 1D scans, destroying spatial structure. There is a need for a global, input-dependent, subquadratic operator that respects native geometry.
AI.method: HyenaND is a subquadratic, global, input-dependent operator acting on native multidimensional data via implicitly parameterized global convolutional kernels. The CUDA implementation nSubQ fuses an FFT-convolution path to achieve O(L log L) scaling. The approach can be stacked in pure HyenaND configurations or as hybrids interleaved with attention layers.
AI.result: Across long-context genomics, computer vision, medical imaging, and PDE modeling, pure HyenaND stacks match the accuracy of strong attention baselines. Hybrid configurations that interleave HyenaND and attention layers outperform both pure attention and strong recurrence-based hybrids.
AI.conclusion: HyenaND provides a viable global receptive-field alternative with subquadratic complexity that respects native data geometry; the FFT-accelerated nSubQ implementation offers practical speedups; the framework yields competitive or superior accuracy across domains and benefits when combined with attention.

title: ModPack: An Extensible Teleoperation Interface for Bimanual Mobile Manipulation
summary: Existing teleoperation systems are often tailored to specific robot hardware and task domains, limiting their scalability and adaptability. We present ModPack, a modular and extensible teleoperation system designed to support diverse robot embodiments and task requirements within a unified framework. At the core of ModPack is a self-contained wearable "backpack" that integrates onboard computation, power, communication, and data storage. Built on top of this shared interface, the system supports plug-and-play capability modules including joint-level teleoperation with haptic feedback, mobile manipulation, and active perception. Experiments across two distinct robot platforms and real-world mobile manipulation tasks demonstrate that ModPack provides a flexible and reusable framework for data collection and policy learning. To support future research, we open-source the complete hardware design and software stack. Project website: https://modpack-robotics.github.io/

AI.tldr: ModPack is a modular, wearable-backed teleoperation framework that unifies diverse robot embodiments and tasks via plug-and-play modules, enabling scalable data collection and policy learning; the authors open-source hardware and software.
AI.motivation: Teleoperation research is hampered by hardware- and task-specific systems that limit scalability. A unified, extensible platform is needed to support multiple robots, tasks, and data-driven learning.
AI.method: Develop ModPack with a self-contained wearable backpack providing computation, power, communication, and storage. Build plug-and-play modules for joint-level teleoperation with haptic feedback, mobile manipulation, and active perception. Validate on two robot platforms with real-world mobile manipulation tasks and release the hardware/software as open-source.
AI.result: Demonstrates flexibility and reusability for data collection and policy learning across different robots and tasks; validated experimentally on two platforms with real-world tasks; complete stack is open-sourced.
AI.conclusion: ModPack offers a scalable, modular teleoperation framework that supports diverse embodiments and task requirements within a unified platform, enabling broader data collection and learning; open-source release facilitates adoption and further research.

title: On 2-Layer k-Matching-Planar Graphs
summary: A graph is $k$-matching-planar if it admits a drawing in the plane such that, for every edge $e$, the edges crossing $e$ contain no matching of size greater than $k$. The class of $k$-matching-planar graphs generalizes other beyond-planar graph classes, such as $k$-planar and fan-planar graphs. In a $2$-layer drawing of a bipartite graph, the vertices of the two bipartition classes are placed on two parallel horizontal lines and edges are drawn as straight-line segments between them. We prove that every graph with a $2$-layer $k$-matching-planar drawing has pathwidth at most $2k+1$. Moreover, for every $k \geq 0$, we construct a graph with a $2$-layer $k$-matching-planar drawing whose pathwidth is $3\lfloor k/2\rfloor + 1$. On the algorithmic side, we consider the one-sided recognition problem where a fixed embedding of the vertices on one side is given. We show that this problem is NP-hard. On the other hand, we prove that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Finally, we prove that the two-sided variant cannot be approximated within any constant factor in polynomial time unless $\operatorname{P}=\operatorname{NP}$.

AI.tldr: Defines k-matching-planar graphs, proves tight pathwidth bounds for 2-layer drawings, constructs matching-width lower bounds, and maps the complexity landscape (NP-hardness, FPT in k, and inapproximability) for related recognition problems.
AI.motivation: Generalizes beyond-planar graph classes and links geometric drawing constraints to width parameters and computational complexity, motivating structural and algorithmic study of this graph family.
AI.method: Combinatorial analysis of 2-layer straight-line drawings, derivation of pathwidth bounds, constructive graph lower bounds, and complexity reductions to establish NP-hardness, fixed-parameter tractability in k, and inapproximability results for two-sided variants.
AI.result: Pathwidth of graphs with 2-layer k-matching-planar drawings is at most 2k+1; there exist graphs with the same drawings having pathwidth 3⌊k/2⌋+1; one-sided recognition is NP-hard but fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by k; two-sided recognition cannot be approximated within any constant factor in polynomial time unless P=NP.
AI.conclusion: The work advances the understanding of k-matching-planar graphs by establishing tight structural bounds and delineating the computational complexity landscape, including precise bounds and hardness/tractability results, which informs future research on beyond-planar graph classes and related algorithms.

title: OpenEvoShield: Dual Non-Stationary Continual Defense for Open-World Multi-Agent System Attacks
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, where adversaries inject malicious instructions through inter-agent communication to propagate harmful behaviors. Unlike static threats, these attacks are doubly dynamic: adversaries refine injection strategies against deployed defenses while normal-agent behavior drifts with system expansion. Existing defenses treat deployment as a closed-world problem and degrade rapidly once either distribution shifts beyond training coverage. We propose OpenEvoShield, a co-evolutionary continual defense framework for LLM-MAS. An asymmetric rate controller (M1) decouples fast attack-side and slow normal-side learning rates from dual drift signals. A normal-boundary updater (M2) maintains a dynamic behavioral boundary at the slow rate, while an EWC-regularized policy ensemble (M3) fast-adapts without catastrophic forgetting. An energy-based multi-granularity detector (M4) fuses node-, subgraph-, and graph-level evidence to classify novel attacks as out-of-distribution. Experiments over 100 deployment rounds across five benchmarks and four MAS topologies show that OpenEvoShield outperforms static and continual baselines, detecting most previously unseen attacks while keeping false positive rates low.

AI.tldr: OpenEvoShield: a co-evolutionary continual defense for LLM-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS) using four modules (M1–M4) to counter evolving adversarial instructions. Demonstrates robust unseen-attack detection across 100 deployment rounds, five benchmarks, and four MAS topologies, outperforming static and continual baselines.
AI.motivation: Adversaries continuously adapt injection strategies against deployed defenses while agent behavior drifts as the system scales; static/coverage-bound defenses degrade under distribution shift, necessitating a co-evolutionary, continual defense with multi-scale detection.
AI.method: A four-module framework: (M1) asymmetric rate controller decouples fast attack-side from slow normal-side learning; (M2) normal-boundary updater maintains a slow-rate dynamic behavioral boundary; (M3) EWC-regularized policy ensemble enables fast adaptation without catastrophic forgetting; (M4) energy-based multi-granularity detector fuses node-, subgraph-, and graph-level cues to detect out-of-distribution attacks. Evaluated over 100 deployment rounds across five benchmarks and four MAS topologies.
AI.result: Outperforms static and continual baselines; detects most previously unseen attacks while maintaining low false positive rates.
AI.conclusion: OpenEvoShield delivers robust, continual defense for LLM-MAS against evolving adversarial instructions, with effective unseen-attack detection and scalable performance across diverse topologies.

title: Crowd4D: Scene-Aware Monocular 4D Crowd Reconstruction
summary: Recovering scene-consistent 4D crowd motion from monocular video in large-scale scenes remains challenging due to severe depth ambiguity and complex scene geometry. Existing monocular crowd reconstruction methods typically rely on single-plane assumptions, leading to unreliable metric scale and spatial drift under complex terrain. We propose Crowd4D, the first scene-aware 4D crowd reconstruction framework that jointly optimizes the crowd and scene from a monocular RGB video in large-scale scenes. Crowd4D explicitly incorporates scene geometry and ensures consistency across image and scene spaces via a multi-stage optimization strategy. A key bottleneck of this task lies in accurate human-scene alignment, particularly in scale and position. However, human and scene reconstructions are typically decoupled. To address this, we introduce the Human-Scene Interaction Proxy, abbreviated as HSIP, as an intermediate representation derived from Scene Interaction Point Clouds and a Scene Interaction Surface, abbreviated as SIPC and SIS. These representations encode explicit scene-aware geometric priors and redefine the optimization space for large-scale monocular 4D crowd reconstruction. To further improve temporal stability under occlusions, we introduce Crowd Structural Coherence Regularization, abbreviated as CSCR, which leverages HSIP-based spatial priors to impose soft temporal consistency on pairwise relative displacements and directions within local crowd neighborhoods. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Crowd4D consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods and enables robust monocular 4D crowd reconstruction in complex, large-scale real-world scenes.

AI.tldr: Crowd4D provides scene-aware monocular 4D crowd reconstruction in large-scale scenes by jointly optimizing crowd and scene, introducing HSIP as an intermediate geometric prior via SIPC and SIS, and CSCR for temporal coherence; it outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Monocular crowd reconstruction suffers from depth ambiguity, scene geometry ignorance, and unreliable metric scale; existing methods often rely on single-plane assumptions, causing spatial drift on complex terrains; need scene-aware, large-scale reconstruction.
AI.method: Multi-stage optimization that jointly optimizes crowd and scene. Introduces Human-Scene Interaction Proxy (HSIP) derived from Scene Interaction Point Clouds (SIPC) and a Scene Interaction Surface (SIS). Uses HSIP as geometric priors to redefine the optimization space. Adds Crowd Structural Coherence Regularization (CSCR) leveraging HSIP priors to impose soft temporal consistency on pairwise displacements/directions within local crowds.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show Crowd4D consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art monocular 4D crowd reconstruction methods in complex, large-scale real-world scenes.
AI.conclusion: Crowd4D is the first scene-aware 4D crowd reconstruction framework. The HSIP/SIPC/SIS representations provide explicit scene-aware priors and reframe the optimization; CSCR improves temporal stability. The method demonstrates robustness and scalability in challenging monocular settings.

title: Bayesian Wind Tunnels for Model Selection
summary:
Prior work has shown that transformers can perform exact Bayesian filtering within a fixed
  hypothesis class. Can they also perform Bayesian model selection -- identifying the correct
  hypothesis class from data? We introduce model-selection Bayesian wind tunnels: controlled
  environments where ground-truth posteriors over hypothesis classes are available in closed
  form. Using fixed-point-free involutions -- whose defining property f(f(x))=x is purely
  relational -- a 2.8M-parameter transformer achieves 0.01-bit entropy agreement with the
  Bayesian optimum (3 seeds), with both integer tokens and opaque symbols whose meanings
  change every episode. This extends to non-nested comparisons: involutions vs. 3-cycles
  (where neither class is a subset of the other) achieve class-posterior MAE under 0.001,
  demonstrating genuine model selection beyond simplicity/subset bias. We then identify a
  sharp perceptual access condition: when the discriminative statistic requires arithmetic --
  modular addition (rotations) or multiplication (f(x)=cx mod p) -- model selection succeeds
  with integer tokens but fails completely with opaque symbols, and this boundary persists
  under 112x scaling (2.8M to 316M parameters). A stationarity control confirms the operative
  factor: opaque tokens with a fixed relabeling succeed (0.009-bit MAE), showing that stable
  semantics, not integer identity, enable circuit compilation. Header subtask diagnostics
  localize the failure to the composition of header inversion with arithmetic rather than
  header parsing itself. Probing frontier LLMs on the same tasks shows qualitative Bayesian
  behavior but a large calibration gap (~55x), measured through lossy probes and therefore
  directional rather than exact.

AI.tldr: Transformers can perform Bayesian model selection under controlled, abstract tasks; a 2.8M-parameter model matches Bayes-optimal posteriors within 0.01 bits for fixed hypothesis classes and achieves sub-0.001 MAE on non-nested class comparisons, but success depends on perceptual access: arithmetic operations are recoverable with integer tokens but not with opaque symbols. Scaling preserves the boundary; semantics stability matters. Frontier LLMs show Bayesian-like behavior with large calibration gaps (~55x).
AI.motivation: To test whether transformers can perform Bayesian model selection (identifying the correct hypothesis class) rather than only exact Bayesian filtering within a fixed class, by constructing model-selection wind tunnels with tractable ground-truth posteriors.
AI.method: Construct model-selection wind tunnels where ground-truth posteriors over hypothesis classes are available. Use fixed-point-free involutions as hypotheses and compare to non-nested alternatives (e.g., 3-cycles). Train a 2.8M-parameter transformer on data with integer tokens and with opaque symbols whose meanings change each episode. Assess posterior accuracy (bits) and mean absolute error (MAE) against Bayesian optimum across seeds. Explore a perceptual access boundary by requiring arithmetic (rotations, modular multiplication) and perform a scaling study up to 316M parameters. Do stationarity controls and header inversion diagnostics to localize failure modes. Probe frontier LLMs for comparison.
AI.result: Achieved 0.01-bit entropy Agreement with Bayes optimum (three seeds) for involutions with 2.8M parameters; non-nested involutions vs 3-cycles yield class-posterior MAE < 0.001. Perceptual boundary: arithmetic-based statistics enable success with integer tokens but fail with opaque tokens; boundary persists under 112× (2.8M to 316M) scaling. Stationarity control shows that stable semantics, not integer identity, enable circuit-like computation; header inversion combined with arithmetic, not header parsing per se, accounts for certain failures. Frontier LLMs show qualitative Bayesian behavior but calibration gaps are large (~55×) as measured by lossy probes.
AI.conclusion: Model-selection capability in transformers emerges under conditions where the perceptual statistics are accessible arithmetically and semantics are stable; without interpretable semantics, even large models struggle with model selection. The results delineate a boundary between tokenizable arithmetic percepts and opaque symbols, and they indicate that calibration gaps remain for large LLMs despite Bayesian-like behavior.

title: Emergent Autonomous Drifting for Collision Avoidance in Real-World Winter Driving Scenarios
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. Accepted at IEEE ITSC 2026
summary: Real-world collision avoidance is a core motivation for studying the dynamics and control of high sideslip drifting in vehicles, yet the practical benefit of such maneuvers has so far primarily been tested in scenarios explicitly engineered to require drifting. In this work, we explore the question of if and when drifting may be optimal for safety in real-world winter driving conditions. We present a drift-capable nonlinear model predictive control (MPC) system designed to handle scenarios grounded in crash fatality data and deploy the controller in a high fidelity simulator across road departure and oncoming vehicle collision avoidance scenarios. The controller naturally initiates and sustains drifting maneuvers to stay on the road when hitting a patch of ice on the rear axle and to avoid an oncoming vehicle that has slid into its lane. Comparisons with a benchmark electronic stability control (ESC) system demonstrate how a drift-capable controller can trade off stability for controllability to precisely maneuver through dangerous winter driving scenarios. A Monte Carlo study over random ice patches further shows that the drift-capable controller achieves lower median lane error than ESC across several speeds, while revealing that drifting emerges predominantly at higher speeds.

AI.tldr: Drift-capable nonlinear MPC improves winter driving safety by enabling controlled drifting; outperforms ESC in lane-keeping errors; drifting more common at higher speeds.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether drifting can be advantageous for safety in real-world winter conditions, extending beyond engineered drifting scenarios.
AI.method: Develop drift-capable nonlinear MPC; validate in a high-fidelity simulator across road departure and oncoming-vehicle scenarios grounded in crash data; compare with ESC; conduct Monte Carlo over random ice patches.
AI.result: Controller initiates and sustains drifting to stay on the road when rear-axle ice is encountered and to avoid an oncoming vehicle; achieves lower median lane error than ESC across speeds; drifting emerges predominantly at higher speeds.
AI.conclusion: Drift-capable control can widen the safety envelope in winter driving by trading stability for controllability; drifting is a viable tool under icy conditions and merits further study and practical consideration.

title: How Close is a Tree to a Euclidean Minimum Spanning Tree?
comment: Extended version of the paper accepted to "34th International Symposium on Graph Drawing and Network Visualization" (GD 2026)
summary: Let $Γ$ be a straight-line crossing-free drawing of a tree $T$. A \emph{bad pair} in $Γ$ is a pair of non-adjacent vertices of $T$ whose Euclidean distance in $Γ$ is smaller than the length of the longest edge in the path connecting them in~$Γ$. When $Γ$ has no bad pairs, $Γ$ is a Euclidean Minimum Spanning Tree of its vertex set (or EMST-drawing for short). Deciding whether a tree of maximum degree at most six admits an EMST-drawing is known to be \NP-hard. In contrast, we characterize those caterpillars that admit an EMST-drawing. The characterization gives rise to a linear-time algorithm that decides if a caterpillar admits an EMST-drawing, and in the affirmative case, computes such a drawing. For caterpillars of maximum degree six, we further present a linear-time algorithm to compute a crossing-free straight-line drawing with the minimum number of bad pairs. For $n$-vertex trees with maximum vertex degree $Δ$, we prove the $Δ^2n\log n$ upper bound on the minimum number of bad pairs. In the special case of stars, we construct a drawing with the minimum number of bad pairs.

AI.tldr: Characterizes EMST-drawings of trees, with NP-hardness for max degree ≤ 6; provides a complete caterpillar characterization and linear-time EMST-drawing algorithm for caterpillars; for max-degree-6 caterpillars, a linear-time method to minimize bad pairs; general Δ-bound on minimum bad pairs (Δ^2 n log n); optimal results for stars.
AI.motivation: Understand the structure of Euclidean Minimum Spanning Tree drawings of trees via the notion of bad pairs; delineate complexity boundaries and develop efficient algorithms for special tree families (caterpillars) to decide and construct EMST-drawings and minimize bad pairs.
AI.method: Theoretical graph-drawing analysis introducing the bad-pair concept; complexity reductions to show NP-hardness for degree-6 trees; structural characterization of caterpillars; design of linear-time algorithms for EMST-drawings on caterpillars; optimization procedures for minimizing bad pairs on restricted trees; derivation of general upper bounds Δ^2 n log n on the minimum number of bad pairs; specialized treatment of stars.
AI.result: A complete characterization of which caterpillars admit EMST-drawings and a linear-time algorithm to decide and construct such drawings; a linear-time algorithm to compute a crossing-free straight-line drawing with minimum bad pairs for caterpillars of max degree 6; a Δ^2 n log n upper bound on the minimum possible number of bad pairs for n-vertex trees with maximum degree Δ; and a construction achieving the minimum number of bad pairs for stars.
AI.conclusion: EMST-drawability is tractable for caterpillars and can be optimized efficiently within restricted tree classes; hardness persists for general trees at degree bound 6, delineating a clear boundary; the Δ^2 n log n bound narrows understanding of bad-pair minimization in broader settings, with stars achieving optimal scenarios; further work likely exists in tightening bounds and extending results to broader tree families.

title: Benchmarking Confidential GPU Inference on NVIDIA H100 under Intel TDX
summary: Confidential computing is becoming a practical deployment requirement for AI inference workloads that process sensitive inputs or protect proprietary model assets. However, the performance cost of enabling confidential execution for GPU-accelerated large language model serving remains workload dependent and operationally important. This paper presents a benchmark study comparing standard non-confidential execution with confidential computing mode on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU hosted in an Intel TDX confidential instance. The evaluation uses two representative language models, Mistral-7B v0.1 and Qwen3-30B-A3B, and measures time to first token, end-to-end request latency, per-request token generation throughput, global token throughput, and closed-loop request throughput under increasing concurrency. In fixed request-rate experiments, confidential mode increases average TTFT by 21.8% for Mistral-7B and 27.8% for Qwen3-30B-A3B, while global token throughput drops by 17.7% and 21.1%, respectively. In closed-loop concurrency experiments, throughput gaps remain in the 11.5-20.2% range, but the larger model reaches its saturation knee earlier under confidential mode. The results suggest that confidential GPU inference can retain usable throughput under load, but capacity planning must account for both the steady throughput penalty and the earlier saturation behavior observed for larger models.

AI.tldr: Confidential computing on a single H100 GPU incurs measurable throughput penalties for LLM inference but remains usable; capacity planning must account for TTFT increase and earlier saturation, especially for larger models.
AI.motivation: Assess practical performance trade-offs of confidential execution for GPU-accelerated LLM serving to inform deployment decisions.
AI.method: Benchmark comparing non-confidential vs confidential mode on one NVIDIA H100 80GB in Intel TDX; two models (Mistral-7B v0.1, Qwen3-30B-A3B); metrics TTFT, end-to-end latency, per-request token throughput, global token throughput, closed-loop throughput; experiments include fixed-rate and increasing concurrency; analyze throughput penalties and saturation behavior.
AI.result: Confidential mode raises TTFT by 21.8% (Mistral-7B) and 27.8% (Qwen3-30B); global token throughput declines by 17.7% and 21.1%; closed-loop throughput gaps 11.5-20.2%; larger model saturates earlier; nonetheless confidential GPU inference can maintain usable throughput under load.
AI.conclusion: Confidential GPU inference is feasible but requires explicit capacity planning to accommodate steady performance penalties and earlier saturation, particularly for larger models.

title: D3VL: Understanding Driving Scenes from 3D Time Series Data and Video with Language Models
summary: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have triggered the development of end-to-end MLLMs for autonomous driving. However, the main emphasis to date has been for MLLMs using 2D images and videos. In contrast, this paper considers MLLM effectiveness using 3D sensors, particularly LiDAR and stereo cameras. LiDAR presents unique challenges to integration within an MLLM, largely because of data sparsity and lack of a grid structure for the data. For similar reasons, fusion of camera and LiDAR data within an MLLM pipeline is also uncommon. However, most autonomous systems rely on LiDAR-based sensing, and incorporating 3D data has been proven to improve performance in traditional 3D scene perception tasks. This paper presents D3VL, a novel MLLM framework that integrates 2D and 3D time-series data in a single but simple architecture. The model aims to answer questions involving traffic scene understanding and safety. D3VL shows an 11% improvement in the KITTI Question-Answering (QA) dataset compared to baseline methods in processing 2D and 3D time-series data. This paper further introduces the Waymo QA dataset extension, which assesses models' capabilities in processing 3D and time-series data under diverse driving conditions. D3VL implementation code and WaymoQA extension can be found on our supplemental website: https://automotivesafety-lvlm.github.io

AI.tldr: D3VL introduces an end-to-end multimodal LLM that fuses 2D and 3D time-series data (LiDAR and stereo) for autonomous driving, achieving an 11% improvement on KITTI QA, and introduces Waymo QA as a 3D/time-series evaluation extension with publicly available code and dataset resources.
AI.motivation: Leverage 3D sensing (LiDAR, stereo) in multimodal LLMs to improve traffic scene understanding and safety, addressing LiDAR data sparsity and lack of grid structure, and to complement traditional 2D MLLMs for autonomous driving.
AI.method: Proposes D3VL, a single-architecture framework that integrates 2D and 3D time-series data (including LiDAR and stereo) within an end-to-end MLLM pipeline, designed for QA-style questions about driving scenes.
AI.result: Demonstrates an 11% improvement over baselines on the KITTI QA dataset when processing 2D and 3D time-series data; introduces the Waymo QA dataset extension to evaluate models under diverse driving conditions.
AI.conclusion: Validates the feasibility and benefits of incorporating 3D modalities into MLLMs for autonomous driving; provides supplemental resources (code and WaymoQA extension) to advance 3D-aware MLLMs in practice.

title: CruiseBench: A Real-Flight-Aligned N-CMAPSS Benchmark for Engine RUL Prediction
summary: Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction estimates how long an engine can continue safe operation and is central to maintenance planning. N-CMAPSS extends C-MAPSS by simulating run-to-failure aero-engine trajectories using recorded real-flight profiles and retaining complete within-flight time series rather than cycle-level snapshots. However, this added realism reduces evaluation control because full-flight records increase data volume and entangle degradation cues with operating-regime variation, complicating preprocessing choices and direct comparisons of RUL modeling performance. To mitigate this issue, this paper proposes CruiseBench, a cruise-stage RUL benchmark derived from N-CMAPSS. It introduces CPM-N-CMAPSS (Cruising-Period Mask for N-CMAPSS), a mask artifact that stores cycle-local cruising intervals identified by the common-altitude method for the nine accessible subdatasets. CruiseBench applies a fixed protocol to the masked rows, using scenario descriptors and measured sensors as inputs while excluding virtual sensors, health parameters, and auxiliary metadata from the feature tensor, preserving native-resolution windows, and applying dataset-wise RUL caps. Experiments with LSTM, GRU, TCN, and TSMixer provide baseline results for this setting. Under CruiseBench-eta5-W256-S10, TSMixer obtains the lowest average RMSE, $3.4\pm1.71$, and Saxena score, $(2.50\pm2.99)\times 10^{4}$. Ablation studies show that flight-stage selection, temporal downscaling method, and RUL-cap threshold affect reported results. With its fixed cruise-stage protocol, CruiseBench provides a reproducible sub-benchmark for controlled RUL model comparison and CPM-N-CMAPSS provides a stage-specific data foundation for future transfer-learning and domain-adaptation studies.

AI.tldr: Introduces CruiseBench, a fixed-cruise-stage RUL benchmark derived from N-CMAPSS, with CPM-N-CMAPSS mask, enabling reproducible RUL model evaluation and domain-transfer groundwork.
AI.motivation: Mitigate data-volume and regime-variation confounds in full-flight RUL records to enable controlled, reproducible RUL model comparisons and facilitate transfer-learning research.
AI.method: Apply a fixed CruiseBench protocol: identify cruise-stage intervals via CPM-N-CMAPSS mask for nine subdatasets; use scenario descriptors and measured sensors as inputs; exclude virtual sensors, health parameters, and metadata; preserve native-resolution windows; apply dataset-wise RUL caps. Evaluate LSTM, GRU, TCN, and TSMixer with benchmarks such as CruiseBench-eta5-W256-S10.
AI.result: TSMixer achieves the best performance with RMSE 3.4±1.71 and Saxena score (2.50±2.99)×10^4 under CruiseBench-eta5-W256-S10. Ablations show that flight-stage selection, temporal downscaling, and RUL-cap threshold significantly affect results; CruiseBench provides a reproducible sub-benchmark and CPM-N-CMAPSS offers a data foundation for transfer-learning and domain adaptation.
AI.conclusion: CruiseBench establishes a controlled, reproducible evaluation framework for RUL modeling and enables stage-specific data analysis; CPM-N-CMAPSS serves as a foundation for future transfer-learning and domain-adaptation studies.

title: Milo, a Fully Autonomous Indoor/Outdoor Robotic Guide Dog
comment: Submitted to CoRL 2026. The Milo project website is available here: https://fgolemo.github.io/milo
summary: Many Blind and Low-Vision (BLV) people rely on guide dogs for moment-to-moment navigation, such as staying on path and avoiding obstacles and pedestrians. However, guide dogs are expensive to acquire and maintain (approximately \$50k USD plus ongoing costs), often involve long waiting lists, and have relatively short life expectancies. While robot guide dogs offer a promising alternative, existing approaches exploring this idea suffer from several drawbacks: They often lack the autonomy required for real-world deployment, relying on prior 3D scans of the environment, external computation, or limited awareness of the handler. In this work, we present Milo, the first open-source, low-cost (approximately \$2k USD) robotic guide dog platform capable of fulfilling the basic collaborative navigation role expected of a guide dog. Milo is fully autonomous, requiring no a priori knowledge of the environment, completely self-contained with all computation performed onboard, and suitable for both indoor and outdoor navigation while avoiding obstacles and pedestrians. Our system consists of a modified Unitree Go2 robot (equipped with onboard compute, sensors, and a handle), a perception stack combining voxel mapping with floor, obstacle, and pedestrian detection, and a navigation stack based on an obstacle-avoidance policy trained in a custom bird's-eye-view simulator. We evaluate Milo in real indoor and outdoor obstacle courses and compare it against a costmap-based baseline, demonstrating smoother navigation and fewer handler collisions. To maximize accessibility for BLV users, we release both the robot hardware instructions and the complete software stack as open source.

AI.tldr: First open-source, low-cost autonomous robotic guide dog platform Milo, built from a modified Unitree Go2, with onboard sensing, perception, and navigation; evaluated vs a baseline; released as open-source.
AI.motivation: Many BLV people rely on guide dogs for navigation but face high acquisition/maintenance costs, long waiting lists, and limited lifespans. Existing robotic alternatives often rely on external computation, prior environmental knowledge, or limited handler awareness. There is a need for an autonomous, self-contained, affordable guide-robot suitable for indoor and outdoor use.
AI.method: Milo is built from a modified Unitree Go2 with onboard compute and a handle. It uses a perception stack combining voxel mapping with floor, obstacle, and pedestrian detection. The navigation stack relies on an obstacle-avoidance policy trained in a custom bird's-eye-view simulator. It requires no a priori environmental knowledge and performs all computation onboard. Real indoor and outdoor obstacle-course experiments compare Milo to a costmap-based baseline; the system is released open-source along with hardware instructions.
AI.result: Experiments on real indoor and outdoor obstacle courses show Milo navigates more smoothly and incurs fewer handler (guide) collisions than the costmap-based baseline.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the feasibility of a low-cost, fully autonomous, self-contained robotic guide dog and promotes accessibility through open-source hardware and software releases, making BLV navigation assistance more available and affordable.

title: FormulaSPIN: Self-Play Fine-Tuning for Natural Language to Spreadsheet Formula Generation
comment: 15 pages,7 figures, 14 tables. Accepted to ACL 2026 Main Conference Oral
summary: Spreadsheet applications are used by hundreds of millions worldwide, yet writing formulas remains a significant barrier. Existing approaches rely on static supervised data, which quickly saturates on limited annotations. In this paper, we introduce FORMULASPIN, a self-play framework that breaks the ceiling of supervised fine-tuning by enabling iterative self-improvement without any additional data. Vanilla SPIN fails on this task: it uniformly penalizes every non-matching output, so execution-equivalent alternatives are punished as negatives in one example while serving as ground truth in another, producing contradictory gradients. Our framework resolves this by exploiting formula generation's unique advantage: binary executability provides implicit supervision that separates semantic errors from valid stylistic variants. We frame training as a two-player game in which the main player learns to prefer ground-truth formulas over those from its previous version, while execution feedback sorts outputs into distinct granularities-enabling an adaptive curriculum that shifts from semantic correctness to stylistic refinement. To further increase accuracy, we incorporate ExecVote, a semantic-level voting mechanism that naturally handles multiple valid formulations. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FORMULASPIN achieves state-of-the-art performance, with 74.9% exact match and 87.1% execution accuracy on NL2FORMULA, matching models trained with additional preference annotations while outperforming both traditional SFT and frontier proprietary models. These findings underscore self-play's potential to tackle scarce data tasks and open the door to extending it beyond executable domains.

AI.tldr: FORMULASPIN leverages self-play with executable supervision and ExecVote to surpass data-scarce NL2FORMULA tasks, achieving 74.9% exact match and 87.1% execution accuracy without extra annotations.
AI.motivation: Address data scarcity in spreadsheet formula generation; overcome SPIN's gradient issues; exploit binary executability to distinguish semantic errors from stylistic variants; enable adaptive curriculum.
AI.method: Two-player self-play training where the main model prefers ground-truth formulas over its previous version; execution feedback creates granular decision boundaries; ExecVote aggregates multiple valid formulations; no additional data required.
AI.result: State-of-the-art results on NL2FORMULA: 74.9% exact match; 87.1% execution accuracy; matches models trained with preference annotations; outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning and frontier models.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates self-play viability for scarce data tasks; potential to extend to other executable domains and non-executable tasks.

title: Synthetic and Derived Training Images for Campus Waste Detection: A Multi-Seed Evaluation with YOLOv8n
summary: Incorrect disposal can contaminate campus recycling streams, and a bin-mounted camera could provide feedback as an item is discarded. We evaluated whether synthetic and derived images improve a YOLOv8n detector for this view. The real dataset contained 148 campus photographs: 86 for training, 31 for validation, and 31 for testing. Twelve joint-training configurations varied the amount and source of added images. We repeated seven principal settings with four matched seeds and computed bootstrap percentile intervals over those seeds. The real-only model reached a mean mAP@0.5 of 0.691 [0.665, 0.722]. Background replacement reduced the mean to 0.560 [0.499, 0.619], isolated-object images gave 0.680 [0.644, 0.724], and the full augmentation pool gave 0.487 [0.438, 0.537]. We also tested hand-and-forearm composites because every real photo showed a held object. Two cutouts in the initial composite set came from test photographs, so we discarded that experiment, rebuilt the set with training-split cutouts, and reran all four seeds. The corrected paired difference was +0.034 [-0.063, 0.199], which does not support a reliable hand-composite effect. Single-seed transfer experiments produced source-dependent rankings between joint mixing and sequential pretraining. None of the evaluated configurations exceeded the real-only baseline. The reported intervals quantify seed variation; the 31-photo test set remains too small for strong class-specific conclusions.

AI.tldr: Augmenting a YOLOv8n detector with synthetic/derived images did not beat the real-data baseline in a small campus recycling dataset; most augmentation strategies reduced performance, with high seed variability preventing robust conclusions.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether synthetic and derived images improve a bin-mounted camera detector for feedback on item disposal, addressing data scarcity and potential domain shift through joint-training augmentations.
AI.method: Use 148 real campus photos (86 train, 31 val, 31 test). Test seven joint-training configurations varying amount/source of added images. Four seeds per setting; bootstrap percentile intervals across seeds. Evaluate mAP@0.5. Test background replacement, isolated-object images, full augmentation pool, and hand/forearm composites. Excluded test-derived composites; rebuilt with training-split cutouts. Report paired differences and seed-dependent rankings.
AI.result: Real-only mAP@0.5 = 0.691 [0.665, 0.722]. Background replacement 0.560 [0.499, 0.619]; isolated-object 0.680 [0.644, 0.724]; full augmentation pool 0.487 [0.438, 0.537]. Corrected hand-composite paired difference +0.034 [-0.063, 0.199], not significant. Single-seed transfers showed source-dependent rankings; none exceeded real-only baseline. The 31-image test set is too small for robust class-specific conclusions.
AI.conclusion: Across the tested configurations, synthetic/derived augmentation did not surpass the real-data baseline. Seed variation matters; data quantity is a limiting factor, and the small test set precludes strong conclusions about specific classes. Future work should emphasize larger datasets, thorough leakage controls, and perhaps alternative augmentation strategies or domain adaptation.

title: Air Quality Arena: A Large-Scale Multi-Region Ground Monitoring Dataset and Benchmark for Air Quality Forecasting with Time-Series Foundation Models
summary: Air pollution causes an estimated 7.9 million premature deaths annually, making accurate forecasting a critical public health priority. Machine learning is increasingly being applied to forecast air pollution levels, yet existing benchmarks remain narrow in both geographic scope and pollutant coverage, and fail to evaluate the latest generation of time series foundation models (TSFMs) on real world, large scale data. We present Air Quality Arena (AQA), a large scale multi-country and multi-pollutant dataset (AQA-Data) and benchmark (AQA-Bench) to address this gap. AQA covers 6 major pollutants over a three year period across 7 diverse countries and 4 continents, with more than 14,000 station-pollutant series, aiming to provide a comprehensive benchmark for air quality tasks. We benchmark this dataset across 11 leading time series foundation models and classical baselines to assess performance on short-term air quality forecasting. Our results demonstrate that TSFMs are effective zero-shot forecasters and consistently outperform classical baselines, with our top-performing model employing a cross-modal architecture that leverages a vision foundation model for time series forecasting. AQA is publicly released at AirQualityArena.github.io

AI.tldr: AQA provides a large-scale, multi-country, multi-pollutant benchmark for short-term air quality forecasting; time series foundation models (TSFMs) excel as zero-shot forecasters and outperform baselines, with a top cross-modal model using a vision foundation model; dataset is publicly released.
AI.motivation: Air pollution causes ~7.9 million premature deaths annually; existing benchmarks are geographically/pollutant-limited and do not evaluate the latest TSFMs on real-world large-scale data, hindering progress in accurate forecasting.
AI.method: Create Air Quality Arena (AQA) consisting of AQA-Data (6 pollutants, 3 years, 7 countries, 4 continents, >14,000 station-pollutant series) and AQA-Bench; benchmark 11 leading TSFMs and classical baselines on short-term forecasting; employ a cross-modal architecture that leverages a vision foundation model for time series forecasting.
AI.result: TSFMs act as effective zero-shot forecasters and consistently outperform classical baselines; the top model uses a cross-modal approach with a vision foundation model for improved forecasting.
AI.conclusion: AQA dataset/benchmark is publicly released, providing a comprehensive resource to advance air quality forecasting and enabling robust evaluation of TSFMs on real-world, large-scale data.

title: Learning Personalized Safety Interventions for Haptic Human-Robot Shared Control
summary: Haptic feedback provides an implicit channel for communicating safety intentions during human-robot shared control. Existing haptic guidance systems typically employ predefined intervention strategies that cannot accommodate the diverse safety preferences of individual users or application scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose a Learning from Haptics (LfH) framework that learns user-preferred safety interventions from sparse demonstrations, eliminating the need for manual trial-and-error design. Our framework is built on a differentiable Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based optimization layer that automatically adjusts the underlying safety parameters to match the demonstrated haptic responses. Instead of tuning controller parameters directly, users teach the system how they expect it to intervene during teleoperation. The resulting haptic guidance reflects the demonstrated intervention preferences while preserving the intuitive interaction of haptic shared control. Simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework can learn personalized safety interventions from sparse user input and reduce the mismatch between the generated haptic feedback and the demonstrated preferences.

AI.tldr: Learning from Haptics (LfH) enables user-specific safety interventions in haptic shared control by a differentiable CBF-based optimization layer that learns from sparse demonstrations, aligning haptic feedback with user intent in simulation and hardware.
AI.motivation: Current haptic guidance uses fixed, predefined interventions that fail to capture diverse safety preferences across users and applications; a data-efficient method to learn personalized interventions is needed.
AI.method: A differentiable Control Barrier Function (CBF)–based optimization layer learns user-preferred safety interventions by adjusting safety parameters to match demonstrated haptic responses; demonstrations teach the system how the intervention should feel during teleoperation without tuning controller gains.
AI.result: Simulation and hardware experiments show LfH can learn personalized safety interventions from sparse user input and reduce the mismatch between produced haptic feedback and demonstrated preferences.
AI.conclusion: LfH offers a data-efficient path to personalized, intuitive haptic guidance in shared control by learning safety interventions; it preserves interaction simplicity while aligning with user expectations, with potential for broader deployment and extension to richer demonstrations.

title: Information Discernment in Large Language Models
summary: LLMs are increasingly used with external knowledge sources like the internet. Do they weigh information appropriately -- updating more for reliable sources (source discernment) and more when claims bring priors closer to the truth (truth discernment)? We formalize this as information discernment and introduce Learn2Discern (L2D), an experimental framework and benchmark grounded in three normative axioms with interpretable metrics. To establish external validity, a pre-registered, quota-matched user study (n=299) confirms that real LLM users endorse all three axioms and report that violations reduce their trust and usage intent. Across 13 models and nearly 670K trials, we find consistent failures across both dimensions: models perform near chance on source and truth discernment, rely on source popularity twice as much as source reliability, and update roughly equally whether a claim improves or worsens their position relative to the ground truth. Models integrate external knowledge most effectively on datasets where their priors are already the most accurate. Newer and larger models improve truth discernment but not source discernment, a blind spot that model complexity does not address. We identify simple inference-time interventions that improve both forms of discernment. We release our dataset and survey as a testbed for a core alignment property that scales in importance as LLMs replace traditional search.

AI.tldr: Introduces Learn2Discern (L2D), a framework and benchmark to quantify LLMs' ability to discern when to update beliefs from external sources by source reliability and truth alignment; finds widespread shortcomings across 13 models and many trials, with improvements mainly in truth discernment but not source discernment; proposes simple inference-time interventions and releases data for benchmarking alignment.
AI.motivation: Address whether LLMs weigh external information appropriately by source trustworthiness and its proximity to truth; formulate information discernment as a formal property with interpretable metrics, and create a scalable benchmark to study it.
AI.method: Develop Learn2Discern (L2D) framework grounded in three normative axioms; conduct a preregistered, quota-matched user study (n=299) for external validity; evaluate 13 models across ~670k trials; measure source discernment and truth discernment; analyze reliance on source popularity vs. reliability; test inference-time interventions; release dataset and survey.
AI.result: Models perform near chance on both source and truth discernment; they lean toward source popularity twice as much as reliability; update about equally whether a claim improves or worsens alignment with ground truth; better integration when priors are already accurate; newer/larger models improve truth discernment but not source discernment; simple inference-time interventions improve both forms; external validity confirmed via user study.
AI.conclusion: Dataset and survey released as a testbed for a core alignment property that grows in importance as LLMs replace traditional search; identifies a persistent blind spot in source discernment and suggests practical interventions to enhance both discernment dimensions.

title: ChronoStitch: Training-Free Composition of Visual KV Memories for Long-Horizon Temporal Reasoning
summary: Long-video question answering requires a model to preserve visual evidence over time without repeatedly reprocessing the same video. A practical approach is to store the vision-language model's internal key-value (KV) cache for each video chunk and retrieve that state at query time. However, independently cached video chunks do not compose correctly: every chunk is prefilled from local rotary position zero, so naive concatenation collides temporal phases and removes the global order required for questions about what happened first, how often events occurred, or what changed across the video. This paper presents ChronoStitch, a training-free method for composing independently stored visual KV memories. The method first re-bases stored post-rotary keys onto a global three-axis multimodal RoPE coordinate system that preserves time, height, and width structure. We show why a one-dimensional scalar re-indexing is geometrically inconsistent for visual tokens because it turns spatial order within a frame into false temporal displacement. We then address the residual content gap left by positional repair: later chunks were originally encoded without attending to earlier chunks. ChronoStitch therefore selectively recomputes a small fraction of high-deviation later-chunk visual tokens while allowing them to attend over the composed cache. On Qwen2.5-VL-3B and the temporal split of TempCompass, ChronoStitch outperforms naive composition and position-only variants, improving event-ordering accuracy while running 3.3x faster than full joint re-prefilling.

AI.tldr: Training-free method ChronoStitch to compose KV caches across video chunks by re-basing on a three-axis RoPE, with selective token recomputation; yields correct temporal order and 3.3x speed-up vs full re-prefill, outperforming naive methods.
AI.motivation: Long-video QA requires preserving visual evidence over time; naive chunk concatenation misaligns temporal order due to independent caches; need a principled, efficient method to maintain global sequence.
AI.method: Base stored post-rotary keys onto a global 3D RoPE coordinate system (time, height, width). Argue 1D scalar reindexing is geometrically inconsistent. Address residual content gap by selectively recomputing a small fraction of high-deviation tokens from later chunks while allowing them to attend over the composed cache.
AI.result: Empirical results on Qwen2.5-VL-3B and TempCompass temporal split: ChronoStitch improves event-ordering accuracy vs naive and position-only variants; 3.3x faster than full joint re-prefilling.
AI.conclusion: ChronoStitch offers a training-free, efficient solution to cache composition for long videos, aligning temporal structure and maintaining accuracy with lower compute.

title: Challenges of Explainability in Continual Learning for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Deep learning models have shown strong potential for time series forecasting, yet their deployment in real-world environmental monitoring remains challenging due to non-stationary dynamics and limited explainability. In this work, we investigate explainability as a central tool for understanding continual learning in adaptive time series forecasting, with Experience Replay strategies. We study neural forecasting architectures such as PatchMixer, PatchTST and DLinear, augmented with attention-based sampling mechanisms to support model adaptation over time. Explainability is leveraged through attention rollout and gradient-based attribution methods (Grad-CAM) to analyze both predictive behavior and sampling strategies within a continual learning framework. Experiments conducted on real-world piezometric time series exhibiting heterogeneous patterns and regime shifts show that analyzing model and sampling behaviors provides valuable insights into the dynamics of the continual learning framework. Beyond predictive performance, our results highlight the challenges and opportunities of using explainability to understand continual learning behaviors, revealing how attribution patterns evolve over time and how they can inform data selection and adaptation strategies in non-stationary forecasting scenarios.

AI.tldr: Explainability-guided continual learning for adaptive time-series forecasting using Experience Replay across PatchMixer, PatchTST, and DLinear, with attention-based sampling and Grad-CAM/attention rollout; applied to piezometric data to reveal non-stationarity dynamics and inform data adaptation strategies.
AI.motivation: Tackle non-stationary environmental time series and the opacity of deep learning forecasts by leveraging explainability to scrutinize continual learning and data sampling under Experience Replay.
AI.method: Augment neural forecasters (PatchMixer, PatchTST, DLinear) with attention-based sampling; implement Experience Replay for continual learning; analyze predictions and sampling with attention rollout and Grad-CAM to interpret model behavior over time on real piezometric time series with regime shifts.
AI.result: Attribution and sampling analyses reveal evolving patterns in continual learning; insights gained into data selection and adaptation strategies beyond standard predictive performance; highlights challenges and opportunities in using explainability to understand continual learning dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Explainability can illuminate how continual learning and sampling evolve in non-stationary forecasting, offering guidance for data selection and adaptation, but raises questions about attribution stability and the generalizability of insights across domains.

title: LENS: LLM-guided Environment Simplification for Planning and Control in Clutter
summary: Despite recent advances in general-purpose robotic manipulation, real-world multi-object clutter remains challenging to handle for today's prevalent approaches. The problem scales in complexity due to more objects and collisions, more unpredictable contact physics, distractors, and task ambiguity. Bridging this gap to real-world deployment requires effective scene abstractions; yet today, producing such abstractions requires extensive task-specific manual engineering, which does not scale. These abstractions are costly to generate and difficult to adjust or fine-tune. We instead propose a plug-and-play fix to automatically generate scene-specific, task-specific, adaptively updating abstractions on top of existing planning and control stacks. LLM-guided Environment Simplification (LENS) produces a de-cluttered abstracted scene representation by merging (e.g., stacked objects) or pruning (e.g., distant objects) scene entities in a closed loop in response to task progress. These dynamic, task-relevant abstractions are versatile and easy to use. In our experiments, we show that LENS improves classical planning, model-based control, and a vision-language-action model, across a diverse set of highly cluttered manipulation scenes. Project website: https://lens-2026.github.io/.

AI.tldr: LENS offers an LLM-guided, adaptive scene abstraction module that prunes/merges clutter to create task- and scene-specific representations, compatible with existing planning and control stacks, improving performance in cluttered manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Real-world multi-object clutter creates large, dynamic decision spaces and requires extensive task-specific engineering for scene abstractions. Automated, adaptive abstractions are needed to scale to deployment.
AI.method: A plug-and-play pipeline that sits above planning/control systems. It uses an LLM to guide environment simplification, performing operations such as merging (e.g., stacked objects) and pruning (e.g., distant objects) in a closed loop driven by task progress.
AI.result: LENS yields improvements across classical planning, model-based control, and a vision-language-action model in diverse, highly cluttered manipulation scenes, demonstrating versatility across architectures.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, task-relevant abstractions are versatile, easy to use, and can bridge the gap to real-world deployment by simplifying clutter while preserving essential task information.

title: NEXUS: Structured Runtime Safety for Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents increasingly execute high-impact actions, making runtime safety monitoring essential. We present NEXUS (Neural EXecution Utility and Safety), a structured-plan safety monitor that applies a formal intervention policy to select among four actions: allow, block, request confirmation, or request revision. NEXUS combines deterministic safety rules, argument-level inspection, and a calibrated logistic-regression risk score for graded escalation. On a 128-instance synthetic benchmark, NEXUS achieves an F1 score of 0.949 and a 4-class intervention accuracy of 0.6406, outperforming rule-only intervention selection by 27.3 percentage points. It also improves over rule-only on R-Judge (F1 = 0.861 vs. 0.849), matches rule-only on AgentHarm due to threat-model limits, and achieves 0% ASR at 99% control allow on IPI. On the rule-blind NEXUS-Stress benchmark, NEXUS reaches an F1 score of 0.881, highlighting the difficulty of fine-grained intervention routing. With 0.205 ms median latency, NEXUS adds under 0.1% overhead to typical agent loops. Code, benchmarks, and the calibrated risk scorer are publicly released.

AI.tldr: NEXUS is a structured-plan safety monitor for tool-using LLMs that provides four intervention actions (allow, block, request confirmation, request revision) via deterministic rules, argument-level inspection, and a calibrated logistic-regression risk score. It achieves strong safety performance with low latency, and code/benchmarks are released.
AI.motivation: Runtime safety for high-impact LLM actions requires more than rule-based checks; a calibrated, graded intervention policy can better balance safety and usability.
AI.method: Four-action policy: allow, block, request confirmation, or request revision. Combines deterministic safety rules, argument-level inspection, and a calibrated logistic-regression risk score to route interventions.
