Evaluated on a 128-instance synthetic benchmark and multiple real benchmarks (R-Judge, AgentHarm, IPI; plus a rule-blind NEXUS-Stress). Median latency 0.205 ms; overhead <0.1% of typical agent loops. Code, benchmarks, and the risk scorer are publicly released.
AI.result: On the 128-instance synthetic benchmark, NEXUS achieves F1 = 0.949 and 4-class intervention accuracy = 0.6406, outperforming rule-only intervention selection by 27.3 percentage points. It improves over rule-only on R-Judge (F1 = 0.861 vs 0.849), matches rule-only on AgentHarm (limited by threat model), and achieves 0% ASR at 99% control allow on IPI. On the rule-blind NEXUS-Stress benchmark, F1 = 0.881. Median latency is 0.205 ms, adding under 0.1% overhead to typical agent loops.
AI.conclusion: NEXUS demonstrates effective, low-latency safety intervention for tool-using LLMs with calibrated risk scoring. It improves over rule-only baselines on several benchmarks and remains resilient under various evaluation settings, though some gains are bounded by threat models. The work provides practical apparatus (calibrated risk scorer, public release) for safer agent execution.

title: VQ-Transplant: Efficient VQ-Module Integration for Pre-trained Visual Tokenizers
summary: Vector Quantization (VQ) underpins modern discrete visual tokenization. However, training quantization modules for state-of-the-art VQ-based models requires significant computational resources which, in practice, all but prevents the development of novel, cutting-edge VQ techniques under resource constraints. To address this limitation, we propose {\bf VQ-Transplant}, a simple framework that enables plug-and-play integration of new VQ modules into frozen, pre-trained tokenizers by replacing their native VQ modules. Crucially, the proposed transplantation process preserves all encoder-decoder parameters, obviating the need for costly end-to-end retraining when modifying the quantization method. To mitigate decoder-quantization mismatch, we introduce a lightweight decoder adaptation strategy (trained for only 5 epochs on ImageNet-1k) to align feature priors with the new quantization space. In our empirical evaluation, we find that VQ-Transplant allows obtaining near state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity for industry-level models like VAR while reducing the training cost by 95\%. VQ-Transplant democratizes quantization research by enabling resource-efficient integration of novel VQ techniques while matching industry-level reconstruction performance.

AI.tldr: VQ-Transplant enables plug-and-play integration of new vector quantization modules into frozen pre-trained tokenizers by swapping VQ modules, preserving encoder-decoder parameters, with a lightweight decoder adaptation trained for 5 epochs; achieves near state-of-the-art reconstruction while reducing training cost by ~95%.
AI.motivation: Reduce the computational burden of developing and evaluating new VQ techniques in VQ-based models by allowing module replacement without end-to-end retraining.
AI.method: Introduce a transplantation framework that swaps the native VQ module in a frozen tokenizer while keeping encoder-decoder parameters fixed; add a lightweight decoder adaptation stage (≈5 epochs on ImageNet-1k) to align feature priors with the new quantization space.
AI.result: Attains near state-of-the-art reconstruction fidelity for industrial models (e.g., VAR) and cuts training cost by about 95%, enabling resource-efficient exploration of novel VQ methods.
AI.conclusion: VQ-Transplant democratizes quantization research by enabling rapid, cost-effective integration of new VQ techniques without compromising reconstruction performance.

title: SUM: Unified Geometric Surgery on Spatio-Temporal Adaptation Vectors for Federated Class Incremental Learning
summary: Real-world intelligent systems often require both distributed collaboration across data-isolated clients and continual adaptation to evolving tasks. This setting naturally gives rise to Federated Class Incremental Learning (FCIL), which combines Federated Learning (FL) and Continual Learning (CL). However, their combination introduces two coupled sources of interference: spatial interference from heterogeneous clients and temporal interference from sequential tasks, jointly leading to Spatial-Temporal Catastrophic Forgetting (ST-CF). Existing approaches typically address spatial and temporal interference with separate mechanisms, often incurring additional client-side computation or communication, while leaving directional interactions among updates during aggregation unregulated. In this paper, we reinterpret FCIL as a unified multi-task learning problem, where both client and task updates are represented as adaptation vectors in a shared parameter space. Based on this view, we propose Unified Geometric Surgery on Spatio-Temporal Adaptation Vectors (SUM), a purely server-side framework that performs geometric surgery on adaptation vectors during aggregation. Spatial SUM mitigates client-level interference within each round, while causal online temporal SUM removes cross-task interference over time without additional client-side computation, communication, or memory beyond standard federated training. Empirically, SUM achieves up to 22% improvement over prior FCIL methods across diverse vision and language benchmarks while remaining robust to unreliable clients and maintaining computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: Unified Geometric Surgery (SUM) for Federated Class Incremental Learning (FCIL) treats client updates and task updates as adaptation vectors in a shared parameter space and performs server-side geometric operations to mitigate spatial and temporal interference. It unifies FL and CL in a single framework, avoiding extra client-side costs.
AI.motivation: FCIL suffers from spatial interference due to heterogeneous, data-isolated clients and temporal interference due to sequential tasks; existing methods address these separately and incur extra client-side computation or communication. A unified, server-side approach could reduce cross-task and cross-client interference without increasing client burden.
AI.method: Represent client and task updates as adaptation vectors in a common parameter space. Apply geometric surgery on these vectors during aggregation: Spatial SUM mitigates intra-round client-level interference; causal online temporal SUM mitigates cross-task interference over time. Implementation is server-side and requires no extra computation/communication/memory on clients beyond standard federated training.
AI.result: SUM yields up to 22% improvement over prior FCIL methods across vision and language benchmarks, demonstrates robustness to unreliable clients, and maintains computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: A server-only, geometrically guided aggregation framework can unify FL and CL, improving performance and robustness in FCIL without increasing client-side overhead.

title: Remote ID Spoofing-Aware Trajectory Planning for Small Unmanned Aerial Systems
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, to be published in IEEE DASC 2026 Conference proceedings
summary: This work presents a decentralized, spoofing-aware trajectory planning framework for small unmanned aerial systems operating under Remote Identification (RID) location spoofing attacks. Existing planners typically assume RID broadcasts are trustworthy, which can increase the risk of loss of separation and mid-air collisions when spoofing occurs. In contrast, the proposed approach explicitly treats RID information as unverified and incorporates physical-layer observations to assess broadcast credibility. Received signal-strength measurements from neighboring aircraft are used to detect spoofing and probabilistically localize a spoofing agent. The resulting uncertainty is converted into a risk-bounded unsafe region using a chance-constrained formulation and integrated into a per-agent Markov decision process-based planner. This enables real-time, decentralized collision avoidance while preserving mission objectives and scalability. Simulation results in a multi-aircraft package delivery scenario demonstrate reduced near mid-air collision events compared to planners that assume truthful RID data, while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time execution.

AI.tldr: Decentralized, spoofing-aware trajectory planning for small UAS under RID spoofing, leveraging RSS-based detection and probabilistic localization to form a risk-bounded region, integrated into a per-agent MDP for real-time collision avoidance.
AI.motivation: RID broadcasts may be spoofed; assuming truthfulness in RID can lead to loss of separation or mid-air collisions. A framework that treats RID data as unverified and uses physical-layer cues is needed for safer autonomy.
AI.method: The method uses received signal-strength (RSS) measurements from neighboring aircraft to detect RID spoofing and probabilistically localize the attacker. The resulting uncertainty defines a risk-bounded unsafe region via a chance-constrained formulation, which is then embedded into a per-agent Markov decision process (MDP) planner for decentralized, real-time collision avoidance while preserving mission objectives.
AI.result: Simulation in a multi-aircraft package-delivery scenario shows fewer near mid-air collision events compared to planners assuming truthful RID data, with computational efficiency suitable for real-time execution.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables real-time, decentralized collision avoidance under RID spoofing, maintaining scalability and mission objectives while reducing near-collision risk.

title: Stochastic Primal-Dual Decoding for Multiobjective Generative Recommender Systems
summary:
Recent advances in recommender systems (RS) have shown substantial performance gains through generative modelling. In practice, recommendation often involves constructing slates -- ordered lists of items -- that must satisfy multiple objectives beyond relevance, such as constraints defined over item attributes or fairness constraints. Existing multiobjective approaches either rely on post-processing techniques designed for non-generative settings, or incorporate auxiliary objectives directly into model training. The former does not explicitly account for the sequential nature of generative RS, while the latter is often impractical in large-scale systems.
  We propose a lightweight, inference-time decoding layer that augments autoregressive generative RS to support multiobjective slate generation without modifying or retraining the underlying model. We formulate decoding as an online constrained optimisation problem, where items are selected sequentially, and trade-offs between relevance and auxiliary objectives are adjusted dynamically based on the remaining constraint slack, i.e., how much of each objective remains to be satisfied. This is implemented via a stochastic primal-dual approximation scheme that balances relevance and auxiliary objectives during generation.
  We provide theoretical guarantees on constraint violation and regret, and evaluate the proposed approach through extensive offline experiments and a large-scale online A/B experiment in a real-world recommender system. Our results show consistent improvements in multiobjective trade-offs, including a +1.8\% gain in the auxiliary objectives achieved at zero cost to user satisfaction.

AI.tldr: An inference-time decoding layer for autoregressive recommender systems enables multiobjective slate generation via online constrained optimization with a stochastic primal-dual scheme, achieving better auxiliary objectives with no loss in user satisfaction, validated offline and in a large-scale online A/B.
AI.motivation: In RS, slate generation must satisfy multiple objectives beyond relevance (e.g., item attributes, fairness). Re-training or post-processing approaches are inadequate: post-processing ignores sequence, retraining is costly for large-scale systems.
AI.method: Introduce a lightweight inference-time decoding layer that performs sequential item selection through an online constrained optimization problem. It dynamically adjusts objective trade-offs using remaining slack and uses a stochastic primal-dual approximation. No retraining of the base autoregressive model.
AI.result: The approach provides theoretical guarantees on constraint violations and regret. Empirical evaluation includes extensive offline experiments and a large-scale online A/B in a real system, showing consistent improvements in multiobjective trade-offs; +1.8% gain in auxiliary objectives with zero cost to user satisfaction.
AI.conclusion: An effective, scalable decoding-time solution for multiobjective slate generation in autoregressive RS, combining online optimization with primal-dual methods to balance relevance and constraints without model retraining.

title: EGRNet: A Lightweight Semantic Segmentation Network with Edge-Gated Refinement and Adversarial Sensing
summary: As autonomous systems and smart cities continue to evolve, the demand for efficient and robust scene understanding becomes increasingly critical. Semantic segmentation plays a key role in enabling autonomous vehicles to comprehend complex urban environments. However, achieving high accuracy with minimal computational cost remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we present Edge-Gated Refinement Network (EGRNet), a lightweight and efficient deep learning model designed for real-time semantic segmentation in urban scenarios. The model incorporates depthwise separable convolutions to reduce computational complexity and dilated residual blocks for capturing rich multi-scale contextual information. Additionally, we introduce a novel Edge-Gated Refinement (EGR) module, which adaptively fuses original and refined features through a learnable gating mechanism, enhancing boundary preservation and edge-sensitive regions. To further improve feature representation, Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) attention is applied across the network. With only 0.46M parameters, EGRNet achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining low computational overhead. When evaluated on the Cityscapes dataset, the model attains a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 65.28%, demonstrating strong accuracy with minimal resource consumption. Moreover, we introduce a lightweight adversarial attack detection strategy, ensuring robustness against adversarial inputs without compromising real-time performance. By combining efficiency, accuracy, and resilience, EGRNet is well-suited for deployment on edge devices in safety-critical real-time applications.

AI.tldr: Edge-Gated Refinement Network (EGRNet) is a lightweight real-time semantic segmentation model for urban scenes, using depthwise separable convolutions, dilated residual blocks, an Edge-Gated Refinement (EGR) module with a learnable gate, and SE attention. It achieves 0.46M parameters, 65.28% mIoU on Cityscapes, and includes a lightweight adversarial attack detection strategy for edge devices.
AI.motivation: Need for accurate semantic segmentation in autonomous systems and edge devices with limited computation, particularly in urban environments, balancing accuracy with low latency and resource usage.
AI.method: A compact network design using depthwise separable convolutions for efficiency, dilated residual blocks for multi-scale context, an Edge-Gated Refinement module that adaptively fuses original and refined features via a learnable gate, SE attention across the network, and a lightweight adversarial attack detection mechanism.
AI.result: Achieves 65.28% mIoU on Cityscapes with only 0.46M parameters, indicating strong accuracy with low computational cost; claims state-of-the-art performance for its size and real-time capability; includes robustness to adversarial inputs through a lightweight detection strategy.
AI.conclusion: EGRNet offers an effective balance of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness suitable for deployment on edge devices in safety-critical, real-time urban perception systems; potential for real-world deployment given the reported metrics.

title: STN-TGAT: Top-K Portfolio Construction via Prior-Guided Graph Attention with Learnable Soft-Threshold Sparsification
summary: This paper tackles the problem of stock ranking and portfolio construction under realistic investment settings by jointly modeling temporal dynamics and cross-sectional dependencies. We propose the Soft-Threshold NMI-prior Transformer Graph Attention Network (STN-TGAT), which integrates a temporal Transformer with a Graph Attention Network to capture long-horizon sequential patterns and dynamic inter-stock relationships. An NMI-based prior graph combined with a soft-threshold sparsification mechanism enhances structural robustness by mitigating noisy correlations while preserving informative connections. The portfolio formation process incorporates practical considerations, including Top-5 selection within the Top-50 $S\&P$ 500 constituents, explicit weight allocation, and transaction cost adjustment, thereby aligning the evaluation with real-world trading conditions. Empirical results on real-world data demonstrate that STN-TGAT consistently outperforms benchmark models from predictive accuracy and investment profitability measured by portfolio returns. These findings suggest that combining decision-aligned training with adaptive relational modeling provides a coherent and practically effective framework for data-driven portfolio construction.

AI.tldr: Introduces STN-TGAT, a Transformer-GAT model with an NMI-prior sparse graph for stock ranking and realistic portfolio construction; achieves superior predictive accuracy and portfolio returns under practical trading constraints.
AI.motivation: Stock ranking and portfolio construction require modeling both temporal dynamics and cross-sectional dependencies while mitigating noisy correlations; existing methods may be fragile under real-world trading frictions.
AI.method: Propose Soft-Threshold NMI-prior Transformer Graph Attention Network (STN-TGAT): a temporal Transformer capturing long-horizon patterns, a Graph Attention Network capturing dynamic inter-stock relationships; an NMI-based prior graph with soft-threshold sparsification for robustness; portfolio formation with Top-5 selection within Top-50 S&P 500 constituents, explicit weight allocation, and transaction cost adjustment.
AI.result: Empirical results on real-world data show STN-TGAT consistently outperforms benchmark models in predictive accuracy and investment profitability (portfolio returns).
AI.conclusion: Combining decision-aligned training with adaptive relational modeling yields a coherent and practically effective framework for data-driven portfolio construction.

title: NavVerse: Benchmarking Indoor-to-Outdoor Embodied Navigation in Continuous Robot Simulation
summary: Robots deployed in delivery, campus, and emergency-response settings often need to navigate from buildings to streets within a single continuous episode. Existing benchmarks usually evaluate indoor and outdoor navigation separately, and many abstract away robot execution, leaving exit finding, boundary traversal, adaptation, and kinodynamic failures underexplored. We introduce NavVerse, a physics-enabled benchmark for indoor-to-outdoor embodied navigation. NavVerse contains 100 indoor scenes, 50 urban outdoor scenes, and 50 indoor-to-outdoor scenes, and 10,000 episodes spanning Object Navigation, Vision-and-Language Navigation, and Place Navigation tasks, where agents search for semantic points of interest such as restaurants or banks. Agents are evaluated through executable robot interfaces using task-success, path-efficiency, and safety metrics. Zero-shot experiments with RL, VLA, and modular baselines show that current agents remain far from solving cross-context navigation: end-to-end VLAs obtain the highest zero-shot success, while the modular method provides the strongest safety profile. PlaceNav further reveals a clear drop from outdoor to indoor-to-outdoor scenes, indicating that adaptation remains major bottleneck.

AI.tldr: NavVerse is a physics-enabled indoor-to-outdoor embodied navigation benchmark with executable robot interfaces, integrating indoor, outdoor, and indoor-to-outdoor scenes across multiple navigation tasks; it reveals significant cross-context navigation challenges and safety/adaptation bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: To evaluate cross-context embodied navigation in continuous episodes from buildings to streets, addressing the gap where indoor and outdoor benchmarks are treated separately and robot execution is often abstracted.
AI.method: Construct NavVerse with 100 indoor scenes, 50 urban outdoor scenes, and 50 indoor-to-outdoor scenes, totaling 10,000 episodes for Object Navigation, Vision-and-Language Navigation, and Place Navigation. Agents are evaluated via executable robot interfaces using metrics for task-success, path-efficiency, and safety. Zero-shot experiments are conducted with RL, VLA, and modular baselines.
AI.result: Zero-shot experiments show end-to-end VLAs achieve the highest zero-shot success but remain far from solving cross-context navigation; modular baselines afford the strongest safety profile. PlaceNav reveals a clear drop in performance from outdoor to indoor-to-outdoor scenes, highlighting adaptation as the major bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Cross-context embodied navigation remains challenging; current agents struggle to adapt across indoor/outdoor boundaries. NavVerse provides a rigorous, physics-enabled platform to study adaptation, safety, and execution with realistic robot interfaces, suggesting the need for better transfer learning, modular safety mechanisms, and integrated perception-action loops.

title: LISA: Linear-Indexed Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Recent advances in long chain-of-thought reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1 have led to increasingly longer inference context lengths under the test-time scaling paradigm. However, the O(n^2) computational complexity of standard self-attention causes inference costs to grow sharply with long sequences, limiting the deployment of long-CoT reasoning in production settings. To address this, we propose LISA (Linear-Indexed Sparse Attention), a plug-and-play attention replacement module that requires no pretraining from scratch. LISA integrates two lightweight components in parallel within the original model: (1) a Linear Attention module that provides long-range memory with O(n) time complexity; (2) a Lightning Indexer that selects the top-M important tokens from the full context to feed into a Sparse Self-Attention. The two branches are fused via a gating mechanism, reducing inference complexity from O(n^2) to O(nM) (M << n) for generating n tokens. We design a two-stage training pipeline: Stage 1 initializes the model by integrating the linear attention to capture long-range dependencies, complemented by a sliding-window attention mechanism that is optimized via knowledge distillation to approximate the full self-attention distribution of a frozen teacher model. In Stage 2, we further introduce the Indexer to replace the static sliding-window mechanism, enabling dynamic token selection from broader contexts. The Indexer is trained using a novel per-head KL divergence loss, which aligns its selection behavior with the attention patterns of the teacher model. Experiments on DeepSeek-distilled-Qwen models demonstrate that LISA achieves a 50% inference speedup under 16K-token context, while improving average performance by 5.6% on reasoning benchmarks including AIME and MATH-500.

AI.tldr: LISA reduces attention complexity from O(n^2) to O(nM) by fusing a Linear Attention module and a top-M Lightning Indexer; trained in two stages with distillation; achieves 50% speedup at 16K context and +5.6% average on AIME and MATH-500.
AI.motivation: Long-context chain-of-thought reasoning is hampered by the quadratic cost of standard self-attention; scalable inference for long sequences is needed.
AI.method: Two parallel branches: (1) Linear Attention with O(n) complexity for long-range memory; (2) Lightning Indexer selecting top-M tokens for Sparse Self-Attention. A gating mechanism fuses branches. Training proceeds in two stages: Stage 1 integrates linear attention with a sliding-window mechanism optimized via knowledge distillation from a frozen teacher to approximate full self-attention; Stage 2 adds the Indexer to enable dynamic token selection. The Indexer is trained with a per-head KL divergence loss to align its selections with the teacher's attention patterns.
AI.result: On DeepSeek-distilled-Qwen models, LISA yields ~50% inference speedup under a 16K-token context and improves average performance by ~5.6% on reasoning benchmarks (AIME, MATH-500).
AI.conclusion: LISA provides a plug-and-play, scalable solution for long-CoT reasoning, reducing inference cost from quadratic to near-linear with maintained or improved accuracy, without full re-pretraining.

title: Pathologist Attention-Aligned Report Generation for Prostate Histopathology
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, accepted for publication at the 29th International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (MICCAI 2026)
summary: The allocation of visual attention by pathologists during cancer diagnosis is a highly selective process that critically shapes the information extracted from whole-slide images (WSIs). Human attention helps medical imaging tasks such as classification and segmentation, and becomes a strong semantic cue for identifying diagnostically informative regions for report generation. In this paper, we introduce human attention into the training of pathologist report generation models. To this end, we collected a multimodal human-attention dataset of 121 prostate WSIs annotated with pathologists' multi-scale viewport trajectories synchronized with the pathologists' verbal descriptions and cursor movements for five clinically relevant components (e.g., Gleason patterns). Using this dataset, we finetune two report generation models with an attention-alignment loss that regularizes the model attention over image patches to match the distribution of pathologist attention. We evaluate our approach on prostate cancer report generation and visual question answering using two models with different internal attention mechanisms (i.e., how image tokens are integrated into the language decoder). Experiments show average gains of 10.9% on NLP-based metrics and 19.3% in accuracy across five clinically relevant report components. Further, model attention maps extracted at inference time, with minimal computational overhead, align more closely with pathologist attention, providing stronger visual support for the generated reports by highlighting the regions that most influence the output.

AI.tldr: Introduces a multimodal human-attention dataset and an attention-alignment training objective to guide pathologist report generation and VQA on prostate WSIs; achieves notable performance gains and more interpretable, pathologist-aligned attention maps.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between AI model attention and diagnostically informative regions by leveraging human visual attention to improve medical report generation and explanatory power.
AI.method: Collect a dataset of 121 prostate whole-slide images with pathologists' multi-scale viewport trajectories, verbal descriptions, and cursor movements; finetune two report-generation models using an attention-alignment loss that regularizes image-patch attention to match pathologist attention; compare models with different internal attention mechanisms; evaluate on prostate cancer report generation and visual question answering; analyze inference-time attention maps.
AI.result: Average improvements of 10.9% on NLP-based metrics and 19.3% in accuracy across five clinically relevant report components; attention maps at inference align more closely with pathologist attention with minimal overhead; enhanced visual support for generated reports.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating human attention through attention-alignment loss improves both performance and interpretability of medical report generation and VQA on WSIs, providing stronger, pathologist-aligned explanatory cues without substantial computational costs.

title: Building Fast, Evaluating Slow: Pipeline Choices Dominate Autointerpretability Score Variance
summary: Cross-paper comparison of sparse autoencoder (SAE) interpretability often relies on autointerpretability scores. In this evaluation pipeline, a language model (LM) explains each feature, and another LM scores the explanation. For these comparisons to be meaningful, scores must reflect stable properties of the features rather than confounding aspects of the evaluation pipeline. Through systematic experiments across four metrics (simulation, detection, fuzzing, purity), two models (Pythia-160M, Apertus-8B), and four axes of methodological variation, we show that this assumption does not hold. Specifically, we find that R1) methodological variance collectively exceeds architectural variance across all metrics and tested models; R2) each metric exhibits a distinct instability profile, with detection being the most stable and fuzzing unreliable across all conditions; R3) top-k feature rankings do not stay consistent across corpus and draw conditions, masking per-feature instability behind stable mean scores; a failure that cannot be detected by monitoring explanation similarity alone. These findings suggest that cross-paper comparisons based on autointerpretability scores may reflect pipeline differences rather than architectural differences, with implications for the ongoing debate on SAE utility. More broadly, unreliable evaluation slows progress in interpretability research at a time when reliable tools for understanding AI systems are needed. To support evaluation, we contribute a variance decomposition approach, a Stability Check, and a Minimum Reporting Checklist.

AI.tldr: Cross-paper autointerpretability scores are dominated by pipeline variance rather than model architecture; instability depends on metric; top-k rankings unstable across corpora; proposes variance decomposition, Stability Check, and a Minimum Reporting Checklist to improve evaluation reliability.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether autointerpretability scores genuinely reflect SAE interpretability or are confounded by evaluation pipelines; enable reliable cross-paper comparisons.
AI.method: Systematic empirical study across four metrics (simulation, detection, fuzzing, purity), two models (Pythia-160M, Apertus-8B), and four axes of methodological variation; compute LM-explanation–based scores; perform variance decomposition; assess per-feature stability and top-k rankings; develop a Stability Check and a Minimum Reporting Checklist.
AI.result: Methodological variance consistently exceeds architectural variance across metrics and models; each metric shows a unique instability profile (detection most stable, fuzzing unreliable); top-k feature rankings are not stable across corpus/dower conditions and can mask per-feature instability; explanation similarity alone fails to reveal this instability.
AI.conclusion: Cross-paper comparisons based on autointerpretability scores may reflect pipeline differences rather than architectural differences; unreliable evaluation hampers interpretability research. Proposes a variance-decomposition framework, a Stability Check, and a Minimum Reporting Checklist to improve evaluation practices.

title: Contact-Persistent Full Actuation for Aerial Physical Interaction
summary: Fully actuated unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are usually certified through rank conditions on a control-allocation matrix or through free-flight tracking performance. For aerial physical interaction, this certification may be incomplete. During sustained contact, part of the available wrench is consumed by the interaction task, and only the residual wrench remains available for stabilization, disturbance rejection, and maneuvering. This paper introduces a control-theoretic framework for \emph{contact-persistent full actuation}. A rigid-body model on $\R^{3}\times\SO\left(3\right)$ is combined with a morphology-dependent wrench map that captures fixed-tilt, variable-tilt, coaxial, and overactuated multirotor architectures. We define feasible wrench sets under actuator limits, residual wrench sets under task loading, and residual authority margins that strengthen the usual rank-based notion of full actuation. The main result shows that contact-persistent full actuation is equivalent to interiority of the task wrench in the constrained feasible wrench polytope, and that the residual authority radius is exactly the distance to the polytope boundary. We further introduce a signed residual-margin certificate for infeasible and boundary cases, a slack-maximizing allocation certificate, and a robust implementability condition that can be used as a margin-aware safety filter. Numerical evaluation on an abstract tilted hexarotor shows that full row rank alone does not imply feasible contact operation. Intermediate tilt angles preserve residual authority during pushing, whereas small or excessive tilts fail because of lateral-force deficiency or hover-margin loss.

AI.tldr: A geometry-based, margin-aware framework for contact-persistent full actuation in UAVs, linking actuator limits, task wrench, and residual authority via a wrench polytope; establishes interiority as feasibility criterion, defines residual margins and certificates, and demonstrates rank alone is insufficient while mid-range tilts improve residual authority.
AI.motivation: Certifying full actuation for aerial physical interaction is incomplete when contact tasks consume wrench; there is a need to quantify feasible residual actuation capacity and provide safety margins.
AI.method: Rigid-body model on SE(3) with a morphology-dependent wrench map for fixed-tilt, variable-tilt, coaxial, and overactuated multirotor architectures. Define feasible wrench sets under actuator limits, residual wrench sets under task loading, and residual authority margins. Prove equivalence between contact-persistent full actuation and interiority of the task wrench in the constrained feasible wrench polytope; define residual authority radius as distance to polytope boundary. Introduce signed residual-margin certificates, slack-maximizing allocation certificate, and a robust implementability condition as a margin-aware safety filter. Numerical evaluation on an abstract tilted hexarotor.
AI.result: The main theoretical result establishes equivalence between contact-persistent full actuation and interiority; residual authority radius equals distance to the polytope boundary. Certificates enable feasibility checks under infeasible or boundary cases; a slack-maximizing allocation certificate and a robust implementability condition form a margin-aware safety filter. Numerical study shows full row rank is not sufficient for feasible contact; intermediate tilt angles preserve residual authority during pushing, while small or excessive tilts fail due to lateral-force deficiency or hover-margin loss.
AI.conclusion: A margin-aware, certificate-based framework is needed for reliable contact propulsion/interaction with UAVs; actuation feasibility hinges on the task wrench’s interiority within the feasible wrench polytope, and optimizing morphology (tilt) can maintain residual authority; rank alone is insufficient for guaranteeing contact feasibility.

title: Profile-Graph Memory for LLM Agents: Implicit Cross-Entity Traversal through Narrative Profiles
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code and MemHop benchmark: https://github.com/ShengtongZhu/ProGraph
summary: Long-term memory is essential for LLM agents that interact across sessions, yet current memory benchmarks primarily evaluate single-hop recall, leaving multi-hop association largely unmeasured. We make three contributions. First, we introduce MemHop, a multi-hop memory benchmark of 1,000 questions at hop depths 1-5 across 10 social-network scenarios, with per-hop evidence annotations. Second, we present Profile-Graph Memory (ProGraph), a two-layer memory architecture combining (i) profile expansion -- substring-matched traversal of entity names that naturally appear in LLM-written profile narratives, a minimal alternative to explicit knowledge-graph construction -- and (ii) compression residuals -- exact dates, quantities, and named items co-extracted with each profile update at zero extra API cost. Third, a full-grid ablation shows cross-benchmark mechanism specialization: profile expansion drives multi-hop reasoning (-22.6pp on MemHop when removed) while compression residuals drive precision recall (-8.6pp on LoCoMo when not co-extracted), with cross-effects under 3pp within a single architecture. ProGraph averages 80.1% on MemHop (matching the FullContext reference) and 78.4% on LoCoMo (exceeding FullContext by 11.3pp), outperforming Mem0, A-Mem, HippoRAG, and RAG on both. We release MemHop, ProGraph, and baseline implementations.

AI.tldr: A multi-hop memory benchmark (MemHop) and a two-layer memory architecture (ProGraph) for LLM agents; MemHop tests multi-hop recall; ProGraph combines profile expansion and compression residuals; ablations show specialization and strong performance; datasets and baselines released.
AI.motivation: Current memory benchmarks emphasize single-hop recall; multi-hop memory and cross-benchmark generalization remain underexplored; need architectures that integrate entity-profile traversal with precise co-extracted data.
AI.method: MemHop: 1,000 questions across hop depths 1-5, 10 social-network scenarios, with per-hop evidence annotations. ProGraph: two-layer memory architecture; profile expansion—substring-matched traversal of entity names in LLM-written profile narratives; compression residuals—exact dates, quantities, and named items co-extracted with each profile update at zero API cost. Full-grid ablation shows cross-benchmark mechanism specialization: profile expansion drives multi-hop reasoning; compression residuals drive precision/recall; cross-effects under 3pp within a single architecture. Evaluation: ProGraph averages 80.1% on MemHop (matching FullContext) and 78.4% on LoCoMo (exceeding FullContext by 11.3pp); outperforming Mem0, A-Mem, HippoRAG, and RAG on both.
AI.result: MemHop provides a challenging, hop-depth-graded benchmark; ProGraph demonstrates a two-layer architecture achieving strong multi-hop memory performance, with ablations validating the roles of profile expansion and compression residuals; code and datasets released.
AI.conclusion: ProGraph achieves competitive multi-hop memory performance with explicit decomposition into profile expansion and compression residuals; MemHop provides a challenging benchmark; released benchmarks and baselines.

title: Domain Shift in Echocardiography: Interpretable Quantification and Prediction of Cross-Dataset Left Ventricular Segmentation
summary: Cross-dataset generalisation remains a major barrier to clinical deployment of echocardiographic left ventricular segmentation, yet the sources of this shift are rarely disentangled. We examined whether transfer degradation could be estimated before deployment using handcrafted ultrasound descriptors, VAE latent features, and segmentation-derived latent features across six echocardiographic datasets. Geometry-aware preprocessing substantially improved several poor transfer cases, suggesting that much of the apparent domain shift reflects field-of-view and framing inconsistencies rather than intrinsic acoustic differences alone. Intensity z-normalisation changed dataset separability by less than 0.005, indicating that brightness and contrast are not the dominant shift axis. Absolute Dice drop on held-out source-target pairs was predicted with an R-squared value of 0.612, an MAE of 0.082, and a Spearman rho of 0.681. The variant without LV and fan-shaped features retained approximately 70% of this explanatory power, supporting mask-free transfer-risk monitoring. The most informative discrepancy measure depended on the representation, with CMD strongest in z-normalised handcrafted features, with an absolute r of approximately 0.86 and an R-squared value of approximately 0.70; log-Wasserstein strongest in VAE space, with an r of approximately -0.90 and an R-squared value of approximately 0.81; and log-MMD strongest in LV-segmentation latent features, with an r of approximately -0.92 and an R-squared value of approximately 0.84. Apparent vendor effects were largely dataset-confounded. Echocardiographic domain shift is therefore structured and measurable, and its impact on segmentation can be partly reduced through geometry-aware preprocessing and anticipated using representation-specific transfer-risk estimation.

AI.tldr: Cross-dataset generalisation in echocardiographic LV segmentation is addressable by geometry-aware preprocessing and transfer-risk estimation using multiple representations; domain shift sources include viewpoint framing; brightness is not the main axis; discrepancy measures capture transfer risk with representation-specific strengths; dataset vendor effects are confounded.
AI.motivation: Identify sources of cross-dataset domain shift and predict segmentation performance drop (Dice) before deployment; evaluate whether preprocessing and representation-based metrics can estimate transfer degradation.
AI.method: Compare handcrafted descriptors, VAE latent features, and LV-segmentation latent features across six datasets; apply geometry-aware preprocessing; assess intensity normalization; compute discrepancy measures (CMD, log-Wasserstein, log-MMD); correlate with Dice drop; test masked variant without LV/fan-shaped features.
AI.result: Geometry-aware preprocessing reduces transfer degradation in some cases; intensity normalization has minimal effect; Dice drop can be predicted with R^2 ~0.612, MAE ~0.082, Spearman ~0.681; strongest discrepancy measures depend on representation: CMD (handcrafted) r~0.86, R^2~0.70; log-Wasserstein (VAE) r~-0.90, R^2~0.81; log-MMD (LV-seg features) r~-0.92, R^2~0.84; removing LV/fan features retains ~70% explanatory power; apparent vendor effects are dataset-confounded.
AI.conclusion: Domain shift in echocardiography is structured and measurable; geometry-aware preprocessing and representation-specific transfer-risk estimation can mitigate and anticipate transfer degradation; caution on vendor confounding requires careful dataset handling.

title: Scale-Aware Learning of Chaotic Dynamics on Unstructured Meshes via Binned Spectral Losses
summary: Surrogate modeling for high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems that exhibit chaos requires mechanisms that preserve not only pointwise accuracy but also the scale-dependent structure of physical fields. Bandwise spectral power losses, such as the binned spectral loss function, provide such supervision on structured grids, where Fourier modes define a standard frequency decomposition. On irregular meshes, however, no canonical Fourier basis exists, and spectral representations must be constructed from graph operators induced by mesh connectivity and geometry. In this study, we extend the binned spectral power loss for application to unstructured-mesh surrogate modeling of nonlinear dynamical systems. This is obtained by replacing Fourier bands with graph-Laplacian frequency bands, and we provide scalable Chebyshev and multilevel approximations for improving long-horizon rollout fidelity. In its full-spectrum form, our approach uses graph Laplacian eigenspaces to provide a graph analogue of Fourier band-power matching, but incurs the high cost of spectral decomposition. As a scalable approximation, we replace exact band projectors with sparse Chebyshev polynomial graph filters, avoiding explicit eigendecomposition. When utilizing multilevel graph architectures, we introduce Graph Laplacian Energy Alignment for Meshes (GLEAM), which applies retained-subspace scale-aware supervision across graph hierarchies so that coarse and fine representations are regularized during autoregressive rollout. Our results show that the proposed spectral losses improve long-horizon rollout fidelity and preserve statistical invariants for the forecasting of turbulent flows on unstructured meshes, compared to deterministic baselines.

AI.tldr: Graph-Laplacian spectral losses with Chebyshev and multilevel approximations (GLEAM) improve surrogate modeling on unstructured meshes by preserving scale-dependent statistics and long-horizon fidelity in chaotic dynamics, e.g., turbulence forecasting.
AI.motivation: To retain scale-aware, physically meaningful structure in high-dimensional chaotic systems when Fourier bases are unavailable on irregular meshes; extend band-power loss to graphs.
AI.method: Replace Fourier bands with graph-Laplacian frequency bands; use sparse Chebyshev polynomial filters and multilevel graph architectures; full-spectrum uses Laplacian eigenspaces; GLEAM aligns energy across graph hierarchies.
AI.result: Improved long-horizon rollout fidelity and preservation of statistical invariants for turbulent flow forecasting on unstructured meshes versus deterministic baselines.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based spectral losses with scalable approximations provide effective, scalable supervision for unstructured-mesh surrogate modeling of chaotic dynamics.

title: Morphing MILR: Design and control of a cable-driven limbless robot with rolling joints for maneuvering in complex environments
summary: Limbless robots offer exceptional mobility in confined and cluttered environments due to their slender bodies and their ability to exploit body-terrain interactions. Recent designs incorporating compliance demonstrate robust locomotion without complex sensing or control; however, these systems typically rely on fixed body configurations, with each morphology specialized for a single locomotion mode or environment. This raises a key challenge: how can a single limbless robot achieve versatile locomotion while preserving the robustness of compliance-mediated locomotion? To address this challenge, we present a cable-driven limbless robot that reconfigures body morphology and compliance to enable diverse locomotion modes. Distributed cable actuation generates traveling body waves, while programmable passive compliance enables robust contact-rich locomotion without terrain knowledge or high-bandwidth feedback. Rolling joints reorient bending planes along the body, enabling rapid reconfiguration and smooth transitions between locomotion styles, and incorporate geared locking to maintain configuration without continuous power. By combining programmable bending compliance and morphology control, the platform achieves lateral undulation, sidewinding, rolling, and twisting within a single system. Experiments demonstrate reliable gait generation, traversal in obstacle-rich environments, and transitions between modes, establishing a versatile limbless platform for navigating complex environments with applications in search and rescue, environmental monitoring, and inspection.

AI.tldr: A cable-driven limbless robot reconfigures body morphology and compliance to enable multiple locomotion modes (lateral undulation, sidewinding, rolling, twisting) within a single platform, using distributed cable actuation for traveling waves, programmable passive compliance for robust contact-rich locomotion, and rolling joints with geared locking for rapid reconfiguration and mode transitions.
AI.motivation: Limbless robots with compliant locomotion excel in rough, confined environments but typically rely on fixed morphologies tailored to a single mode; this limits versatility and robustness across varied terrains. A single, reconfigurable system could preserve compliance benefits while enabling diverse locomotion strategies.
AI.method: A cable-driven architecture distributes actuators along the body to generate traveling waves. Programmable passive bending compliance provides robustness during contact-rich locomotion without terrain knowledge or high-bandwidth feedback. Rolling joints reorient bending planes to enable rapid morphology changes and smooth transitions between locomotion styles, with geared locking to maintain configurations without continuous power. The system combines programmable bending compliance with morphology control to realize lateral undulation, sidewinding, rolling, and twisting in one platform.
AI.result: The platform achieves multiple locomotion modes within one robot (lateral undulation, sidewinding, rolling, twisting). Experiments demonstrate reliable gait generation, traversal in obstacle-rich environments, and smooth transitions between modes, indicating a versatile, robust limbless platform.
AI.conclusion: Integrating programmable bending compliance with reconfigurable morphology yields a versatile limbless robot capable of diverse locomotion modes without sacrificing robustness. The approach broadens applicability to complex environments (e.g., search and rescue, environmental monitoring, inspection) by enabling smooth mode transitions and reliable terrain interaction.

title: Lifted Representation Hypothesis in Language Models
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, ICML 2026 Workshop: Philosophy Meets Machine Learning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often answer queries by mapping individual observations to more general rule-like structures. However, it remains unclear how these structures are stored, selected, and revised. To study this process, we propose thelifted representation hypothesis: LLMs update memory through shared latent structures rather than isolated instance-level facts. This view frames lifting as an efficient use of symmetry across instances, and shattering as the refinement of coarse lifted structures into more specific subtypes. We evaluate LLMs' lifting and shattering through controlled exception-learning experiments across in-context learning, LoRA, and full fine-tuning. We find that LLMs are vulnerable to shattering failures when data are governed by nested rules and exceptions, while lifting often occurs prematurely. These results highlight the need to study the relation between data and rule structures in LLMs.

AI.tldr: The lifted representation hypothesis posits that LLMs store and revise rule-like knowledge via shared latent structures (lifting) and refine them (shattering); experiments show premature lifting and shattering failures with nested-rule data, underscoring the need to align data and rule structures.
AI.motivation: To understand how LLMs store, select, and revise rule-like memory representations, and to explain how generalizations emerge from concrete observations.
AI.method: Controlled exception-learning experiments evaluating lifting and shattering across in-context learning, LoRA, and full fine-tuning.
AI.result: Lifting often occurs prematurely, while LLMs are vulnerable to shattering failures when data are governed by nested rules and exceptions; memory updates rely on shared latent structures and symmetry across instances.
AI.conclusion: The data–rule structure relationship is crucial; future work should explore how data design and training regimens can induce more robust lifting and more reliable shattering in LLMs.

title: A Unified Variational Framework for Deep Weakly Supervised Image Segmentation
summary: We propose a unified variational framework for image segmentation under sparse pixel-level supervision. Our method is based on a simplex-constrained Potts model with a smooth perimeter regularizer, yielding a convex, smooth energy functional that can be used as a training loss in weakly supervised deep learning paradigms or optimized efficiently using iterative methods. Sparse labels are incorporated into the data fidelity term by constructing a fuzzy membership function via a function extension problem in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS), which can effectively capture inhomogeneous intensity statistics. The derived discrete loss for training standard networks demonstrates robustness and consistent improvements over non-training and partial cross-entropy (PCE) baselines in experiments, achieving comparable performance without requiring ground-truth segmentation images.

AI.tldr: A convex, smooth variational framework for weakly supervised image segmentation using a simplex-constrained Potts model with a smooth perimeter term and RKHS-based fuzzy memberships to encode sparse labels, yielding a trainable loss that improves performance without ground-truth segmentations.
AI.motivation: To enable effective image segmentation under sparse pixel-level supervision by unifying variational methods with deep learning, and to robustly handle inhomogeneous intensity statistics without needing full ground-truth masks.
AI.method: Develop a simplex-constrained Potts model with a smooth perimeter regularizer to create a convex, differentiable energy. Incorporate sparse labels into the data fidelity by constructing a fuzzy membership function via a function extension problem in an RKHS, capturing inhomogeneous intensities. Derive a discrete loss from this energy for training standard networks and for efficient optimization.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows robustness and consistent improvements over non-training and partial cross-entropy baselines in various experiments. The approach achieves comparable performance to fully supervised methods without requiring ground-truth segmentation images.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a practical, trainable loss for weakly supervised segmentation that blends variational principles with deep learning, handles label sparsity and intensity inhomogeneity via RKHS-based memberships, and can be optimized efficiently rather than requiring full segmentation labels.

title: Neural Operator Surrogates for Two-Dimensional Neutron Flux Estimation
comment: to be submitted to ANS Winter 2026
summary: This work extends our one-dimensional single-sweep neural-operator studies to two dimensions. We consider one-group transport with isotropic scattering. As in the one-dimensional work, we use Fourier neural operators (FNOs) to approximate the high-fidelity scalar flux. Additionally, we also investigate U-shaped neural operators (UNOs) in this study. We consider three surrogates. The first two map the material and source fields directly to the flux, one using an FNO and one using a UNO. The third is an FNO that additionally takes the scalar flux after one source iteration, the single-sweep approximation, as an input. Each case is solved to high fidelity with a verified discrete-ordinates solver, and an average relative L_2 error norm is used to characterize the quality of the inferred maps. We train every surrogate over three random seeds so that differences between them can be assessed against run-to-run variability. Two questions guide the study: whether the single-sweep input improves accuracy over the direct maps, and whether training on the logarithm of the flux improves accuracy in the strongly attenuated regions relevant to shielding.

AI.tldr: Extends 1D neural-operator transport surrogates to 2D for isotropic scattering, evaluating FNO and UNO architectures across three surrogates, including a single-sweep input variant and a log-flux variant; assesses accuracy with average relative L2 error against high-fidelity solvers, with three seeds to gauge variability; aims to answer if single-sweep inputs and log-flux training improve performance.
AI.motivation: Develop fast, accurate surrogate models for 2D neutron transport by comparing neural-operator architectures and input strategies, addressing accuracy in strongly attenuated regions relevant to shielding.
AI.method: Train three surrogate models (FNO-direct, UNO-direct, FNO-with-single-sweep-input) mapping material/source fields to flux; introduce a log-flux variant; compare to high-fidelity discrete-ordinates solver using average relative L2 error; each model trained with three random seeds for variability assessment.
AI.result: Abstract outlines planned experiments and evaluation metrics but does not report quantitative results; expects comparative performance across surrogates and guidance on the benefits of single-sweep input and log-flux training.
AI.conclusion: The study seeks to determine (i) whether incorporating the single-sweep input improves accuracy over direct maps and (ii) whether log-flux training enhances accuracy in strongly attenuated regions, with implications for selecting neural-operator architectures for 2D transport surrogates.

title: EgoRecovery: Acquiring Failure Recovery Ability Through Human Recovery Demonstration
summary: Robust embodied robots should be able to recover from failures and retry tasks in order to operate reliably in unstructured and noisy real-world environments. Achieving this capability requires training policies on data that captures recovery behaviors. However, collecting such data through robot teleoperation is difficult to scale, as it is time-consuming to induce diverse failure states, perform corrective actions, and reset the environment. This challenge is further exacerbated by the high diversity of failure modes, which demands substantially more recovery data than success demonstrations. In this work, we show that egocentric human data capturing failure recovery processes provides a scalable alternative. By efficiently arranging task-level failure configurations and recording short recovery segments, human operators can generate more than 10x as much valid recovery data per hour compared to robot teleoperation under our protocol. To address the embodiment gap between human and robot, we propose EgoRecovery, a co-training framework for learning recovery behavior, where human recovery demonstrations are aligned to a compact corrective-intent space shared with robot data, which captures the timing and magnitude of correction. Only a small number of robot recovery demonstrations are required to connect this intent to executable robot actions. At deployment, a learned recovery gate predicts when correction is needed from robot observations and activates the corrective intent only in recovery states. Experiments on real-world recovery tasks show that EgoRecovery improves success from failure starts over robot-only recovery, direct co-training with human recovery data, and direct intent-transfer baselines.

AI.tldr: EgoRecovery enables scalable recovery policy learning by pairing egocentric human failure-recovery data with robot data in a shared corrective-intent space, requiring few robot cues to map intent to action, leading to >10x more data and improved recovery performance over baselines.
AI.motivation: To create data-efficient, robust recovery policies for embodied robots by leveraging scalable human demonstration data and bridging the embodiment gap between humans and robots.
AI.method: Collect egocentric human recovery data organized by task-level failure configurations and short recovery segments; align this data to a compact corrective-intent space shared with robot data; train with both human and robot demonstrations; use a small set of robot demonstrations to connect intent to executable actions; deploy a recovery gate that predicts when to apply corrective intent from robot observations.
AI.result: The approach yields >10x more valid recovery data per hour than robot teleoperation; improves success from failure starts over robot-only recovery and other baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of cross-domain recovery learning.
AI.conclusion: EgoRecovery provides a scalable path to learning robust recovery behaviors by aligning human recovery intent with robot actions in a shared space, reducing robot data requirements while improving recovery performance.

title: GraphContainer: A Unified Platform for Comparing and Debugging Graph RAG Methods
summary: Graph RAG mitigates hallucinations and stale knowledge in LLMs, particularly for multi-hop question answering. However, existing approaches remain highly fragmented and incompatible. The structural heterogeneity of graph formats across different frameworks and the lack of granular visualization tools make it exceedingly difficult to evaluate and compare retrieval behaviors. To bridge this gap, we propose GraphContainer, a novel platform designed to unify and visualize diverse graph RAG workflows. GraphContainer features two key components: (1) a Unified Graph Representation (UGR) layer that seamlessly standardizes multi-format graphs, and (2) a Graph Recorder that tracks and visually renders the step-by-step retrieval process. Through an interactive web interface, we demonstrate GraphContainer's ability to import heterogeneous graphs and perform live, traceable visual debugging of graph RAG methods. Ultimately, we show how GraphContainer enables controlled comparisons of various graph formats and retrieval strategies, lowering the barrier for researchers and practitioners to design optimal graph RAG pipelines. A demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/O02eNJLwkU0.

AI.tldr: A platform GraphContainer unifies diverse graph RAG workflows via UGR and a Graph Recorder for live visual debugging and controlled comparison.
AI.motivation: Graph RAG helps mitigate hallucinations and stale knowledge in LLMs for multi-hop QA, but heterogeneous graph formats and lack of granular visualization hinder evaluation and comparison. A unified, traceable visualization tool is needed to standardize and compare retrieval behaviors across frameworks.
AI.method: Introduce Unified Graph Representation (UGR) to standardize multi-format graphs; implement Graph Recorder to capture and visually render step-by-step retrieval; provide an interactive web interface for importing heterogeneous graphs, live visual debugging, and controlled comparisons of formats/strategies.
AI.result: Demonstrates import of heterogeneous graphs and live, traceable debugging; enables controlled comparisons of graph formats and retrieval strategies; video demonstration provided.
AI.conclusion: GraphContainer lowers barriers for researchers and practitioners to design and optimize graph RAG pipelines by standardizing formats and visually tracking retrieval processes, enabling more reliable evaluation.

title: PhenSPINE: A Standardized Benchmark for Spine Pathology Diagnosis
comment: 12 pages, figures, Accepted at CITA 2026 (The 15th Conference on Information Technology and its Applications, Scopus)
summary: The accurate diagnosis of spinal pathologies depends heavily on radiological interpretation, yet automated systems are hindered by the lack of diverse, high-quality benchmarks. In this study, we present PhenSPINE, a Magnetic Resonance Imaging dataset comprising 16,813 images from 250 patients, curated to facilitate advanced deep learning research. We propose a robust diagnostic benchmark that integrates state-of-theart convolutional backbones with a Positional Encoding mechanism to explicitly model the anatomical context of intervertebral discs. Evaluating across four standard MRI sequences, our experiments demonstrate that the Sagittal T2-weighted sequence offers the most robust diagnostic value, achieving a superior Macro F1-score of 50.31%. We find that multisequence fusion strategies yield inferior performance compared to this single-sequence baseline, as the images across sequences in our dataset are significantly compromised by noise interference from surrounding anatomical regions. This work establishes a robust baseline and offers critical insights into sequence selection for spine analysis.

AI.tldr: PhenSPINE offers a large spine MRI dataset and a benchmark integrating positional encoding with CNN backbones; sagittal T2 is the strongest single-sequence predictor with Macro F1 50.31%; multisequence fusion underperforms due to noise.
AI.motivation: Address lack of diverse, high-quality spine MRI benchmarks to advance deep learning for automated diagnosis.
AI.method: Dataset collection (16,813 images from 250 patients) across four MRI sequences; propose diagnostic benchmark with convolutional backbones plus a positional encoding mechanism to capture intervertebral disc anatomy; evaluate different sequences and fusion strategies.
AI.result: Sagittal T2-weighted sequence yields Macro F1 score 50.31%; multi-sequence fusion underperforms single-sequence baseline due to noise from surrounding anatomy; single-sequence baseline is robust.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a robust baseline, provides insights into sequence selection for spine analysis.

title: The Orthogonalized Read Is a Removable Training Scaffold for Recurrent Memory
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures. Code, per-seed results, and checkpoints: https://github.com/no-way-labs/recurrent-memory-scaffold
summary: A recent report finds that orthogonalizing the mLSTM memory matrix at read time (five Newton-Schulz iterations, trained through) substantially improves noisy associative recall. The effect replicates, but it is not a memory improvement. Training on this task is a long chance plateau followed by a sharp escape, and the orthogonalized read acts by re-conditioning the learning problem during the plateau. Three properties establish this. It must be self-consistent: an exact recursive least-squares read (the Mesa layer) reproduces it, while straight-through halves, delta-rule writes, frozen random keys, and plain normalization all fail. It is uniform: across a learning-rate x hardness grid it multiplies the escape hazard roughly six-fold with no detectable hardness dependence, widening the workable learning-rate corridor that narrows for the baseline. And it is removable: applied to failed models at inference it rescues none, and annealed away on an escape-triggered schedule it leaves numerically stock mLSTMs at full accuracy. Much of the published gain needs no architecture at all -- solved-rate at a fixed budget measures escape hazard, which follows a heat/noise law (learning-rate elasticity +3.0, gradient-noise elasticity -1.65) under which the original vocab-96 result is a large-batch noise condition rather than a capacity one. Decoding the memory state directly shows failed models carry roughly half their associations in linearly recoverable form: the plateau is a readout failure over half-written storage. Two conclusions travel beyond the intervention: recall benchmarks used for architecture selection partly measure trainability, and the system is a fully instrumented model organism of "emergence," in which a sharp behavioral threshold demonstrably arises from a censored metric over gradually accumulating structure.

AI.tldr: Orthogonalizing the mLSTM read with Newton-Schulz iterations improves noisy associative recall via training-dynamics re-conditioning, not through genuine memory expansion; the effect is replicable by a Mesa (recursive least-squares) read, scales with training difficulty and learning-rate, and reveals an emergent threshold rather than architecture-level improvement.
AI.motivation: To distinguish whether orthogonalized reads provide true memory capacity gains or merely alter trainability and optimization dynamics; to understand the mechanisms and generality of the observed boost in recall under noise.
AI.method: Apply five Newton-Schulz iterations to orthogonalize the memory read at read time; compare with baselines (straight-through, delta-rule writes, frozen random keys, plain normalization); validate via an exact recursive least-squares (Mesa) read; analyze escape hazard across learning-rate × problem hardness; decode memory state to assess recoverability; test removability at inference and under annealing; model the effect with a heat/noise law.
AI.result: The orthogonalized read yields substantial improvement in noisy associative recall but does not increase true memory capacity. The Mesa read reproduces the effect, indicating the mechanism is about read-time conditioning of the learning problem. Across lr × hardness grids, the escape hazard increases roughly six-fold with little hardness dependence, widening the workable learning-rate corridor for the baseline but not for the improved model. At inference, applied to failed models, the intervention rescues none; annealing away on a schedule leaves full accuracy intact in stock mLSTMs. Much of the gain arises from trainability rather than storage capacity; decoded states show failed models keep about half of their associations in linearly recoverable form, implying plateau-wide readout failure of half-written storage. A heat/noise law (learning-rate elasticity +3.0, gradient-noise elasticity -1.65) governs the results; the original vocab-96 result reflects a large-batch noise condition rather than capacity. Two broad conclusions emerge: recall benchmarks used for architecture selection partly measure trainability, and the system behaves as an emergent, fully instrumented model organism with a sharp behavioral threshold arising from gradually accumulating structure.
AI.conclusion: The intervention highlights the central role of trainability and emergent thresholds in architectural gains. It cautions against equating improved recall with genuine memory enhancement and suggests that many reported gains may derive from optimization dynamics sensitive to learning rate, noise, and task structure. It also provides a framework (Mesa read; heat/noise law) to diagnose when such interventions yield robust, architecture-invariant improvements versus transient training-time artifacts.

title: Defer to Plan: Adaptive Multi-Agent Fusion for End-to-End V2X Driving
summary: Vehicle-to-everything-aided autonomous driving (V2X-AD) significantly enhances driving performance through information sharing. However, existing collaborative perception methods only optimize module-level perception capabilities and fail to effectively serve the ultimate planning and control tasks. We propose an end-to-end collaborative driving system that directly optimizes planning task performance. The system employs MotionNetwork to fuse historical temporal information, utilizes attention mechanisms to efficiently compress spatial features into compact tokens, and adaptively fuses multi-agent features through an autoregressive decoder. Additionally, we introduce Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to enhance the model's representation capacity for heterogeneous features. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves a driving score of 79.72, surpassing the state-of-the-art CoDriving baseline (77.15) by 3.33% in closed-loop evaluation while maintaining communication efficiency.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end V2X collaborative driving framework that optimizes planning by fusing temporal data, tokenizing spatial features with attention, adaptively fusing multi-agent info via autoregressive decoding, and using Mixture-of-Experts to handle heterogeneous features; achieves 79.72 driving score, outperforming CoDriving baseline.
AI.motivation: Limitations of modular, perception-centric collaboration; need end-to-end optimization of planning control in V2X for improved decision making and efficiency.
AI.method: MotionNetwork for temporal fusion; attention-based spatial feature tokenization; autoregressive decoder for adaptive multi-agent fusion; Mixture-of-Experts to enhance representation of heterogeneous features.
AI.result: Closed-loop driving score of 79.72, beating CoDriving by 3.33% (77.15) while maintaining communication efficiency.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end collaborative driving improves planning performance and efficiency; MoE enhances handling of heterogeneous features; promising direction for V2X-AD systems.

title: AdaRoPE: Not All Attention Heads Should Rotate and Scale Equally
summary: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is widely adopted in Transformers to encode positional information, yet standard implementations enforce a uniform frequency schedule and scaling across all attention heads. Using simplified retrieval tasks and length generalization scenarios, we show -- both empirically and theoretically -- that heads with different functional roles require distinct frequency ranges and attention scaling factors to operate effectively. Ignoring this structure leads to suboptimal utilization of embedding dimensions and degraded performance, particularly under long-context settings. To address these limitations, we propose AdaRoPE, which equips each attention head with learnable rotation frequencies and attention scaling factors. Pretrained LLMs with AdaRoPE consistently outperform existing RoPE variants, including partial RoPE and NoPE baselines. For context extension, we further show that uniform frequency and attention scaling, used in methods such as YaRN, are suboptimal. By applying head-specific scaling, AdaRoPE enables better context extension while better preserving short-context performance in both the extrapolation setting and the long-context continued pretraining setting. These results highlight the importance of optimizing rotary position embedding at the level of individual attention heads.

AI.tldr: AdaRoPE introduces per-head learnable rotation frequencies and attention scaling factors for Rotary Position Embedding, outperforming uniform RoPE variants in long-context, extrapolation, and context extension tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard RoPE uses a uniform frequency schedule across all attention heads, assuming identical positional roles. Empirical and theoretical evidence suggests heads have distinct functional roles requiring different frequency ranges and scaling for effective attention, especially with long contexts.
AI.method: Propose AdaRoPE where each attention head has its own learnable rotation frequency and attention scaling. Conduct experiments on simplified retrieval tasks and length generalization, plus evaluation on pretrained LLMs, comparing against partial RoPE and NoPE; analyze context extension scenarios and YaRN-style uniform frequency baselines.
AI.result: AdaRoPE-equipped pretrained LLMs consistently outperform existing RoPE variants (including partial RoPE and NoPE). Head-specific scaling improves context extension and long-context performance, preserving short-context performance in extrapolation and continued pretraining settings.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing rotary position embeddings at the per-head level yields better utilization of embedding dimensions and improved long-context and extrapolation performance; per-head frequency and scaling customization is beneficial for RoPE-based transformers.

title: SafeGen: Goal-Conditioned Video Diffusion of Safety-Critical Scenarios for VLM-Based Autonomous Driving
summary: VLMs are increasingly deployed in AD systems, creating an urgent need for rigorous safety evaluation under rare yet safety-critical scenarios. Among these, interactions with vulnerable road users represent a major source of real-world failures. However, existing safety-critical scenario generation methods predominantly rely on simulator-based pipelines, which suffer from a substantial sim-to-real gap and often fail to capture realistic, diverse, and unforeseen human-vehicle interaction dynamics. We present SafeGen, a goal-conditioned diffusion framework for safety-critical scenario generation in VLMADs. Our key insight is to formulate scenario generation as a goal-conditioned diffusion process, where a predefined catastrophic end-state serves as a strong supervisory signal, guiding the generation of temporally coherent video trajectories that naturally evolve toward safety-critical outcomes. Building on this formulation, we introduce Context Grounded End State Reasoning, which leverages VLMs to analyze benign driving contexts and infer latent vulnerabilities in human-vehicle interactions, producing structured end-state specifications that induce high-risk scenarios. Conditioned on these targets, we further propose End State Conditioned Video Evolution, which grounds semantic threats into physically plausible visual dynamics. Specifically, we instantiate high-risk agents within the scene via depth-aware geometric projection, followed by boundary-conditioned diffusion to generate intermediate frames with consistent motion patterns and temporal coherence. Extensive experiments across 3 VLMADs demonstrate that SafeGen increases the Judge Overall Score, a metric using a VLM judge to evaluate VLMADs' understanding and decision-making, by 24.25% on average compared to SoTA baselines. Furthermore, fine-tuning a VLMAD improves performance in real-world driving scenes by an average of 15.9%.

AI.tldr: SafeGen uses goal-conditioned diffusion to generate safety-critical driving scenarios for VLMADs, with end-state reasoning and video evolution, achieving strong judge-based scores and real-world gains.
AI.motivation: To close the sim-to-real gap and capture diverse, realistic, and unforeseen human-vehicle interactions for safety evaluation in VLM-enabled AD systems.
AI.method: Formulate scenario generation as a goal-conditioned diffusion toward a catastrophic end-state; Context Grounded End State Reasoning via VLMs to derive latent vulnerabilities; End State Conditioned Video Evolution with depth-aware projection and boundary-conditioned diffusion to produce temporally coherent frames.
AI.result: Judge Overall Score improves by 24.25% over SOTA baselines; fine-tuning VLMAD yields 15.9% real-world driving performance gain.
AI.conclusion: SafeGen provides a scalable framework for safety-critical scenario generation and evaluation, mitigating sim-to-real gaps; further validation and broader generalization are potential avenues.

title: LAARA: Layer-Aware Adaptive Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation is widely used for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet existing methods typically assign the same adapter rank to every transformer layer despite their heterogeneous adaptation requirements. In this work, we show theoretically and empirically that uniform rank allocation is fundamentally suboptimal. Motivated by this observation, we propose LAARA (Layer Aware Adaptive Rank Allocation framework), a search-free framework that dynamically allocates ranks using lightweight diagonal Fisher estimates computed during training. LAARA combines projection-wise normalization, logarithmic compression, blended adapter importance estimation, and a vote-to-change dampening mechanism to produce stable and efficient rank adaptation. Experiments on GLUE and MathInstruct benchmark demonstrate that LAARA consistently matches or outperforms popular state of the art approaches such as LoRA, AdaLoRA, DyLoRA, and Bitfit while using significantly fewer trainable parameters. Our results show that Fisher-guided rank allocation provides a principled and effective foundation for adaptive parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The code is publicly available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LAARA-D305/LAARA.py

AI.tldr: LAARA is a search-free, layer-aware rank allocation framework for Low-Rank Adaptation that uses diagonal Fisher estimates during training to dynamically allocate adapter ranks per layer, achieving competitive performance with fewer trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Uniform rank allocation across transformer layers is suboptimal due to heterogeneous adaptation needs; adaptive, parameter-efficient fine-tuning is desirable.
