AI.method: Compute lightweight diagonal Fisher information during training to estimate per-layer adapter importance; apply projection-wise normalization, logarithmic compression, blended adapter importance estimation, and a vote-to-change dampening mechanism to dynamically allocate ranks without search.
AI.result: On GLUE and MathInstruct, LAARA matches or outperforms LoRA, AdaLoRA, DyLoRA, and Bitfit while using significantly fewer trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: Fisher-guided, layer-aware rank allocation provides a principled and effective foundation for adaptive parameter-efficient fine-tuning; code is publicly available.

title: V2F: Vision-Informed Grasp Force Prediction for Damage-Aware Robotic Handling of Date Fruits
comment: Accepted to IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026
summary: This paper presents a vision-informed grasp force prediction framework for robotic handling of date fruits. Addressing the dual challenge of high detachment forces and low bruise thresholds, we first conduct mechanical characterization on date samples to define a safe grasping envelope and quantify the relationship between fruit geometry and bioyield stress. In this work, we develop a Vision-to-Force (V2F) pipeline that combines computer vision-based segmentation, active-contour refinement, and geometric feature extraction with a physics-informed residual neural network that augments a Hertz contact equation. The resulting model maps non-contact visual descriptors and cultivar metadata to predict a safe grasp force with mean validation performance of $R^2 \approx 0.7$ across unseen cultivar groups, which is a good result given the inherent mechanical variability of biological tissue. Experimental validation using a gripper and load cell indicates that the predicted forces enable stable manipulation of different types of date fruits, with residual deformations below 1 mm and no observable damage. These results show that pre-emptive, vision-driven force estimation% can replace slow and potentially damaging tactile exploration , enabling safer robotic handling of fragile fruits.

AI.tldr: Vision-informed grasp force prediction for date fruits achieving R^2 ~ 0.7 across unseen cultivars, enabling safe, damage-free manipulation by predicting safe grasp forces from visual cues and cultivar metadata.
AI.motivation: Fragile fruit handling requires accurate, safe grasp forces to prevent bruise damage. Date fruits exhibit high detachment forces and low bruise thresholds, making tactile-only exploration slow and risky.
AI.method: A Vision-to-Force (V2F) framework combining computer vision segmentation, active-contour refinement, geometric feature extraction, and a physics-informed residual neural network that augments a Hertz contact model. The model maps non-contact visual descriptors and cultivar metadata to predicted safe grasp forces.
AI.result: Mean validation R^2 ≈ 0.7 on unseen cultivars; experimental validation shows stable manipulation with residual deformations <1 mm and no observable damage. Demonstrates potential to replace tactile exploration with vision-driven force estimation.
AI.conclusion: Vision-driven force estimation can enable safer robotic handling of fragile fruits and reduce reliance on slow tactile exploration, improving efficiency and reducing damage during automation.

title: Statistically Grounded Sparse-Feature Interventions for Activation-Space Control in Large Language Models
summary: Activation steering offers a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for behavioral control of large language models, but SAE-based steering methods often rely on learned steering objectives or single-criterion feature selection. We introduce a transparent SAE-feature steering pipeline that first applies a six-condition reliability filter, then ranks sparse features through an unweighted Borda consensus over three complementary statistics: $F$-test, KSG mutual information, and Cohen's $d$. The resulting steering direction is constructed as a Cohen's-$d$-weighted combination of SAE decoder rows, providing an optimization-free direction motivated by Fisher-LDA under approximate SAE-feature decorrelation. Across three Gemma-family models, four behavioral domains, and 356 layer-strength configurations, the method produces measurable domain-specific shifts while revealing a substantial gap between raw attribute movement and quality-preserving generation. In the strongest configuration, logical-correctness steering reaches a primary-score delta of $+1.16$ in Gemma~2 9B; however, our broader finding is that usable steering is highly localized by model, domain, layer, and strength. These results argue that activation-steering evaluations should report quality-conditioned success alongside raw behavioral shift. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/Oshayer-Siddique/LLM-Steering-Using-SAE.

AI.tldr: A transparent activation-steering pipeline using SAE features with a six-condition reliability filter and Borda-based feature ranking, producing a Cohen's d–weighted steering direction; results show model-, domain-, layer-, and strength-specific effectiveness and a need to report quality-conditioned success.
AI.motivation: To address opacity and inconsistency in SAE-based activation steering, and to link feature movement to quality-preserving generation with an optimization-free, interpretable method.
AI.method: Apply a six-condition reliability filter; rank sparse features via an unweighted Borda consensus over F-test, KSG mutual information, and Cohen's d; construct steering direction as a Cohen's d–weighted combination of SAE decoder rows; leverage Fisher-LDA-like decorrelation; evaluate across Gemma-family models, four behavioral domains, and 356 layer-strength configurations.
AI.result: Observed measurable domain-specific shifts and a large gap between raw attribute movement and quality-preserving generation; strongest config yielded a +1.16 primary-score delta for logical correctness in Gemma-2 9B; overall, usable steering is highly localized by model, domain, layer, and strength.
AI.conclusion: Activation-steering evaluations should report quality-conditioned success alongside raw behavioral shift; code and data are available at the provided GitHub link.

title: Point-Selection Fine-Tuning Framework for Robust Point Cloud Classification
summary: Noisy and corrupted points can substantially degrade point cloud recognition performance, especially under challenging corruption settings. In particular, full fine-tuning of 3D pre-trained models may amplify the influence of outliers and overwrite robustness priors learned during pre-training, while naive parameter-efficient adaptation remains sensitive to corrupted tokens. To address this issue, we propose PSFT, a point-selection fine-tuning framework that improves robustness while remaining parameter-efficient. PSFT first estimates point-wise influence from pre-pooling features and adaptively retains minimally influential points to suppress outliers. Based on the selected subset, a prompt generation branch predicts layer-wise prompt tokens and injects them into a frozen backbone for lightweight downstream adaptation. To further mitigate residual noise after selection, we append a lightweight feature filter with bottleneck MLP transformation and Beta-gated residual blending to refine patch-token representations before prediction. Extensive experiments show that PSFT consistently reduces corruption error on ModelNet-C and ModelNet40-C across all tested 3D pre-trained backbones, while achieving the strongest ScanObjectNN-C results with ULIP-2 and Uni3D-B among the evaluated tuning strategies. Our implementation can be found at https://github.com/CVChMA/PSFT/tree/master.

AI.tldr: PSFT is a parameter-efficient, robust fine-tuning framework for 3D pre-trained models that selects low-influence points and uses a prompt-based adaptation plus a lightweight feature filter to mitigate noise, achieving reduced corruption errors across ModelNet-C/ModelNet40-C and strong results on ScanObjectNN-C.
AI.motivation: 3D pre-trained models are vulnerable to noise and outliers, and full fine-tuning can erase robustness learned during pre-training; naive parameter-efficient adaptation remains sensitive to corrupted tokens. A robust, efficient approach is needed.
AI.method: 1) Estimate point-wise influence from pre-pooling features and retain minimally influential points to suppress outliers. 2) On the selected subset, a prompt-generation branch predicts layer-wise prompt tokens that are injected into a frozen backbone for lightweight downstream adaptation. 3) Append a lightweight feature filter with bottleneck MLP transformation and Beta-gated residual blending to refine patch-token representations before prediction.
AI.result: PSFT consistently reduces corruption error on ModelNet-C and ModelNet40-C across tested 3D pre-trained backbones; achieves the strongest ScanObjectNN-C results with ULIP-2 and Uni3D-B among evaluated tuning strategies.
AI.conclusion: PSFT provides a robust, parameter-efficient adaptation mechanism for 3D pre-trained models under corruption, leveraging targeted point selection, prompt-based integration, and a lightweight filtering stage to mitigate residual noise across multiple benchmarks.

title: Predicting Groundwater Arsenic Concentrations Using Graph Neural Networks
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, AAAI '26 AI4ES workshop acceptance
summary: Arsenic contamination in groundwater presents a longstanding public health crisis in the United States, especially for households depending on private wells. Accurate and spatially informed prediction of arsenic concentration is vital to identify high-risk areas and focus mitigation efforts. However, there is a lack of generalizable models for representing continuous variation in arsenic concentrations across regions. In this work, we pose arsenic prediction as a regression task and construct a spatially integrated dataset to aggregate over 74,000 arsenic samples from the Water Quality Portal (WQP), Mineral Resources Data System (MRDS), and Gridded National Soil Survey Geographic Database (gNATSGO). Specifically, we use a variety of techniques including kNearest Neighbors (k-NN) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to join arsenic measurement points from across the United States by location. Building on this dataset, we evaluate a diverse suite of machine learning models, including tree-based ensemble approaches, multilayer perceptrons, and spatially aware graph neural networks (GNN). Our findings show that while gradient-boosted trees are still considered state-of-the-art in the field of tabular data, GNNs are able to further account for spatial dependence to match or outperform the results of gradient-boosted trees. These results demonstrate that graph-based and spatially informed learning can enhance environmental prediction and provide a foundation for improved groundwater risk mapping and monitoring.

AI.tldr: A study assembles a large, spatially integrated arsenic dataset across the US and compares models ranging from gradient-boosted trees to graph neural networks for continuous arsenic concentration prediction, highlighting spatially aware learning as a potential enhancement over traditional tabular models.
AI.motivation: Arsenic in private-well groundwater is a public health risk with spatially varying concentrations. There is a need for generalizable, spatially aware predictive models that can leverage diverse data sources to map arsenic risk.
AI.method: Construct a spatially integrated dataset (~74,000 samples) by joining WQP, MRDS, and gNATSGO data with k-NN and GIS-based spatial joins. Train and evaluate multiple models: gradient-boosted trees, multilayer perceptrons, and spatially aware graph neural networks (GNNs).
AI.result: Gradient-boosted trees remain strong baselines on tabular data, but GNNs that incorporate spatial dependencies can match or surpass them, suggesting spatial structure improves predictive performance for arsenic concentration.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based and spatially informed learning can enhance environmental prediction and support improved groundwater risk mapping and monitoring across regions.

title: Clinical Pathways as Safety Specifications for Physical AI in Hospital Wards
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the 1st IJCAI Workshop on Safe Physical AI (SPAI 2026), held in conjunction with IJCAI-ECAI 2026, Bremen, Germany
summary: Ensuring safety in Physical AI systems operating in real-world environments is a critical challenge, particularly in hospital wards where vulnerable patients, clinical staff, medical devices, and assistive robots coexist. In this paper, we reinterpret Clinical Pathways as explicit runtime safety specifications for embodied medical AI. We propose a conceptual robotic architecture that integrates wearable sensors, smart medical devices, and assistive robotic components into a unified framework for real-time safety monitoring. At its core, a Runtime Safety Monitor (RSM) evaluates multimodal physiological and system-level signals against clinically defined constraints derived from the prescribed care process. Rather than relying solely on statistical anomaly detection, the proposed approach combines temporal prediction, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and constraint-based verification to identify safety violations. The RSM targets three classes of events: physiological deviations from prescribed care, hardware and communication failures, and potential data tampering or misuse. This work contributes to Safe Physical AI by operationalizing domain-specific clinical knowledge as enforceable safety constraints, bridging learning-based perception and runtime safety monitoring to assist nursing staff in real-world hospital wards.

AI.tldr: A conceptual Runtime Safety Monitor (RSM) framework that enforces safety constraints for embodied medical AI in hospital wards, integrating wearables, smart devices, and assistive robots to monitor safety in real time using constraint-based verification and temporal prediction rather than solely anomaly detection.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical integration of Physical AI in clinical environments; need explicit, enforceable safety specifications derived from clinical workflows to protect patients, staff, and devices.
AI.method: Proposes a unified robotic architecture with wearables, smart medical devices, and assistive robots. Introduces a Runtime Safety Monitor (RSM) that assesses multimodal physiological and system-level signals against clinically defined constraints from prescribed care pathways. Combines temporal prediction, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and constraint-based verification to detect safety violations across physiological, hardware/communication, and data integrity domains.
AI.result: Conceptual framework and architectural proposal; no reported empirical results in the abstract (the work outlines design, constraints, and safety-monitoring approach).
AI.conclusion: Operationalizing domain-specific clinical knowledge as runtime safety constraints can bridge perception and safety monitoring, supporting nursing staff and enhancing Safe Physical AI in real-world hospital wards.

title: Logic-Guided Data Extraction with Answer Set Programming and Large Language Models
comment: 42nd International Conference on Logic Programming, to appear in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming (TPLP)
summary: When Large Language Models (LLMs) are used for semantic data extraction from unstructured text, producing candidate relational facts from natural language, they may remain unreliable for tasks requiring complex combinatorial reasoning and global consistency. This paper proposes a logic-guided data extraction framework combining LLM-based extraction with Answer Set Programming (ASP). The LLM produces candidate facts, whereas ASP performs validation, inference, consistency checking, and control. Unlike existing pipelines that query the LLM independently for all target predicates, the proposed approach uses ASP reasoning to identify which predicates are logically admissible at each stage and to guide extraction queries. By interleaving LLM calls with ASP derivation, the framework infers logically implied facts without further extraction and detects inconsistencies early. We formalize the pipeline and prove that, under mild assumptions, it is equivalent to the baseline approach with respect to the final extracted facts, while requiring fewer LLM calls. We also introduce a caching mechanism for logic-based control queries, exploiting monotonicity of conjunctive queries over incrementally constructed fact sets to reduce solver invocations. Experiments on ASP-derived benchmarks show that the framework reduces LLM calls and improves extraction quality by mitigating spurious outputs, demonstrating the value of non-monotonic logic programming for controlled semantic extraction.

AI.tldr: A logic-guided data extraction framework that integrates LLM-based extraction with Answer Set Programming (ASP) to validate, infer, and enforce consistency. By interleaving LLM calls with ASP derivations and caching control queries, it reduces required LLM interrogations while maintaining extraction quality, and is shown equivalent to a baseline in final facts under mild assumptions.
AI.motivation: LLMs can be unreliable for tasks requiring complex combinatorial reasoning and global consistency in semantic data extraction. Existing pipelines query the LLM independently for all targets, leading to spurious outputs. A principled, logic-guided approach can enforce consistency and minimize calls.
AI.method: LLM produces candidate facts; ASP performs validation, inference, consistency checking, and control. The pipeline interleaves LLM calls with ASP derivations; ASP determines which predicates are logically admissible at each stage and guides extraction queries. A caching mechanism for logic-based control queries exploits monotonicity of conjunctive queries over incrementally constructed fact sets to reduce solver invocations. The authors formalize the pipeline and prove equivalence to the baseline with respect to final extracted facts under mild assumptions. They also leverage non-monotonic logic programming to handle inconsistencies and derive implied facts without extra extraction.
AI.result: Empirical results on ASP-derived benchmarks show reduced LLM calls and improved extraction quality by mitigating spurious outputs. The framework demonstrates the value of non-monotonic logic programming for controlled semantic extraction.
AI.conclusion: Integrating LLM-based extraction with ASP reasoning yields efficient, higher-quality semantic extraction with fewer LLM queries, validated both theoretically (equivalence to baseline) and empirically (fewer calls, better accuracy).

title: A Unified Tokenization Framework for Pain Recognition using Heterogeneous 3D Modalities
comment: Accepted at the 28th ACM International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI 2026)
summary: Pain is a complex and pervasive phenomenon affecting a large percentage of the population, and accurate assessment is essential for effective clinical management and intervention. Computational pain recognition systems enable continuous monitoring, support clinical decision-making, and help mitigate pain-related distress and functional decline. This study introduces a unified tokenization framework for heterogeneous 3D modalities in pain recognition that provides a single processing pipeline across behavioral and brain-activity 3D data, without requiring separate architectures for each modality or handcrafted inductive biases. The framework preserves spatial, temporal, and time--frequency structure while mapping diverse inputs into a shared token space. Extensive experiments show that the proposed approach effectively processes facial videos and fNIRS data in both raw-signal and spectrogram-based representations. On the AI4Pain benchmark dataset, the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining high computational efficiency and enabling real-time assessment on both GPU and CPU hardware.

AI.tldr: A unified tokenization framework for multimodal 3D pain recognition that processes facial videos and fNIRS in a single pipeline, preserving spatial/temporal/time-frequency structure and achieving state-of-the-art, real-time performance on AI4Pain.
AI.motivation: Pain assessment requires integrating heterogeneous 3D modalities (behavioral and brain activity) with minimal handcrafted biases; existing approaches often use separate architectures per modality, limiting efficiency and cross-modal learning.
AI.method: Introduce a unified tokenization framework that maps diverse 3D inputs into a shared token space while preserving spatial, temporal, and time-frequency structures. Applicable to both raw signals and spectrogram-based representations, enabling a single processing pipeline across facial videos and fNIRS data without modality-specific inductive biases.
AI.result: On AI4Pain, achieves state-of-the-art performance with high computational efficiency and real-time capability on both GPU and CPU hardware.
AI.conclusion: A single, unified processing framework for heterogeneous 3D pain-related data that simplifies architecture, maintains structural fidelity, and enables real-time, cross-modal pain assessment.

title: Decodable but Not Detectable: A Leakage Fingerprint for Near-OOD Benchmarks
summary: While auditing a perturbation-based OOD detector on a document benchmark, we recorded an AUROC of 0.326 -- well below the 0.5 chance level. The cause is a benchmark leak: the designated "OOD" class is one the model was trained on, so its examples sit inside the in-distribution fit set and the detector is penalized for correctly ranking them as familiar. Deleting the class and retraining 35 models across two domains raises the score to 0.911. We distill the contamination into a leak fingerprint -- near-perfect supervised decodability (AUROC approximately 1) coupled with unsupervised detection collapsed below 0.65 -- and validate it on a controlled battery of 52 settings (20 leaked, 32 clean) across ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 on CIFAR-10/100, achieving sensitivity 18/20 and specificity 31/32 in embedding space; the matched fit-set-exclusion controls are perfect at 20/20. An in-the-wild audit of 24 standard near/far OOD benchmark pairs fires on exactly one (the intrinsically hard CIFAR-100 vs CIFAR-10 pair) and on no far-OOD pair, confirming specificity and that standard cross-dataset construction is clean. Under the corrected protocol, perturbation signals are decodable but not detectable: a supervised reader recovers the OOD signal (AUROC 0.87-1.00) while no unsupervised detector does, and the perturbation method does not improve on plain Mahalanobis distance. We provide a theoretical account of why and, for transparency, retract an earlier circular correlation. The contributions are a corrected protocol and a validated leak diagnostic, not a new OOD method.

AI.tldr: Corrects OOD evaluation by exposing a benchmark leak; provides a leak diagnostic and a validated protocol rather than a new OOD method.
AI.motivation: Address benchmark leakage and unreliable claims in perturbation-based OOD detection; establish a robust evaluation protocol and a leak-diagnostic tool.
AI.method: Identify leakage by discovering that the designated OOD class was trained on; remove the class and retrain 35 models across two domains; distill a leak fingerprint (near-perfect supervised decodability AUROC ~1, unsupervised detection <0.65); validate on 52 settings (20 leaked, 32 clean) across ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 on CIFAR-10/100; use matched fit-set-exclusion controls; conduct an in-the-wild audit on 24 benchmark pairs; assess corrected protocol where perturbation signals are decodable but not detectable; supervised reader achieves AUROC 0.87-1.00 while unsupervised detectors fail; show Mahalanobis distance is no better; provide theoretical explanation and retract prior circular correlation.
AI.result: Leak fingerprint identified; high decodability of leak signal with weak unsupervised detection; controls achieve perfect results; alternative cross-dataset leakage observed in certain pairs; corrected protocol improves reliability; perturbation-based methods do not outperform plain Mahalanobis distance; validated diagnostic and protocol rather than a novel OOD method.
AI.conclusion: The work presents a corrected evaluation protocol and a validated leak diagnostic for OOD assessment, not a new OOD method.

title: SOPD-SocialNav: Selective On-Policy Distillation for Vision-Language Social Navigation
comment: This paper has been accepted to 2026 WRC Symposium on Advanced Robotics and Automation (WRC SARA)
summary: Vision-language models have shown strong potential for social robot navigation by leveraging rich semantic understanding of complex environments and human behaviors. However, large scale VLMs are difficult to deploy on resource-constrained robotic platforms, while lightweight VLMs often lack sufficient social reasoning capability. To address this problem, we propose SOPD-SocialNav, a selective on-policy distillation (SOPD) method that transfers social navigation knowledge from a large teacher VLM to a lightweight student VLM. SOPD introduces an entropy-based token selection mechanism that uses teacher uncertainty to identify socially informative decision tokens, while suppressing gradients from low-entropy tokens corresponding to trivial navigation states. A temperature-controlled Jensen-Shannon divergence objective is then used to align the student and teacher distributions on the selected tokens. Experiments on the SNEI and MUSON benchmarks demonstrate that SOPD consistently outperforms supervised fine-tuning, off-policy distillation, and standard on-policy distillation baselines in action prediction, perception consistency, and reasoning consistency. Real-world deployment on a Scout Mini robot further shows that the distilled model can generate more socially appropriate navigation behaviors in conversational and queuing scenarios. These results suggest that SOPD is an effective strategy for building lightweight yet socially aware VLM-based navigation systems.

AI.tldr: Selective on-policy distillation (SOPD) transfers social navigation knowledge from a large VLM to a lightweight one by using entropy-based token selection and a temperature-tuned Jensen-Shannon objective; it improves action, perception, and reasoning consistency on SNEI/MUSON and shows better real-world social navigation on a Scout Mini.
AI.motivation: Enable socially capable navigation on resource-constrained robots by leveraging large vision-language models without incurring their computational burden; standard fine-tuning and distillation often fail to preserve social reasoning.
AI.method: SOPD selects socially informative decision tokens using teacher uncertainty (entropy). It suppresses gradients from low-entropy, trivial states. It then minimizes a temperature-controlled Jensen-Shannon divergence between teacher and student distributions on the selected tokens to align the policies.
AI.result: On SNEI and MUSON benchmarks, SOPD outperforms supervised fine-tuning, off-policy distillation, and standard on-policy distillation in action prediction, perception consistency, and reasoning consistency. Real-world deployment on a Scout Mini shows more socially appropriate navigation in conversational and queuing scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Selective on-policy distillation is an effective strategy to produce lightweight but socially aware VLM-based navigation systems, enabling practical deployment without sacrificing social reasoning.

title: Geometry-Guided Constraint Learning for LLM Safety Classification
summary: Safety as Polytope (SaP) learns linear half-space constraints in LLM hidden space but requires per-category tuning of the constraint count K. We show that sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature extraction resolves this: K=2 becomes optimal for 12/14 categories on Qwen3.5-9B, achieving 96-99% accuracy per category on our BeaverTails classification benchmark, largely eliminating the need for exhaustive sweeps (K=4-25 with random initialization). This convergence to two planes is consistent with the Linear Representation Hypothesis, providing suggestive evidence that safety boundaries in this setting admit a low-dimensional linear description in the SAE feature space. Building on this geometric perspective, we introduce a cone constraint whose learnable aperture adapts to each category's cluster concentration, stabilized by a three-phase training

AI.tldr: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features enable safety boundaries in LLM latent space to be modeled by two linear planes per category (K=2), avoiding exhaustive K-sweeps. This yields 96-99% per-category accuracy on BeaverTails for 12/14 categories on Qwen3.5-9B and aligns with the Linear Representation Hypothesis. The authors further introduce a category-adaptive cone constraint with a learnable aperture and a three-phase training regime, stabilizing and generalizing the boundary description.
AI.motivation: Address the need to tune the number of linear constraints (K) for Safety as Polytope (SaP) by exploiting latent low-dimensional linear structure in SAE-extracted features, aiming to reduce manual sweeps and improve robustness across categories.
AI.method: 1) Train sparse autoencoders on LLM latent representations to obtain SAE features. 2) Evaluate safety boundaries using K=2 versus larger K across 14 categories on Qwen3.5-9B; BeaverTails classification benchmark. 3) Observe two-plane convergence and test the Linear Representation Hypothesis. 4) Propose a cone constraint with a learnable aperture per category and train with a three-phase protocol to stabilize adaptation to cluster concentration.
AI.result: Two planes (K=2) suffice for 12/14 categories, achieving 96-99% accuracy per category on BeaverTails; significant reduction of K-sweep needs (from K=4-25 with random initializations). Empirical convergence supports a low-dimensional linear safety boundary in SAE space; introduction of a category-specific cone constraint with adaptive aperture and tri-phase training.
AI.conclusion: Safety boundaries in SAE feature space admit a low-dimensional linear description, consistent with the Linear Representation Hypothesis. The proposed cone constraint enables per-category adaptation with stable training, potentially reducing complexity in SaP deployments.

title: ReFace: Reorganizing Facial Spatiotemporal Representations for Improved Pain Assessment
comment: Accepted at the 14th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII 2026)
summary: Automatic pain assessment from facial video remains challenging due to the spatial heterogeneity of pain-related facial cues. This study proposes ReFace, a spatial reorganization pipeline that divides facial input into four spatial quadrants before tokenization, rather than processing the entire face as a single region. Evaluated on the AI4Pain dataset, the proposed approach achieves $56.00\%$ accuracy on the test set using video only, achieving the highest reported accuracy under the fixed AI4Pain benchmark protocol among the compared methods. Notably, the four-quadrant configuration processes the same total pixel budget as the full-face input, yet achieves higher accuracy, suggesting that spatial reorganization can improve performance under the proposed tokenization design. A single quadrant region, processing just one quarter of those pixels, remains competitive at a fraction of the computational cost.

AI.tldr: Spatial quadrant reorganization (ReFace) for video-based pain assessment improves accuracy under fixed pixel budget, achieving 56% on AI4Pain test and outperforming full-face baselines; four-quadrant setup beats full-face, while a single quadrant offers cost-effective performance.
AI.motivation: Pain-related facial cues are spatially heterogeneous; existing methods using full-face tokenization may miss localized cues or waste budget; reordering into quadrants could better allocate capacity to informative regions.
AI.method: Divide facial input into four spatial quadrants prior to tokenization (spatial reorganization). Evaluate on AI4Pain dataset with video input, comparing four-quadrant vs full-face vs single-quadrant under identical pixel budgets.
AI.result: Achieves 56.00% accuracy on test set with video only; highest reported accuracy under fixed AI4Pain benchmark among compared methods; four-quadrant yields higher accuracy than full-face at the same total pixel budget; single-quadrant performs competitively at reduced computation.
AI.conclusion: Spatial quadrant reorganization enhances video-based pain assessment under the specified tokenization design, with potential for more efficient and accurate models by focusing on informative facial regions.

title: Cross-Subject Semantic Decoding with Shared-Space Alignment for Generalized Neural Representation Learning
summary: Generalizing across subjects remains challenging in invasive neural recordings because electrode configurations, anatomical structures, and neural signal patterns vary substantially across individuals. To investigate such inter-subject variability, we propose a cross-subject semantic decoding framework that aligns neural responses to speech perception from multiple subjects into a shared latent space and learns a mapping from the aligned neural representations to contextual embeddings. More specifically, using electrocorticography data collected during natural language comprehension, we estimate the shared space using the shared response model and train a decoder to predict contextual semantic embeddings from projected neural responses. For a held-out subject, we estimate a subject-specific projection into the predefined shared space, and directly apply the pretrained decoder without any retraining. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms baseline methods across evaluation settings and exhibits a reduced performance drop from source subject to held-out subject testing, indicating improved cross-subject generalization. These results suggest that aligning neural activity into a shared latent space, while decoding in a semantic embedding space, provides an effective strategy for improving cross-subject generalization by reducing subject-specific differences in neural responses while effectively capturing shared stimulus-related representations.

AI.tldr: Cross-subject semantic decoding for invasive ECoG by aligning neural responses to a shared latent space with a Shared Response Model, then decoding to contextual semantic embeddings; a held-out subject is projected into the shared space and decoded without retraining; shows improved cross-subject generalization.
AI.motivation: Inter-subject variability in invasive neural recordings (electrode configurations, anatomy, signal patterns) undermines generalization; a shared, stimulus-aligned representation could mitigate subject-specific differences.
AI.method: Record ECoG during natural language comprehension; estimate a shared latent space using the Shared Response Model; train a decoder to map projected neural responses to contextual semantic embeddings. For a held-out subject, compute a subject-specific projection into the shared space and apply the pretrained decoder without retraining.
AI.result: The framework outperforms baselines across evaluation settings and reduces the performance drop when generalizing from source to held-out subjects, indicating improved cross-subject generalization.
AI.conclusion: Aligning neural activity into a shared latent space and decoding in a semantic embedding space effectively captures shared stimulus-related representations while reducing subject-specific variability, supporting improved cross-subject generalization.

title: KineBench: Benchmarking Embodied World Models via IDM-Free Kinematic Grounding
summary: Evaluating the physical consistency of embodied world models(EWMs) is a critical open challenge. While closed-loop evaluation via simulator rollouts offers a more faithful assessment of physical plausibility than open-loop alternatives, existing frameworks almost exclusively rely on Inverse Dynamics Models(IDMs) for action extraction. Due to the intricate mapping from 2D pixel space to 3D kinematic space, the learned IDMs can be brittle to data outside their training distribution, resulting in unreliable action extraction from the generated videos with novel objects and scenarios. This creates an unavoidable attribution ambiguity between world model inaccuracies and extractor errors. To reduce this ambiguity, we present KineBench, an IDM-free closed-loop benchmark for EWMs, built upon an explicit kinematic grounding pipeline. Given a generated video, KineBench employs cascaded visual foundation models to directly extract 6D end-effector poses from individual frames, which are then executed in a physics simulator for closed-loop validation. Beyond execution-based task success, KineBench incorporates two classical 3D kinematic metrics--Spectral Arc Length (SPARC) and the Maruyama Manipulability Index--to characterize trajectory smoothness and kinematic feasibility from a robot-centric perspective. Built on 20 diverse manipulation tasks in ManiSkill3, KineBench evaluates EWMs across four progressive suites: basic execution, task transfer, visual out-of-distribution generalization, and complexity-conditioned scaling. Evaluation across frontier models reveals task-complexity-bounded nonlinear scaling in embodied video generation, providing empirical guidance for future data-scaling strategies.

AI.tldr: Introduces KineBench, an IDM-free closed-loop benchmark for embodied world models, using direct 6D pose extraction and physics-based validation with SPARC and Maruyama metrics; demonstrates task-complexity-limited nonlinear scaling across ManiSkill3 tasks.
AI.motivation: Reduce attribution ambiguity between world model errors and action extractor errors by eliminating inverse dynamics models and adopting explicit kinematic grounding for evaluation of embodied video generation.
AI.method: KineBench uses cascaded visual foundation models to extract 6D end-effector poses from individual frames, executes these poses in a physics simulator for closed-loop validation, and augments evaluation with SPARC (trajectory smoothness) and Maruyama Manipulability Index (kinematic feasibility); built on ManiSkill3 with 20 diverse manipulation tasks, across four suites: basic execution, task transfer, visual out-of-distribution generalization, and complexity-conditioned scaling.
AI.result: Demonstrates task-complexity-bounded nonlinear scaling in embodied video generation across frontier models; provides empirical guidance for data-scaling strategies and enables more robust EWM evaluation without IDM-induced attribution ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: IDM-free, kinematic-grounded benchmarking is feasible and informative for EWMs, clarifying how performance scales with task complexity and guiding future data-collection and model development.

title: Rethinking Uncertainty Evaluation in Large Language Models
summary: Calibration is the primary criterion for evaluating LLM confidence, but it is insufficient: it admits trivially incoherent estimators, depends on the evaluation distribution, and does not test the extent to which the estimation can be interpreted as a consistent, underlying probability function. What we actually need is for LLM confidence estimates to satisfy the conditions required of coherent probabilistic beliefs. We formalize these conditions along three axes (structural coherence, faithfulness, and usefulness) and operationalize them as the C1 metrics. Widely used estimators systematically violate these conditions despite appearing well-calibrated: models assign lower confidence to logically easier questions 31\% of the time, and common interventions reducing RMSCE leave structural violations unchanged, suggesting that calibration is orthogonal to probabilistic validity. RLHF and chain-of-thought improve usefulness metrics without restoring coherence. Our results show current LLM confidence estimates cannot be interpreted as coherent probabilities; our framework provides the tools to measure and close this gap.

AI.tldr: Current calibration of LLM confidence fails to be a coherent probabilistic belief; introduces C1 metrics across structural coherence, faithfulness, and usefulness; RLHF and chain-of-thought improve usefulness but not coherence; framework to measure and close the gap.
AI.motivation: Calibration alone is insufficient for interpreting LLM confidence as probabilities. A coherent probabilistic interpretation requires structural coherence, faithful reflection of evidence, and practical usefulness.
AI.method: Formalize three axes of coherence and define C1 metrics to operationalize them; empirically assess widely used estimators; analyze effects of interventions like RLHF and chain-of-thought on these axes.
AI.result: Widely used estimators violate coherence; better calibration does not imply probabilistic validity; 31% of cases where easier questions receive lower confidence; RMSCE-reducing interventions do not fix structural violations; RLHF/CoT improve usefulness but not coherence.
AI.conclusion: A framework (C1) is needed to measure and guide the alignment of LLM confidence with coherent probabilistic beliefs; current confidence estimates cannot be interpreted as such, and the framework can guide improvements.

title: An Exploratory Analysis of Pain Localization via Explainable Computational Modeling
comment: Accepted at the 14th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII 2026)
summary: Automatic pain localization, which involves identifying the anatomical origin of pain from peripheral physiological signals without patient self-report, is a clinically critical but largely unaddressed problem, particularly for non-verbal patients. This paper presents a systematic comparison of classical feature engineering and deep sequence learning for subject-independent three-class pain localization using the AI4Pain 2026 Challenge dataset, which comprises four synchronously recorded wearable modalities: electrodermal activity, blood volume pulse, respiration, and peripheral oxygen saturation recorded from 65 participants under controlled TENS-induced pain. A 115-dimensional hand-crafted feature set spanning time-domain, frequency-domain, modality-specific, and cross-modal descriptors is benchmarked against end-to-end deep architectures. Extremely Randomized Trees achieves the highest macro-F1 of 0.539, outperforming the best deep model by 7.4 percentage points, with EDA spectral features emerging as the dominant discriminators. A consistent 26-point gap between pain detection (F1\,=\,0.815) and localization (F1\,=\,0.552) across all models points to a fundamental ceiling imposed by the anatomical diffuseness of peripheral autonomic pathways at 10-second resolution.

AI.tldr: Classical feature engineering with Extremely Randomized Trees outperforms end-to-end deep models for subject-independent three-class pain localization on the AI4Pain 2026 dataset; EDA spectral features dominate; a ~26-point gap between pain detection and localization suggests a ceiling due to peripheral autonomic signal diffuseness at 10-second resolution.
AI.motivation: Evaluate whether traditional hand-crafted features can outperform deep learning for pain localization from wearable signals, in a subject-independent setup, and assess the contribution of modalities and feature types as well as the practical limits imposed by physiology and temporal resolution.
AI.method: Comparison between a 115-dimensional hand-crafted feature set (time-domain, frequency-domain, modality-specific, cross-modal) and end-to-end deep architectures across four wearables (EDA, BVP, respiration, SpO2) for three-class pain localization on the AI4Pain 2026 dataset (65 participants, TENS-induced pain). Performance is measured with macro-F1; feature importance and modality contributions are analyzed.
AI.result: Extremely Randomized Trees achieved the highest macro-F1 of 0.539, outperforming the best deep model by 7.4 percentage points. EDA spectral features emerged as the dominant discriminators. Pain detection accuracy (F1 = 0.815) substantially exceeds localization accuracy (F1 = 0.552), indicating a ~26-point gap likely due to the anatomical diffuseness of peripheral autonomic pathways at 10-second resolution.
AI.conclusion: Classical feature-based methods can surpass deep learning in this setting under the current data and resolution. The localization ceiling appears to be constrained by physiological signal properties and the chosen temporal granularity; improvements may require better temporal resolution, richer labeling, or hybrid approaches that leverage physiology-informed priors.

title: From Trajectories to Prefixes: Reusing Teacher Trajectories via Replayed Prefixes and Online Continuation
summary: Small language models are attractive backbones for interactive agents, but direct distillation from strong teacher trajectories often turns rich multi-turn behavior into one-shot imitation targets. This is inefficient in long-horizon environments, where early decisions shape later states and rewards. We propose Prefix-GRPO, a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes teacher trajectories into replay-aligned prefix queries and online continuations. Each prefix is replayed in the environment to recover a valid intermediate state, after which the student continues online interaction and receives task reward. Unlike response-only GRPO, Prefix-GRPO also applies clipped policy updates to historical assistant tokens inside the replayed prefix, using a policy-distilled SFT checkpoint to estimate their old log-probabilities. This unifies prefix learning and continuation learning within the same policy-optimization form. Experiments on TextCraft, BabyAI, and ALFWorld show that Prefix-GRPO improves small-model agents over distillation and standard RL baselines, while ablations show that replay alone is insufficient without explicit prefix-token optimization. The implementation and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/HappynessI/Prefix_GRPO.

AI.tldr: A RL framework Prefix-GRPO that uses replay-aligned prefix queries and online continuation to train small language models, outperforming distillation and standard RL on multi-turn tasks.
AI.motivation: To overcome inefficiency of distilling strong teacher trajectories into small LMs for long-horizon interactive environments, preserving multi-turn behavior.
AI.method: Decompose trajectories into prefixes and continuations; replay prefixes to recover intermediate state; then the student continues online; apply clipped policy updates to tokens inside the replayed prefix using a policy-distilled SFT checkpoint to estimate their old log-probabilities; unify prefix learning and continuation in a single policy optimization objective.
AI.result: Experiments on TextCraft, BabyAI, ALFWorld show improved performance over distillation and RL baselines; ablation shows replay alone insufficient without explicit prefix-token optimization; code released at the provided repository.
AI.conclusion: Prefix-GRPO provides a unified, practical method to leverage teacher trajectories for small LMs in interactive environments, improving sample efficiency and preserving long-horizon behavior.

title: EA-Nav: Learning Safe Visual Navigation Policies with Embodiment Awareness
summary: Cross-embodiment navigation is a key challenge in embodied intelligence. Due to differences in embodiment, the same visual observation may imply different actions for different agents, making prediction ambiguous when relying solely on vision. Existing studies mainly rely on reinforcement learning, which requires large-scale interaction and careful reward design, making it difficult to support scalable pretraining and real-world adaptation. In contrast, imitation-learning-based approaches remain limited. To address these challenges, we propose an imitation-learning-based embodiment-aware navigation framework with a modular multi-stage design. In pretraining, we construct a cross-embodiment navigation dataset from Internet videos and introduce embodiment geometry as conditional tokens to reduce action ambiguity under the same observation. In fine-tuning, we design a multimodal information injection mechanism based on a decoupled architecture. Specifically, we design a trajectory augmentation strategy to generate high-risk samples, which are used to train spatial perception and risk-aware correction separately, thereby explicitly incorporating embodiment geometry for safe navigation. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively improves navigation performance across different embodiment settings, demonstrating the effectiveness of incorporating embodiment geometry into embodied navigation.

AI.tldr: Imitation-learning-based cross-embodiment navigation with embodiment-aware pretraining and a decoupled fine-tuning architecture improves navigation across different embodiments by encoding embodiment geometry as conditional tokens and using trajectory-based risk augmentation.
AI.motivation: Cross-embodiment navigation faces action ambiguity: the same observation can imply different actions across agents. RL-based methods require extensive interaction and meticulous reward design, while imitation-learning approaches struggle with embodiment heterogeneity and safety. The work aims to enable scalable pretraining and robust real-world adaptation by explicitly modeling embodiment geometry.
AI.method: 1) Pretraining on a cross-embodiment navigation dataset derived from Internet videos, with embodiment geometry encoded as conditional tokens to reduce action ambiguity. 2) Fine-tuning with a multimodal injection mechanism in a decoupled architecture. 3) Trajectory augmentation to create high-risk samples, used to train spatial perception and risk-aware correction separately, explicitly incorporating embodiment geometry for safety.
AI.result: The approach improves navigation performance across different embodiments, demonstrating that incorporating embodiment geometry into embodied navigation can enhance performance and safety in cross-embodiment scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating embodiment geometry via conditional tokens and a decoupled, risk-aware fine-tuning pipeline yields better cross-embodiment navigation performance and provides a scalable path for pretraining and real-world adaptation.

title: Spectral-LSH: Sub-Quadratic Prompt Compression via Krylov-Projected Locality-Sensitive Hashing
summary:
Long-prompt inference remains expensive because prefill attention scales quadratically with sequence length. We propose Spectral-LSH, a training-free prompt compression method that operates before the prompt enters the language model. Spectral-LSH approximates the dominant components of an implicit attention-kernel operator using a Krylov subspace method together with random features, avoiding explicit $O(N^2)$ attention-kernel materialization. It then applies SimHash in the resulting attention eigenspace to group similar tokens and aggregate them into macro-tokens with causal positional assignments.
  We evaluate Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on C4. Our experiments reveal a compression-ratio phase transition. Below $ρ= 4 \times$, local token redundancy is low enough that lightweight chunking typically provides the best latency--quality trade-off. Above $ρ= 8 \times$, the spectral path preserves quality that chunking loses. At $ρ= 16 \times$, Qwen2.5-7B (adaptive) reduces the PPL ratio from 353.409 to 196.963, while Qwen2.5-14B (adaptive) reduces it from 9.533 to 3.427.
  On a small long-context structured stress test containing JSON-like, code-like, and table-like inputs, local LSH also improves every metric over chunking at $8 \times$. The adaptive backend captures both regimes by using the chunk path at low compression and spectral clustering at high compression, although chunking remains the fastest backend in total latency.

AI.tldr: Spectral-LSH is a training-free prompt compression that pre-processes prompts before the LM by approximating dominant attention-kernel components via Krylov subspaces and random features, followed by SimHash-based grouping into macro-tokens with causal positions; it enables long-context inference with adaptive latency-quality trade-offs and notable perplexity reductions at high compression.
AI.motivation: To mitigate the quadratic scaling of prefill attention in long prompts without fine-tuning, enabling efficient long-context decoding with maintained or improved quality.
AI.method: Spectral-LSH combines a Krylov subspace method with random features to approximate the dominant components of the implicit attention-kernel, avoiding explicit O(N^2) computation. It then applies SimHash in the derived attention eigenspace to cluster tokens into macro-tokens, assigning causal positional information. An adaptive backend switches between chunking (low compression) and spectral clustering (high compression); chunking remains fastest in total latency.
AI.result: Demonstrates a compression-ratio phase transition: below 4× compression, chunking yields best latency-quality; above 8×, spectral path preserves quality that chunking loses; at 16×, adaptive Qwen2.5-7B reduces perplexity from 353.409 to 196.963, and adaptive Qwen2.5-14B reduces from 9.533 to 3.427. On a small long-context stress test (JSON/code/table-like inputs), local LSH improves all metrics over chunking at 8×. The adaptive backend blends approaches to cover regimes, though chunking remains fastest for total latency.
AI.conclusion: Spectral-LSH provides a scalable, training-free mechanism for long-context prompt compression that adapts between chunking and spectral clustering. It achieves substantial quality gains at high compression while maintaining efficient latency, suggesting broad applicability for long-context inference across LLMs and prompts.

title: Efficient Tracking and Understanding Object Transformations
summary: Tracking objects through state transformations is essential for understanding real-world dynamics. However, existing methods are computationally expensive. TubeletGraph recently showed impressive capabilities, but its inference cost (~$4.4$ seconds per object-frame on VOST) precludes any real-time deployment possibilities. We observe that TubeletGraph's overhead arises from building a spatiotemporal partition of the input video: (1) entity segmentation is computed densely for every frame regardless of whether a transformation occurs, and (2) every entity in the scene is tracked, scaling cost with scene complexity rather than the number of transformations of interest. To address both, we propose FluxGraph, a reactive variant that uses SAM2's internal multi-mask disagreement as a lightweight trigger for transformation detection, and removes the need for tracking all entities in the given video. FluxGraph is ~$3.3\times$ faster than TubeletGraph on VOST while improving tracking performance and preserving state graph quality. Furthermore, we also observe consistent speedups of $3.7-10.7\times$ across VSCOS, M$^3$-VOS, and DAVIS17 while maintaining performance. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/YihongSun/FluxGraph.

AI.tldr: FluxGraph is a reactive, trigger-driven variant of TubeletGraph that uses SAM2 multi-mask disagreement to detect object transformations and avoids tracking all entities, achieving ~3.3x speedup on VOST and 3.7-10.7x on other datasets while maintaining or improving tracking quality; code released.
AI.motivation: Overhead in TubeletGraph due to dense per-frame segmentation and tracking every scene entity leads to high compute and non-real-time performance.
AI.method: Use SAM2's internal multi-mask disagreement as a lightweight trigger for transformation detection; only track entities when a transformation occurs; remove dense tracking of all entities; construct a state graph based on transformations rather than full spatiotemporal partition.
AI.result: Speedups: ~3.3x on VOST; improved tracking performance and state graph quality; broader speedups 3.7-10.7x on VSCOS, M3-VOS, DAVIS17; code available.
AI.conclusion: FluxGraph makes reactive, transformation-driven tracking efficient while preserving quality, enabling closer to real-time deployment; demonstrates that gating computation with a trigger reduces unnecessary segmentation/tracking; generalizes across datasets.

title: Memory Merge DQN: Sensitivity Weighted Target Updates for Stable Value Learning
summary: Deep Q-networks use target networks to stabilise bootstrapped value learning, but the standard hard copy update also introduces a tradeoff. Holding the target network fixed, improves short term stability, yet each hard update abruptly replaces the target parameters with the newest online network and discards recent parameter history. This can produce sudden changes in the bootstrap target and may remove value function structure that remains useful later in training. This paper introduces Memory Merge DQN, a target network update mechanism that maintains a short memory of recent historical online network copies and constructs the target network by merging network parameters based on the Q-value sensitivity rather than copying only the newest online network. Memory Merge gives greater influence to parameters that remain locally important for current Q-value behaviour, while using a recency prior to keep the merged target close to the latest online parameters. The method is inspired by Fisher Weight Model Merging, but uses Q-value sensitivity rather than Fisher information as the weighting signal. This paper evaluates Memory Merge DQN on Atari environments against DQN, Averaged DQN, DQN with layer normalisation, and PQN (with gradient clipping). The results show that Memory Merge DQN is highly competitive and it achieves the largest number of first place final performance results among the evaluated methods, beats DQN, Averaged DQN, and PQN (with gradient clipping), and produces substantial gains in several games where preserving useful value-function parameters appears beneficial. These findings suggest that selectively merging recent parameter weights and history can improve the stability and final performance of DQN agents, and that target network design is an important mechanism for preserving useful value function structure during long horizon value learning.

AI.tldr: Memory Merge DQN introduces a target-network update that merges a short memory of recent online network copies using Q-value sensitivity weights and a recency bias, improving stability and final Atari performance compared to standard DQN variants.
AI.motivation: To address instability from hard target-network updates in DQN and to avoid discarding useful parameter history by only copying the latest online network.
AI.method: Maintain a short memory of recent online networks and construct the target network by merging their parameters. Weights are assigned based on Q-value sensitivity (not Fisher information) with a recency prior to favor newer copies. Inspired by Fisher Weight Model Merging, but applied to Q-values.
AI.result: Memory Merge DQN is highly competitive on Atari, achieving the largest number of first-place final results among the methods tested (DQN, Averaged DQN, DQN with layer normalization, PQN with gradient clipping). It yields substantial gains in multiple games where preserving useful value-function parameters is beneficial.
AI.conclusion: Selective parameter-weight and history merging in the target network can enhance stability and final performance in long-horizon value learning, underscoring the importance of target-network design for preserving useful value-function structure.

title: What Matters in Humanoid General Motion Tracking? An Empirical Study
summary: Humanoid general motion tracking requires policies that can follow diverse whole-body references while maintaining balance. Building such policies involves many practical design choices, and their individual effects are often hard to assess. We address this issue with an empirical study of common modeling and training factors used in recent humanoid motion-imitation pipelines. To make the study controlled and reproducible, we developed YAHMP, an open-source modular framework for training, evaluating, and deploying whole-body motion tracking policies on the Unitree G1. Within YAHMP, we define a nominal configuration and compare variants that differ in motion-command representation, observation history, action representation, actuation profile, hand-force randomization during training, and training approach. We evaluate the resulting policies on a test set of retargeted human motions and compare the nominal policy with TWIST2 as an external baseline trained on the same motion set. The results distinguish choices with clear tracking effects from choices that mainly change actuation effort, training complexity, or physical interaction capability. Finally, we deploy YAHMP policies zero-shot on the real Unitree G1, demonstrating diverse whole-body motion tracking, balance under external perturbations, and forceful interaction.

AI.tldr: Empirical study of modeling/training factors in humanoid motion-imitation using YAHMP; identifies which design choices critically affect tracking vs. actuation/training/interaction; demonstrates zero-shot deployment on a Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Disentangle the effects of common design choices in whole-body humanoid motion tracking and provide a reproducible, modular framework for systematic evaluation.
AI.method: Develop YAHMP, define a nominal configuration, compare variants across motion-command representation, observation history, action representation, actuation profile, hand-force randomization during training, and training approach; evaluate on a test set of retargeted human motions; compare nominal policy with TWIST2 baseline trained on the same motions; deploy policies zero-shot on the real Unitree G1.
AI.result: The study separates factors that clearly impact tracking performance from those that mainly influence actuation effort, training complexity, or physical interaction capability; real-world deployment shows diverse whole-body motion tracking, balance under perturbations, and forceful interaction.
AI.conclusion: YAHMP provides a reusable, open-source framework for controlled experiments in humanoid motion imitation and offers practical guidance on which design choices matter for tracking performance and real-world deployment.

title: Beyond Tracking or Shortcut: Composition-Bounded Predictive States in Poker Autoregressive Models
summary: Hidden-state probes often recover latent labels in imperfect-information sequence models, but this alone does not establish that a model maintains a posterior belief distribution over hidden states. This paper studies this ambiguity in a no-range Limit Hold'em autoregressive model trained only on action and value targets, not on an opponent's hand or range. Opponent-range probes are positive after action/value controls in two of three seeds, and the behavior head predicts held-out actions about five percentage points above a baseline using only observable public history. However, visible public betting composition explains more opponent-range signal than residual hidden states, suggesting that most recoverable information comes from betting summaries. Action/value+composition baselines reach 16.5-16.7% top-10 accuracy while composition-residual hidden probes fall to 11.4-12.2%, and matched-composition comparisons are negative in every seed. We call this evidence pattern composition-bounded predictive support: hidden states remain behavior-predictive and opponent-range correlated, but most recoverable range information is explained by visible betting composition rather than residual hidden-state structure. This is a case-study claim about opponent-range representational evidence, not exact Bayesian posterior tracking or a causal belief mechanism. Synthetic control and oracle validations show that the same diagnostics accept posterior-sensitive states and reject raw composition states under matched controls. Thus positive belief probes should be interpreted through targeted alternatives before being treated as evidence of belief tracking.

AI.tldr: In a no-range Hold’em autoregressive model trained only on actions and values, apparent evidence that hidden states track opponent beliefs largely derives from observable betting composition, not residual hidden-state information; supports a composition-bounded interpretation of belief probes and urges caution in treating such probes as evidence of true posterior belief tracking.
AI.motivation: Clarify whether hidden-state probes truly indicate posterior belief tracking in imperfect-information sequence models, or merely reflect observable features like betting composition.
AI.method: Train an autoregressive model on action/value targets without opponent hands; test opponent-range probes under action/value controls across seeds; compare with baselines including composition and matched-composition; use top-k action prediction as a proxy for range signal; employ synthetic control and oracle validations to test sensitivity to genuine posterior vs composition.
AI.result: Opponent-range probes can be positive after action/value controls in some seeds, but public betting composition explains more of the range signal than residual hidden states. Action/value+composition baselines achieve ~16.5-16.7% top-10 accuracy; composition-residual probes yield ~11.4-12.2%; matched-composition comparisons are negative across seeds. Overall, evidence supports composition-bounded predictive patterns where hidden states remain predictive but largely reflect observable betting stats rather than hidden-range structure.
AI.conclusion: Positive belief probes should be interpreted with targeted alternatives; the data suggest that observed belief-related signals largely arise from betting composition rather than genuine hidden-state posterior tracking. The work emphasizes representational evidence about opponent-range inferences and validates the need for controls to distinguish true belief tracking from composition-driven signals.

title: Extending a Large View Synthesis Model for Multi-view Panoptic Segmentation
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. 31 pages, 7 figures, 9 tables. Project page: https://kwonyoung9120.github.io/PanopticLVSM/
summary: Large view synthesis models synthesize novel views through cross-view attention without explicit 3D representations, and recent studies have shown that they learn accurate spatial correspondence from RGB supervision alone. We observe that this correspondence generalizes beyond appearance. When non-photorealistic signals such as binary encoded panoptic labels are passed through the model, they are propagated to novel views with consistent spatial structure. These results indicate that the correspondence learned for RGB view synthesis can also propagate view-independent per-pixel labels. From this observation, we present the first work to extend large view synthesis models beyond appearance rendering to 3D scene understanding. We propose a panoptic segmentation pipeline that reuses a frozen view synthesis model to propagate panoptic labels from input views to novel views, without 3D reconstruction or any segmentation-specific training of the view synthesis model. Given panoptic labels on the input views, we encode them into binary channel representations and pass them through the same model to render target-view segmentation. On ScanNet, our method achieves segmentation quality on par with Gaussian based approaches requiring explicit 3D reconstruction, while outperforming them in novel view synthesis by more than 7 dB. The label propagation also transfers across datasets, surpassing these approaches on Replica without any fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: A large view synthesis model trained on RGB data learns cross-view spatial correspondence that can propagate non-photorealistic labels. The authors reuse a frozen view synthesis model to propagate panoptic labels for segmentation without 3D reconstruction or segmentation-specific training, achieving competitive results on ScanNet and strong generalization to Replica across datasets.
AI.motivation: To extend the capabilities of large view synthesis beyond appearance rendering to 3D scene understanding by leveraging the learned correspondence for per-pixel labels.
AI.method: Encode panoptic labels into binary channels and feed them through the same frozen view synthesis model used for RGB rendering to produce target-view panoptic segmentation, requiring no 3D reconstruction or segmentation-specific fine-tuning.
AI.result: On ScanNet, segmentation quality matches Gaussian-based methods that rely on explicit 3D reconstruction, while achieving >7 dB improvement in novel view synthesis. Label propagation generalizes across datasets, outperforming baselines on Replica without fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The cross-view correspondence learned for RGB view synthesis extends to view-invariant per-pixel labels, enabling a simple yet effective panoptic segmentation pipeline via label propagation with a frozen model and without 3D reconstruction.

title: Leveraging Offline Supervision for Efficient and Generalizable Reinforcement Learning in Large-Scale Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: It is commonly observed that online reinforcement learning (RL) produces better-performing strategies than offline methods across a broad range of performance measures. In particular, RL-trained policies exhibit stronger out-of-distribution (OOD) behavior, where models trained only with imitation learning approaches often struggle. A recent study introduced an OOD-focused benchmark and reported that RL-trained vision-language-action (VLA) policies achieve noticeably better OOD performance and slightly better in-distribution (IND) performance than their counterparts trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In this work, we investigate whether hybrid offline-online training can combine the advantages of both approaches. Specifically, we study RL methods regularized by offline supervision via either offline data or an offline-trained reference policy. We evaluate these approaches on the OOD benchmark and compare them with both offline-only training and standard RL. Our results show that although offline training achieves limited OOD performance by itself, incorporating offline supervision into RL preserves strong OOD capability while substantially improving training efficiency. In particular, the guided methods reach performance close to that of standard RL while requiring roughly half of the training budget. Rather than producing a trade-off between speed and OOD performance, the hybrid approach retains strong OOD capability while achieving this efficiency gain. Project page: https://alstar8.github.io/offline-supervision-vla-rl

AI.tldr: Hybrid offline-online RL with offline supervision (data or reference policy) on an OOD-focused VLA benchmark preserves strong OOD performance and improves training efficiency, achieving near-RL results with ~50% of the training budget.
AI.motivation: RL often outperforms offline methods in out-of-distribution (OOD) settings; offline imitation can lag in OOD generalization. The study investigates whether augmenting RL with offline supervision can retain OOD robustness while speeding up training.
AI.method: Regularize RL with offline supervision via offline data or an offline-trained reference policy. Evaluate on an OOD benchmark for vision-language-action policies, comparing against offline-only and standard RL baselines.
AI.result: Offline supervision in RL yields strong OOD capability and substantially improves training efficiency; guided methods attain performance close to standard RL while using roughly half of the training budget.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid offline-online training is a practical approach to combine the strengths of offline supervision and RL, achieving robust OOD performance with significant training efficiency gains.

title: Diffusion ReRoll: Revisable Denoising for Robotic Sequential Prediction
summary: We propose Diffusion ReRoll, a diffusion-based framework for robotic sequential prediction that enables revisable denoising over horizons. Existing diffusion-based sequence predictors typically perform a single monotonic denoising process. In contrast, Diffusion ReRoll selectively re-noises regions that have become locally stable while the remaining regions continue denoising, so the re-noised regions can be refined again using context from the rest of the horizon. This structured re-noising enables iterative cross-horizon revision, allowing earlier and later segments to revise one another, while maintaining local consistency. We evaluate Diffusion ReRoll against full-sequence diffusion and causal denoising based on Diffusion Forcing across long-horizon planning, policy learning, and unified video-action modeling. On OGBench PointMaze and AntMaze, Diffusion ReRoll achieves relative gains in average success rate of 21% over Diffusion Forcing in matched guidance-based planning and 23% over Diffuser in matched goal-inpainting. In diffusion-policy-style action prediction, Diffusion ReRoll improves average success by 56.5% relative to Diffusion Policy across different prediction horizons and history lengths on the LIBERO-10 multi-task benchmark. In unified video-action prediction, Diffusion ReRoll improves policy and inverse dynamics performance, especially under out-of-distribution evaluation, and achieves the best action-video consistency. These results support structured re-noising as an effective mechanism for revisable robotic sequence generation.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based framework enabling revisable, iteratively refined denoising across horizons, outperforming baselines in long-horizon robotic tasks.
AI.motivation: Address the rigidity of monotonic, full-sequence denoising in existing diffusion-based sequence predictors and enable revisable cross-horizon refinement.
AI.method: Introduce Diffusion ReRoll: selectively re-noises regions that have become locally stable while continuing denoising elsewhere, enabling iterative cross-horizon revision and preserved local consistency.
AI.result: Significant improvements across long-horizon planning, policy learning, and video-action modeling: ~21% relative gains over Diffusion Forcing and ~23% over Diffuser in planning and goal-inpainting; ~56.5% relative improvement over Diffusion Policy in LIBERO-10; improved policy/inverse dynamics and action-video consistency, especially under out-of-distribution evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Structured re-noising is an effective mechanism for revisable robotic sequence generation, enabling mutual revision between earlier and later segments while maintaining consistency.

title: Mitigating Scaffolding Collapse in Socratic Tutors via Representation Alignment
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based Socratic tutors increasingly guide students through multi-turn questioning, but they can suffer from scaffolding collapse: under sustained student pressure, a tutor gradually abandons guided inquiry and reveals solutions directly. Prior defenses primarily constrain observable responses through prompting, preference optimization, or filtering, leaving the internal representation drift that precedes trajectory-level collapse largely unaddressed. We propose Scaffold-Preserving Representation Alignment, a two-stage framework that first warms up a Socratic tutor with supervised fine-tuning, then combines trajectory-weighted direct preference optimization with a margin-preserving representation loss anchored to frozen reference states. Our method is designed to maintain separation between scaffold-preserving and collapse-inducing hidden states across dialogue turns. We evaluate our method across five STEM disciplines and five red-teaming attack strategies. On Qwen3-8B, our method lowers Collapse Rate to 32%, delays average collapse onset beyond nine turns, and keeps over-refusal low, suggesting that representation-level alignment can improve the robustness of long-horizon Socratic tutoring under our red-teaming protocol.

AI.tldr: Two-stage scaffold-preserving representation alignment for LLM Socratic tutors; aligns hidden states to prevent scaffold collapse, reducing collapse rate and delaying onset under red-teaming.
AI.motivation: Address hidden-state drift leading to scaffold collapse in long-horizon Socratic tutoring; existing defenses focus on outputs, not internal representations.
AI.method: Stage 1: supervised fine-tuning to warm-start; Stage 2: trajectory-weighted direct preference optimization with margin-preserving representation loss anchored to frozen reference states to separate scaffold-preserving vs collapse-inducing states.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B across five STEM disciplines and five red-teaming strategies, collapse rate reduced to 32%, onset delayed beyond nine turns, and over-refusal remains low.
AI.conclusion: Representation-level alignment can enhance robustness of long-horizon Socratic tutoring beyond output-level constraints.

title: Global Building Area Estimation Products: How Accurate Are They?
summary: Geo-spatial rasters of building footprint area are useful for a variety of tasks, such as monitoring urbanization, improving energy efficiency, and tracking greenhouse gas emissions. There are now multiple global building raster datasets, however there lacks an independent, comprehensive, and fair assessment of their accuracy. In this work, we evaluate the accuracy of four major global building products: Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL), Microsoft's TEMPO (TEMPO), The Global Building Atlas (GBA), and Overture. As ground truth for assessing their accuracy, we use ORBITaL-Net, a globally diverse dataset of manually labeled building footprints. To ensure fairness, we evaluate products on grids of multiple spatial resolutions, and several conventional performance metrics. Our results indicate that either GBA or TEMPO generally achieves the highest overall accuracy, depending upon the particular evaluation criteria. We also stratify the accuracy of each product by several factors: geographic location, population density, and income groups. The results reveal that product accuracy can sometimes vary significantly with respect to these factors. Notably, all products are significantly less accurate in Africa and Asia. Most products also suffer significant accuracy reduction in high-density urban areas.

AI.tldr: Independent, multi-criteria evaluation of four global building rasters (GHSL, TEMPO, GBA, Overture) using ORBITaL-Net as ground truth across multiple resolutions; GBA or TEMPO often top performers, but accuracy varies by region, density, and income, with notably lower accuracy in Africa/Asia and dense urban areas.
AI.motivation: There is no comprehensive, independent benchmark comparing global building raster products across scales and contexts; stakeholders need fair, multi-faceted accuracy assessments to inform data selection and improvement.
