AI.motivation: Standard planners optimize tasks in isolation, creating escalating future costs in persistent, shared environments. A scalable, modular approach is needed to account for others' constraints without costly joint rollouts.
AI.method: A factored, anticipatory planning framework where a planner proposes candidate plans and selects one that minimizes immediate cost plus aggregated expected future cost across all robots, estimated via independent per-robot learned estimators, enabling modular deployment.
AI.result: In two domains (two-robot home; three-robot restaurant) with persistent tasks: reductions of 10.43% vs myopic and 4.03% vs selfish anticipatory planning in the two-robot home; 17.41% and 13.24% in the three-robot restaurant.
AI.conclusion: Courteous anticipatory planning offers scalable, modular multi-robot coordination by decoupling future-cost estimation, achieving meaningful total-cost reductions across long task sequences in diverse persistent domains.

title: Sophisticated Policies from Epistemic Priors
summary: Sophisticated Inference is a variant of active inference often associated with recursive belief modeling and tree search. We argue that its central computational role is simpler: within a planning horizon, it makes active inference closed-loop by allowing future actions to depend on future states and observations. This closed-loop structure can be represented in the epistemic-prior variational free energy framework. Epistemic priors supply the active-inference objective, while a joint posterior over future states and actions supplies the state-contingent control structure. We evaluate this decomposition in the Reactivity Maze, a stochastic benchmark designed to separate epistemic incentive from inner-horizon closed-loop control. The comparison includes three variational objectives with the same state-action posterior family, an action-state factorized active inference objective, Sophisticated Inference, and standard Expected Free Energy planning. The results show that neither ingredient is sufficient on its own. Methods without an epistemic component do not seek information, while methods that prevent future actions from depending on future states cannot turn information into reliable goal-reaching. By contrast, both Sophisticated Inference and full-joint epistemic-prior active inference solve the environment by combining epistemic drive with closed-loop inference. These results show that the advantage associated with Sophisticated Inference need not be specific to tree search itself. It arises from the closed-loop form of active inference, and this form can be represented in epistemic-prior variational inference when the posterior keeps future actions dependent on future states.

AI.tldr: Sophisticated Inference’s practical advantage comes from closed-loop planning within active inference, via a joint future-state–future-action posterior and epistemic priors. Its benefits are not unique to tree search but arise from closed-loop inference, which can be captured in epistemic-prior variational inference.
AI.motivation: Clarify the computational role of Sophisticated Inference in active inference and its relation to planning, and test this in a benchmark separating epistemic incentive from inner-horizon control (Reactivity Maze).
AI.method: Represent closed-loop planning within an epistemic-prior variational inference framework. Compare multiple variational objectives that share the same state-action posterior: three generic objectives, an action-state factorized active inference objective, Sophisticated Inference, and standard Expected Free Energy planning. Evaluate on the Reactivity Maze benchmark designed to disentangle epistemic drive from horizon-spanning control.
AI.result: Epistemic-only methods fail to seek information; methods that disallow future actions from depending on future states fail to convert information into goal-directed behavior. By contrast, both Sophisticated Inference and full-joint epistemic-prior active inference solve the task by combining epistemic drive with closed-loop inference.
AI.conclusion: The observed advantage stems from the closed-loop form of active inference, not from tree search per se; this form is representable in epistemic-prior variational inference when the posterior maintains dependency of future actions on future states.

title: Lean-SAM2: Target-Anchored Memory and Encoder Acceleration for SAM2
summary: The Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) has advanced temporal promptable segmentation, yet its deployment remains hindered by heavy memory cross-attention overhead and redundant full-frame visual feature extraction. While recent methods explore efficiency via heuristic memory pruning and window-based sparse routing, they typically suffer from catastrophic performance degradation in complex segmentation scenarios replete with occlusions and distractors. To resolve these limitations, we propose \textbf{Lean-SAM2}, a holistic lightweight framework designed to address the above vulnerabilities while systematically eliminating computational redundancies. Specifically, Lean-SAM2 integrates three collaborative mechanisms: (1) Target-Anchored Memory Pruning (TAMP) safeguards target tokens against deceptive attention by modulating raw attention significance with semantic consistency against prompt-derived foreground anchors; (2) Temporal Condensation with Insurance Memory (TCIM) condenses historical context via a visibility-gated fusion while conditionally archiving high-confidence entries in a parallel insurance bank; and (3) Target-Anchored Risk-Aware Routing (TARR) selectively activates the heavy image encoder for target-related windows based on anchor similarity, utilizing a risk-aware fallback policy to trigger full-frame refreshes during volatile transitions. Extensive evaluations across multiple challenging benchmarks demonstrate that Lean-SAM2 establishes a superior balance between accuracy and efficiency. For example, on the LVOSv2 validation dataset, Lean-SAM2 achieves overall inference speedups of $1.412\times$ and $1.417\times$ on the SAM2.1-Large and SAM2.1-Base+, respectively, significantly outperforming Efficient-SAM2 while boosting the corresponding $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ scores by $5.0\%$ and $3.6\%$. Code is available at https://github.com/DeawhaleQwQ/Lean-SAM2.

AI.tldr: Lean-SAM2 proposes a holistic lightweight framework with three collaborative modules (TAMP, TCIM, TARR) to reduce memory overhead and redundant feature extraction in SAM2, delivering notable speedups and accuracy gains on LVOSv2 compared to Efficient-SAM2.
AI.motivation: Mitigate heavy memory cross-attention and full-frame feature extraction bottlenecks in Segment Anything Model 2, especially under occlusions and distractors, while maintaining or improving segmentation accuracy.
AI.method: Three mechanisms: (1) Target-Anchored Memory Pruning (TAMP) filters attention using semantic consistency with prompt-derived anchors; (2) Temporal Condensation with Insurance Memory (TCIM) condenses history via visibility-gated fusion and archives high-confidence entries in an insurance bank; (3) Target-Anchored Risk-Aware Routing (TARR) selectively activates the heavy image encoder for target windows based on anchor similarity, with a risk-aware fallback to full-frame refreshes during transitions.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on LVOSv2 shows speedups of 1.412x (SAM2.1-Large) and 1.417x (SAM2.1-Base+) over Efficient-SAM2, with J&F score improvements of 5.0% and 3.6% respectively.
AI.conclusion: Lean-SAM2 achieves a favorable accuracy–efficiency balance with strong empirical gains; code is available at the provided repository.

title: Adaptive Multi-Expert Graph Transformer for Interpretable EEG-Based Diagnostics
summary: Electroencephalographic (EEG) abnormalities arise from dynamic changes in neural synchrony across spatial and temporal scales, yet many computational approaches reduce these dynamics to static features. We present a Spatial Multi-Expert Graph Transformer that models each EEG recording as a sequence of dynamic functional connectivity graphs. Time-resolved connectivity is estimated using the weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI), and hierarchical graph encoding aggregates information from electrode to regional and global levels. A multi-expert transformer architecture enables subtype-aware reasoning, with a gating mechanism adaptively fusing expert outputs for global abnormality prediction. Experiments on the TUAB dataset show competitive abnormal EEG detection performance and demonstrate the potential of dynamic graph modeling with adaptive expert fusion for interpretable, subtype-aware spatial--temporal analysis.

AI.tldr: A dynamic, hierarchical, multi-expert graph transformer for EEG abnormality detection via time-resolved wPLI connectivity graphs, enabling subtype-aware, interpretable spatial-temporal analysis and competitive TUAB performance.
AI.motivation: Addresses the limitation of static EEG features by capturing time-varying functional connectivity across electrode, regional, and global scales; supports subtype-aware diagnosis through adaptive expert fusion.
AI.method: Model EEG as a sequence of graphs; estimate time-resolved connectivity with the weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI); hierarchical graph encoding from electrode to regional to global levels; a multi-expert transformer with a gating mechanism adaptively fusing expert outputs for global abnormality prediction.
AI.result: On the TUAB dataset, the approach achieves competitive abnormal EEG detection performance and demonstrates the potential of dynamic graph modeling with adaptive expert fusion for interpretable, subtype-aware spatial–temporal analysis.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic graph modeling with adaptive expert fusion is a promising framework for spatial-temporal EEG analysis and subtype-aware diagnostics; further work could extend evaluation, interpretability analyses, and comparison with other dynamic graph methods.

title: Closing the Lab-to-Store Gap: A Data-Efficient Post-Training and Experience-Driven Learning VLA Framework for Retail Humanoids
comment: 8 pages. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Closing the gap between benchmark performance and reliable real-world operation remains a central challenge for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) humanoid robots, which must handle execution errors, distribution shifts, and environmental variability. This paper presents DEED (Data-Efficient Post-Training and Experience-Driven Learning), a systems-level approach evaluated on a supermarket chip-restocking task using a Unitree G1-Edu humanoid robot and the GR00T N1.6 foundation model. DEED comprises three key components: (1) a data-efficient post-training pipeline with control-frequency alignment, data curation, task-relevant visual highlighting, and reduced VLA dependence; (2) a real-world study of experience-driven refinement, adapted from RECAP via a text-based advantage prefix and a vision-language value function; and (3) a latent-space analysis tool for studying in- and out-of-distribution behavior. Our results suggest that bridging the lab-to-store gap is primarily a systems integration challenge rather than an architectural one: careful data design and targeted post-training can transform a policy that fails under naive fine-tuning into a competent real-world system using only a single GPU.

AI.tldr: DEED offers a data-efficient, post-training, and experience-driven framework to close the lab-to-store gap in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) humanoids, emphasizing data design and systems integration over architectural novelty; demonstrated on a supermarket restocking task with a Unitree G1-Edu and GR00T N1.6, claiming real-world competence using a single GPU.
AI.motivation: Bridge the persistent gap between benchmark performance and reliable real-world operation for VLA humanoids in variable, error-prone environments; improve sample efficiency and deployment practicality via post-training data design and experience-driven refinement.
AI.method: Three components: (1) data-efficient post-training pipeline with control-frequency alignment, data curation, task-relevant visual highlighting, and reduced VLA dependence; (2) experience-driven refinement inspired by RECAP, using a text-based advantage prefix and a vision-language value function for real-world adaptation; (3) a latent-space analysis tool to study in- and out-of-distribution behavior.
AI.result: The authors claim the lab-to-store gap is primarily a systems integration challenge; with careful data design and targeted post-training, a policy that fails under naive fine-tuning can become a competent real-world system using only a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: If validated, the work underscores data-centric, post-training strategies as a path to practical deployment in VLA robotics, shifting emphasis from architectural novelty to robust data design and integration. Further validation across tasks and environments is needed to assess generality and reproducibility.

title: Knowledge-Centric Self-Improvement
summary: Self-improving AI systems typically treat the agent as the object that improves, by optimizing prompts, workflows, harnesses, or even the agent's own code. This agent-centric view can make improvements expensive to maintain and difficult to transfer, because gains become tied to a particular agent design, task distribution, or adaptation run. We study a complementary paradigm: knowledge-centric self-improvement, in which agents remain generic and disposable while the persistent object is a curated knowledge base that agents can leverage for future tasks. We conduct controlled case studies to operationalize this idea via a simple protocol. Agents attempt one task, then contribute evidence-grounded insights to a shared knowledge base via task-level and cross-task forums, followed by knowledge distillation. Because self-improvement is contained in the knowledge rather than the agent, improvement can be more inspectable, transferable, and portable. Across abstract reasoning, coding, and terminal benchmarks, this protocol improves solve rates while reducing dollar cost relative to agent-centric baselines. The resulting distilled knowledge also transfers to held-out tasks and across LLM families, indicating that the improvement is not merely an LLM- or run-specific behavior. These results support a new view of self-improving agentic systems: progress can be driven primarily by the curated persistent knowledge. Code is available at https://github.com/recursive-knowledge/KSI.

AI.tldr: Shifts self-improvement from agent-centric optimization to a persistent, curated knowledge base (KB). Agents contribute evidence-grounded insights to the KB and undergo knowledge distillation, enabling transferability, inspectability, and portability of improvements across tasks and model families, reducing costs.
AI.motivation: Agent-centric self-improvement ties gains to a specific agent design and task run, hindering maintainability and transfer. A knowledge-centric paradigm uses a persistent KB that agents can reuse, enabling more robust, transferable improvements.
AI.method: Controlled case studies across abstract reasoning, coding, and terminal benchmarks. A simple protocol: agents attempt a task, then contribute evidence-grounded insights to a shared KB via task-level and cross-task forums, followed by knowledge distillation. The KB captures improvements; subsequent tasks can leverage distilled knowledge.
AI.result: The protocol improves solve rates and reduces dollar cost versus agent-centric baselines. Distilled knowledge transfers to held-out tasks and across LLM families, indicating improvements are not tied to a specific model or run. The KB enables more inspectable, transferable, and portable improvements.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-centric self-improvement, via a curated persistent knowledge base and distillation, is a viable, transferrable paradigm for self-improving agents, potentially enabling broader reuse and portability across tasks and model families. Code is available at the provided GitHub repository.

title: MoAKE: Toward Unified All-in-One Action Quality Assessment via Mixture of Action Knowledge Experts
summary: Action Quality Assessment (AQA) aims to objectively evaluate performance quality from action videos. Most existing methods follow a ``one-by-one'' paradigm, training a separate model for each action type. This setting limits real-world deployment, as it requires prior action-type knowledge to select the corresponding model and suffers from poor generalization across diverse actions. To address these limitations, we study the challenging task of all-in-one AQA, which aims to assess heterogeneous actions within a single unified model. We propose a novel Mixture of Action Knowledge Experts (MoAKE) framework, designed to mitigate negative knowledge transfer caused by large semantic discrepancies among actions. MoAKE learns complementary experts that capture diverse action patterns within a shared semantic space and dynamically aggregates their knowledge to adapt the assessment to the input action. Each expert is tailored with segment-aware prototypes to handle varying temporal lengths, together with an Adaptive Intra- and Inter-Segment Relationship Modeling (AIISRM) module to model multi-granularity temporal dynamics. Furthermore, we establish comprehensive benchmarks for all-in-one as well as zero/few-shot AQA. Extensive experiments on three long-term datasets demonstrate that MoAKE significantly outperforms existing methods in the all-in-one setting, while also achieving consistent generalization on three short-term datasets under zero/few-shot evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/XuHuangbiao/MoAKE.

AI.tldr: MoAKE: a unified all-in-one AQA model using a mixture of action experts with segment-aware prototypes and multi-granularity temporal modeling, achieving strong all-in-one and zero/few-shot performance.
AI.motivation: Current AQA typically trains separate models per action type, hindering deployment and generalization. A unified model with modules to handle heterogeneous actions and temporal dynamics is needed to reduce negative transfer and improve scalability.
AI.method: Introduce Mixture of Action Knowledge Experts (MoAKE) that learns complementary experts in a shared semantic space. Each expert uses segment-aware prototypes to address varying action lengths. An Adaptive Intra- and Inter-Segment Relationship Modeling (AIISRM) module captures multi-granularity temporal dynamics. Experts are dynamically aggregated based on input. The approach includes benchmarks for all-in-one and zero/few-shot AQA and reports results on three long-term datasets; code is released.
AI.result: MoAKE significantly outperforms existing methods in the all-in-one setting and shows consistent generalization on three short-term datasets under zero/few-shot evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MoAKE framework effectively mitigates negative knowledge transfer in all-in-one AQA, enabling robust, scalable assessment across diverse actions, with broad applicability and strong empirical results; the authors release code for reproducibility.

title: Unlearning as Distribution Restoration: A Controlled Counterfactual Study, a Validated Selective Screen, and the Limits of Oracle-Free Certification
summary: Machine unlearning is commonly evaluated by matching a retrained oracle on trained probes. In a controlled nonce-fact testbed with a matched retraining reference, we find this criterion can favor methods that retain held-out knowledge: candidates it rates adequate score held-out forget facts $-2.82$ nats below the never-learned level (cluster CI $[-3.16,-2.48]$). We recast unlearning as restoration to the matched reference and audit oracle-free screens and certificate-style criteria across 45 model-seed cells spanning five open architecture families. The reference itself falsifies an absolute retain/round-trip certificate: the injected model, which retains the retain set by construction, fails the fixed retain threshold in 41/45 cells and its own round trip in 31/45, and the reference fully certifies in only 1/45. A base-anchored held-out screen remains strong as a selective necessary test: on a sealed challenge suite it rejects the injected model in 45/45 cells, accepts the reference in 44/45, and partially detects entity-routing suppression (35/45); it is a necessary test with measured sensitivity, not a sufficiency certificate. A damage-relative recalibration anchored to the reference's own operating point certifies a small subset in 15/45 cells; where it does not abstain, its picks lie within retraining noise (0.80 nats) on the axes it optimizes, while the common trained-probe criterion sits 5.17 nats away (a supporting comparison, not a head-to-head benchmark). A fixed-magnitude logit-suppression attack defeats the full forward battery in 12/45 cells, so forward-only certification is not sound; our method is an empirical selective test for methods-as-produced. An identifiability theorem delimits which facts admit an oracle-free forget threshold at all, with TOFU as the predicted boundary case.

AI.tldr: Proposes oracle-free, reference-based evaluation for machine unlearning; shows standard retrained-probe metrics can mis-rate methods, and introduces screens, recalibrations, and an identifiability theorem (TOFU) to bound forget thresholds across many seeds and architectures.
AI.motivation: Address the misalignment between common unlearning evaluations (retrained oracle on probes) and true forgetting, by developing reference-based, oracle-free criteria that better distinguish forgetting from retained knowledge.
AI.method: Recast unlearning as restoration to a matched reference; audit with oracle-free screens and certificate-style criteria across 45 model-seed cells spanning five open architectures; introduce a base-anchored held-out test, damage-relative recalibration, and a fixed-magnitude logit-suppression attack; prove an identifiability theorem to bound forget thresholds (TOFU).
AI.result: The reference often invalidates absolute forget thresholds; the base-anchored held-out test is a robust, necessary test; recalibration identifies a small subset with retraining noise matching; the forward training-probe criterion is not sound; a logit-suppression attack defeats forward metrics in many cases; the approach yields an empirical selective test for methods.
AI.conclusion: An empirical selective testing framework with oracle-free criteria and a TOFU-based boundary provides a more reliable assessment of unlearning than traditional retrained-probe metrics, though no absolute certificate guarantees forgetting across all settings.

title: Distributed Motion Planning with Safety Guarantees for Self-Reconfiguring Robotic Boats
summary: Aquatic self-reconfigurable robots must assemble into desired shapes while ensuring safe interactions among multiple agents. This paper proposes a hybrid framework that combines distributed Model Predictive Control (MPC) with Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) for multi-agent shape formation and reconfiguration. Given a desired shape and target assignment, a distributed MPC scheme, solved via the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM), computes coordinated trajectories through local optimization and information exchange. To ensure safety in real time, distributed CBF-based filters are applied to enforce inter-agent collision avoidance. The proposed approach leverages the predictive capabilities of MPC to mitigate local minima, while CBFs provide formal safety guarantees despite the nonconvexity of the underlying optimization problem. Simulation results with up to 25 agents and experimental validation with four physical robots demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of the framework.

AI.tldr: Hybrid distributed MPC with ADMM and distributed CBF-based safety for multi-agent shape formation in aquatic robots; demonstrates scalability in simulation (up to 25 agents) and real-world feasibility with 4 robots.
AI.motivation: Achieve scalable, safe, and coordinated reconfiguration of multi-agent aquatic robots under nonconvex optimization and real-time safety constraints.
AI.method: Distributed MPC (solved via ADMM) computes coordinated trajectories with local optimization and info exchange; distributed CBF-based filters enforce inter-agent collision avoidance in real time, providing safety guarantees despite nonconvexity.
AI.result: Simulation with up to 25 agents; experimental validation with four physical robots showing effectiveness and scalability of the framework.
AI.conclusion: Combines predictive MPC planning with formal safety via CBFs to mitigate local minima and ensure safety in nonconvex multi-agent optimization; suitable for scalable shape formation and reconfiguration in aquatic swarms.

title: Edge Intelligence in Civil Aviation: Paradigms, Techniques, and Applications
summary: Civil aviation is safety critical and its operations, from flight decks and towers to ramps and maintenance, generate massive, heterogeneous data at the network edge. Yet cloud centric deployment of large Artificial Intelligence (AI) models often produces high task latency, lacks offline capability in communication denied environments, and requires centralizing sensitive data, raising privacy and sovereignty risks. Edge AI moves perception, prediction, and decision logic closer to the data producers via compression, collaborative inference, and split learning, thereby reducing latency, bandwidth, and exposure while enabling graceful operation during disconnections. This paper provides a panoramic view and a common understanding of edge intelligence tailored to civil aviation. We firstly articulate the operational motivations for edge AI, and then review recent techniques for edge inference and edge learning. We then introduce the organizational computing paradigms and the respective configurations in civil aviation environments; finally, we describe the emerging applications and the future research trends of edge intelligence in civil aviation. We argue that a refined edge solution can complement cloud foundations to deliver low latency, privacy preserving, and resilient AI services across the civil aviation lifecycle.

AI.tldr: Edge intelligence in civil aviation aims to move AI inference and learning closer to data sources to cut latency, reduce bandwidth, and preserve privacy, especially in disconnected environments. The work provides a panoramic view, a unified framework, and future research directions, highlighting how edge solutions complement cloud deployments across the aviation lifecycle.
AI.motivation:
- Civil aviation generates massive, heterogeneous data at the network edge; safety-critical operations demand low latency and resilience. 
- Cloud-centric AI faces high task latency, offline/denied-environment limitations, and privacy/sovereignty risks due to data centralization. 
- Edge AI promises reduced latency, bandwidth, and exposure, plus graceful operation during disconnections, aligning with regulatory and safety requirements.
AI.method:
- Conducts a panoramic view and literature review of edge intelligence applied to civil aviation. 
- Reviews techniques for edge inference (compression, collaborative inference, split learning) and edge learning. 
- Introduces organizational computing paradigms and configurations relevant to civil aviation environments. 
- Describes emerging applications and outlines future research directions.
AI.result:
- Provides a unified understanding and taxonomy of edge intelligence in civil aviation. 
- Outlines concrete techniques for edge inference and edge learning and maps them to aviation use cases. 
- Proposes organizational computing paradigms and deployment configurations suitable for aviation environments. 
- Identifies emerging applications and sketches a research roadmap for edge intelligence in civil aviation.
AI.conclusion: A refined edge solution can complement cloud foundations, delivering low-latency, privacy-preserving, and resilient AI services across the civil aviation lifecycle, including during disconnections and in privacy-constrained contexts.

title: Memory-Augmented Multimodal Large Language Models for Small Object Understanding in Streaming Aerial Videos
summary: Language-guided aerial perception aims to understand user-specified tiny targets in complex unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) scenes. In real UAV deployment, the UAV must respond while it flies, so such perception runs in an online streaming manner, where frames arrive sequentially and the model responds to each one without access to future frames. However, applying current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to this setting raises two challenges. First, targets viewed from the air are often tiny, yet the visual compression in existing MLLMs treats all regions equally and discards their fine-grained details. Second, understanding a continuous stream requires past-frame context, yet retaining the entire history is infeasible on resource-constrained onboard hardware, whereas discarding it causes the target to drift or disappear. We address the tiny object and streaming challenges from both data and method perspectives. From the data perspective, we present \textbf{DroneEyes}, the \textbf{first} pixel-level and open-vocabulary referring-segmentation dataset for tiny aerial targets, comprising $2,140$ high-definition videos and $176,623$ pairs across Object Description and Referring Expression tasks, with dense per-frame masks. From the method perspective, we propose \textbf{SkyAnchor}, an MLLM with two designs to the above challenges: a Semantics-Aware Token Router that preserves small-target under a reduced visual-token budget, and a Hierarchical Memory Bank that keeps the target consistently understood on streams.

AI.tldr: Introduces DroneEyes, a pixel-level, open-vocabulary referring-segmentation dataset for tiny aerial targets, and SkyAnchor, an MLLM with a Semantics-Aware Token Router and a Hierarchical Memory Bank to enable online, streaming, open-vocabulary referring segmentation in UAV scenes.
AI.motivation: Real-time UAV perception requires identifying tiny targets in complex aerial scenes. Existing MLLMs struggle with fine-grained tiny-object details due to uniform token budgets and fail to maintain long-term target consistency in streaming settings due to limited memory.
AI.method: Data: DroneEyes dataset with 2,140 high-definition videos and 176,623 description/referring-expression pairs, providing dense per-frame masks for tiny aerial targets. Model: SkyAnchor with (1) Semantics-Aware Token Router that allocates a reduced visual-token budget to preserve small-target semantics, and (2) Hierarchical Memory Bank to retain target understanding across frames in streaming input.
AI.result: The abstract does not report quantitative results; it highlights the introduction of the dataset and the model design aimed at addressing tiny-target and streaming challenges in online UAV perception.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes a new dataset and a specialized MLLM architecture to advance pixel-level, open-vocabulary referring segmentation of tiny aerial targets in online UAV streams, setting the stage for more robust real-time perception in drone applications.

title: Marine Engine Fault Dataset: Open-Access Data under Controlled Reference and Fault Scenario Conditions
comment: submitted to a journal and currently is under review, 34 pages, 13 Figures
summary: Open-access datasets for marine-engine predictive maintenance remain scarce, particularly those from controlled fault experiments with documented operating conditions, subsystem-level interventions and system-level measurements. This work presents the Marine Engine Fault Dataset, an openly available dataset from a turbocharged, intercooled three-cylinder marine diesel engine operated on a testbed under both reference and fault-scenario conditions. The experimental campaign combined a reference-performance program across the 30-90% load range with scenario-based tests in which abnormal conditions were introduced after stabilized fault-free operation, enabling controlled comparison between baseline and fault-affected behaviour. Five anomaly classes were implemented through physical interventions affecting major engine subsystems: cooling-water pump cavitation, compressor air-filter clogging, air-cooler fouling, injection-valve nozzle clogging and turbine degradation induced through increased exhaust-side restriction. The released data comprise multi-sensor time-series of operating, thermal, pressure, flow and combustion-related variables, with a separate reference-performance record and metadata for structured reuse. Technical validation shows that the reference measurements remain physically coherent across the operating range and that the imposed anomalies produce interpretable response patterns consistent with the affected subsystems, including progressively distinguishable behaviour where different severities were implemented. By combining controlled fault realization, multi-load operation and system-level measurements within a real marine-engine platform, the dataset provides a well-documented benchmark for anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, degradation modelling and related condition-monitoring studies in maritime machinery.

AI.tldr: Open-access Marine Engine Fault Dataset from a testbed diesel engine; controlled fault experiments across loads; multi-sensor time-series; five anomaly classes; validated for anomaly detection and fault diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Addresses scarcity of openly available, well-documented marine engine datasets for predictive maintenance and benchmarking.
AI.method: On a turbocharged, intercooled three-cylinder marine diesel engine testbed, perform reference program across 30-90% load; introduce fault scenarios after stabilized fault-free operation; five fault classes via physical interventions (cooling-water pump cavitation, compressor air-filter clogging, air-cooler fouling, injection-valve nozzle clogging, turbine degradation due to exhaust-side restriction); collect multi-sensor time-series of operating, thermal, pressure, flow, and combustion variables; provide a separate reference-performance record and metadata.
AI.result: Demonstrates coherence of reference data across the operating range; anomalies produce interpretable patterns aligned with affected subsystems; severity levels yield progressively distinguishable behavior; enables benchmarking for anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, degradation modelling, and condition monitoring in maritime machinery.
AI.conclusion: Provides a reproducible, well-documented benchmark by combining controlled fault realization, multi-load operation, and system-level measurements on a real marine engine platform, supporting diverse health-monitoring studies in maritime propulsion.

title: Distributed Acoustic Localization Array Deployed Using a Soft Everting Vine Robot
comment: Sebastian Lorca Godoy, Ciera McFarland, Michael Val, Antonio Alvarez Valdivia, Nathaniel Hanson, and Margaret McGuinness, "Distributed Acoustic Localization Array Deployed Using a Soft Everting Vine Robot", in IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems, 2026
summary: Soft robot exteroception is increasingly being explored for a variety of field applications. In this work, we present a sound-based system for localizing disaster victims in confined and unstructured environments, based on a distributed acoustic sensing architecture embedded along the body of a soft everting vine robot. We propose a dynamic Steered Response Power with Phase Transform framework that supports both far-field direction-of-arrival estimation and near-field three-dimensional source localization as the robot approaches the sound source. To better understand the design and control space related to localizing sound using a soft, shape-morphing robot body, we conduct experiments measuring the accuracy of these methods for a five-microphone array attached to the robot body using three placements relative to the outer membrane of the robot (inside the pressurized body, inside the inner tail, and outside the outer wall) and in four robot configurations (linear, double linear, circular, and sinusoidal). We measure the change in accuracy as the signal-to-noise ratio, the direction of approach, and the distance of the sound source from the center of the array change. Finally, we demonstrate a vine robot growing into an arbitrary shape while carrying microphones along its outer wall, and show that a sound source located with the array's near field can be localized with high accuracy after only three microphones have everted from the robot body. These results highlight the potential of distributed acoustic sensing for reliable victim localization using soft growing robots.

AI.tldr: Proposes a sound-based localization system for disaster victim localization using a distributed microphone array along a soft growing vine robot, employing a dynamic SRP-PHAT framework for both far-field DOA and near-field 3D localization; evaluates microphone placement, robot shape, and SNR; demonstrates near-field localization with minimal microphones.
AI.motivation: Enable robust victim localization in confined/unstructured environments by leveraging exteroceptive sensing on deformable, self-growing soft robots, addressing challenges posed by changing geometry and microphone deployment.
AI.method: Develop a Dynamic SRP-PHAT framework for far-field DOA and near-field 3D localization. Deploy a five-microphone array on a soft vine robot and test three microphone placements (inside pressurized body, inside inner tail, outside outer wall) across four configurations (linear, double linear, circular, sinusoidal). Vary SNR, approach direction, and source distance to assess accuracy. Demonstrate the robot growing into arbitrary shapes while carrying microphones and show near-field localization with only three everted microphones.
AI.result: The approach yields high near-field localization accuracy with as few as three everted microphones and demonstrates viable sound-based victim localization along a soft, morphing body. Accuracy is influenced by microphone placement, robot configuration, and SNR, with performance tracking as source approaches.
AI.conclusion: Distributed acoustic sensing on soft, morphing robots is a viable path for victim localization in challenging environments. The dynamic SRP-PHAT framework supports both DOA and near-field localization, and microcontroller-based microphone deployment along the outer wall enables effective localization even as the robot shape changes.

title: Symbol and Footprint Database for Electronic Components by Agentic Recognition and Generation
summary: A rich and recognizable component library is the cornerstone of printed circuit board (PCB) design and generation. Traditionally, engineers manually create symbols and footprints and design PCB schematics, which is time-consuming and error-prone. Leveraging multimodal large language models (MLLMs), we develop SFgen, an agentic recognition and generation flow of symbol and footprint for electronic components. SFgen achieves 86% accuracy for symbol generation and 80% accuracy for footprint generation. We use the SFgen method to create SFnet, a database of symbols and footprints. It now has 1000 components and is expanding constantly, which lays the foundation for automatic generation of PCB designs.

AI.tldr: SFgen is a multimodal LLM-driven flow for symbol and footprint recognition/generation in PCB design; achieves 86% symbol and 80% footprint accuracy; SFnet database has 1000 components enabling automatic PCB design generation.
AI.motivation: To reduce manual, error-prone symbol and footprint creation in PCB design and accelerate design throughput.
AI.method: Developed SFgen—an agentic recognition and generation flow using multimodal LLMs for symbols and footprints; built SFnet as a growing database of symbols/footprints (1000 components) to support automatic PCB design generation.
AI.result: Achieved 86% symbol generation accuracy and 80% footprint generation accuracy; SFnet contains 1000 components and is expanding.
AI.conclusion: SFgen and SFnet establish a foundation for scalable, automatic PCB design through multimodal AI-assisted symbol/footprint generation, potentially reducing design time and errors.

title: Robust Activation Map Rectification for Weakly Supervised Volumetric Segmentation: Temporal Coherence as a Free Lunch
summary: Weakly supervised segmentation relies heavily on class activation maps (CAMs) to initially localize target regions. However, CAMs are often noisy and prone to catastrophic failures. Existing remedies typically introduce additional training stages or prototype learning, increasing computational cost and reducing robustness. In this paper, we propose a training-free prototype-free framework that rectifies unreliable CAMs by exploiting temporal and structural coherence in volumetric data as a free lunch. Our approach is built on two key components. First, we introduce Variance-Reduced Activation Aggregation (VRAA) which suppresses noise and amplify coherent semantic signals. We provide a theoretical justification by modeling CAMs as high-dimensional random vectors and show that aggregation yields provable variance reduction. Second, we design a Bidirectional Extremity Rectification (BER) mechanism that detects and rectifies implausible activations through bidirectional extremity checks, effectively mitigating extreme-value failures without learning additional parameters. Our method is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated with existing pipelines. Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements over state-of-the-art weakly supervised methods, achieving up to 20% Dice and 40% mIoU gains while reducing inference time by more than 5 times. These results indicate that leveraging coherence as an implicit inductive bias yields a principled and efficient approach to stabilizing weakly supervised volumetric segmentation. Our code will be available.

AI.tldr: A training-free, prototype-free framework for refining weakly supervised CAMs in volumetric segmentation using VRAA and BER, achieving robustness and speedups.
AI.motivation: Weakly supervised segmentation relies on CAMs that are noisy and brittle; existing remedies add training stages or prototypes, increasing cost and reducing robustness. A training-free, prototype-free approach leveraging coherence in volumetric data is desirable.
AI.method: Variance-Reduced Activation Aggregation (VRAA) suppresses noise and amplifies coherent semantic signals by aggregating CAMs, with a theoretical variance-reduction justification. Bidirectional Extremity Rectification (BER) performs bidirectional extremity checks to detect and rectify implausible activations, mitigating extreme-value failures without learnable parameters. The framework is model-agnostic and integrates into existing pipelines.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on public benchmarks show substantial gains over state-of-the-art weakly supervised methods, achieving up to 20% Dice and 40% mIoU improvements, while reducing inference time by more than 5x.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging coherence as an implicit inductive bias yields a principled and efficient approach to stabilizing weakly supervised volumetric segmentation; the method is training-free, prototype-free, and broadly applicable, with code to be released.

title: Guardrails as Scapegoats: Auditing Unfaithful Safety Refusals in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the ACM KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI
summary: Evaluation frameworks for tool-augmented LLM agents focus overwhelmingly on capability metrics or explicit tool crashes, leaving silent infrastructure failures and HTTP 200 responses with empty, null, or malformed payloads largely unaudited. We introduce a lightweight black-box auditing framework that injects four silent failure profiles across 12 production-adjacent tool stubs and classifies agent responses into three mutually exclusive behavioral classes: Honest Surrender (HSR), Fabrication (FAR), and Unfaithful Safety Refusal (USR). Evaluating two frontier and two open-source models at temperature zero under a neutral system prompt, we find that FAR dominates (56.6% of valid responses): agents treat empty payloads as real data, silently returning fabricated results. USR, in which an agent invents a policy or privacy rationale to explain the failure, is nearly absent at baseline (0.25%, one instance across 396 valid trajectories). Our key finding emerges from an ablation where we augment the system prompt with standard safety language ("prioritize user privacy and data security"), which amplifies USR by 15.6x (from 0.25% to 3.95%; 95% CI on ablation rate: 2.2%-6.4%; Fisher's exact test, p < 0.001). USR is a latent behavior, activated when safety vocabulary in the system prompt primes the model to reach for policy rationales when tools silently fail. Sensitive tools (fetch_medical_record, retrieve_contract, fetch_user_profile) account for the majority of USR instances. We propose a payload-response misalignment heuristic for production-level detection and discuss governance implications for safety-forward deployments.

AI.tldr: Silent infrastructure failures in tool-augmented LLMs are underaudited; a black-box framework reveals Fabrication (FAR) dominates valid responses, USR is rare at baseline but amplified by safety prompts; sensitive tools drive USR; a payload-response misalignment heuristic is proposed for production detection and governance implications are discussed.
AI.motivation: Address the gap in auditing silent, infrastructure-level failures in production-adjacent tool usage by LLM agents, beyond visible capability metrics and explicit tool errors.
AI.method: Black-box audit with four silent failure profiles across 12 tool stubs; classify agent outputs into Honest Surrender (HSR), Fabrication (FAR), Unfaithful Safety Refusal (USR); evaluate two frontier and two open-source models at temperature 0 with a neutral system prompt; ablate safety language in the system prompt; analyze prevalence and statistical significance; identify sensitive tools driving USR; propose a payload-response misalignment detection heuristic.
AI.result: Fabrication (FAR) dominates with 56.6% of valid responses; USR baseline 0.25% (one instance across 396 trajectories); safety-language ablation raises USR to 3.95% (95% CI 2.2%-6.4%), p<0.001; USR tends to involve sensitive tools (fetch_medical_record, retrieve_contract, fetch_user_profile); a payload-response misalignment heuristic is proposed for production detection.
AI.conclusion: USR is latent but can be amplified by safety-oriented prompts; silent-tool failures require robust detection and governance; the proposed payload-response misalignment heuristic offers a practical detection mechanism for production deployments.

title: Towards Miniature Humanoid Tele-Loco-Manipulation Using Virtual Reality and Reinforcement Learning
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Accepted manuscript. Published in the 2025 IEEE-RAS 24th International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids), pp. 1233-1240
summary: Full-sized humanoid robot capabilities have grown exponentially in recent years, aiming towards general-purpose deployment in human environments. A popular control method used by manufacturers utilizes Virtual Reality for upper-body teleoperation and Reinforcement Learning for lower-body balance and locomotion control. As a result, a single remote operator can see, manipulate, and navigate about a real, distant physical environment. This powerful control stack is often relegated to expensive full-sized robots, many of which are inaccessible to the research community. Miniature humanoids are more prevalent, but employ less biomimicry in their design (e.g. fewer sensors, Degrees of Freedom, etc) and lack similar developments. This paper describes a compliant full-body telepresence control stack developed from the ground up for miniature humanoids. Framework experimentation on ROBOTIS OP3 hardware showcases walking at speeds up to 0.45 m/s independent of arm motions. Tele-loco-manipulation is demonstrated via a cube relocation experiment with an expert human operator. On average, the teleoperated system moved 2 different 40 g cubes within 10 mins, walking a total distance of 5 m. Overall, the developed system shows potential for miniature humanoid tele-loco-manipulation.

AI.tldr: A compliant telepresence stack enables miniature humanoids to perform teleoperation and tele-manipulation, achieving autonomous-like balance via RL while a human operator remotely controls upper body; demonstrated on ROBOTIS OP3 with 0.45 m/s walking, cube relocation, and 5 m total travel in 10 minutes.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between full-sized humanoid teleoperation and miniature platforms by enabling full-body telepresence on smaller robots, addressing limited biomimicry and sensor DOF in miniaturized designs, and expanding research access.
AI.method: Developed a ground-up compliant full-body telepresence control stack for miniature humanoids, implemented on ROBOTIS OP3. Combines VR-based upper-body teleoperation with reinforcement-learning-driven lower-body locomotion control to enable tele-loco-manipulation.
AI.result: Walking at up to 0.45 m/s with arm motions decoupled from the legs; tele-loco-manipulation demonstrated via a cube relocation task using an expert operator; two 40 g cubes moved within 10 minutes, totaling 5 m of walking.
AI.conclusion: The proposed stack demonstrates the viability of miniature humanoid tele-loco-manipulation and offers a pathway to broader adoption in research environments, with room for improvements in payload, robustness, and task complexity.

title: Silent Failures in Multimodal Agentic Search:A Diagnostic Taxonomy and Cross-Judge Evaluation
summary: Multimodal agentic search systems increasingly rely on external tools to answer knowledge-intensive visual questions. However, existing evaluations mainly focus on final-answer accuracy and may miss failures in the search trajectory. In this work, we study such hidden reliability issues as silent failures. We introduce a six-category taxonomy covering modality shortcuts, phantom grounding, wrong-evidence-right-answer cases, over-retrieval laundering, cross-modal contradiction, and provenance hallucination. Based on this taxonomy, we build a trajectory-level diagnostic pipeline that evaluates both answer correctness and evidence-grounding quality under a unified ReAct-style scaffold. Experiments on MMSearch-Plus trajectories across four frontier multimodal models show that surface accuracy consistently overestimates true trajectory-level correctness. We further use cross-judge validation, blank-image stress tests, and tool ablations to show that silent failures are capability-dependent and often shift rather than disappear. Home-page: https://github.com/DingWu1021/silent-failures-multimodal-agentic-search

AI.tldr: Introduces a six-category taxonomy of silent failures in multimodal agentic search and a trajectory-level diagnostic pipeline under a ReAct-style scaffold; shows surface accuracy overestimates trajectory correctness; silent failures persist and vary by capability across four frontier models; provides benchmarks and code.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations emphasize final-answer accuracy and overlook failures in the search trajectory, i.e., silent reliability issues in multimodal agentic search.
AI.method: Define a six-category taxonomy: modality shortcuts, phantom grounding, wrong-evidence-right-answer, over-retrieval laundering, cross-modal contradiction, and provenance hallucination. Build a trajectory-level diagnostic pipeline evaluating both answer correctness and evidence-grounding quality under a unified ReAct-style scaffold. Evaluate MMSearch-Plus trajectories across four frontier multimodal models. Use cross-judge validation, blank-image stress tests, and tool ablations.
AI.result: Surface accuracy consistently overestimates true trajectory-level correctness. Silent failures are capability-dependent and tend to shift rather than disappear. Cross-judge validation, blank-image stress tests, and ablations corroborate these reliability issues.
AI.conclusion: Silent failures are a critical issue in multimodal agentic search. The work provides a taxonomy and a trajectory-level diagnostic pipeline to assess grounding and provenance, highlighting that surface metrics can misrepresent true reliability; code and data are made available at the provided home page.

title: Current Injection Spiking Neural Network for Infrared and Visible Image Fusion
summary: Infrared and visible image fusion (IVIF) integrates the complementary information of two modalities into a single image with richer scene content. While existing methods are largely built on artificial neural networks (ANNs), which densely compute over all activations, spiking neural networks (SNNs) communicate through sparse binary spikes and compute only where and when a spike occurs, offering a route to more energy-efficient fusion. However, directly applying SNNs to IVIF creates a fundamental tension: cross-modal fusion relies on fine-grained responses from both modalities, whereas binary spikes can discard complementary cues that remain below the firing threshold. The membrane potential retains these subthreshold responses before firing, letting both modalities jointly shape the output when integrated at this stage. Building on this, we propose CIS-Fuse, a spiking network that performs cross-modal fusion directly at the membrane-potential level. At its core is the current injection spiking (CIS) operator, which injects one modality as a gated auxiliary current into the driving neuron of the other, so the two integrate before spike firing, with a per-channel learnable injection strength that adaptively regulates the modulation magnitude. Building on CIS, we construct a bidirectional cross-modal fusion (BCMF) module and deploy it on a dual-branch architecture with asymmetric stacking depths, where the two branches develop a clear functional specialization. Extensive experiments on four IVIF benchmarks and on downstream detection and segmentation show that CIS-Fuse achieves fusion quality on par with state-of-the-art ANN-based methods while inheriting the energy efficiency of spike-based computation, with roughly an order of magnitude lower inference energy than the similarly-sized ANN-based DCEvo. Code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: CIS-Fuse is a spiking-network approach for infrared-visible image fusion that fuses information at the membrane-potential level using a current injection spiking (CIS) operator, enabling cross-modal interaction with adaptive per-channel injection. It achieves fusion quality competitive with state-of-the-art ANN methods while offering significant energy efficiency, outperforming similar-sized ANN baselines in energy consumption.
AI.motivation: Address the inherent tension in IVIF between requiring fine-grained cross-modal cues and the sparsity of spike-based computation. By fusing at the membrane-potential level, subthreshold information from both modalities can jointly shape the output, enabling effective cross-modal fusion with energy efficiency.
AI.method: Introduce the current injection spiking (CIS) operator that injects one modality as an auxiliary current into the driving neuron of the other modality. The two modalities integrate before spike firing, with a per-channel learnable injection strength. Build a bidirectional cross-modal fusion (BCMF) module on a dual-branch architecture with asymmetric depths, enabling specialization of each branch. Perform fusion directly at the membrane-potential stage rather than after spike generation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four IVIF benchmarks and downstream detection/segmentation show fusion quality on par with state-of-the-art ANN-based methods, while delivering roughly an order of magnitude lower inference energy than a similarly-sized ANN-based DCEvo. Code will be released.
AI.conclusion: CIS-Fuse demonstrates that cross-modal fusion can be effectively realized at the membrane-potential level in SNNs, marrying competitive fusion performance with the energy efficiency advantages of spike-based computation. The approach shows promise for energy-efficient IVIF and potentially other cross-modal tasks; future work may explore broader benchmark validation and hardware implementation.

title: REGEN: Replay-recycling for Expert-to-Generalist distillation with Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large-scale online reinforcement learning (RL) is the predominant means of eliciting advanced abilities including long-term reasoning and agentic tool use in large language models (LLMs). However, continuing to scale it across vast task domains of interest remains challenging in both computational infrastructure and cost, especially when considering RL as merely a one-off learning stage. Recently, a widely used technique for distilling knowledge across various domains and training stages, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), helps to decouple the RL stage, saving costs, while maintaining generality across vast domains. Nonetheless, similar to online RL, MOPD requires coupled inference and backward passes, which continues to limit its scalability and computational efficiency. To address these challenges, we propose REGEN: Replay-recycling for Expert-to-Generalist Distillation with Offline RL. Instead of distilling from multiple teacher models, REGEN trains a generalist by simply recycling the replay memory -- the free by-product of the teachers' specialized RL training -- and employing offline RL algorithms. REGEN completely decouples the rollout sampling from the backward training process and thus greatly reduces the training cost. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following, REGEN matches the accuracy of MOPD at substantially lower cost. It potentially turns online RL into a data synthesis process instead of a one-off learning stage, and can potentially be extended to large-scale post-training without requiring heavy computational load.

AI.tldr: REGEN leverages replay memory from teacher RL training to train a generalist via offline RL, decoupling rollout sampling from training, achieving MOPD-level accuracy at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Large-scale online RL with LLMs is costly and scales poorly across many domains; existing multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) is effective but still couples rollout with backward updates, hindering scalability.
AI.method: Recycle the teachers' replay memory and apply offline RL to train a generalist, thereby decoupling rollout sampling from backward training and avoiding on-policy backpropagation during distillation. Evaluated on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following.
AI.result: REGEN matches the accuracy of MOPD at substantially lower cost and can turn online RL into a data synthesis process, with potential for scalable post-training.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling data collection from training and leveraging offline RL on replay data, REGEN offers a cost-efficient path to scale generalist agents across diverse domains, with room for extension to larger-scale post-training.

title: Koopman Dreamer: Spectrally Constrained Latent Dynamics for Stable World-Model Imagination
summary: Latent world models improve sample efficiency in continuous control by optimizing policies over imagined latent trajectories, but common neural transitions offer limited direct control over modal persistence and error accumulation in long rollouts. We propose Koopman Dreamer, a Dreamer-style world model with a spectrally constrained deterministic latent dynamics core. Its Koopman-inspired backbone uses two-dimensional rotation--scaling blocks with bounded radii to represent damping, rotation, and near-periodic modes. Linear and low-rank bilinear action terms capture global and state-dependent control effects, while stochastic-state modulation supplies local correction information. To reduce the mismatch between posterior-conditioned training and prior-only imagination, the model combines posterior-conditioned EMA teacher targets with one-step consistency, multi-step rollout, and open-loop observation-prediction objectives. We further derive a multi-step rollout-error bound that separates amplification by the spectral backbone and bilinear interaction from the additive effects of stochastic-state mismatch and modeling residuals, clarifying the trade-off between error attenuation and long-term information retention. Experimental results on proprioceptive continuous-control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite and UAV-LiDAR autonomous navigation demonstrate that Koopman Dreamer improves the stability of long-horizon latent rollouts and achieves stronger closed-loop control performance on tasks that rely on high-quality multi-step imagination.

AI.tldr: A Koopman-inspired Dreamer with a spectrally constrained latent dynamics core improves stability of long-horizon imagined rollouts and closed-loop control in continuous control tasks.
AI.motivation: Improve sample efficiency and long-horizon planning reliability by mitigating modal persistence and error accumulation in latent rollouts of Dreamer-like world models.
AI.method: A spectrally constrained deterministic latent dynamics core built from two-dimensional rotation–scaling blocks with bounded radii to capture damping, rotation, and near-periodic modes; linear and low-rank bilinear action terms for global/state-dependent control; stochastic-state modulation for local corrections. Training combines posterior-conditioned EMA teacher targets with one-step consistency, multi-step rollout, and open-loop observation-prediction objectives. A multi-step rollout-error bound is derived to separate amplification from spectral/bilinear interactions versus stochastic-state mismatch and residuals.
AI.result: Experiments on proprioceptive continuous-control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite and UAV-LiDAR autonomous navigation show improved stability of long-horizon latent rollouts and stronger closed-loop control on tasks requiring high-quality multi-step imagination.
AI.conclusion: Koopman Dreamer demonstrates improved long-horizon stability and control by integrating a spectral backbone with structured control and EMA-based training; the derived bound clarifies the trade-off between error attenuation and information retention in long rollouts.

title: Rewarding Better Thinking for LLM Preference Alignment
summary: LLM preference alignment aims to optimize models toward human preferences across diverse user instructions. Reinforcement learning has become a major post-training approach for this goal, but existing proxy rewards are often outcome-level, mainly evaluating the final response while providing limited guidance for the reasoning trajectory. This can make credit assignment coarse when multiple responses receive similar final scores, leaving trajectory-level preferences under-specified. To address this limitation, we propose Thinking Checklist Reward (TCR), a process-oriented reward for RL-based preference alignment. TCR converts preference pairs into sample-specific thinking checklists and uses them to evaluate whether the generated reasoning trace addresses the preference-implied considerations. To reduce overlap with outcome-level supervision, TCR further introduces an exponential moving average (EMA) residual formulation to isolate a complementary thinking surplus beyond what is predictable from the outcome reward. Experiments on five models from three model families show that TCR consistently improves alignment performance across diverse benchmarks, with ablations further validating the importance of EMA-based residual formulation and sample-specific checklist supervision.

AI.tldr: Proposes Thinking Checklist Reward (TCR), a process-oriented RL reward that evaluates model reasoning traces against preference-implied considerations, using an EMA residual to separate outcome-based signal; demonstrates improved alignment across models and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Outcome-level proxy rewards in RL-based preference alignment provide coarse credit assignment, especially when multiple responses share similar final scores; trajectory-level preferences and reasoning traces demand more granular supervision.
AI.method: Convert preference pairs into sample-specific thinking checklists; evaluate whether the generated reasoning trace addresses the preference-implied considerations; introduce an EMA residual formulation to isolate a surplus beyond outcome reward; train with TCR rewards; evaluate on five models from three families; perform ablations on EMA residual and sample-specific checklist supervision.
AI.result: TCR consistently improves alignment performance across diverse benchmarks; ablations show the importance of EMA-based residual formulation and sample-specific checklist supervision.
AI.conclusion: Process-oriented thinking-checklist rewards can provide finer-grained guidance for RL-based preference alignment, improving trajectory-level guidance and overall alignment across diverse models; EMA residual further enhances the signal by decoupling outcome-based supervision.

title: MTVDiff: Multimodal Conditional Latent Diffusion for Enhanced Thermal-to-Visible Face Translation
summary: Thermal-to-visible face translation presents fundamental challenges including geometric discontinuities, semantic attribute mismatches, and identity degradation. We propose MTVDiff, a novel multimodal latent diffusion framework that synergistically integrates depth and textual information to address these limitations while preserving identity characteristics. The MTVDiff framework presents three core technical contributions: (1) a Dual-Branch Cross-Attention Fusion (DBCAF) module for multi-scale thermal-depth feature extraction and fusion; (2) a Gated Text-to-Visual Feature Alignment mechanism for semantically-guided generation; and (3) Spatial Feature Transformations (SFT) for adaptive multimodal prior integration. Extensive experiments on the MCXFace and SpeakingFaces datasets demonstrate that our multimodal approach significantly outperforms existing GAN-based and diffusion-based approaches across multiple metrics, achieving substantial improvements in both image quality and face verification performance, with FID reductions of up to 48.3% and Rank-1 accuracy improvements of up to 8.9\%. Our work provides a robust solution for face recognition systems operating under varying illumination conditions and advances the state-of-the-art in cross-spectral facial image translation through effective multimodal integration.

AI.tldr: Multimodal diffusion framework MTVDiff translates thermal to visible faces by integrating depth and textual cues to preserve identity, using a dual-branch cross-attention fusion, gated text-to-visual feature alignment, and spatial feature transformations; it achieves state-of-the-art cross-spectral translation on MCXFace and SpeakingFaces with notable FID reductions and Rank-1 gains.
AI.motivation: Address the key challenges in thermal-to-visible face translation: geometric discontinuities, semantic attribute mismatches, and identity degradation under varying illumination.
AI.method: MTVDiff employs a latent diffusion backbone with three innovations: (1) DBCAF for multi-scale fusion of thermal-depth features; (2) Gated Text-to-Visual Feature Alignment for semantic guidance; (3) SFTs to integrate multimodal priors adaptively. The approach leverages depth and text cues to guide realistic, identity-preserving translation.
AI.result: Empirical results show substantial improvements over GAN- and diffusion-based baselines on MCXFace and SpeakingFaces, with up to 48.3% FID reduction and up to 8.9 percentage-point Rank-1 accuracy gains; the method improves image quality and face verification performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multimodal MTVDiff advances cross-spectral facial translation by effectively integrating depth and textual information within a diffusion framework, offering a robust solution for recognition under varying illumination and setting new state-of-the-art in this domain.

title: Predictive Extrema, Unprofitable Policies: An AI-Assisted Audit of Candle-Based Binance Spot Timing Models
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables. Simulation-only negative empirical study and human-supervised AI-assisted evidence audit. No live trading or investment advice. Code and available artifacts: https://github.com/AyoubJadouli/Quantbot-Research-Framework
summary: We audit whether candle-based machine-learning models can turn predictions of cryptocurrency extrema or short-horizon outcomes into positive Binance Spot paper policies after assumed costs. Numerical results come from scripted fixed-seed model runs and deterministic simulators; human-supervised AI agents supported the July 20 evidence-integrity revision through literature retrieval, separately tasked critique, artifact reconciliation, documentation, and source packaging, not trading decisions. The strongest later-period evidence, conditional on extensive predecessor search, is negative: an unchanged ten-pair mandatory-daily selector lost 6.72\% over 19 July cycles at an assumed 31-bps completed-cycle cost, with 3 wins and 16 losses. In short model-specific July evaluations, the validation-selected local-minimum policy returned -1.79\%, while the local-maximum sell-to-cash/re-entry policy underperformed continuous holding by 2.80\%; their gross mean advantages of 11.11 and 12.21 bps were below even the 21-bps stress. A Gurgul-inspired, OHLCV-only daily adaptation attained minimum/maximum ROC AUC of 0.874/0.896 but average precision of only 0.134/0.116 and lost 44.30\% over seven cycles, versus -41.20\% for buy-and-hold. A forensic audit also downgraded an earlier One4All "30-day holdout": its dates had influenced prior architecture work, its four-hour outcome horizon was not purged at split boundaries, it used same-close entry, and its raw result directories were absent. Across the tested, mostly exploratory protocols, event-ranking performance did not establish positive executable policy value. Every operational decision remains NO\_TRADE.

AI.tldr: Candle-based ML models fail to generate positive executable policies for cryptocurrency trading after costs; across multiple protocols, NO_TRADE dominates with negative or marginal results.
AI.motivation: Assess whether candle-based ML can translate predictions of extrema or short-horizon outcomes into profitable Binance Spot policies under realistic costs, using fixed-seed experiments and human-in-the-loop validation.
AI.method: Fixed-seed model runs and deterministic simulators; evaluation of multiple policy variants (ten-pair daily selector, validation-selected local-minimum, local-maximum sell-to-cash/re-entry, OHLCV daily adaptation, One4All holdout). Metrics include cycle-level PnL, costs in basis points, ROC AUC, and average precision; cross-protocol audit with evidence-validation steps, not trading decisions.
AI.result: Across tested protocols, no positive executable policy value was found. Notable figures include a -6.72% result over 19 July cycles at 31 bps cost for a ten-pair selector; local-minimum policy at -1.79% and local-maximum policy at -2.80% vs continuous holding, with gross means of 11.11 and 12.21 bps but below a 21 bps stress. OHLCV adaptation achieved ROC AUC ~0.874–0.896 but precision ~0.134–0.116 and -44.30% over seven cycles vs -41.20% buy-and-hold. One4All holdout was found flawed (dates influenced prior work, horizons not purged, same-close entry, missing raw directories). Overall, event-ranking did not establish positive executable policy value; NO_TRADE remains the default.
AI.conclusion: No profitable executable policy emerged across protocols; methodology issues (holdout leakage, data reuse) and modest performance gains suggest candle-based ML in this setup does not yield actionable trading policies after costs.

title: Know Your Agent: Reconnaissance-Driven Pentesting of AI Agents
summary: Traditional pentesting uses reconnaissance at each step to uncover unseen weaknesses, build stronger attacks, and advance the objective; we argue that AI agents require the same treatment. We formalize agent reconnaissance by modeling the process and identifying the knowledge assets it seeks to extract: what they are, how they are used, and which agent weaknesses they exploit to give adversaries leverage in indirect prompt injection attacks. We instantiate these insights in Know Your Agent (KYA), a framework that automates black-box, reconnaissance-driven pentesting by probing agents, building target profiles, and using those profiles to craft stronger attacks. We evaluate KYA on agent-security benchmarks and a real-world coding agent, and release KYA, its benchmarks, and baseline implementations for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: Proposes Know Your Agent (KYA), a framework for automated reconnaissance-driven pentesting of AI agents; formalizes agent reconnaissance and uses it to build attack profiles; evaluated on benchmarks and a real-world coding agent; releases artifacts for reproducibility.
AI.motivation: AI agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection and other weaknesses; traditional pentesting emphasizes reconnaissance and knowledge asset extraction; there is a need to systematically model and exploit agent weaknesses to improve security.
AI.method: Formalize agent reconnaissance as a modeled process; identify knowledge assets (what they are, how used, and which weaknesses are exploited); instantiate Know Your Agent (KYA) to perform black-box reconnaissance, build target profiles, and craft stronger attacks.
AI.result: KYA evaluated on agent-security benchmarks and a real-world coding agent; artifacts (KYA, benchmarks, baselines) released for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: Reconnaissance-driven pentesting is a viable, reproducible approach to AI-agent security; KYA provides a concrete framework to identify and exploit agent weaknesses, informing defense and safer design.

title: LAVIFT: Latent-Action-Guided Vision Fine-Tuning for Surgical Interaction Recognition
summary: Understanding instrument-tissue interactions is essential for context-aware surgical AI and autonomous robotic surgery. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and vision encoders offer an alternative to conventional interaction classifiers by transferring broad visual and semantic knowledge. However, adapting them to fine-grained surgical interactions remains challenging: (1) freezing the vision encoder depends entirely on pretrained representations that may retain noise and provide weak spatial localization, while (2) full fine-tuning can improve global semantic alignment without ensuring that the encoder learns meaningful features in the correct action region. We address these limitations by introducing LAViFiT, an end-to-end latent-action-guided framework for vision-language fine-tuning. An inverse dynamics model captures the visual changes induced by each action, while a forward world model drives the encoder to represent action-relevant regions. A patch-level SIG Regularizer further prevents local feature collapse without additional supervision, such as bounding boxes or pseudo-labels. Experiments across multiple encoders and datasets improve recognition and image-text alignment, while representation analyses show stronger grounding over the complete instrument-tissue interaction region and more spatially coherent features.

AI.tldr: LAViFiT is an end-to-end latent-action-guided fine-tuning framework that uses inverse dynamics and forward world models, plus a patch-level SIG Regularizer, to adapt vision-language models for fine-grained instrument–tissue interaction in surgery, improving recognition and image-text alignment with stronger spatial grounding.
AI.motivation: Adapting pretrained vision-language models to fine-grained instrument–tissue interactions is challenging. Freezing vision encoders risks noisy representations and weak localization; full fine-tuning can improve semantic alignment but may not yield meaningful action-region features. A method is needed to learn action-relevant, spatially grounded features without heavy supervision.
AI.method: LAViFiT integrates (i) an inverse dynamics model that captures visual changes induced by each action, (ii) a forward world model that directs the encoder to emphasize action-relevant regions, and (iii) a patch-level SIG Regularizer to prevent local feature collapse without bounding boxes or pseudo-labels. It performs end-to-end latent-action-guided fine-tuning of vision-language models across multiple encoders and datasets to improve recognition and image-text alignment.
AI.result: Experiments show improved recognition and image-text alignment across encoders/datasets, with representation analyses indicating stronger grounding across the full instrument-tissue interaction region and more spatially coherent features.
AI.conclusion: LAViFiT effectively aligns vision-language representations with the complete instrument–tissue interaction region, yielding better action-grounded features and improved performance for context-aware surgical AI without requiring heavy supervision.

title: Generating Bearing Vibration Signals at User-Specified Fault Probabilities Using PR-GAN and Counterfactual Methods
summary: In bearing vibration datasets, most samples receive predicted fault probabilities close to 0 or 1, while samples with intermediate (gray-zone) probabilities are rare. Such borderline samples are important because they reflect conditions in which maintenance decisions may require additional inspection or a conservative response and are useful for studying decision boundaries. To address this scarcity, this paper proposes and compares two approaches that generate vibration signals whose predicted fault probability matches a target probability of 0.25, 0.50, or 0.75. We use the average output of a heterogeneous ensemble classifier with different architectures and random initializations as a fixed, gradient-accessible probability oracle. The first, training-based approach, Probability-Regularized Generative Adversarial Network (PR-GAN), extends Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) and edits a real signal through a residual generator while pushing the classifier output toward the target probability. The second is a training-free, per-sample Wachter-style counterfactual (CF) procedure that directly optimizes each input signal to reach the target probability while remaining close to the source signal. We evaluate both methods on the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) and Paderborn bearing datasets using mean absolute target-probability error, time-domain total variation, and frequency-domain log power spectral density (log-PSD) differences. Across all settings, CF reaches the target with a mean absolute probability error of 0.005-0.008 and a within-tolerance success rate of 1.000 on retained samples, whereas PR-GAN's mean error is 0.046-0.059 with success rates between 0.501 and 0.680.
