CF therefore steers the probability more reliably and requires smaller average L1 changes, whereas PR-GAN has a lower reported runtime in most settings.

AI.tldr: Two approaches to generate bearing-vibration signals with target fault-probability: a training-based PR-GAN and a training-free counterfactual CF; CF outperforms PR-GAN in probability accuracy and L1 perturbation, with higher reliability; PR-GAN faster in runtime but less precise.
AI.motivation: Address scarcity of gray-zone samples (intermediate fault probability) to study decision boundaries and maintenance actions in bearing fault diagnosis.
AI.method: PR-GAN extends Wasserstein GAN with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) by using a residual generator to modify real signals while pushing the heterogeneous ensemble classifier toward the target probability. The CF method applies a per-sample Wachter-style counterfactual optimization to the input signal, directly optimizing it to reach the target probability while keeping it close to the source signal; the probability oracle is a gradient-accessible ensemble classifier.
AI.result: CF achieves mean absolute target-probability error of 0.005–0.008 and 100% success on retained samples; PR-GAN achieves 0.046–0.059 error with 0.501–0.680 success rates. CF also requires smaller average L1 changes; PR-GAN generally reports faster runtime in most settings.
AI.conclusion: Training-free counterfactuals provide more reliable steering of predicted fault probability and better signal fidelity for gray-zone samples, while the trained GAN-based method is faster but less precise. Both methods are evaluated on CWRU and Paderborn bearing datasets using MAE of target probability, time-domain total variation, and log-PSD differences.

title: DocOps: A Verifiable Benchmark for Autonomous Agents in Complex Document Operations
summary: As autonomous agents rapidly evolve, their ability to reliably manipulate ubiquitous digital documents has become critical for enabling general-purpose AI assistants and automating complex workspace workflows. In this paper, we introduce DocOps, a deterministically verifiable evaluation framework underpinned by a hierarchical taxonomy that deconstructs document operations inspired by real-world practices into atomic dimensions and escalating workflow complexities. Based on DocOps, we systematically evaluate representative closed- and open-source models across various agentic harnesses, revealing that even the most advanced frontier configurations still exhibit profound limitations when handling highly coupled, long-range tasks. Furthermore, a fine-grained analysis of existing agents' manipulation behaviors uncovers 3 key failure modes: long-term state tracking collapse, shallow semantic verification, and destructive editing of structural metadata. Ultimately, our work exposes the capability boundaries of agents in maintaining global document consistency, shedding light on the future design of robust, non-destructive agents for complex digital ecosystems.

AI.tldr: DocOps is a deterministic, hierarchically structured evaluation framework for document operations that benchmarks agentic models across workflows, revealing fundamental limits and three primary failure modes in maintaining document integrity.
AI.motivation: To ensure reliable, non-destructive manipulation of digital documents by autonomous agents, enabling robust general-purpose AI assistants and automation of complex workflows.
AI.method: Introduce a hierarchical DocOps taxonomy that breaks down document operations into atomic dimensions and escalating workflow complexity; perform systematic evaluation of representative closed- and open-source models across various agentic harnesses; conduct fine-grained analysis of manipulation behaviors to identify failure modes.
AI.result: Even frontier configurations exhibit significant limitations on highly coupled, long-range tasks; three key failure modes are identified: (1) long-term state tracking collapse, (2) shallow semantic verification, and (3) destructive editing of structural metadata; results delineate capability boundaries and inform non-destructive, robust agent design.
AI.conclusion: DocOps exposes the boundary conditions of agent capabilities in maintaining global document consistency and points to future design directions for robust, non-destructive agents in complex digital ecosystems.

title: OSVE: One Step Video Editing with One Step Diffusion Models
summary: Text-guided video editing with diffusion models is impractically slow, hindered by costly multi-step sampling and inversion. We present OSVE, the first framework to successfully adapt one-step Text-to-Image (T2I) models for high-quality video editing, addressing the core challenges of inversion, editability, and temporal consistency. To bypass slow iterative inversion, we train a learnable encoder that predicts the initial noise for each frame in a single forward pass. This encoder is trained with a novel Structure-Aware Editing (SAE) loss on a curated dataset of structurally-aligned image pairs, teaching it to preserve the source video's geometry during edits. For temporal coherence, we introduce Unified-Frame Editing (UFE), a technique that concatenates frame latents to facilitate cross-frame attention in a single generation step. Furthermore, for long videos, a sliding-window strategy with an anchor frame maintains global consistency. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that OSVE achieves editing quality comparable or superior to state-of-the-art multi-step methods, while operating approximately 155--171 times faster. This breakthrough paves the way for practical, real-time video editing applications. Code is available at https://github.com/KU-VGI/OSVE.

AI.tldr: OSVE enables real-time, one-step text-guided video editing by adapting text-to-image diffusion models with a learnable initial-noise predictor, a Structure-Aware Editing loss, Unified-Frame Editing for cross-frame attention, and a sliding-window strategy for long videos, achieving 155–171x speedups with comparable or superior quality.
AI.motivation: To overcome the computational bottlenecks of diffusion-based video editing (slow iterative inversion, costly multi-step sampling) and to achieve temporally coherent edits suitable for practical use.
AI.method: Introduce a learnable encoder that predicts the initial noise for each frame in a single forward pass. Train it with a Structure-Aware Editing (SAE) loss on a dataset of structurally-aligned image pairs to preserve source geometry. Use Unified-Frame Editing (UFE) by concatenating frame latents to enable cross-frame attention in one generation step. For long videos, apply a sliding-window with an anchor frame to maintain global consistency.
AI.result: OSVE achieves editing quality comparable or superior to state-of-the-art multi-step methods while being approximately 155–171 times faster. Code is released at the provided repository.
AI.conclusion: A practical, real-time video editing framework is possible by re-purposing one-step T2I diffusion models with architecture and loss designs that address inversion, editability, and temporal coherence, paving the way for real-time video editing applications.

title: MoA-Structured Decode Attention DNF Derivation, KV-Cache Accumulation, GQA/MQA, and OpenACC Kernel
summary: We derive four memory-optimal inference artifacts for transformer attention using the Mathematics of Arrays (MoA), each following directly from the forward-pass Denotational Normal Form (DNF) of with the query-row index fixed to the current decode step. The artifacts are: (1)~a single-query decode DNF in which the $ψ$-reduction eliminates the $K^\top$ buffer algebraically, achieving $(d_k + nd_k+ nd_v+ d_v)\times4\,{B}$ Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) traffic result numerically verified to $\|{err}\|_\leq2\times10^{-7}$; (2)~a C/OpenACC Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) kernel with Operational Normal Form (ONF) stride arithmetic and hardware-coalesced memory access, verified to $\|\mathrm{err}\|_\infty=0$ (exact IEEE-754 floating-point arithmetic); (3)~a multi-step KV-cache with $O(d_k+d_v)$ per-step append via MoA concatenation $\#$; and (4)~Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and Multi-Query Attention (MQA) derived via $ψ$-selection, achieving a proven $\frac {h_q} { h_{kv} }$ reduction in KV traffic. All programs are verified against PyTorch scaled_dot_product_attention.

AI.tldr: Four memory-optimal inference artifacts for transformer attention derived with Mathematics of Arrays (MoA) and Denotational Normal Form (DNF) with fixed query row. (1) single-query decode DNF removing K^T buffer, giving (d_k + n d_k + n d_v + d_v) × 4 B DRAM traffic; (2) an ONF-stride GPU kernel with coalesced memory access and zero error; (3) a multi-step KV-cache with per-step append O(d_k+d_v) via MoA concatenation; (4) GQA and MQA via ψ-selection achieving a proven h_q/h_kv reduction in KV traffic. All verified against PyTorch scaled_dot_product_attention.
AI.motivation: Reduce memory traffic and improve throughput of transformer attention during inference by deriving memory-optimal artifacts with formal MoA/DNF tooling and providing verifiable results.
AI.method: Apply Mathematics of Arrays (MoA) to the forward-pass Denotational Normal Form (DNF) with the query-row fixed to the current decode step; derive four artifacts: (1) decode DNF with ψ-reduction to eliminate K^T; (2) ONF GPU kernel with stride arithmetic and coalesced memory access; (3) multi-step KV-cache with O(d_k+d_v) per-step append via MoA concatenation; (4) GQA/MQA via ψ-selection; validate against PyTorch scaled_dot_product_attention.
AI.result: Memory traffic: (d_k + n d_k + n d_v + d_v) × 4 B DRAM; numerical error ≤ 2×10^-7; ONF kernel yields zero ∞-norm error (exact IEEE-754); per-step KV-cache complexity O(d_k+d_v); proven KV traffic reduction factor h_q/h_kv for GQA and MQA; experimental verification against PyTorch.
AI.conclusion: Presents a set of memory-optimal inference artifacts enabling efficient, verifiable transformer attention: decode simplification, GPU-optimized kernel, incremental KV-cache, and A-language–driven GQA/MQA with provable KV-traffic reductions; validated against standard attention implementation.

title: JANUS: Foreseeing Latent Risk for Long-Horizon Agent Safety
summary: Agent safety is moving from content moderation toward preventing operational failures before tool-using agents act. We propose Janus, a foresight-oriented framework for long-horizon agent safety that trains guards to anticipate delayed risks from partial trajectories. Janus synthesizes diverse agent trajectories via multi-agent simulation and learns a shared policy with two coupled tasks: an anticipation task that forecasts safety-relevant futures and an adjudication task that decides safety from both the observed prefix and anticipated future. The two tasks are jointly optimized with CoAA-RL, which rewards forecasts by their utility for downstream safety judgment. The resulting guard model, Vanguard, blocks unsafe actions before execution. Across four agent-safety benchmarks, Vanguard improves average protection by 15.9 percentage points over baseline guards while increasing benign task completion by 5.1 percentage points.

AI.tldr: Proposes Janus, a foresight-oriented framework for long-horizon agent safety that trains anticipators and adjudicators to prevent delayed safety failures; evaluated with Vanguard guards improving protection and task completion on four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address the safety gap for tool-using agents by forecasting future safety-relevant outcomes from partial trajectories and preventing unsafe actions before execution.
AI.method: Use multi-agent simulation to synthesize diverse trajectories; train a shared policy with two coupled tasks (anticipation of future safety states and adjudication of safety from observed and anticipated info) optimized via CoAA-RL; deploy Vanguard to block unsafe actions pre-execution.
AI.result: Vanguard improves average protection by 15.9 percentage points and benign task completion by 5.1 percentage points across four agent-safety benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Joint anticipation–adjudication with forecast-guided rewards yields effective preemptive safety for long-horizon agents and modest, but consistent, gains in task performance.

title: StrokeSeg2: Stroke Lesion Segmentation in Clinical Research Workflows
summary: Deep learning frameworks like nnU-Net achieve state-of-theart brain lesion segmentation performance but remain difficult to deploy in clinical research environments due to, among other reasons, software dependencies and computational requirements. We introduce StrokeSeg2, a lightweight, modular, cross-platform C++/Qt framework designed to adapt resource-intensive 3D stroke segmentation pipelines into portable and reproducible applications. To improve compatibility with standard clinical workstations, we investigate the combined effect of architectural compression through knowledge distillation and inference optimisation using ONNX Runtime with Float16 quantisation. Across heterogeneous hardware configurations (CPU, integrated GPU, and dedicated GPU) architectural distillation emerged as the primary contributor to efficiency gains, contributing to over 90% reduction in energy consumption and an average 84% reduction in inference time. Specifically, we identify a 0.84M-parameter student model as the most favourable trade-off, reducing the original 102.3M-parameter teacher architecture to a 2.1 MB disk footprint while preserving robust lesion localisation and competitive segmentation performance. This small footprint supports the development of a self-contained installer for clinical workstation targets. Finally, StrokeSeg2 packages these optimisations into standalone installers for Windows, macOS, and Linux. By providing both graphical and commandline interfaces without Docker or external environment dependencies, StrokeSeg2 facilitates deployment of high-performance segmentation workflows for routine clinical research pipelines.

AI.tldr: StrokeSeg2 presents a lightweight, portable C++/Qt framework that repackages 3D stroke segmentation into standalone, docker-free applications. It combines architectural distillation (teacher 102.3M to 0.84M) with ONNX Runtime Float16 quantisation to achieve major efficiency gains across CPU/GPU, enabling easy clinical deployment via Windows/macOS/Linux installers with GUI/CLI access.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between state-of-the-art brain lesion segmentation (e.g., nnU-Net) and practical clinical research deployment, addressing software dependencies, hardware constraints, and portability.
AI.method: Develop a cross-platform C++/Qt framework (StrokeSeg2) and evaluate architectural distillation (teacher→student with 0.84M parameters) plus ONNX Runtime Float16 quantisation across CPU, integrated GPU, and dedicated GPU. Package into standalone installers for Windows, macOS, and Linux with GUI and CLI interfaces, avoiding Docker or external dependencies.
AI.result: Distillation dominates efficiency gains (>90% energy reduction and ~84% faster inference overall). The 0.84M-parameter student reduces model size from 102.3M to 2.1 MB on disk while maintaining robust lesion localization and competitive segmentation. Standalone installers enable self-contained deployment across platforms with no external dependencies.
AI.conclusion: Architectural distillation is the main driver of efficiency in this deployment pipeline. StrokeSeg2 demonstrates feasible, portable, high-performance brain lesion segmentation workflows for routine clinical research without Docker, improving adoption in clinical workstations.

title: Total Variation Distance Estimation in Autoregressive Models
comment: 39 pages, 11 figures, code is available at https://github.com/XunZhiyang/llm-tv-estimation
summary: Modern LLM deployments use a number of implementation choices and inference optimizations (e.g., batching, custom kernels, and quantization) on top of fixed weights, so two engines serving "the same model" can produce meaningfully different distributions. We study the problem of estimating the total variation (TV) distance between two length-$n$ autoregressive distributions to additive error $\varepsilon$, under three access models. (1) Under sample access, we use $\widetilde{O}(n^2 K/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, where $K$ is the maximum support of the next-token distribution. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(n^3 m/\varepsilon^5)$-query estimator of Meel et al. (2025), where $m \geq K$ is the total size of the token alphabet. (2) Under logit access, we use $O(n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, and this is tight. (3) Under noisy logit access, we smoothly interpolate between the above two guarantees: if probability values are given to relative error $σ$, we use $\widetilde{O}((n+n^2σ^2)/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. We complement our theoretical results with an empirical evaluation of our algorithms, for example measuring the distance between SGLang and vLLM serving identical weights. Our experiments highlight the robustness and practicality of estimating the total variation distance, which remains estimable where the KL divergence is infinite. Our code is available at https://github.com/XunZhiyang/llm-tv-estimation.

AI.tldr: Estimates the total variation distance between two length-n autoregressive distributions under three access models with new query complexities and empirical validation; improves prior work; supports robust auditing of LLM deployments.
AI.motivation: Quantify how deployment choices and inference optimizations affect the output distribution of autoregressive models, enabling cross-engine comparability and auditing.
AI.method: Develops TV-distance estimators for three access models: (1) sample access with Õ(n^2 K/ε^2) queries; (2) logit access with Õ(n/ε^2) queries (optimal); (3) noisy logit access, interpolating between the two: Õ((n+n^2 σ^2)/ε^2) queries. Provides lower bounds and empirical evaluation comparing engines (e.g., SGLang vs vLLM).
AI.result: New upper bounds for sample-based TV estimation; tight bound for the logit access case; interpolation result for noisy logit access; empirical results show TV is estimable even when KL divergence is infinite; code released.
AI.conclusion: Total variation distance between autoregressive model outputs is practically estimable under realistic access models, enabling robust auditing of LLM deployments and comparison across engines despite implementation differences.

title: Long-Term Sequential Decision Making under Risk
comment: Accpeted in Forty-Second Annual Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2026)
summary: We study finite-horizon MDP planning under \emph{root-based} (resolute) risk objectives that apply a rank-dependent functional to the distribution of total returns. Such objectives are non-linear in the return distribution and generally break Bellman optimality, so direct optimization by scenario-tree enumeration is intractable. We propose \textbf{ERQDP}, an enumeration-free and sampling-free method that solves a rank--quantile surrogate via exact DP (Dynamic Programming), evaluates candidate policies exactly by DP over return Probability Mass Functions (PMFs) on a discretized return grid (with an explicit rounding bound), and refines the surrogate in an anytime loop that reports an explicit upper--lower gap (certificate) for the target objective up to discretization budgets. Across tested benchmarks, ERQDP returns certified solutions or explicit residual gaps, enables fast risk-parameter sweeps with substantial runtime gains, and supports both risk-averse and risk-seeking behaviors.

AI.tldr: ERQDP is an enumeration-free, sampling-free DP method for finite-horizon MDPs with root-based risk objectives; it optimizes a rank-quantile surrogate exactly, evaluates policies via DP over discretized return PMFs with rounding bounds, and refines the surrogate in an anytime loop that provides explicit upper–lower certificates.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear, rank-dependent risk objectives under finite-horizon MDPs break Bellman optimality and render scenario-tree enumeration intractable; there is a need for tractable, certified, risk-aware planning techniques.
AI.method: Propose ERQDP which solves a rank-quantile surrogate using exact DP; evaluates candidate policies by DP over return PMFs on a discretized return grid with an explicit rounding bound; iteratively refines the surrogate in an anytime loop, reporting an explicit upper–lower gap (certificate) for the objective within discretization budgets.
AI.result: Empirical benchmarks show ERQDP yields certified solutions or explicit residual gaps, enables fast risk-parameter sweeps with substantial runtime gains, and supports both risk-averse and risk-seeking behaviors.
AI.conclusion: ERQDP provides a scalable, certification-enabled framework for finite-horizon risk-aware MDP planning under non-linear objectives, offering exact DP optimization on a surrogate, discretization-based evaluation with provable bounds and practical performance benefits.

title: MV-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Coordinated Multi-View Interface Construction
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly expected to automate visualization development by generating code directly from visual designs. However, existing evaluations mainly focus on single-chart generation and overlook coordinated multi-view interface construction, which requires joint reasoning about data semantics, view coordination, and interaction logic. Consequently, MLLM capabilities in this setting remain underexplored, and the field lacks a dedicated benchmark for systematic assessment. We introduce MV-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on coordinated multi-view interface construction. Instead of relying on incomplete or inconsistent open-source implementations, we use Tableau workbook files as ground truth because they explicitly encode data bindings, visual mappings, and interactions. We develop a multi-stage pipeline that converts these specifications into executable web interfaces through structured intermediate representations. The benchmark contains 92 base interfaces and 1,048 verified instances created by recombining chart types, datasets, and interaction patterns. Each instance includes executable code, a rendered interface, a dataset, and interaction annotations. We evaluate five state-of-the-art MLLMs in a single-pass setting using metrics for visual fidelity, data binding correctness, and interaction completeness. The strongest model achieves 75.45 percent accuracy in visual layout reproduction, but only 21.71 percent in data binding and 11.68 percent in interaction completeness. These results show that current MLLMs can reproduce visual appearance but remain limited in generating the data semantics and interactive logic required by coordinated multi-view interfaces. Iterative refinement improves code executability but does not substantially reduce the gap in data binding and interaction generation.

AI.tldr: MV-Bench: a benchmark for evaluating multimodal LLMs on coordinated multi-view interface construction, using Tableau workbooks as ground truth. It includes 92 base interfaces and 1,048 recombined instances with executable code, rendered interfaces, datasets, and interaction annotations. Five SOTA MLLMs are evaluated; results show strong visual layout reproduction (≈75.5%), but weak data binding (≈21.7%) and interaction completeness (≈11.7%). Iterative refinement improves code executability but does not significantly close the data binding and interaction gaps.
AI.motivation: There is a gap in evaluating MLLMs on coordinated multi-view interface construction, as existing work focuses on single-chart generation and lacks a dedicated benchmark that captures data semantics, view coordination, and interaction logic.
AI.method: Construct a pipeline that converts Tableau specifications into executable web interfaces via structured intermediate representations. Build MV-Bench from Tableau workbooks by recombining chart types, datasets, and interaction patterns to create 1,048 verified instances. Each instance includes executable code, a rendered interface, a dataset, and interaction annotations. Evaluate five SOTA MLLMs in a single-pass setting using metrics for visual fidelity, data binding correctness, and interaction completeness.
AI.result: Strongest model achieves 75.45% visual layout accuracy; 21.71% data binding accuracy; 11.68% interaction completeness. Iterative refinement improves executability but leaves large gaps in data semantics and interactive logic.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs reproduce visual appearance well but struggle with data semantics and interactive logic required for coordinated multi-view interfaces; further research is needed to close these gaps, including enhancing data binding and interaction generation and exploring iterative refinement strategies.

title: Do Sheaf Neural Networks Use Holonomy? A Measure--Intervene--Control Study
summary: Geometric architectures are often justified by internal mechanisms such as rotations, yet task performance alone cannot show whether those mechanisms drive predictions. Using sheaf neural networks (SNNs) as a testbed, we introduce the first basis-independent measurement of trained triangle-loop products, separating rotation, stalk-space area, and orientation. In a custom high-homophily GraphUniverse regime, Neural Sheaf Propagation (NSP) increases the triangle-weighted mean two-dimensional SO(2) loop rotation from 0.010 to 0.388 radians for triangle counting, while the community-detection comparison ends at 0.029 radians. Across the training-set-size experiment, replacing all learned SO(2) transports with identities sharply increases test error, establishing post-training sensitivity to the complete learned connection. However, a graph-summary ridge predictor is more accurate, diagonal maps also improve, and fixed-degree graphs develop increasing rotation without outperforming the training-mean predictor. This measure-intervene-control study separates geometric change, connection sensitivity, and evidence for triangle-specific computation.

AI.tldr: Introduces a basis-independent measurement of trained triangle-loop products in sheaf neural networks to separate rotation, area, and orientation; shows NSP-induced rotation changes and sensitivity to learned transports; graph-based predictors can outperform direct rotation metrics, enabling a measure-intervene-control framework for triangle-specific computation.
AI.motivation: Diagnose whether geometric inductive biases in sheaf neural networks drive predictions by moving beyond task performance to internal geometric mechanisms; develop a basis-independent metric and test interventions.
AI.method: Define a basis-independent triangle-loop product metric and decompose it into rotation (SO(2)), stalk-space area, and orientation. Apply in a high-homophily GraphUniverse regime with Neural Sheaf Propagation (NSP). Assess triangle counting and compare with community detection. Perform ablations by replacing learned SO(2) transports with identities; evaluate a graph-summary ridge predictor; examine diagonal maps and fixed-degree graphs; vary training-set size.
AI.result: Triangle-loop rotation under NSP rises from ~0.010 to ~0.388 radians for triangle counting; community-detection measure peaks around ~0.029 radians. Replacing learned transports with identities markedly increases test error, showing sensitivity to learned connections. Graph-summary ridge predictor is more accurate; diagonal maps improve; fixed-degree graphs develop increasing rotation without outperforming the training-mean predictor.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a measure–intervene–control framework to separate geometric change, connection sensitivity, and triangle-specific computation, demonstrating that internal geometric mechanisms contribute to computation beyond task performance.

title: MOF-Sleuth: Tool-Grounded Reward Alignment for Explainable Fine-Grained MOF CIF Auditing
summary: Large metal-organic framework (MOF) databases support simulation, screening, and machine learning through crystallographic information files (CIFs). Subtle chemical and structural errors in these inputs can compromise downstream results and hinder manual inspection. LLM advances in computational chemistry offer paths beyond predictive screening toward fine-grained diagnosis with evidence-grounded explanations. However, two challenges remain: (i) limited fine-grained attribution: MOF-specific validators and machine-learning models scale detection but provide fixed checks, readiness scores, or coarse labels rather than evidence-grounded explanations; and (ii) unreliable CIF reasoning: direct LLM auditing is costly and unreliable because chemical evidence is implicit across atom-site records and requires geometric, connectivity, occupancy, and charge calculations. Both stem from weak coupling between chemical evidence and language-model explanation. We introduce MOF-Sleuth, a reinforcement-guided CIF auditing agent with two modules: a deterministic Forensic Lab and a Sleuth reasoning engine. The Lab derives composition, geometry, connectivity, occupancy, coordination, and charge evidence, and Sleuth uses this evidence to produce an evidence-grounded explanation, error types, and a binary decision. Reward-guided reinforcement learning (RL) turns tool measurements into chemical explanation-level supervision, rewarding not only the final answer but also cited chemical evidence and evidence-supported diagnoses. We introduce Chemically Grounded Diagnosis (Chem-GD), a metric that assesses whether a correct diagnosis is explained by factual, relevant CIF-derived evidence. Across four benchmarks, MOF-Sleuth establishes state-of-the-art performance among LLM-based approaches and MOF-specific machine-learning methods, demonstrating gains in detection, attribution, and grounded explanation quality.

AI.tldr: MOF-Sleuth presents a reinforcement-guided CIF auditing agent with two modules (Forensic Lab and Sleuth) that produce evidence-grounded explanations for MOF CIF quality issues, using reward-driven RL and a Chem-GD metric; achieves state-of-the-art performance on four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Subtle errors in metal-organic framework CIFs undermine downstream simulations, screening, and ML. Current validators offer coarse labels without evidence-grounded explanations, and LLM-based auditing struggles due to implicit chemical evidence distributed across atom-site records. A tightly coupled system that derives chemical evidence and explains it with evidence-grounded reasoning is needed.
AI.method: Two-module architecture: Forensic Lab computes chemical evidence (composition, geometry, connectivity, occupancy, coordination, charge) from CIFs; Sleuth uses this evidence to generate explanations, categorize errors, and make a binary pass/fail decision. Training uses reward-guided reinforcement learning to supervise both final diagnoses and cited chemical evidence/explanations. Introduces Chemically Grounded Diagnosis (Chem-GD) metric to assess whether diagnoses are justified by factual CIF-derived evidence. Evaluated on four benchmarks, compared against LLM-based and MOF-specific ML baselines.
AI.result: MOF-Sleuth achieves state-of-the-art performance among LLM-based approaches and MOF-specific ML methods, with improvements in detection accuracy, attribution of errors to underlying chemical evidence, and quality of grounded explanations.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that coupling deterministic chemical evidence extraction with RL-guided, evidence-grounded explanations yields superior CIF auditing for MOFs. The Chem-GD metric provides a principled measure of explainability, suggesting broader applicability to chemistry-domain LLM auditing and data curation workflows.

title: LoRFT: Benchmarking Long-Range Vehicle Trajectory Reconstruction from Fixed Highway Cameras
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Code and processed annotations: https://github.com/YvfanZhu/LoRFT
summary: Long-range vehicle trajectories provide important spatio-temporal evidence for traffic safety analysis, autonomous driving evaluation, and data-driven traffic management, yet continuously recovering them from fixed highway cameras remains difficult. As vehicles recede into distant road regions, perspective compression and scale decay often fragment or prematurely terminate automatic tracklets, even when their continuation remains identifiable from motion consistency across neighboring frames. We formulate this problem as recovering the far-range continuation of a vehicle trajectory from a reliable near-field tracklet. We introduce LoRFT, to our knowledge the first open benchmark dedicated to long-range vehicle trajectory reconstruction from fixed highway cameras. LoRFT comprises 22 expressway surveillance scenes, 366,109 video frames, 6,601 manually verified trajectories, 2,694,889 bounding boxes, road-geometry annotations, scene-level splits, and evaluation scripts. We further propose Map-RSTNet, a map-aware residual sequence-to-sequence model that reconstructs distant trajectories in a road-geometry-aligned state space and dynamically refreshes local road geometry during decoding. On LoRFT, Map-RSTNet reduces ADE, FDE, and 5-second RMSE by 11.0%, 15.4%, and 10.5%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate that road-geometry-aware reconstruction can extend usable trajectory records from existing fixed-camera infrastructure. LoRFT provides a reproducible testbed for long-range vehicle trajectory reconstruction.

AI.tldr: Introduces LoRFT benchmark for long-range vehicle trajectory reconstruction from fixed highway cameras and proposes Map-RSTNet, a map-aware residual seq-to-seq model that uses road geometry to reconstruct distant trajectories, achieving improvements on ADE/FDE/5s RMSE on LoRFT.
AI.motivation: Long-range trajectories are difficult to recover due to perspective compression and scale decay; a reproducible, diverse benchmark is needed; leveraging road geometry can improve reconstruction fidelity.
AI.method: LoRFT dataset with 22 expressway scenes, 366,109 frames, 6,601 validated trajectories, 2,694,889 bounding boxes, plus road-geometry annotations and evaluation scripts. Map-RSTNet is a map-aware residual sequence-to-sequence model that reconstructs distant trajectories in a road-geometry-aligned state space and dynamically refreshes local road geometry during decoding.
AI.result: On LoRFT, Map-RSTNet reduces ADE by 11.0%, FDE by 15.4%, and 5-second RMSE by 10.5% relative to the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Road-geometry-aware reconstruction can extend usable trajectory records from fixed-camera infrastructure; LoRFT provides a reproducible testbed for long-range trajectory reconstruction.

title: Geospatial Diffusion-based Evolution Synthesis (GeoDES) for Storm-Centered Weather Augmentation
summary: While machine learning-based weather models hold significant promise, they struggle to predict the detailed structure of large-scale weather systems such as cyclonic storms. Regional models are constrained by limited historical records within fixed geographic boundaries, while global models are computationally expensive and often operate at resolutions too coarse to capture fine-grained storm dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Geospatial Diffusion-based Evolution Synthesis (GeoDES) model, a custom image-to-video diffusion model. By focusing generation strictly on the evolving storm structure, GeoDES synthesizes physically consistent, high-fidelity weather events suitable for stress-testing forecast models and expanding meteorological datasets. Evaluations demonstrate that GeoDES outperforms prior methods on key metrics, achieving $52\%$ lower Peak Vorticity Error and $8\%$ higher Anomaly Correlation Coefficient than the next strongest methods on the North Atlantic test set.

AI.tldr: GeoDES is a geospatial diffusion model that synthesizes evolving storm structures to augment weather datasets and stress-test forecast models, claiming significant accuracy improvements on North Atlantic storms.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of regional and global weather models: regional models have limited history; global models are expensive and coarse. A synthetic, high-fidelity, physically consistent method could provide abundant, diverse storm scenarios for evaluation and data augmentation.
AI.method: A custom image-to-video diffusion architecture (GeoDES) that generates evolving storm structures, focusing generation on the storm evolution to ensure physical consistency and high fidelity.
AI.result: GeoDES achieves 52% lower Peak Vorticity Error and 8% higher Anomaly Correlation Coefficient on the North Atlantic test set compared to the next strongest methods.
AI.conclusion: GeoDES provides a scalable means to synthesize physically plausible, high-fidelity weather events for stress-testing forecast models and expanding meteorological datasets.

title: SenWorld: A Digital-Twin Simulation for Generating Context-Rich Evaluation Data
summary: Smartphone personal assistants reason over longitudinal personal data, yet evaluating them requires context-rich evaluation data whose correct answers are known, and real device traces are too privacy-sensitive to share. To address this challenge, we present SenWorld, a physically grounded, deterministic, event-sourced digital-twin simulation that generates such data with ground truth fixed by construction. In SenWorld, personas live through a full day in a world built from real map, weather, holiday, and network data; every observable signal is archived in full-system snapshots; and each evaluation case is labeled by a pointer to an existing record rather than by post-hoc annotation or a large language model (LLM) judge. We evaluate this method with 16 personas in Beijing. The generated data closely matches the held-out real-user benchmark in category distribution (Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) 0.070) and in the daily rhythm of communication records (JSD below 0.1), though generated records remain shorter than real ones. Without scripted interaction, personas form a fully reciprocated dialogue subgraph and differentiated behavioral repertoires. Projected into 717 evaluation cases, the generated data exposes 78 failures in a production smartphone assistant, concentrating on call and Short Message Service (SMS) records while contacts, schedules, and alarms never fail. The snapshot pointer confirms each failure as an assistant-side retrieval error, with no LLM judge involved. Overall, SenWorld offers a privacy-safe, reproducible, and distribution-checked path to evaluation data whose labels are fixed by construction.

AI.tldr: SenWorld is a deterministic, event-sourced digital-twin that generates ground-truth, privacy-safe evaluation data for smartphone assistants by simulating 16 Beijing personas over a day using real-world context; it closely matches real benchmarks and reveals retrieval-errors in production systems without relying on LLM judges.
AI.motivation: Evaluating context-rich smartphone assistants requires evaluation data with known ground truth that respects user privacy; real traces are privacy-sensitive and cannot be shared widely, hindering reproducibility and benchmarking.
AI.method: Build a physically grounded, deterministic digital twin (SenWorld) with event-sourced logs. Personas live a full day in a world constructed from real map, weather, holidays, and network data. All signals are captured in full-system snapshots; evaluation cases are labeled by references to existing records (not post-hoc judgments). 16 Beijing personas are simulated; data is compared to held-out real benchmarks; 717 evaluation cases generated without scripted interactions; failures identified as assistant-side retrieval errors via snapshot pointers.
AI.result: Generated data closely matches held-out benchmarks: Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) of 0.070 for category distribution and <0.1 for daily rhythm of communication; generated records are shorter than real ones; 78 failures surfaced in a production smartphone assistant, concentrated in calls and SMS; contacts, schedules, and alarms did not fail; snapshot pointers validate failures as retrieval errors without LLM judging; data is privacy-safe, reproducible, and distribution-checked.
AI.conclusion: SenWorld provides a privacy-safe, reproducible, and distribution-checked path to evaluation data for smartphone assistants with ground-truth labels built by construction, enabling robust, shareable benchmarking without reliance on LLM judges; limitations include shorter generated traces and potential generalization to other settings.

title: WearWow: Native 2K Multi-Garment Virtual Try-On via Adaptive Token Packing and Preference Alignment
summary: Synthesizing native 2K multi-garment virtual try-on is a formidable frontier in digital fashion, critically bottlenecked by two fundamental limitations: the O(N^2) memory explosion induced by 2k conditions, and the spectral bias of diffusion models that over-smooths high-frequency fabric details. We present WearWow, an end-to-end, mask-free generative framework that pioneers ultra-high-resolution multi-garment synthesis. To mitigate the memory explosion , we propose Adaptive 2D Token Packing (ATP). ATP leverages inherent garment sparsity to algorithmically pack heterogeneous items onto a unified 2D canvas and prune uninformative background tokens, minimizing the effective sequence length and subsequent memory overhead while rigorously preserving 2D spatial priors. To rectify texture degradation, we introduce the Multi-dimensional Try-on Reward (MTR) system. MTR synergizes a Semantic Guidance Reward to explicitly drive tactile restoration with a Cloth Distribution Reward to implicitly anchor the physical distribution, a joint formulation that effectively mitigates the severe reward hacking. Furthermore, we curate WearWow-2K, an extreme-quality dataset comprising native 2K triplets, providing physically correct spatial interactions that naturally empower the model's mask-free generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that WearWow establishes a new state-of-the-art, exceeding existing commercial baselines in native 2K multi-garment synthesis.

AI.tldr: WearWow presents a end-to-end, mask-free ultra-high-resolution (native 2K) multi-garment synthesis framework. It introduces Adaptive 2D Token Packing (ATP) to reduce memory by packing garments onto a unified 2D canvas and pruning background tokens, and Multi-dimensional Try-on Reward (MTR) to improve texture fidelity via Semantic Guidance Reward and Cloth Distribution Reward, supported by WearWow-2K, a high-quality 2K dataset. It reports state-of-the-art results against commercial baselines.
AI.motivation: The work targets two core bottlenecks in native 2K multi-garment virtual try-on: (i) O(N^2) memory growth caused by 2K token-level conditions, and (ii) diffusion models' spectral bias that over-smooths high-frequency fabric details. Mask-free generation at ultra-high resolution requires scalable memory and faithful texture rendering, which are not fully addressed by prior methods.
AI.method: Adaptive 2D Token Packing (ATP): exploits garment sparsity to pack heterogeneous garments on a single 2D canvas and prune uninformative background tokens, reducing the effective sequence length and memory usage while preserving 2D spatial priors. Multi-dimensional Try-on Reward (MTR): combines a Semantic Guidance Reward to drive tactile restoration with a Cloth Distribution Reward to anchor physical distribution, forming a joint objective that mitigates reward hacking. WearWow-2K: a native-2K dataset of 2K-resolution triplets with physically correct spatial interactions to enable mask-free, high-fidelity generation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art performance for native 2K multi-garment synthesis, surpassing existing commercial baselines.
AI.conclusion: WearWow demonstrates a scalable, end-to-end solution for ultra-high-resolution mask-free multi-garment generation with memory-efficient token handling and improved texture fidelity, underpinned by a high-quality 2K dataset.

title: SynPre-FL: Synthetic data-driven pretraining integrated Federated Learning training framework
summary: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to privacy-preserving clinical risk prediction, but its deployment remains limited by restricted data sharing, client heterogeneity, class imbalance, and the lack of realistic tabular electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks. Synthetic data generation may alleviate data scarcity, yet its integration with federated optimisation has received limited systematic study. We propose SynPre-FL, a unified framework combining high-fidelity synthetic EHR generation with synthetic-pretrained FL for robust prediction under non-IID conditions. A latent autoencoder-diffusion model generates privacy-preserving synthetic cohorts, which are used to warm-start federated training. This pretraining is followed by heterogeneity-aware optimisation using class-balanced local objectives, proximal regularisation, and adaptive server aggregation. Post-hoc calibration and federated-safe explainability support reliable and interpretable risk estimates. Experiments show that the synthetic generator preserves univariate, bivariate, and multivariate structure while protecting against membership-inference and reconstruction attacks. The generated data achieve strong downstream utility under TSTR, TRTS, and model-based evaluations. Across federated settings with 5, 10, and 15 heterogeneous clients, SynPre-FL consistently improves robustness and scalability over baseline methods, especially under severe non-IID fragmentation. Calibration improves probability reliability, while SHAP analysis produces stable and clinically coherent feature attributions across federation sizes. SynPre-FL therefore provides a practical and reproducible framework for combining synthetic data with FL to enable privacy-aware, interpretable, and robust clinical prediction from distributed tabular EHR data.

AI.tldr: SynPre-FL combines high-fidelity synthetic EHR generation with synthetic-pretrained federated learning to improve privacy, robustness, and interpretability in non-IID distributed tabular data.
AI.motivation: Federated learning for clinical risk prediction is limited by restricted data sharing, client heterogeneity, class imbalance, and lack of realistic tabular EHR benchmarks. Synthetic data can alleviate scarcity, but its integration with federated optimization requires systematic study.
AI.method: Train a latent autoencoder–diffusion model to generate privacy-preserving synthetic EHR cohorts. Use these cohorts to warm-start federated training, followed by heterogeneity-aware optimization using class-balanced local objectives, proximal regularisation, and adaptive server aggregation. Apply post-hoc calibration and federated-safe SHAP explainability.
AI.result: Synthetic data preserve univariate, bivariate, and multivariate dependencies and resist membership inference and reconstruction attacks. Downstream utility is strong under TSTR, TRTS, and model-based evaluations. Across federated settings with 5, 10, and 15 heterogeneous clients, SynPre-FL improves robustness and scalability over baselines, especially under severe non-IID fragmentation. Calibration improves probability reliability; SHAP yields stable, clinically coherent feature attributions across federation sizes.
AI.conclusion: SynPre-FL offers a practical and reproducible framework to combine synthetic data with federated learning for privacy-aware, interpretable, and robust prediction from distributed tabular EHR data.

title: EvoThink: Evolving Thinking in Large Reasoning Models via Self-Pruning and Aha-Moment Preference Optimization
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) often suffer from overthinking due to redundant verification steps. Existing approaches for mitigating overthinking, such as fast-slow thinking switching and reasoning trajectory compression, fail to make a fine-grained distinction between beneficial and redundant steps within the LRM's reasoning process, and may thus impair reasoning capability in their pursuit of efficiency. To simultaneously improve reasoning efficiency and capability, we propose EvoThink, a framework that reduces redundant verification and encourages the exploration of new reasoning paths. EvoThink comprises two key components: Self-Pruning Training (SPT), an unsupervised method that iteratively prunes redundant reasoning steps and self-trains on the concise trajectories; and Aha-Moment Preference Optimization (AMPO), which, inspired by genetic algorithms, identifies valuable failed reasoning attempts, synthesizes from-wrong-to-right aha-moment data, and optimizes the model to internalize this reasoning pattern. Extensive evaluations across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks demonstrate that EvoThink not only substantially reduces inference-time token usage but also improves the reasoning capability of LRMs.

AI.tldr: EvoThink reduces redundant reasoning steps in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) by pruning and learning from efficient trajectories and aha-moments; it combines Self-Pruning Training (SPT) and Aha-Moment Preference Optimization (AMPO) to cut verification overhead while boosting reasoning capability.
AI.motivation: LRMs often overthink due to redundant verification steps; existing mitigation methods either lack fine-grained discrimination between useful vs. redundant steps or trade efficiency for capability. A method that selectively prunes useless steps and learns from productive missteps could improve both efficiency and reasoning quality.
AI.method: SPT: unsupervised iterative pruning of redundant reasoning steps with self-training on concise trajectories. AMPO: inspired by genetic algorithms; selects valuable failed reasoning attempts, derives from-wrong-to-right aha-moments, and optimizes internal reasoning patterns.
AI.result: EvoThink substantially reduces inference-time token usage and enhances reasoning capability across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: A coordinated framework combining pruning of redundant steps and learning from productive missteps yields both efficiency gains and improved reasoning performance for LRMs.

title: G-MAD: A Game-Based Data Generation Framework for Multi-View RGB-T Aerial Object Detection
summary: This work introduces G-MAD, an open-source framework that uses Arma3 to generate synchronized multi-view RGB-T data for aerial object detection. G-MAD addresses key limitations of real-world aerial dataset construction, including limited viewpoint control, imperfect RGB-T alignment and high annotation cost. The framework supports structured scenario specification, controllable multi-view camera placement, simultaneous visible/thermal capture, and automatic bounding box annotation using engine-level geometric metadata. These capabilities enable controlled studies of viewpoint variation, multi-modal fusion, and synthetic-to-real transfer in aerial object detection. Besides, using G-MAD, we construct and release AMOD, a new large-scale multi-view aerial RGB-T object detection benchmark. The source code and the dataset are available at https://unique-chan.github.io/G-MAD-Project.

AI.tldr: G-MAD is an open-source Arma3-based framework that generates synchronized multi-view RGB-T data for aerial object detection, enabling controlled viewpoint studies, multi-modal fusion analysis, and synthetic-to-real transfer; it also releases AMOD, a large-scale benchmark.
AI.motivation: Real-world aerial datasets face limitations such as restricted viewpoint control, imperfect RGB-T alignment, and high annotation costs. A controllable, automated, and scalable synthetic data pipeline can address these challenges and facilitate systematic studies of viewpoint variation and sensor fusion.
AI.method: Utilizes Arma3 within a framework (G-MAD) to specify structured scenarios, place multiple synchronized RGB and thermal cameras, capture aligned modalities, and automatically annotate bounding boxes using engine-level geometric metadata. Produces a large-scale multi-view RGB-T dataset (AMOD) for aerial object detection, with open-source code and dataset released.
AI.result: Introduction of AMOD, a new large-scale multi-view aerial RGB-T object detection benchmark. Open-source code and dataset are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: G-MAD enables controlled experiments on viewpoint variation, multi-modal fusion, and synthetic-to-real transfer in aerial object detection and provides a reusable platform for future research.

title: The C-index illusion: discrimination without calibration in published survival models
summary: "Stop Chasing the C-index when Evaluating Survival Analysis Models" (ICML 2026, Spotlight) argued normatively, on synthetic data, that evaluating survival models by discrimination alone, i.e. the concordance index, produces systematically misleading model comparisons, because the metric ignores calibration and time-dependent accuracy. Whether this matters for real, published, non-clinical models has not been tested. We reproduce three published survival-ML models across three structurally distinct domains (hard-drive failure, peer-to-peer credit default, and user disengagement on digital platforms), validate our evaluation instrument against the anchor paper's own synthetic experiment, and test five pre-registered hypotheses under a Holm-corrected family-wise error rate. Three of five reject. A model that reproduces the published discrimination almost exactly (C = 0.9595 vs. 0.958 reported) fails a formal calibration test at p = 2.6e-136; a broad feature-ablation search finds no single attribute responsible for this discrimination, so the calibration failure is not an artifact of a trivial shortcut. A lender's estimated default risk is biased upward by roughly two percentage points, growing to nearly four points in the riskiest segment, when loan prepayment is treated as non-informative censoring rather than as a competing risk. A platform's churn model shows probability estimates that degrade with the prediction horizon even as its global discrimination stays within the pre-registered C-index band. A direct test of whether metric choice inverts which model is preferred does not reject, though with limited power given only two to three models per domain; the failure mode we document is better characterized as misplaced confidence in a chosen model than as choice of the wrong one. We release a reusable, pre-registered evaluation harness with full code and a single annotated notebook.

AI.tldr: Replication and evaluation study showing that concordance index (C-index) alone can mislead survival-model comparisons in real data; three of five preregistered hypotheses refuted, with significant calibration issues and impact of competing risks; release of a preregistered evaluation harness.
AI.motivation: Test whether evaluating survival models by discrimination alone (C-index) is sufficient in real-world, non-clinical domains and validate the anchor paper’s synthetic findings using multiple datasets and pre-registered hypotheses.
AI.method: Reproduce three published survival-ML models across three domains (hard-drive failure, P2P credit default, user churn); validate evaluation against the anchor paper’s synthetic setting; test five preregistered hypotheses with Holm-corrected FWER; conduct calibration tests, assess effects of treating competing risks, and evaluate horizon-dependent calibration; provide a reusable, preregistered evaluation harness with code.
AI.result: Three of five preregistered hypotheses are rejected; a model with nearly identical C-index still fails a formal calibration test (p ≈ 2.6e-136); feature ablation does not single out a cause for miscalibration; effect of treating prepayment as non-informative censoring biases default risk estimates upward (2–4 percentage points); churn model shows horizon-dependent calibration degradation despite stable discrimination; a direct test of metric choice changing preferred model shows limited power and does not reject; overall, calibration and horizon effects can invalidate conclusions drawn from discrimination alone; a preregistered evaluation harness is released.
AI.conclusion: Discrimination (C-index) alone is insufficient to compare survival models in real data; calibration and time-dependent accuracy must be incorporated; competing risks materially affect risk estimates; preregistered evaluation tools enable more robust, transparent model comparison and reduce overconfidence in model choice.

title: The Giant Hippocampus: From Structural Monoculture to a System of Systems
summary: AI researchers describe state-of-the-art models as one thing repeated at scale: the Transformer, wired identically for text, pixels, or speech. Neuroscientists describe the cortex as a mosaic - dense Layer 4 in visual cortex for spatial encoding, thick Layers 5/6 in motion cortex for temporal integration - different jobs solved by different structures. This paper argues the gap is a structural error, not a stylistic one, and is measurable. A century of cytoarchitecture, from Brodmann to single-cell Patch-seq, shows distinct cognitive functions are implemented by qualitatively different structures, not by rescaling one template. The convolutional neural network is the field's own proof: local receptive fields and hierarchical depth encoded this prior directly, reaching strong image recognition on far less data than later architectures needed. The paper traces how this lesson was discarded: the "Hardware Lottery" made the Transformer the path of least resistance, not the principled choice, and Mixture-of-Experts, often cited as diversity, in fact partitions parameters among identical experts. A functionalist analysis shows the Transformer is best understood as a functional analog of the hippocampal formation, not a general-purpose cortex - the same mistake as treating cortex as one giant Broca's area, except the field has now standardized on a giant hippocampus, applied to tasks it was never built for: audition, executive gating, working memory. The paper closes with an alternative: a Heterogeneous Topological Network, a System of Systems in which distinct modules keep the inductive bias their computation demands and communicate through standardized interfaces. This is a design discipline for AI architects, not cognitive science: specify modularity before training, using structural evidence as a design input rather than reverse-engineering architecture from a trained model's behavior.

AI.tldr: Transformers are not a universal cortex; the paper argues cognitive functions arise from qualitatively different neural structures, not simply scaled templates. It critiques the Hardware Lottery and Mixture-of-Experts, reframes current diversity, and advocates a Heterogeneous Topological Network—modular, system-of-systems designs guided by structural neuroscience.
AI.motivation: Address the mismatch between AI architectures (single-template transformers) and biological cortex, arguing that cognitive functions are implemented by distinct structures; emphasize structural evidence as a design input for AI architectures.
AI.method: Historical and functionalist analysis across neuroscience (cytoarchitecture to Patch-seq) and AI practice; critique of hardware-driven choices; evaluation of Mixture-of-Experts and Transformers; proposal of a prescriptive architectural design framework.
AI.result: A heterogenous topology design is proposed as a more faithful, scalable architecture; Transformers are viewed as a functional analog of hippocampus rather than a general cortex; Mixture-of-Experts is mischaracterized as diversity; call for modular systems with standardized interfaces and task-aligned inductive biases.
AI.conclusion: Adopt a design discipline that specifies modularity and inductive biases before training, guided by structural neuroscience; replace post hoc architecture discovery with prescriptive, architecture-level design informed by biology.

title: SIINR: Structurally Informed Implicit Neural Representations for super-resolution with uncertainty quantification of clinical quality diffusion MRI datasets
summary: Diffusion Magnetic Resonance Imaging (dMRI) is a powerful tool for probing brain microstructure, but clinical acquisitions are often limited by low out-of-plane resolution, resulting in degraded structural information and reduced utility for advanced analysis. We introduce SIINR (Structurally Informed Implicit Neural Representations), a general framework for super-resoltion of clinical dMRI datasets while quantifying uncertainty in the reconstructed outputs. SIINR utilizes a supervised 3D U-net as a prior and combines it with a self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) that fuses the high-resolution prior and the original low-resolution data. The INR enables joint modeling across spatial and angular domains, enforces data consistency, and provides analytic approximate posterior distributions for downstream uncertainty quantification. We validate the framework on a diverse set of open-access dMRI datasets, demonstrating that SIINR outperforms standard interpolation methods in both quantitative error metrics and qualitative anatomical fidelity. Experiments on clinical cases, including subjects with multiple sclerosis and brain lesions, illustrate the framework its ability to propagate intensity changes and flag uncertain regions in challenging scenarios. SIINR is flexible, modular, and can be adapted to different upsampling ratios and downstream tasks, providing a principled approach for enhancing clinical dMRI and supporting robust interpretation of derived neuroimaging metrics.

AI.tldr: SIINR combines a supervised 3D U-net prior with a self-supervised implicit neural representation to upsample clinical diffusion MRI, enabling joint spatial-angular modeling, data consistency, and uncertainty quantification; it outperforms interpolation and handles lesions, offering a modular, task-adaptive framework.
AI.motivation: Clinical dMRI suffers from low out-of-plane resolution, leading to degraded structural information and unreliable downstream metrics. There is a need for a method that leverages priors while providing uncertainty estimates for robust interpretation.
AI.method: A two-component framework: (1) a supervised 3D U-net prior; (2) a self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) that fuses the high-resolution prior with the low-resolution data across spatial and angular domains. The INR enforces data consistency, models across spatial-angular domains, and yields analytic approximate posterior distributions for uncertainty. The approach is validated on open-access dMRI datasets and tested on clinical cases (e.g., multiple sclerosis with brain lesions).
AI.result: SIINR outperforms standard interpolation in quantitative error metrics and qualitative anatomical fidelity. It can propagate intensity changes in challenging cases and flag uncertain regions, demonstrating robust performance and uncertainty awareness.
AI.conclusion: SIINR offers a principled, flexible, and modular framework for clinically relevant diffusion MRI super-resolution, capable of adapting to different upsampling ratios and downstream tasks while providing uncertainty quantification to support robust interpretation of derived metrics.

title: Trustworthy Privacy-Preserving Multimodal Federated Learning for Personalised Breast Cancer Prediction
summary: Federated learning has emerged as a potential solution to privacy concerns associated with using sensitive health data for training predictive models, particularly in personalised cancer care. This research investigates whether federated learning can support the development of robust models for predicting tumour progression in breast cancer patients while addressing four critical deployment pillars: transparency, scalability, security, and fairness. This study evaluates a federated learning framework using multimodal data, including clinical information, tumour characteristics, biomarker data, and patient demographics, alongside medical imaging data such as MRI scans, to model changes in tumour characteristics over time. The performance of the federated approach was compared with that of a centralised model trained on aggregated data. The report then further examines strategies to enhance secure model updates, maintain performance across patient subgroups, and support scalability across institutions. The findings assess whether federated learning can achieve predictive performance comparable to centralised learning while preserving data locality. These results contribute to understanding the feasibility of privacy-preserving, multimodal predictive modelling and support future applications such as digital twins to assist clinicians and patients in personalised treatment planning.

AI.tldr: Federated learning with multimodal breast cancer data to predict tumour progression; compares with centralized model; evaluates transparency, scalability, security, and fairness; explores secure updates and subgroup performance; aims for data locality preservation and potential digital twin applications.
AI.motivation: Privacy and regulatory constraints in using sensitive health data; need robust, scalable, and fair predictive models leveraging multimodal data.
AI.method: Develop and evaluate a federated learning framework integrating clinical, biomarker, imaging (MRI), tumor characteristics, and demographics; compare to centralized model; assess security strategies for updates; analyze performance across patient subgroups and scalability across institutions; discuss implications for digital twins.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; indicates comparative evaluation between FL and centralized model; no concrete performance metrics; mentions feasibility and strategies to preserve performance and scalability.
AI.conclusion: Federated learning is a feasible approach for privacy-preserving multimodal predictive modelling in personalised cancer care; can achieve performance comparable to centralized learning under appropriate strategies; emphasizes transparency, security, scalability, and fairness; supports future digital twin applications, with need for subgroup fairness and cross-institution scalability.

title: Coordinating from Memory: Graph-Structured Experience Reuse for Multi-Agent Adaptation in Dynamic Manufacturing
summary: Dynamic manufacturing environments require multi-agent systems to coordinate effectively under frequent operational disturbances such as machine failures, urgent job arrivals, and processing time variations. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches treat each disturbance episode independently, discarding valuable coordination experience that could accelerate future adaptation. In this paper, we propose a Graph-Structured Experiential Memory (GSEM) framework for multi-agent coordination in dynamic manufacturing. The framework encodes historical coordination episodes as heterogeneous relational graphs that capture task dependencies, machine states, and inter-agent collaboration patterns. When a new disturbance occurs, a graph neural network-based retrieval mechanism identifies structurally similar past episodes, enabling experience-guided policy adaptation rather than learning from scratch. Experiments on dynamic flexible job-shop scheduling benchmarks with three disturbance types show that GSEM reduces makespan by 4.1%-10.0% and adaptation time by 33%-38% compared to the strongest memory-augmented baseline, with the advantage increasing under higher disturbance frequency. Ablation studies and cross-disturbance transfer experiments further validate the necessity of graph-structured encoding and similarity-based retrieval and demonstrate the cross-disturbance generalizability of learned coordination patterns.

AI.tldr: Graph-Structured Experiential Memory (GSEM) enables graph-based retrieval of past coordination episodes to guide policy adaptation in dynamic manufacturing, yielding improvements in makespan and adaptation time, with better cross-disturbance transfer.
AI.motivation: Dynamic manufacturing with frequent disturbances causes coordination challenges; existing multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches treat disturbances episode-by-episode, losing potentially valuable prior coordination experience.
AI.method: GSEM encodes historical coordination episodes as heterogeneous relational graphs capturing task dependencies, machine states, and inter-agent collaboration. A graph neural network-based retrieval mechanism identifies structurally similar past episodes to guide policy adaptation rather than learning from scratch.
AI.result: Experiments on dynamic flexible job-shop scheduling benchmarks with three disturbance types show makespan reductions of 4.1%-10.0% and adaptation-time reductions of 33%-38% compared to the strongest memory-augmented baseline, with larger gains at higher disturbance frequency. Ablation studies and cross-disturbance transfer experiments validate the necessity of graph-structured encoding and similarity-based retrieval, and demonstrate cross-disturbance generalizability of learned coordination patterns.
AI.conclusion: Graph-structured encoding and similarity-based retrieval are crucial for effective cross-disturbance coordination in dynamic manufacturing; GSEM offers faster adaptation and better generalization by leveraging past experiences.

title: ETPDesigner: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Interactive Multimodal Electronic Theater Program
summary: Electronic Theater Programs (ETPs) serve as critical promotional media in the performing arts, comprising a multi-page collection of heterogeneous visual assets such as theatrical posters, performance details, and character portraits. However, existing text-to-image paradigms struggle with such complex design tasks due to their inability to comprehend long-context narratives and maintain visual consistency across multiple distinct pages. To address this, we introduce ETPDesigner, a collaborative Multi-Agent framework that directly synthesizes high-quality ETPs from raw dramatic scripts. Emulating a professional design pipeline, our framework orchestrates specialized agents for semantic script analysis, core poster synthesis, functional background generation, and the stratified composition of character assets. Central to ETPDesigner is a global style anchor mechanism that extracts visual priors from the core poster to enforce strict aesthetic uniformity across all generated components. Furthermore, we elevate the ETP from a static publication to an immersive interactive companion. By integrating portrait animation, customized speech synthesis, and persona-grounded Large Language Models (LLMs), our system enables users to engage in real-time, voice-enabled conversations with the generated virtual characters. To rigorously benchmark this task, we construct ETP-Pro, a domain-specific benchmark of professional theater posters and high-quality character portraits. Extensive evaluations demonstrate our method's superiority in producing semantically faithful, aesthetically consistent, and highly interactive program sets.

AI.tldr: Proposes ETPDesigner, a multi-agent system that composes coherent, multi-page Electronic Theater Programs from scripts, using a global style anchor for aesthetic consistency and an interactive avatar extension. Introduces ETP-Pro benchmark and demonstrates superior semantic fidelity, visual coherence, and interactivity.
AI.motivation: ETPs are complex, multi-page promotional artifacts requiring long-range narrative understanding and cross-page visual consistency. Current text-to-image methods struggle to maintain coherence across pages and integrate interactive components.
AI.method: A collaborative multi-agent pipeline: (1) semantic script analysis agent, (2) core poster synthesis agent, (3) functional background generation agent, (4) stratified character asset composition agent; a global style anchor captures visual priors from the core poster to enforce uniform aesthetics across all pages; an interactive extension adds portrait animation, speech synthesis, and persona-grounded LLMs.
AI.result: ETPDesigner yields semantically faithful, aesthetically consistent, and highly interactive ETPs; ETP-Pro provides a domain-specific benchmark for professional theater posters and character portraits; extensive evaluations demonstrate superiority over baselines.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully translates dramatic scripts into cohesive, multi-page, and interactive theater programs with strong style consistency, and the introduced benchmark enables targeted evaluation for future work in design-aware generation and interactive media.

title: Agent-Centric Animal Pose Forecasting
summary: Understanding animal behavior at an algorithmic level -- what animals attend to, how they form internal models and plans, and how this maps to action -- remains a central challenge in neuroscience and ethology. Data-driven generative models offer a path toward this understanding. We introduce a framework for training agent-centric autoregressive models of animal behavior from tracked pose, applicable to single animals and to groups in which each agent senses and responds to its conspecifics. Our models input egocentric sensory observations and output egocentric movements, mirroring the biological constraint that animals observe and act on the world from their own reference frame. Social behavior emerges from agents independently sensing and responding to one another. This agent-centric formulation requires managing many parallel representations of the same data, along with ML-specific transformations like discretization. We release a general-purpose library focused on the composable sequences of operations that translate between these representations. We show that trained models capture the distribution of social behavior in groups of courting Drosophila, and our library includes quantitative tools for measuring fit. We demonstrate how the library supports systematic comparison across input and output representations and that it adapts straightforwardly to a new domain.

AI.tldr: Agent-centric autoregressive models trained on tracked pose to model social animal behavior, scalable to groups, with a library of representation-translation tools; demonstrated on courting Drosophila with quantitative fit and cross-representation comparability.
AI.motivation: Delineate the algorithmic level of animal behavior by learning generative, egocentric models that map observations to actions; enable interpretable, comparison-friendly analysis of social interactions and multi-agent dynamics.
AI.method: Train agent-centric autoregressive generative models using egocentric observations to predict egocentric movements. In groups, each agent senses and responds to conspecifics; manage parallel representations and apply discretization. Release a modular library of operations to translate between different input/output representations and evaluate fit.
AI.result: The models capture the distribution of social behavior in courting Drosophila groups; the library provides quantitative tools to measure fit and to compare input/output representations; the approach generalizes to new domains.
AI.conclusion: This framework advances understanding of social behavior in an algorithmic, model-based way and provides practical, adaptable tools for systematic representation comparison across domains.

title: CLARK: Closed-loop Learning for Adaptive Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs
comment: 18 pages, 3 Figures, 1 algorithm, 3 tables, submitted to The International Semantic Web Conference'26
summary: Machine Learning models are widely used for automating classification tasks by extracting statistical patterns from data. However, their performance deteriorates if the data distribution changes, making them ill-suited to handle uncertain and evolving information. Moreover, they provide limited support for integrating prior knowledge. To address these limitations, we present CLARK (Closed-loop Learning for Adaptive Reasoning over Knowledge Graphs), a framework that integrates knowledge graphs, symbolic rule mining, and probabilistic reasoning under the Logic Programs with Markov Logic Networks (LP$^{\text{MLN}}$) formalism. Starting from CACTUS-derived KGs, CLARK translates graph structure into an LP$^{\text{MLN}}$ program and iteratively enriches it with candidate rules proposed by symbolic learners. These rules are calibrated through probabilistic weight learning, enabling reasoning under uncertainty and refinement of the underlying graph structure. We evaluate CLARK on two medical datasets, analysing both rule quality and downstream classification performance. Results demonstrate that CLARK leads to improved classification performance and more generalisable inference. Overall, CLARK provides a principled approach to constructing adaptive, interpretable, knowledge-driven models for classification.

AI.tldr: CLARK unifies knowledge graphs, symbolic rule mining, and LP^MLN-based probabilistic reasoning to iteratively refine graph structure and rules, achieving improved classification and generalization on medical data.
AI.motivation: Machine learning models struggle with distribution shift, uncertainty, and limited incorporation of prior knowledge; there is a need for adaptive, interpretable, knowledge-driven classification frameworks.
AI.method: Initialize with CACTUS-derived KGs, convert graph structure into an LP^MLN program, iteratively propose candidate rules from symbolic learners, calibrate their weights via probabilistic learning, and refine both graph structure and rules; evaluate on two medical datasets focusing on rule quality and downstream classification performance.
AI.result: CLARK yields improved classification performance and more generalizable inference; enhanced rule quality; demonstrates a principled, adaptive framework that integrates KG, symbolic learning, and probabilistic reasoning.
AI.conclusion: A principled approach for adaptive, interpretable knowledge-driven classification that combines knowledge graphs, symbolic rule mining, and LP^MLN-based probabilistic reasoning, with demonstrated gains on medical data.

title: OffNadirLoc: Benchmark and Framework for Challenging UAV-to-Satellite Geo-Localization under Large Off-Nadir Views
summary: Cross-view geo-localization between UAV and satellite imagery remains a fundamental yet highly challenging task, especially under large off-nadir views where drastic perspective distortions, occlusions, and appearance gaps occur. Existing benchmarks and methods primarily focus on near-nadir scenarios and often overlook the importance of structural scene understanding and intra-domain relational constraints, limiting their performance in real-world deployments. In this work, we introduce OffNadirLoc, a new benchmark for large off-nadir UAV-to-satellite geo-localization. To tackle the unique challenges posed by off-nadir perspectives, we further propose ONLoc, a framework that incorporates a structure-aware contextual weighting mechanism to dynamically emphasize reliable local features while suppressing ambiguous or repetitive regions.
