Additionally, we design a view-coherent learning strategy, which treats one satellite image and the corresponding UAV images from multiple views as a cohesive semantic group. This set-level supervision enables the model to learn viewpoint-invariant and discriminative features, making it more effective at capturing multi-view consistency than conventional pairwise contrastive learning. Extensive experiments on the OffNadirLoc benchmark and four near-nadir datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches while exhibiting strong zero-shot generalization to unseen datasets without additional training. The code will be released at https://montalario.github.io/offnadirloc/.

AI.tldr: New OffNadirLoc benchmark plus ONLoc framework for UAV-to-satellite geo-localization under large off-nadir views; uses structure-aware weighting and view-coherent set-level learning, achieving state-of-the-art results and strong zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: To address drastic perspective distortions, occlusions, and appearance gaps in off-nadir UAV-to-satellite matching; existing benchmarks focus on near-nadir and neglect structural scene understanding and intra-domain constraints, limiting real-world performance.
AI.method: 1) Structure-aware contextual weighting to emphasize reliable local features while suppressing ambiguous or repetitive regions; 2) View-coherent learning: treat one satellite image and multiple UAV views as a cohesive semantic group with set-level supervision to learn viewpoint-invariant, discriminative, and multi-view-consistent features.
AI.result: Experiments on OffNadirLoc and four near-nadir datasets show the method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods and exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to unseen datasets without additional training.
AI.conclusion: OffNadirLoc and ONLoc improve cross-view geo-localization under off-nadir perspectives and generalize across datasets; code will be released publicly.

title: End-to-End Differential Privacy in Training Deep Neural Network Classifiers
summary: Differentially private machine learning enables model training on sensitive data while ensuring that individual data is unlikely to be recoverable from the parameters of the resulting model. However, existing work often privatizes both training inputs and their labels, and these protections may be conservative when labels are public or can be safely made public. Therefore, in this work we propose a novel private training framework that instead privatizes training inputs while keeping labels public. We consider neural networks with softmax output layers, and thus the mapping from training inputs to the output of the softmax layer is a mapping onto the unit simplex. We randomize softmax outputs during training by applying the Dirichlet mechanism to enforce differential privacy for the training inputs, hence the ``end-to-end'' label. Because training data is reused across multiple training epochs, we use the notion of \Renyi differential privacy to formulate tight bounds on the strength of privacy provided by the Dirichlet mechanism across repeated uses. We show empirically that we attain new state-of-the-art accuracy when training from scratch on CIFAR10, MNIST, MedMNIST, FashionMNIST, and SVHN across all privacy budgets evaluated. Notably, when implementing $(ε, δ)$-differential privacy with $δ=10^{-5}$, we improve the prior state-of-the-art accuracy from $78.37\%$ to $88.17\%$ at $ε=4$ on CIFAR10, and our approach has $82.96\%$ accuracy even for $ε=1$, which significantly outperforms prior work.

AI.tldr: Proposes input-private training for neural networks by applying Dirichlet DP to the softmax outputs, keeping labels public; uses Rényi DP for tight across-epoch composition; reports state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10, MNIST-family datasets, and SVHN, including 88.17% at ε=4 (δ=1e-5) and 82.96% at ε=1.
AI.motivation: Existing differential privacy approaches often privatize both inputs and labels; if labels can be public, privatizing inputs alone can improve utility while preserving privacy. The mapping from inputs to softmax outputs lies on the unit simplex, enabling a Dirichlet mechanism to enforce DP. Reusing data across epochs necessitates tight accounting, for which Rényi DP is employed.
AI.method: Use neural networks with softmax output layers. Apply the Dirichlet mechanism to the softmax outputs during training to privatize the training inputs while keeping labels public. Use Rényi differential privacy to analyze privacy loss across repeated training epochs (composition).
AI.result: Empirically achieves new state-of-the-art accuracy on from-scratch training across CIFAR-10, MNIST, MedMNIST, FashionMNIST, and SVHN for various privacy budgets. In particular, with δ=1e-5, ε=4 yields 88.17% on CIFAR-10 (improving from 78.37%), and the method attains 82.96% accuracy at ε=1.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates that privatizing only inputs can attain strong utility under DP, surpassing prior input-privatization results and achieving competitive performance across diverse datasets. Rényi DP provides tight privacy accounting across epochs, suggesting practical applicability for privacy-preserving learning when labels can be public.

title: Safe Remediation as Risk-Constrained Intervention Decision in Microservice Systems
summary: In modern IT operations (IT-Ops), the cost of an incorrect repair often exceeds the cost of no action at all. Yet existing automated remediation systems are designed to generate actions rather than to decide whether intervention is warranted, leaving safety as an afterthought enforced by manual approval. This paper makes three contributions to close this gap: (i) we reformulate safe remediation as a risk-constrained intervention decision problem and cast it as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP), in which the agent maximizes repair success subject to a bounded false remediation rate (FRR); (ii) we introduce a three-dimensional risk decomposition comprising blast radius, reversibility, and epistemic uncertainty, providing operators with an interpretable per-action safety interface; and (iii) we design a context-adaptive human-in-the-loop (HITL) gate that turns escalation from a binary failsafe into a bandwidth-aware control layer responsive to on-call load and business criticality. The full policy is learned offline from historical incident logs, enabling explicit control of the expected FRR. Experiments on the Train Ticket microservice benchmark with Chaos Mesh fault injection and an RCAEval-aligned fault taxonomy show that our framework reduces FRR by 39% while improving repair success by 2.5 points over a strong runbook baseline, and reduces on-call escalation load by 17% relative to a fixed-threshold variant.

AI.tldr: A CMDP-based framework for safe IT remediation that optimizes repair success under a bounded false remediation rate, with interpretable risk-driven safety interface and a context-aware HITL gate; trained offline on incident logs; empirically reduces false remediation rate by 39%, increases repair success by 2.5 points, and lowers on-call escalation by 17%.
AI.motivation: In IT-Ops, incorrect repairs can be costlier than inaction. Current automated remediation often acts without assessing whether intervention is warranted, risking safety and escalations. The work aims to integrate safety into autonomous remediation by explicitly constraining risk, providing interpretability, and enabling a flexible human-in-the-loop mechanism.
AI.method: Formulate safe remediation as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) maximizing repair success subject to a bound on the false remediation rate (FRR). Introduce a three-dimensional risk decomposition (blast radius, reversibility, epistemic uncertainty) for per-action safety interpretability. Design a context-adaptive, bandwidth-aware HITL gate to manage escalations based on on-call load and business criticality. Learn the policy offline from historical incident logs to enable explicit control of expected FRR.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on the Train Ticket microservice benchmark with Chaos Mesh fault injection and RCAEval-aligned fault taxonomy shows: (1) FRR reduced by 39%, (2) repair success improved by 2.5 percentage points over a strong runbook baseline, and (3) on-call escalation load reduced by 17% relative to a fixed-threshold variant.
AI.conclusion: The framework delivers a safety-conscious, interpretable, and adaptive remediation policy that can explicitly cap risk while improving operational outcomes. It demonstrates that CMDP-based safe decision making, combined with risk-informed interfaces and a HITL gate, yields tangible reductions in unsafe interventions and operator load. Potential limitations include offline training generalization, distribution shift, and real-time scaling; future work could extend the approach to broader IT domains, refine the risk decomposition, and explore online adaptation.

title: Forecasting the Number of Harvest-ready Fruits of Sweet Peppers Using Multimodal Time-Series Data
summary: Accurate yield forecasting at the individual-plant level is critical for precision agriculture and supply-chain planning, yet public datasets capturing both visual growth dynamics and per-plant measurement labels are scarce. In this paper, we introduce a novel, annotated image time-series dataset of 691 sweet pepper plants monitored over two growing seasons, comprising 4837 images with per-plant fruit counts categorized by maturity. We propose a multimodal deep learning framework that fuses high-dimensional image features, extracted using the DinoV3 encoder, with numerical count measurements. Our architecture utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to model temporal dependencies and handles irregular sampling intervals common in greenhouse monitoring. Through quantitative experiments, we demonstrate that this multimodal approach reduces RMSE over a persistence baseline by 33% and 38% in the 2022 and 2023 seasons, respectively, with a further 1.2% average gain over a measurement-only model. Furthermore, we employ Deep Ensembles and Gaussian Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) to provide calibrated uncertainty estimates, with an Uncertainty Calibration Error (UCE) ranging from 0.39 to 0.89 depending on the cross-season evaluation direction, offering a principled confidence signal for real-world agricultural decision-making. We release the dataset and code to support reproducible research and to accelerate development of data-driven yield forecasting methods for horticultural crops.

AI.tldr: New annotated image time-series dataset for sweet pepper plants with per-plant fruit counts; a multimodal method fusing DinoV3 image features with numerical counts using LSTM to forecast yield under irregular sampling; shows large RMSE reductions and calibrated uncertainty; dataset and code released.
AI.motivation: Public datasets that jointly capture visual growth dynamics and per-plant labels are scarce, hindering data-driven yield forecasting in horticulture.
AI.method: Multimodal framework: visual features extracted with DinoV3 encoder, combined with numerical counts, fed into an LSTM to model temporal dynamics and handle irregular sampling. Uncertainty quantified via Deep Ensembles and Gaussian NLL; cross-season evaluation. Dataset of 691 plants, 4837 images, two growing seasons.
AI.result: RMSE reduced by 33% (2022) and 38% (2023) over a persistence baseline; +1.2% average gain over measurement-only model. Uncertainty Calibration Error (UCE) 0.39–0.89 across cross-season directions. Dataset and code released.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a valuable dataset and a robust multimodal forecasting framework with calibrated uncertainty for per-plant yield forecasting in horticulture, supporting reproducibility and practical decision-making.

title: The Mechanism Matters: When Knowledge Graphs Help Reinforcement Learning
summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are widely used to inject prior knowledge into reinforcement learning (RL), yet the literature is dominated by single-domain, positive-result method papers, so we lack a systematic account of when KG structure helps an agent, when it is neutral, and when it hurts. We conduct a controlled study that independently varies the RL task, the injection mechanism (state features, action masking, or potential-based reward shaping), and KG quality. Using a synthetic, fully controllable KG over MiniGrid environments, we report three findings. First, on compositional sparse-reward tasks structured KG guidance improves sample efficiency and solve reliability (70% to 97% of seeds), and a shuffle control that permutes the KG's edges while preserving their count collapses the benefit toward baseline (masking p=0.0001; shaping p=0.006), so the gain is structural rather than generic regularization. Second, KG value scales with the amount of task-relevant knowledge the graph contains. Third, and most consequential, safety depends on the mechanism: soft, optimality-preserving injection benefits from correct knowledge and harmlessly ignores incorrect knowledge, whereas hard masking is brittle, forbidding essential actions when the KG is incomplete or corrupted and making a wrong KG worse than none. A UMLS-derived clinical case study on sepsis management under offline RL is a careful null, underscoring that benefits require task structure the chosen mechanism can exploit. Our results give practitioners concrete guidance on how, and how much, to trust a KG when using it to guide RL.

AI.tldr: Structured KG guidance can improve RL sample efficiency and reliability when the KG is task-relevant and injected via soft, optimality-preserving mechanisms; benefits vanish with randomization of KG structure and are brittle under hard masking when KG is incomplete or corrupted; a clinical offline RL case study showed null benefits, highlighting the need for task-aligned KG use.
AI.motivation: There is a large literature on Knowledge Graphs (KGs) in RL, but no systematic account of when KG structure helps, is neutral, or harms performance across tasks, injection mechanisms, and KG quality.
AI.method: Controlled study varying the RL task, the KG injection mechanism (state features, action masking, or potential-based reward shaping), and KG quality using a synthetic, fully controllable KG over MiniGrid environments; includes a shuffle control that permutes KG edges (preserving edge count) to test structural benefits; plus a UMLS-derived clinical case study on sepsis management under offline RL as a null baseline.
AI.result: Three core findings: (1) On compositional sparse-reward tasks, structured KG guidance improves sample efficiency and solve reliability (70%–97% of seeds); shuffle control collapses the benefit toward baseline (masking p=0.0001; shaping p=0.006), indicating the gain is structural, not generic regularization. (2) KG value scales with the amount of task-relevant knowledge in the graph. (3) Safety depends on mechanism: soft, optimality-preserving injection benefits from correct knowledge and ignores incorrect knowledge, while hard masking is brittle, can forbid essential actions when KG is incomplete or corrupted, and can make a wrong KG worse than none. The UMLS-derived clinical case study on sepsis management under offline RL yields a null, underscoring that benefits require task structure the chosen mechanism can exploit. Practical guidance is provided on how much to trust a KG when guiding RL.
AI.conclusion: Guidance for practitioners: adopt task- and mechanism-aware KG integration; prefer soft, optimality-preserving injections with high-quality, task-relevant KG; avoid hard masking unless the KG is verified for completeness and correctness; ensure the KG encodes structure that the task can leverage to realize gains.

title: EvoDRC: A Self-Evolving Agentic Framework for Automated DRC Violation Repair
summary: Design rule check (DRC) closure remains a major bottleneck in advanced-node physical design. Although detailed routers are rule-aware, residual design rule violations (DRVs) often require manual engineering change order iterations. Automating this process is challenging because repairs must account for complex geometric interactions, preserve circuit connectivity, and avoid introducing new violations. We present EvoDRC, a skill-evolution framework for agentic block-level DRC repair. EvoDRC initializes layer-specific repair skills using knowledge distilled from an unrelated reference design and continuously evolves these skills using traceable repair experience collected from the target design. EvoDRC decomposes the layout into bounded repair regions and assigns an LLM repair agent to each region. Local DRC analysis, connectivity-checking, and impact-preview tools provide feedback on proposed modifications. Repair operations and their resulting DRV changes are stored in a knowledge database and used to evolve the repair skills. Experiments on seven block-level designs from the DAC26 DRC Benchmark show that EvoDRC achieves a 73.5\% overall reduction compared to the reported baseline.

AI.tldr: EvoDRC is a region-based, skill-evolution framework for block-level DRC repair that bootsraps repair skills via knowledge distillation from a reference design and evolves them through repair experience. It assigns an LLM repair agent to bounded layout regions, uses local checks and impact previews, and maintains a knowledge database to improve skills. On seven block-level designs from the DAC26 DRC Benchmark, it achieves a 73.5% overall reduction versus a baseline.
AI.motivation: DRC closure remains a bottleneck in advanced-node physical design. Despite rule-aware routers, residual DRVs require manual, iterative repairs that are difficult due to complex geometry, connectivity constraints, and the risk of creating new violations. Automating this process demands region-aware planning, robust feedback, and a traceable learning signal.
AI.method: Decompose the layout into bounded repair regions and assign an LLM-based repair agent to each region. Initialize layer-specific repair skills using knowledge distilled from an unrelated reference design. Continuously evolve these skills via traceable repair experience collected from the target design. Use local DRC analysis, connectivity checks, and impact previews to assess proposed modifications. Store repair operations and resulting DRV changes in a knowledge database to drive future skill evolution.
AI.result: Evaluated on seven block-level designs from the DAC26 DRC Benchmark, EvoDRC achieves a 73.5% overall reduction compared to the reported baseline.
AI.conclusion: EvoDRC effectively combines region-level LLM agents, skill evolution through a knowledge base, and feedback loops to substantially reduce DRC repair effort, demonstrating scalable automation potential for block-level designs in advanced-node processes.

title: STEREOFLOW: Progressive Stereo Matching with StereoDiT and Transition Flow Matching
summary: Stereo matching is a fundamental task in 3D reconstruction. Despite remarkable advances, the prevailing paradigms formulate stereo matching as a deterministic regression problem, collapsing the multimodal distribution modeling into a single-point estimation. This formulation suffers from a regression-to-mean bias, frequently struggling with ambiguous regions. In contrast, we introduce a prior-guided generative framework that integrates deterministic matching regression and generative distribution modeling within a complementary formulation. Built upon this formulation, we introduce StereoFlow through three key components: (i) a two-stage progressive cascade matching network that progressively produces multi-resolution stereo conditions with complementary matching cues; (ii) a pixel diffusion transformer (termed StereoDiT) with a frequency-decoupled architecture for modeling correspondence ambiguity; (iii) a few-step flow matching objective (termed Transition Flow Matching) for efficient optimization. In summary, \textsc{\textbf{StereoFlow}} achieves strong geometric consistency and rich fine-grained details in ill-posed, discontinuous regions and under zero-shot generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed StereoFlow establishes multiple state-of-the-art results across benchmarks, including Scene Flow, KITTI, ETH3D, and Middlebury.

AI.tldr: StereoFlow couples prior-guided generative modeling with deterministic stereo regression to address multimodal disparity, introducing a two-stage cascade matcher, a diffusion-based pixel transformer (StereoDiT), and a few-step transition-flow objective; achieving state-of-the-art results on major stereo benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Deterministic stereo regression suffers from regression-to-mean in ambiguous, multimodal regions and fails to capture the true disparity distribution. A prior-guided generative framework can model distributional ambiguity while preserving geometric consistency.
AI.method: (i) Two-stage progressive cascade matching network producing multi-resolution stereo cues; (ii) Pixel diffusion transformer (StereoDiT) with a frequency-decoupled architecture to model correspondence ambiguity; (iii) Transition Flow Matching for few-step optimization within a generative-distribution framework.
AI.result: StereoFlow yields strong geometric consistency and rich details in ill-posed/discontinuous regions, with zero-shot generalization, achieving state-of-the-art performance across Scene Flow, KITTI, ETH3D, and Middlebury.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework demonstrates that integrating deterministic matching regression with diffusion-based distribution modeling yields robust, high-fidelity stereo matching across diverse datasets and evaluation metrics.

title: SCPP: A Unified Python Library for Soft Clustering
summary: In this paper, we present SCPP (Soft Clustering Python Package), an open-source Python framework for soft clustering. SCPP establishes a canonical, scikit-learn-compatible estimator interface that standardizes model training, prediction, membership representation, evaluation, and benchmarking across heterogeneous soft clustering methods, including fuzzy, probabilistic, graph-based, matrix factorization, and deep learning methods. The framework currently integrates 40 representative algorithms together with a comprehensive benchmarking comprising datasets, clustering quality metrics, and standardized runtime, memory, and scalability evaluation. SCPP further provides extensive documentation, practical examples, automated testing, and seamless integration with the scientific Python ecosystem, enabling reproducible experimentation and straightforward extension with new algorithms. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/soft-clustering/soft-clustering.

AI.tldr: A new open-source framework, SCPP, provides a scikit-learn–compatible interface for soft clustering, integrating 40 algorithms and a comprehensive benchmarking suite to enable reproducible experiments.
AI.motivation: Addresses fragmentation in soft clustering methods by delivering a unified, extensible platform with a standardized API, benchmarking, and ecosystem integration for reproducible research and fair comparisons.
AI.method: Develop SCPP with a canonical estimator interface; integrate 40 representative soft clustering algorithms across fuzzy, probabilistic, graph-based, matrix factorization, and deep learning families; build comprehensive benchmarking with datasets, clustering quality metrics, and standardized runtime/memory/scalability evaluation; provide documentation, automated tests, and seamless Python ecosystem integration.
AI.result: A unified framework offering standardized APIs for training, prediction, and membership representation, plus extensive benchmarking and documentation; code publicly available at GitHub.
AI.conclusion: SCPP enables reproducible experimentation and straightforward extension with new algorithms, promoting broader adoption and fair cross-method comparisons in soft clustering.

title: Global Difference Constraint Propagation for Constraint Programming
summary: Difference constraints of the form $x - y \leq d$ are well studied, with efficient algorithms for satisfaction and implication, because of their connection to shortest paths. Finite domain propagation algorithms, however, typically do not make use of these algorithms, and treat each difference constraint as a separate propagator. Propagation does guarantee completeness of solving, but can be needlessly slow. In this paper we describe how to build a (bounds consistent) global propagator for difference constraints that treats them all simultaneously. SAT modulo theory solvers have included theory solvers for difference constraints for some time. While a theory solver for difference constraints gives the basis of a global difference constraint propagator, we show how the requirements on the propagator are quite different. Crucially, we show how to explain propagations by a global difference constraint propagator, in order to use it within a lazy clause generation solver. We give experiments showing that treating difference constraints globally can substantially improve on the standard propagation approach.

AI.tldr: A global, bounds-consistent propagator for a set of difference constraints is proposed, treating all constraints simultaneously rather than individually, leveraging shortest-path insights and enabling explanations for lazy clause generation in SMT; experiments show substantial performance gains over standard propagation.
AI.motivation: Finite-domain propagation often treats each x - y ≤ d constraint separately, which can be slow even though propagation is complete. A global approach can tighten domains more efficiently and support explanation in SAT/SMT contexts.
AI.method: Develop a single global, bounds-consistent propagator that handles all difference constraints together; integrate the propagator into a lazy clause generation SMT framework by providing explanations for propagations; compare performance against standard per-constraint propagation via experiments.
AI.result: The global propagator yields substantial performance improvements over standard propagation; it also provides propagations explanations suitable for integration with lazy clause generation SMT solvers.
AI.conclusion: Global, bounds-consistent propagation for difference constraints is beneficial in finite-domain and SMT settings, offering both efficiency gains and better explainability within lazy clause generation.

title: Toward Seasonal Guidelines for Robust Deep-Learning Sentinel-2 Building Detection in Different Area Types
summary: Sentinel-2 imagery offers open access, global coverage, and frequent revisit times, making it attractive for practical building mapping at scale; however, its native 10m resolution makes building vs non-building classification challenging, particularly for small or sub-pixel buildings, and performance can vary with both seasonality and the heterogeneity of built-up environments. This paper introduces a Sentinel-2 building-detection framework designed to systematically quantify these effects and to support more formalised, practice-oriented model selection. We construct a dedicated multi-temporal Sentinel-2 dataset over the Warsaw region and derive binary ground-truth masks by rasterising official Polish topographic database (BDOT10k) building footprints onto the Sentinel-2 pixel grid. Using two established convolutional segmentation backbones (U-Net and DeepLabV3+), we first perform scene-specific fine-tuning to select a robust architecture and identify the best monthly models for L1C and L2A products separately. We then conduct cross-temporal inference by applying each best monthly model to all scenes, enabling an assessment of (i) which months provide favourable training and inference conditions, (ii) how performance transfers between seasons, (iii) the impact of processing level, and (iv) how these effects differ across built-up typologies. Based on these results, we provide practical guidance for routine Sentinel-2 building classification under varying acquisition periods and settlement characteristics.

AI.tldr: Multi-temporal Sentinel-2 building-detection framework assessing how seasonality, product level, and urban typology affect 10m imagery for building mapping; offers guidance for model selection and deployment.
AI.motivation: Address limitations of 10m Sentinel-2 for building mapping (e.g., small/sub-pixel buildings) and understand how acquisition time and heterogeneity of built-up areas affect model transferability.
AI.method: Construct a Warsaw-specific multi-temporal Sentinel-2 dataset; create ground-truth masks by rasterising BDOT10k footprints onto the Sentinel grid; evaluate U-Net and DeepLabV3+ with scene-specific fine-tuning; select best monthly models for L1C and L2A; apply cross-temporal inference to analyze training/inference months, seasonal transfer, processing level effects, and typology differences; derive practical guidance.
AI.result: Determine which months yield best training/inference performance, quantify transferability across seasons, assess the impact of L1C vs L2A, and compare performance across built-up typologies; provide practical guidelines for routine Sentinel-2 building classification under varying acquisition periods and settlement characteristics.
AI.conclusion: A systematic, practice-oriented framework to quantify seasonality and product-level effects in Sentinel-2 building detection, informing model selection, preprocessing, and deployment across diverse environments.

title: HypEMBER: Hypernetwork-based Ensemble for Robust Policy Learning of Parametrized Dynamical Systems
summary: In this work we investigate reinforcement learning (RL) as a framework for the robust control of parametrized dynamical systems in presence of measurements and model uncertainties. High-dimensional state spaces, expensive numerical solvers, the partial knowledge of the governing equations, and the dependence on physical parameters that may be uncertain or difficult to estimate accurately, make the use of standard RL approaches computationally unfeasible. Indeed, lack of robustness and poor generalization across parameter variations are further amplified in presence of noisy or incomplete measurements, ultimately hampering control performance. To address these challenges, we introduce HypEMBER, a novel RL framework based on the combination of hypernetworks and ensemble learning. In the proposed approach, both the policy and value functions are represented through hypernetworks that generate the weights of the underlying models conditioned on the physical parameters of the system, thereby enabling parametric generalization across different dynamical regimes. In addition, an ensemble of policy and value approximators is employed to quantify epistemic uncertainty, leading to improved exploration strategies and enhanced robustness during and after training. The performance of the proposed framework is assessed on two representative parametrized control problems: (i) the one-dimensional Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation and (ii) a particle-navigation task in a two-dimensional time-dependent gyre flow, focusing on robustness with respect to measurement noise and parameter misspecification. Numerical results demonstrate that HypEMBER consistently improves training stability and sample efficiency, while achieving superior robustness to uncertainties affecting both the system dynamics and the available observations, in comparison with state-of-the-art RL methods.

AI.tldr: HypEMBER combines hypernetworks and ensembles to enable parametric generalization and robust RL for parametrized dynamical systems; shows improved training stability, sample efficiency, and robustness on Kuramoto–Sivashinsky and gyre flow tasks.
AI.motivation: Address computational infeasibility, limited robustness, and poor generalization of standard RL in high-dimensional, uncertain dynamical systems with noisy/partial measurements by enabling parametric generalization across regimes.
AI.method: Use hypernetworks to generate policy and value network weights conditioned on physical parameters; employ an ensemble of policy/value models to quantify epistemic uncertainty, improving exploration and robustness; evaluate on two parametrized control problems.
AI.result: HypEMBER improves training stability and sample efficiency and achieves superior robustness to uncertainties in dynamics and observations compared with state-of-the-art RL baselines.
AI.conclusion: HypEMBER provides a scalable framework for robust RL in parametrized dynamical systems, enabling generalization across parameter variations and maintaining performance under measurement noise and model misspecification.

title: Reading and Steering Representations of Materials-Science Mechanisms in an Open-Weight Language Model
summary: Large language models can answer scientific questions, yet a correct output does not reveal whether the model represents or uses the governing physics. Here we show that materials science mechanism information in the open-weight google/gemma-4-E4B-it model has three experimentally separable forms: concepts are readable in individual hidden states, constitutive orientation is carried by controlled transformations between states, and selected internal representations causally control engineering answers. We combine matched direct and Jacobian vocabulary readouts, option-free state geometry, a 60-law counterfactual benchmark and causal interventions. In 50 held-out materials descriptions, three independently fitted Jacobian lenses reproduced concept ranks, and target-free word sets from both readouts enabled blinded identification of 9 of 10 mechanism families. A separate 72-prompt benchmark produced mechanism-specific hidden-state neighborhoods, but an exact graph audit showed that this apparent physical organization was equally explained by numerical comparison. We therefore compared otherwise identical prompts in which only the direction of the physical input was reversed, asking whether the resulting hidden-state movement followed the supplied constitutive law. These state transformations ordered direct, physically neutral and inverse laws across 60 frozen relations and correctly oriented 39 of 40 directional laws, whereas lexical controls were near chance. Bidirectional interventions shifted answer probabilities toward or away from the physically appropriate outcome across all 12 matched cases, while counterfactual state patches transferred opposing decision signals across mechanisms and answer formats. Physical relationships were therefore more visible in controlled state changes than in absolute states alone.

AI.tldr: Mechanism information in a materials-science oriented LLM is encoded in multiple separable forms (hidden-state concepts, state-transformation orientation, and causal control of answers). These forms can be read and manipulated via Jacobian/readout techniques and causal interventions, revealing physics beyond static activations.
AI.motivation: To determine whether governing physics is represented in open-weight LLMs, and to delineate how mechanism information is encoded (concept readability, constitutive orientation, and causal control) using targeted readouts, state-geometry, and causal interventions.
AI.method: Analyze google/gemma-4-E4B-it with matched direct and Jacobian vocabulary readouts, option-free state geometry, a 60-law counterfactual benchmark, and causal interventions. Use 50 held-out material descriptions with three Jacobian lenses to reproduce concept ranks and blinded mechanism identification via target-free word sets. Employ a separate 72-prompt benchmark for hidden-state neighborhoods, perform an exact graph audit, reverse input directions to test constitutive law following, apply 60 frozen-relations directional tests, and use bidirectional interventions and counterfactual patches to probe causal signals.
AI.result: Three separable forms of mechanism information are observed: (1) concepts readable in individual hidden states; (2) constitutive orientation carried by controlled state transformations; (3) selected internal representations that causally influence engineering answers. Jacobian readouts reproduce concept ranks; 9/10 mechanism families identified blind; directionality tests correctly oriented 39/40 directional laws, lexical controls near chance; some organization can be explained by numerical similarity via graph audit; interventions shift probabilities toward/away from physics-aligned outcomes; counterfactual patches transfer opposing signals across mechanisms; controlled state changes reveal physics more clearly than absolute states.
AI.conclusion: Mechanism information about physics in LLMs is encoded in separable, causally consequential ways that become detectable primarily through controlled state changes and Jacobian readouts, rather than from static activations alone. This supports using targeted state manipulations and readouts to diagnose physical reasoning in LLMs and highlights potential confounds (numerical similarity) that must be considered in interpretation.

title: A Systematic Benchmark of Intensity Normalisation Methods for 3D Knee MRI Segmentation and Cross-Domain Generalisability
comment: This preprint has not undergone peer review or any post-submission improvements or corrections. The Version of Record of this contribution is published in 3Oth Annual Conference on Medical Image Understanding and Analysis, MIUA 2026. Code is available at https://github.com/oliverjm1/mri_normalisation
summary: Robust out-of-the-box performance is essential for the clinical deployment of deep learning models in medical imaging. An important but underexplored factor affecting model generalisability is intensity normalisation, particularly for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), where image intensities vary across scanners and protocols. In this study, we systematically compared seven normalisation methods and their impact on the performance of a 3D U-Net model for meniscus segmentation from knee MRI. The methods included standard scaling approaches, histogram-based techniques, and a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM)-based method. Models were trained on the IWOAI 2019 dataset and evaluated on both internal and external test sets (SKM-TEA) to assess generalisability. Performance was similar internally but differences were significant on external data, with Z-score, Nyúl histogram matching, and CLAHE showing greater robustness than other methods. However, these differences were small compared to the significant performance drop observed between datasets. Overall, while intensity normalisation had a measurable effect on model generalisability, its impact was limited relative to the effects of domain shift, highlighting the need for complementary strategies for robust deployment.

AI.tldr: Intensity normalization modestly influences cross-domain generalization for knee MRI segmentation; Z-score, Nyúl histogram matching, and CLAHE show relatively higher robustness across scanners, but domain shift dominates.
AI.motivation: Assess how seven normalization methods affect generalizability of a deep learning knee MRI segmentation model across datasets.
AI.method: Train 3D U-Net on IWOAI 2019; apply seven normalization methods (standard scaling, histogram-based, and GMM) to input; evaluate on internal and external SKM-TEA test sets.
AI.result: Internal performance similar across methods; external performance varies; some methods (Z-score, Nyúl histogram matching, CLAHE) more robust; differences smaller than the drop due to dataset shift.
AI.conclusion: Intensity normalization has a measurable but limited impact on generalizability; domain shift remains the primary challenge; complementary strategies needed for robust clinical deployment.

title: Anatomy of a Sound Neural Reasoner: One-Shot Amortization, First-Pass Poisoning, and Search Inertness in Clue-Rich Completion
summary: Neural solvers are built to deduce, branch, and revise intermediate states. The Lattice Deduction Transformer (LDT) appears to do exactly that. In clue-rich Sudoku, it does not: one forward pass commits essentially the entire grid (every blank cell on standard 6x6, 94-96% on augmented 9x9), turning the iterative solver into a one-shot predictor wrapped in an exact verifier. All hard-slice failures are decided before search begins, when the first pass confidently deletes a value required by the true solution. We call this first-pass poisoning. Adding learned branching, MRV, backtracking, value exclusion, and shared nogoods (CoLT) does not change which Sudoku instances are solved; it cuts repeated invalid derivations 1,497-fold. At the frozen training budget, constraint-graph attention alone matches full-CoLT accuracy, while positional tables recover only under substantially longer training, indicating an optimization and sample-efficiency advantage rather than an absolute capacity difference. The diagnosis predicts two effective interventions. Digit-permutation augmentation raises 9x9 accuracy from below 1% to 96.5 +/- 0.3 across three training seeds on a symmetry-disjoint split. Test-time union over symmetry-transformed passes raises all three hard-slice checkpoints from 72.8-78.9% to 100% without retraining. On from-scratch graph coloring, one-shot behavior disappears and search changes accuracy. In clue-rich completion, LDT-like systems are one-shot amortized predictors rather than learned search procedures: accuracy is determined by calibration and symmetry, while search primarily removes computational waste.

AI.tldr: Lattice Deduction Transformer largely behaves as a one-shot predictor in clue-rich Sudoku; first-pass poisoning triggers hard failures before any search; adding traditional search aids mainly reduces wasted derivations rather than expanding solvable instances; symmetry and data augmentation produce major accuracy gains; overall, these systems act as calibrated predictors rather than true search procedures for Sudoku.
AI.motivation: Investigate why LDT fails to be an iterative solver in clue-rich Sudoku, quantify the impact of adding branching/search heuristics, and identify interventions that recover or outperform one-shot behavior, with comparisons to constraint-graph attention and CoLT under a fixed training budget.
AI.method: Empirical analysis on clue-rich Sudoku: evaluate LDT with/without learned branching, MRV, backtracking, value exclusion, and shared nogoods (CoLT); compare to constraint-graph attention and full-CoLT; assess the impact of digit-permutation augmentation and test-time symmetry ensembling; examine one-shot behavior in from-scratch graph coloring; analyze first-pass poisoning as a failure mode.
AI.result: Hard failures occur in the first forward pass (first-pass poisoning) before search. Additional interventions (MRV, backtracking, value exclusion, CoLT) do not change which instances are solved but cut repeated invalid derivations (~1497×). Under frozen training budget, constraint-graph attention matches full-CoLT; positional tables require longer training and show no edge in capacity. Digit-permutation augmentation raises 9x9 accuracy to ~96.5% across seeds; test-time union over symmetry lifts all hard-slice checkpoints to 100% without retraining. From-scratch graph coloring eliminates one-shot behavior; interpretation: LDTs for clue-rich completion are one-shot amortized predictors, with accuracy governed by calibration and symmetry rather than search efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Two effective interventions emerge: (1) digit-permutation augmentation substantially improves accuracy, and (2) test-time symmetry ensembling yields near-perfect performance without retraining. The core insight is that, in clue-rich Sudoku, LDT-style models function as calibrated predictors with search primarily removing computational waste; to enhance robustness, emphasize symmetry-aware training and data augmentation rather than relying on extended search.

title: PRO-LONG: Programmatic Memory Enables Long-Horizon Reasoning
summary: Long-horizon tasks require sustained perception, reasoning, and exploration, and are a persistent challenge for large language model (LLM) agents. This gap is reflected in their limited performance on continual learning benchmarks such as ARC-AGI-3, especially when models are evaluated out of the box. Various agent harnesses have been proposed to close this gap, and each commits to a strategy for handling long sequences of observations, i.e., what information to save from the environment and how to load it into model context, a choice we argue is particularly consequential. Existing methods for context management face a significant tradeoff, as preserving more information makes retrieving relevant details less tractable. We propose PRO-LONG, a minimal context management framework built around programmatic memory for LLM agents in long-horizon, exploratory settings. PRO-LONG addresses the tradeoff by keeping a complete, structured interaction log and capitalizing on recent progress in coding agents to search this history efficiently. On the full ARC-AGI-3 public game set, PRO-LONG improves over a base coding agent by an average of 18.0 percentage points across frontier models, and matches or exceeds state-of-the-art specialized harnesses (up to 76.1% pass@1) while using 4.2-5.8x fewer tokens. With Fable 5, PRO-LONG achieves 97.4% best@2 at a total cost of \$1,750. Relevant code and logs are available at https://github.com/alexisfox7/PRO-LONG.

AI.tldr: PRO-LONG is a minimal context-management framework that uses a complete, structured interaction log and programmatic memory to enable efficient long-horizon planning for LLM agents, improving performance on ARC-AGI-3 with fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon tasks strain LLM agents due to the need to retain and retrieve relevant information across extended interactions; existing methods face a tradeoff between storing more data and making retrieval tractable.
AI.method: Introduce PRO-LONG, a programmatic memory framework that preserves a full interaction log and leverages coding agents to efficiently search this history; evaluated on ARC-AGI-3 and with Fable 5.
AI.result: On ARC-AGI-3 public game set, PRO-LONG improves base coding agent by 18.0 percentage points on average across frontier models and matches or exceeds state-of-the-art harnesses (up to 76.1% pass@1) while using 4.2-5.8x fewer tokens. With Fable 5, achieves 97.4% best@2 at a total cost of $1,750.
AI.conclusion: A minimal, structured memory approach can mitigate the information-tradeoff in context management for long-horizon LLM agents, delivering strong performance gains with lower token costs and good scalability.

title: Importance-Aware OBS Pruning for Diffusion Models
summary: We propose importance-aware pruning for diffusion models, a training-free framework that prioritizes preserving parameters critical to semantically salient image regions. To do so, we incorporate spatial importance maps -- derived from conditioning signals or model attention -- into the pruning objective. This produces parameter rankings aligned with perceptual relevance rather than uniform reconstruction error. On MS-COCO dataset, our proposed approach consistently retains subject fidelity and structural correctness at high compression ratios where conventional pruning causes visible degradation. These results demonstrate that content-aware objectives are key to perceptually faithful compression of generative models.

AI.tldr: Training-free, content-aware pruning for diffusion models that uses spatial importance maps to prioritize parameters affecting salient regions, outperforming uniform error-based pruning at high compression on MS-COCO.
AI.motivation: Preserve perceptual fidelity in compressed diffusion models by weighting pruning decisions toward parameters that influence semantically important content rather than optimizing only generic reconstruction error.
AI.method: Incorporate spatial importance maps (from conditioning signals or model attention) into the pruning objective, yielding parameter rankings aligned with perceptual relevance without additional training.
AI.result: On MS-COCO, the approach consistently preserves subject fidelity and structural correctness at high compression ratios where traditional pruning causes degraded outputs.
AI.conclusion: Content-aware objectives are essential for perceptually faithful compression of generative models; targeting perceptually relevant parameters improves pruning outcomes.

title: Expert-Guided Forecast Editing for Time-Series Foundation Models
summary: Time-series foundation models can forecast across heterogeneous domains without task-specific training, but their forecasts are fixed once produced and cannot directly incorporate task-specific expert feedback. We study expert-guided forecast editing: a frozen foundation model generates candidate future trajectories, and an expensive expert evaluator scores them to guide forecast revision. Under a tight query budget, two natural strategies sit at opposite ends: best-of-$N$ purely exploits the foundation model's predictive distribution, while optimization approaches mostly explore the forecast horizon as an unstructured high-dimensional vector. Each extreme is individually sub-optimal. We introduce \textbf{DEFT}, an expert-guided forecast editing framework that balances the two by first exploiting the foundation model's predictive samples in a decomposed trend--seasonal space, then exploring around them via component-wise refinement. DEFT queries the expert only on complete trajectories, then reuses scores for the trend and seasonal components that appeared in the queried recombinations. This lets each expert query provide structured component-level feedback while keeping the foundation model frozen. We compare DEFT against direct search approaches, including best-of-$N$, cross-entropy methods, and Bayesian optimization, under matched expert-query budgets. Across two forecasting benchmarks consisting of 78 datasets, three time-series foundation models, four feedback types, and seven query budgets, DEFT consistently improves the effectiveness of expert guidance. A molecular-dynamics case study further suggests that the same principle extends to more physically grounded feedback, supporting the hypothesis that sparse test-time guidance should be spent balancing prior exploitation with structured exploration.

AI.tldr: DEFT is an expert-guided forecast-editing framework for time-series foundation models that decomposes forecasts into trend and seasonal components and balances exploitation of model samples with structured exploration via expert feedback, outperforming standard baselines under limited queries.
AI.motivation: Enable task-specific improvements for frozen time-series foundation models by leveraging scarce, high-value expert feedback at test time, without costly fine-tuning.
AI.method: Iteratively exploit the foundation model's predictive samples in a decomposed trend–seasonal space, then perform component-wise refinement. Query the expert on complete trajectories and reuse the resulting scores to guide component-level updates. Compare against best-of-N, cross-entropy methods, and Bayesian optimization under matched query budgets across diverse datasets, models, and feedback types.
AI.result: DEFT consistently improves forecast-accuracy gains from expert feedback across 78 datasets, 3 foundation models, 4 feedback types, and 7 budgets, outperforming baseline search strategies. A molecular-dynamics case study suggests the approach generalizes to physics-based feedback.
AI.conclusion: Sparse test-time guidance should balance prior exploitation with structured, component-wise exploration; DEFT offers a practical, model-free (frozen) framework that efficiently leverages expert feedback to edit forecasts.

title: TRUST-ESD: A Risk-Calibrated and Governance-Aware AI Framework for Enterprise Strategic Decision Support Under Uncertainty
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to APWeb-WAIM 2026, Danang, Vietnam, September 7-9, 2026
summary: Enterprise strategic decision support requires AI systems that are not only accurate, but also uncertainty-aware, risk-calibrated, explainable, and governance-compliant. This paper proposes TRUST-ESD, a risk-calibrated and governance-aware framework for enterprise decision support under uncertainty. TRUST-ESD evaluates feasible counterfactual strategies through predictive utility estimation, conformal uncertainty calibration, CVaR-based downside-risk scoring, risk-memory retrieval, policy-as-code governance, explainability, and human oversight. Unlike prediction-only methods that select actions by maximum expected utility, TRUST-ESD recommends strategies that balance value, reliability, risk exposure, and compliance. Experimental results show that TRUST-ESD improves risk-adjusted utility by 7.95%, reduces risk exposure by 23.22%, reduces CVaR by 23.78%, lowers calibration error by 13.89%, improves explanation fidelity by 10.90%, and increases governance compliance by 9.76% compared with strong uncertainty-aware baselines, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy. Ablation and case-study analyses further confirm that uncertainty calibration, downside-risk scoring, risk memory, explainability, and governance validation jointly improve trustworthy enterprise decision-making.

AI.tldr: TRUST-ESD is a risk-calibrated, governance-aware framework for enterprise decision support under uncertainty that combines predictive utility estimation, conformal uncertainty calibration, CVaR-based downside-risk scoring, risk-memory retrieval, policy-as-code governance, explainability, and human oversight to balance value, reliability, risk, and compliance.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI decision support requires not only accuracy but also uncertainty awareness, risk control, explainability, and governance, which prediction-only methods fail to provide.
AI.method: The framework integrates (1) predictive utility estimation, (2) conformal uncertainty calibration, (3) CVaR-based downside-risk scoring, (4) risk-memory retrieval, (5) policy-as-code governance, (6) explainability, and (7) human oversight to generate risk-aware strategy recommendations rather than maximizing expected utility.
AI.result: TRUST-ESD improves risk-adjusted utility by 7.95%, reduces risk exposure by 23.22%, lowers CVaR by 23.78%, reduces calibration error by 13.89%, improves explanation fidelity by 10.90%, and boosts governance compliance by 9.76% relative to strong uncertainty-aware baselines, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty calibration, downside-risk scoring, risk memory, explainability, and governance validation jointly improve trustworthy enterprise decision-making; ablation and case studies corroborate the benefits of the integrated components.

title: GaussianSeed: Hierarchical Gaussian Seeding for High-Resolution 3D Occupancy Prediction
summary: Vision-centric 3D occupancy prediction provides dense scene representations essential for autonomous driving and robotic navigation, yet existing methods struggle to scale to high voxel resolutions due to prohibitive computational costs. To address this, we introduce GaussianSeed, a progressive multi-scale Gaussian occupancy prediction framework that organizes primitives into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy. Benefiting from this hierarchical design, GaussianSeed effectively circumvents the memory bottlenecks inherent in dense representations, successfully scaling to a $0.1\text{m}$ spatial resolution while maintaining real-time inference capabilities. To comprehensively evaluate high-resolution geometric perception, we further construct TJScenes, a panoramic six-camera occupancy dataset with highly detailed $0.1\text{m}$ annotations. Extensive experiments on Occ3D-nuScenes and TJScenes demonstrate that GaussianSeed delivers the lowest latency among all evaluated methods while maintaining highly competitive accuracy, advancing the efficiency-quality frontier of high-resolution 3D occupancy prediction.

AI.tldr: GaussianSeed introduces a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine Gaussian occupancy framework that uses multi-scale primitives to achieve high-resolution (0.1 m) 3D occupancy prediction with real-time inference, addressing memory bottlenecks of dense representations. It is complemented by TJScenes, a six-camera panoramic occupancy dataset. Experiments on Occ3D-nuScenes and TJScenes show the method has the lowest latency with competitive accuracy, advancing the efficiency-quality frontier for high-res 3D occupancy prediction.
AI.motivation: Dense, high-resolution 3D occupancy maps are essential for autonomous driving and robotics, but densely-voxel representations at fine resolutions suffer prohibitive memory and compute costs. There is a need for scalable, real-time high-resolution occupancy prediction.
AI.method: A progressive multi-scale framework (GaussianSeed) that organizes occupancy primitives as a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of Gaussian components (primitives) to represent occupancy. This hierarchical, probabilistic representation reduces memory overhead compared to dense voxels and enables refinement from coarse to fine resolutions, achieving 0.1 m spatial resolution with real-time inference. Additionally, TJScenes is introduced as a panoramic six-camera occupancy dataset with detailed 0.1 m annotations to benchmark high-resolution geometry perception.
AI.result: GaussianSeed successfully scales to 0.1 m resolution while preserving real-time inference. It achieves the lowest latency among evaluated methods on Occ3D-nuScenes and TJScenes, while maintaining highly competitive accuracy compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: The work pushes the efficiency-quality frontier for high-resolution 3D occupancy prediction by combining a memory-efficient, hierarchical Gaussian representation with a real-time capable pipeline and provides a challenging new dataset (TJScenes) to enable comprehensive evaluation.

title: Efficient Clustering with Provable Guardrails for LLM Inference at Scale
comment: Accepted for presentation at ICML HiLD workshop 2026 (non-archival)
summary: Scaling LLM-based applications to millions of users is bottlenecked by the inference cost and latency of modern foundation models. A natural fix is to cluster the inputs and call the LLM only on cluster representatives, letting other members inherit the output -- but this is only safe if each member is measurably close to its representative. Existing clustering methods do not offer such per-sample quality control at scale: none jointly guarantee a minimal within-cluster similarity, exact matching of categorical attributes, and scalability to tens of millions of samples. We propose a two-stage algorithm that generates initial clusters with Mini-batch K-Means, then greedily selects representatives within each initial cluster -- a step equivalent to the Johnson-Chvatal heuristic for Set Cover over alpha-balls in embedding space. The algorithm enforces the similarity and attribute guardrails exactly by construction, and runs in $O(nd + n^2 d/K)$ time and $O(nd + n^2/K^2)$ memory for $n$ samples, feature dimension $d$, and $K$ initial clusters -- linear in $n$ when $K$ grows proportionally with $n$. We provide benchmarks against common clustering methods on internal and public datasets: our method not only delivers per-sample guardrails but also runs 10-1000x faster and scales to data sizes where most standard methods become intractable. Deployed on 38 million customers for a persona-based recommender, the clustering method cut downstream cost and latency by 50-fold while preserving personalization and unblocked the production launch.

AI.tldr: Two-stage clustering approach to enable safe, scalable LLM inference by selecting cluster representatives with guardrails; achieves per-sample similarity and attribute constraints, with favorable complexity and large-scale success (38M users).
AI.motivation: Reduce inference cost/latency of massive LLM-based applications by using clustered inputs so only representatives are processed, while ensuring per-sample similarity and categorical attribute consistency.
AI.method: Stage 1: Mini-batch K-Means to form K initial clusters. Stage 2: greedily pick representatives within each cluster, analogous to Johnson–Chvátal set cover on alpha-balls in embedding space; enforces similarity and attribute constraints by construction; analyzes time/memory: O(nd + n^2 d/K) time, O(nd + n^2/K^2) memory; scalable when K grows with n.
AI.result: Benchmarks show 10–1000x speedups over standard clustering methods; scales to tens of millions of samples; deployed to 38 million customers with persona-based recommender, cutting downstream cost and latency by ~50x while preserving personalization.
AI.conclusion: The method provides per-sample guardrails and scalability, making safe input clustering viable for large-scale LLM inference; suitable for production deployment; practical gains demonstrated; potential exploration of robustness and parameter sensitivity.

title: CUSUM-Shaped Inference-Time Monitoring and Targeted Re-Decoding for Quantized Small Language Model Reasoning
summary: Quantized small autoregressive reasoning models can enter long, repetitive, or unproductive trajectories, yet inference-time compute is usually allocated without observing how a trajectory develops. Building on an earlier token-level e-CUSUM controller, we develop MGT-B (Monitoring-Guided Test-time Backtracking), a revised external controller that maps overlapping windows of pre-sampling uncertainty and degeneration features to position-conditional empirical tail probabilities, accumulates mixture betting factors with a CUSUM-shaped reset, and responds to an alarm by estimating a rollback point, restoring token and key-value-cache state, and performing constrained re-decoding. To audit whether the effect persists on problem identities first observed after the manual choice of log threshold h = 10, we retrospectively exclude 260 IDs present in pre-threshold artifacts and retain the chronologically first post-threshold pair for each remaining ID, yielding a 240-pair chronology-audit set. On this set, accuracy changes from 82/240 to 88/240 (+2.50 percentage points; 13 corrections, 7 regressions; exact McNemar p = 0.2632; paired bootstrap 95% interval [-1.25, +6.25]). A broader 467-pair historical-coverage set of seed-matched pairs changes accuracy from 146/467 to 167/467 (+4.50 points; McNemar p = 0.000753), but includes 200 seed-1 IDs available before or during threshold selection and is reported only as an exploratory estimate. All 316 no-alarm outputs in the 467-pair set are identical to vanilla, while the 151 alarmed trajectories contain 29 corrections and 8 regressions. Neither analysis is confirmatory, and the empirical factors are not established as a valid e-process or e-detector. The results support a selective monitoring-and-repair mechanism for the studied MATH-500 setting, rather than a general or theoretically certified reasoning improvement.

AI.tldr: MGT-B is a monitoring-guided external controller for quantized autoregressive models that triggers backtracking and constrained re-decoding when early warnings appear, with retrospective and historical audits showing modest, non-definitive gains in accuracy for a MATH-500 setting.
AI.motivation: Mitigate long, repetitive, or unproductive inference trajectories in quantized AR models by adding an external, windowed monitoring and rollback mechanism.
AI.method: Develop MGT-B that maps overlapping windows of pre-sampling uncertainty and degeneration features to position-conditional empirical tail probabilities, accumulates mixture betting factors with a CUSUM-shaped reset, and on alarm estimates a rollback point to restore state and re-decode under constraints. Conduct chronology-audit and historical-coverage audits around a log-threshold h=10 using seed-matched identities, compute McNemar tests and bootstrap intervals to assess persistence of the effect.
AI.result: Chronology-audit (240 pairs): accuracy 82/240 -> 88/240; +2.50 pp; 13 corrections, 7 regressions; McNemar p=0.2632; bootstrap 95% CI [-1.25, +6.25]. Historical-coverage (467 pairs): accuracy 146/467 -> 167/467; +4.50 pp; McNemar p=0.000753; no-alarm outputs identical to vanilla (316/467); alarmed trajectories: 29 corrections, 8 regressions. Exploratory, not confirmatory; factors not established as valid e-process/e-detector.
AI.conclusion: The results tentatively support selective monitoring and repair for the studied MATH-500 setting, but do not establish general or theoretically certified reasoning improvements.

title: Factor-Informed Uncertainty Distillation for Gaze Estimation
summary: Deep gaze estimation works well in controlled capture but degrades in unconstrained settings, where systems must reject unreliable predictions. Single-pass uncertainty (e.g., heteroscedastic regression) infers uncertainty from pixels without explicit input-validity cues, while sampling based methods are often too costly for real time use. We propose Factor-Informed Uncertainty Distillation (FIUD), a teacher-student framework that aligns uncertainty with interpretable image-quality failure modes. A gradient-boosting teacher predicts expected gaze error from factors such as illumination, sharpness, eye visibility and symmetry; a neural student distills these signals via curriculum learning and ranking supervision into a lightweight single-pass uncertainty head. Across ETH-XGaze, Gaze360, and MPIIFaceGaze (>300k samples), FIUD improves uncertainty, error rank correlation and selective prediction versus deterministic and sampling-based baselines, with the largest gains in unconstrained settings.

AI.tldr: A teacher-student framework (FIUD) distills factor-based uncertainty into a lightweight single-pass head for gaze estimation, improving uncertainty calibration and selective prediction in unconstrained settings.
AI.motivation: Gaze estimation performance degrades in unconstrained settings; existing single-pass uncertainty methods lack input-validity cues and sampling methods are too costly for real-time use.
AI.method: A gradient-boosting teacher predicts expected gaze error from factors like illumination, sharpness, eye visibility and symmetry; a neural student, trained with curriculum learning and ranking supervision, distills these signals into a lightweight single-pass uncertainty head.
AI.result: On ETH-XGaze, Gaze360, and MPIIFaceGaze (over 300k samples), FIUD improves uncertainty estimates, error rank correlation, and selective prediction vs deterministic and sampling-based baselines, with the largest gains in unconstrained settings.
AI.conclusion: FIUD effectively aligns uncertainty with interpretable image-quality failure modes and yields better uncertainty estimation and selective prediction for gaze estimation in unconstrained environments.

authors: Venkata Naga Sai Vishnu Rohit Pulipaka
title: How Fast Can Reward Models Score? A Systems Study of C++ and PyTorch Inference Runtimes for RLHF
summary: In RLHF pipelines, reward scoring blocks policy updates. Slow scoring bottlenecks the entire loop, since no update runs until every rollout gets a score. And yet most setups just default to PyTorch eager mode or torch.compile, no one checks if that's actually fastest. Scoring itself is small. Rollout generation eats far more of a typical RLHF step. But scoring and generation fight over the same CPU and GPU resources, so a faster scoring engine doesn't shrink step time on its own. It mainly frees up capacity generation can use instead. We built a native C++ inference engine on ONNX Runtime. First step: confirm correctness. Output matched the PyTorch reference to 5.7 x 10^-6 on CPU and 4.2 x 10^-3 on GPU, close enough to trust. Then we tested it against PyTorch eager mode, torch.compile, and FastAPI, on both CPU and GPU. CPU was decisive. Our engine beat every baseline, confidence intervals didn't even overlap. GPU gave a different view: we beat PyTorch and FastAPI, but torch.compile came out ahead. Further testing traced the speedup to ONNX Runtime itself, not C++ as a language. And batching strategy mattered more than either the language or the runtime choice, more than we expected. The results are from repeated, independent runs, since single runs just aren't reliable enough to trust.

AI.tldr: Replacing PyTorch-based reward scoring in RLHF with a native C++ ONNX Runtime inference engine yields CPU-dominated speedups and highlights batching as a critical performance lever; GPU results are mixed, with torch.compile sometimes leading. Repeated independent runs confirm results; speed gains stem from ONNX Runtime rather than language.
AI.motivation: RLHF reward scoring is a bottleneck that delays policy updates; typical workflows rely on PyTorch eager/compile without validating fastest configuration. Empirical speed comparison and correctness verification are needed to guide implementation choices and resource allocation between scoring and generation.
AI.method: Developed a native C++ inference engine on ONNX Runtime for reward scoring. Validated numerical correctness against a PyTorch reference (output matched within 5.7e-6 CPU, 4.2e-3 GPU). Benchmarked against PyTorch eager mode, torch.compile, and FastAPI on CPU and GPU, with emphasis on batching strategies. Used repeated independent runs to ensure reliability.
AI.result: CPU: the ONNX-based engine outperformed all baselines with non-overlapping confidence intervals. GPU: the engine beat PyTorch and FastAPI, but torch.compile sometimes led. Speedups traced to ONNX Runtime behavior; the batching strategy had a larger impact than language or runtime choice.
AI.conclusion: A purpose-built ONNX Runtime scoring engine can accelerate RLHF steps by freeing generation to utilize resources more effectively. The most impactful factor is batching strategy, and CPU performance is decisive. Results emphasize that ONNX Runtime choice (and not just language) drives speedups, with robust validation via repeated runs.

title: PoTRE: Test-Time Reasoning inspired by Cognitive Heterogeneity
comment: Accepted at Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR 2026)
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at many tasks, they frequently struggle with complex reasoning that requires long-horizon planning and iterative error correction. Furthermore, standard single-stream prompting proves brittle when models encounter novel abstractions or rigorous domain constraints. We introduce PoTRE (Poly-Topological Reasoning Ensembles), a heterogeneous framework that decouples inference into four agents: (1) Adversarial Refinement Agent, (2) Hierarchical strategic Planning Agent, (3) Spectrum Search Agent, and (4) Direct Chain Agent. A final Task-Adaptive Aggregation Layer dynamically reconciles these perspectives -- via final candidate selection, semantic synthesis, or neuro-symbolic verification -- to produce a robust global solution. We evaluate PoTRE on three frontier benchmarks: ARC-AGI-2, Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), and PRBench Finance. PoTRE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy of 49.92% on HLE, surpassing the previous best official score. We demonstrate that this architectural heterogeneity achieves improved reasoning performance using similar or fewer inference tokens compared to heavily scaled homogeneous baselines.

AI.tldr: PoTRE is a four-agent heterogeneous framework for robust long-horizon reasoning in LLMs, combining Adversarial Refinement, Hierarchical Planning, Spectrum Search, and Direct Chain with a Task-Adaptive Aggregation Layer to reconcile perspectives. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on Humanity's Last Exam (49.92%) and shows improved reasoning with similar or fewer inference tokens versus strong homogeneous baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with long-horizon planning, iterative error correction, and brittleness when facing novel abstractions or strict domain constraints under standard single-stream prompting. A heterogeneous, modular inference architecture could enhance robustness and efficiency.
AI.method: Decouples inference into four specialized agents: (1) Adversarial Refinement Agent, (2) Hierarchical Strategic Planning Agent, (3) Spectrum Search Agent, (4) Direct Chain Agent. A Task-Adaptive Aggregation Layer dynamically reconciles these perspectives via final candidate selection, semantic synthesis, or neuro-symbolic verification to produce a robust global solution. Evaluation on ARC-AGI-2, Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), and PRBench Finance.
AI.result: PoTRE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy of 49.92% on HLE, surpassing the previous official best. Demonstrates improved reasoning performance with similar or fewer inference tokens compared with heavily scaled homogeneous baselines.
AI.conclusion: Architectural heterogeneity in prompting can enhance reasoning quality and efficiency by leveraging complementary inference strategies and a dynamic aggregation layer; PoTRE provides a robust, modular approach that could generalize to other complex reasoning tasks.

title: Development of an automated, reliable, and clinically meaningful artificial intelligence (AI) tool for diagnosing cardiac disease from conventional cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) images
summary: Aims: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging enables non-invasive assessment of myocardial structure, function, and pathology, but requires substantial experience in interpretation of CMR images that could be supported by artificial intelligence (AI)-based models. However, use of AI models for enhanced CMR reading is limited by labor-intensive data curation, suboptimal model performance, and unclear implementation pathways. Methods and results: We developed an automated data curation pipeline for CMR-based cardiovascular disease (CVD) diagnosis, integrating open-source locally-run large language models (LLMs) to extract diagnostic labels from narrative CMR reports and preprocessing multimodal imaging data, including cine and late-gadolinium-enhancement (LGE) CMR sequences. Three vision foundation models (DINO, VST, UMedPT) were fine-tuned across these modalities in a two-stage approach. The dataset comprised hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM), cardiac amyloidosis (CA), and normal controls (NOR). A total of 988 curated cases were randomly divided into 742 for training and 246 for validation. Fine-tuned AI-models achieved high discriminative diagnostic performance on an independent test set comprising 1067 patients , with individual AUC-ROC values of up to 0.937 for the correct diagnosis of HCM and 0.945 for cardiac amyloidosis. Ensemble strategies combining multiple models and modalities further improved AI-based diagnostic accuracy and robustness, achieving the highest overall diagnostic performance for HCM (AUC=0.959, CI [0.936-0.978]), CA (AUC=0.966, CI [0.939-0.986]), NOR (AUC=0.872, CI [0.852-0.894]), DCM (AUC=0.848, CI [0.808-0.885]) and ICM (AUC=0.840, CI [0.809-0.868]). All training and inference code, along with the trained model weights, are publicly available on https://github.com/sinaamirrajab/CMR_CVD.

AI.tldr: Multimodal CMR AI with automated data curation using LLMs, fine-tuned vision models on cine and LGE data, achieving high AUCs across HCM, CA, NOR, DCM, ICM; ensemble methods boost performance; code/weights publicly available.
AI.motivation: To reduce labor-intensive data curation and improve AI-assisted CMR interpretation by automating diagnostic-label extraction from narrative reports and leveraging multimodal imaging for robust disease classification.
AI.method: Automated data curation pipeline using locally-run large language models to extract diagnostic labels from CMR reports; preprocessing cine and LGE images; fine-tune three vision foundation models (DINO, VST, UMedPT) in a two-stage approach on a multiclass CMR dataset (HCM, DCM, ICM, CA, NOR; 988 cases; 742 train, 246 validation); evaluate on independent test set of 1067 patients; ensemble strategies across models and modalities.
AI.result: High discriminative performance: HCM AUC 0.937; CA AUC 0.945 on independent test; NOR AUC 0.872; DCM AUC 0.848; ICM AUC 0.840. Ensemble results: HCM AUC 0.959 (CI 0.936–0.978); CA AUC 0.966 (CI 0.939–0.986); NOR AUC 0.872 (CI 0.852–0.894); DCM AUC 0.848 (CI 0.808–0.885); ICM AUC 0.840 (CI 0.809–0.868). All training/inference code and weights are publicly available at the provided GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates feasible automated CMR data curation and robust multimodal AI for CVD diagnosis, achieving high AUCs across multiple cardiomyopathy categories and normals, with publicly accessible resources to support reproducibility and potential clinical deployment; external validation and generalizability remain areas for further work.

title: Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable Activation Explanations
summary: Natural-language autoencoders score explanations of hidden activations by reconstruction: an explanation is deemed faithful if the activation can be regenerated from it. The test is structurally insensitive to individual false claims: if flipping a claim does not change the reconstruction, the claim is never penalized. We show the test is passed in two ways, neither faithful. On a released Qwen-2.5-7B verbalizer, explanations reconstruct well above chance while ~2% of specific claims are reconstruction-dependent, so the score tracks gist, not specific facts. Under exact synthetic ground truth, the standard recipe develops co-adapted private codes (false wording the reconstruction depends on) in 5/5 runs, and fixes that leave the target model unchanged do not help. We contribute two audit protocols, the grounded-vs-true cross and the evaluator swap, and RECAP (Readable Encodings via Co-trained Auxiliary Predictors): linear heads trained alongside the target model to keep designated content decodable. On RECAP-trained sandbox models, fresh verbalizers state the designated content truly and the codes vanish, at a +0.001-nat cost. This replicates on a pretrained Pythia-160M: the content becomes reliably probe-decodable, though a fresh verbalizer conveys it only in part (truth 0.44-0.46 vs a near-zero control). For interpretability, high reconstruction does not certify individual claims. For AI safety, RECAP makes designated internal content independently checkable against probes rather than asserted by prose a model can game: an independent probe scores the verbalizer's true claims above its false ones (AUC 0.96, vs 0.82 without RECAP). Against an adversary that edits an explanation to maximize the reconstruction score while lying (suppressing ~87% of its lie penalty), the RECAP probe still flags the lies (AUC 0.95) while the control probe collapses to chance (0.51).

AI.tldr: RECAP introduces editable, co-trained auxiliary predictors to produce decodable encodings of designated content in NL autoencoders, enabling independent verification of claimed internal content and addressing reconstruction-faithfulness limitations.
AI.motivation: Current reconstruction-based faithfulness tests can be gamed and do not guarantee claim-level truth. The work seeks audit protocols and a method to produce verifiable internal encodings.
