AI.method: Analyze explanations via reconstruction, identify co-adapted private codes, propose two audits (grounded-vs-true cross, evaluator swap), and introduce RECAP (linear heads trained with the model to keep designated content decodable). Evaluate on Qwen-2.5-7B and Pythia-160M across various conditions; compare independent probes vs prose assertions and adversarial edits.
AI.result: Reconstruction-based tests can pass while not ensuring truth of specific claims; high reconstruction correlates with gist, not facts. RECAP reduces leakage and yields verifiable decodability: true content decodes reliably with fresh verbalizers; independent probes score true vs false claims highly (AUC ~0.96) vs weaker baselines; adversarial edits still detectable (AUC ~0.95).
AI.conclusion: High reconstruction alone is insufficient for claim-level interpretability. RECAP provides independent verifiability of designated internal content and improves AI safety by enabling external probes to verify claims rather than relying on prose; results generalize across different model scales and setups.

title: ENTRAP-VL: A Taxonomic Probe for Dual Contextual Entrainment in Vision-Language Models
summary: Contextual entrainment is the tendency of a model to let auxiliary context in its input pull its output, independently of whether that context is relevant, true, or even meaningful. Recently, it has been identified and given a mechanistic account in unimodal language models. Whether and how it manifests in vision-language models (VLMs) is, by contrast, largely unexamined, and the field lacks a purpose-built instrument with which to investigate it. We take the position that studying contextual entrainment in VLMs requires more than porting an existing text-only benchmark to the multimodal setting: it requires a taxonomically structured, dual-modality instrument whose conditions are constructed around the item at hand (the depicted image in the textual stream, the textual query in the visual stream). We argue that the move to VLMs is substantive rather than incremental. It makes entrainment a dual phenomenon, drivable independently by textual and by visual context, and it opens a veracity distinction (context that is false of the depicted scene yet possible in the world) that has no counterpart in the unimodal, world-knowledge-only formulation of prior work. To make this position concrete and actionable, we introduce ENTRAP-VL (ENTRainment Assessment Probe for Vision and Language), a manually curated dataset of 1,500 items across eight categories, organized by a taxonomy that spans two axes, i.e., the association of context with the item and its relationship to truth, and split into a textual-entrainment stream (eight context conditions) and a visual-entrainment stream (three context conditions). We do not claim to measure entrainment in any particular model; we provide the instrument, the taxonomy that motivates it, and the evaluation protocols it enables, so that the community can investigate the phenomenon rigorously. We will release the dataset and its documentation publicly.

AI.tldr: Introduces ENTRAP-VL, a taxonomy-driven, dual-modality instrument for studying contextual entrainment in vision–language models; 1,500 items across eight textual-context and three visual-context conditions; provides evaluation protocols and will release the dataset publicly.
AI.motivation: Addresses the gap that, unlike unimodal language models, vision–language models allow entrainment to be driven by both textual and visual context, creating a dual phenomenon with veracity distinctions; existing benchmarks are insufficient for multimodal entrainment.
AI.method: Proposes ENTRAP-VL: a manually curated dataset of 1,500 items across eight textual-entrainment conditions and three visual-entrainment conditions, organized by a taxonomy with two axes (association to the item; truth relation). It defines a textual-entrainment stream and a visual-entrainment stream, and provides evaluation protocols. The dataset and documentation will be publicly released.
AI.result: The paper delivers an instrument and taxonomy (ENTRAP-VL) with dataset design and evaluation protocols; it does not present model-specific experimental results.
AI.conclusion: ENTRAP-VL offers a structured, multimodal tool to rigorously study contextual entrainment in vision–language models, enabling veracity-aware assessment and guiding future research; public release planned.

title: Analytic Distribution of Classifier-Free Guidance for Schedule Design
summary: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is the default mechanism for conditional generation in diffusion models, but the distribution sampled by its deterministic guided dynamics is not captured by the usual product-distribution heuristic $p_0^ωq_0^{1-ω}$. We analyze CFG through the probability flow ODE and derive exact analytic path-integral representations of the induced distributions for both constant and time-dependent guidance. The resulting formulas show that CFG modifies $p_{t_0}$ by an exponential path-integral correction, and that a time-dependent schedule enters this correction through the weight $ω(t)-1$. This characterization explains how score discrepancies accumulate along sampling trajectories and motivates Distribution-Guided CFG (DG-CFG), a schedule that balances timestep contributions while accounting for signal strength and low-noise score-error amplification. A toy model with analytic scores closely verifies the predicted distributions. On Stable Diffusion~1.5, DG-CFG improves generation and yields a stronger diversity--fidelity trade-off across guidance strengths, with especially clear gains when strong guidance causes saturation and quality degradation in constant and heuristic schedules. Across NFE budgets, DG-CFG reaches fixed image-quality targets with fewer sampling steps, reducing the sampling cost needed to achieve target metrics.

AI.tldr: CFG sampling deviates from the naive p0^ω q0^{1-ω}; exact path-integral corrections derived via the probability-flow ODE; DG-CFG schedule improves diversity–fidelity and sampling efficiency, validated on Stable Diffusion 1.5 and a toy model.
AI.motivation: Understand the exact distribution induced by classifier-free guidance (CFG) during diffusion sampling, explain how score discrepancies accumulate, and mitigate saturation and score-error amplification through a better guidance schedule.
AI.method: Derive exact analytic path-integral representations of the induced distributions for constant and time-dependent CFG via the probability-flow ODE; identify exponential path-integral corrections and the role of ω(t) through ω(t)-1; propose Distribution-Guided CFG (DG-CFG) scheduling; validate with a toy model and Stable Diffusion 1.5 experiments; evaluate across different guidance strengths and number of function evaluations (NFE).
AI.result: CFG induces an exponential path-integral correction to p_t, with time-dependent guidance entering through ω(t)-1. DG-CFG provides a more balanced contribution across timesteps, improving the diversity–fidelity trade-off, particularly under strong guidance where constant/heuristic schedules saturate. In experiments, DG-CFG yields better image quality for given guidance and reduces required sampling steps to reach target metrics, demonstrating improved efficiency across NFE budgets.
AI.conclusion: Probabilistic interpretation of CFG reveals corrective path-integral terms that accumulate along sampling trajectories. A schedule-aware DG-CFG can balance contributions and signal strength, achieving higher-quality, diverse generations with fewer steps; validated on a toy model and SD 1.5.

title: SoftReason: A Fully Differentiable Neuro-Soft-Symbolic Deductive Reasoning Architecture over High-Dimensional Perceptual Data
summary: In many reasoning problems, the premises are not observed as discrete symbols, but must be inferred from high-dimensional inputs. Further, the predicate vocabulary, argument structure, and trusted evidence are supplied by a Knowledge Graph (KG), or rule definitions. Classical neuro-symbolic pipelines have a discrete interface between perception and deduction. We present a neuro-soft-symbolic architecture for differentiable deductive reasoning over latent perceptual facts and knowledge-provided predicates. SoftReason removes the gradient gap by representing the deductive state as a local soft interpretation tensor over candidate constants and predicates. Perception proposes probabilistic base facts, KG triples enter as high-confidence soft evidence, and every query anchor, predicate choice, and closure update remains differentiable. Our core innovation is a learned differentiable lift of the immediate-consequence operator. It uses predicate-definition embeddings and latent composition channels to form soft body-predicate mixtures, aggregate over all possible witnesses, propose query-conditioned head facts, and update the interpretation through a monotone probabilistic OR. We instantiate the framework on Knowledge-aware Visual Question Answering (KVQA), and demonstrates how SoftReason supports end-to-end perceptual grounding, KG evidence injection, and differentiable deductive closure in one trainable architecture.

AI.tldr: Introduces SoftReason, a differentiable neuro-soft-symbolic framework that performs deductive reasoning over latent perceptual facts and KG-provided predicates, enabling end-to-end training for KVQA.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between continuous perceptual inputs and symbolic reasoning by integrating latent facts with knowledge-graph predicates in a differentiable pipeline.
AI.method: Proposes a local soft interpretation tensor over candidate constants and predicates; perception provides probabilistic base facts; KG triples enter as soft evidence; introduces a learnable differentiable lift of the immediate-consequence operator using predicate-definition embeddings and latent composition channels; forms soft body-predicate mixtures; aggregates witnesses; proposes query-conditioned head facts; updates via a monotone probabilistic OR; instantiated for Knowledge-aware Visual Question Answering (KVQA) to enable end-to-end grounding, KG evidence injection, and differentiable deductive closure in a single trainable architecture.
AI.result: Demonstrates end-to-end perceptual grounding, KG evidence injection, and differentiable deductive closure within a single trainable architecture; demonstrated on KVQA with qualitative end-to-end integration of perception and knowledge-based reasoning.
AI.conclusion: SoftReason enables differentiable deductive reasoning over latent perceptual facts and knowledge-provided predicates, closing the gradient gap between perception and symbolic reasoning and enabling joint grounding and reasoning in knowledge-driven visual question answering and related tasks.

title: RIM: A Retrieval-In-Matching Framework for Cross-Domain Global Visual Localization of UAVs
comment: 56 pages, 10 figures, and 18 tables. Supplementary material is included
summary: Global visual localization of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) using remote-sensing reference maps has attracted increasing attention. However, acquisition-time and imaging-platform differences between UAV and reference imagery induce substantial cross-domain appearance and viewpoint shifts, challenging robust six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) pose estimation. We address these shifts by sampling UAV-viewpoint reference views from Google 3D Tiles across locations, altitudes, and orientations. A two-stage cross-domain fine-tuning recipe adapts SALAD using pose-near positives and geographically distant hard negatives, while local geometric consistency re-ranks the Top-K candidates. We further propose Retrieval-In-Matching (RIM), which freezes the adapted DINOv2-B retriever and distils a local-descriptor decoder that reuses its token field alongside a shallow VGG19 detail stream. One query-side DINOv2-B forward thus serves both SALAD retrieval and local description, eliminating a second foundation-model backbone while preserving retrieval descriptors by construction. We evaluate RIM zero-shot on the reconstructed EPFL Urbanscape and self-collected Chang'an Park datasets, both geographically disjoint from the training data. RIM outperforms ten recent retrieval baseline families. At 25/50 m under the full 3D distance metric, it improves Recall@1 over SALAD by 8.55/13.77 percentage points on EPFL and 4.45/8.94 points on Park. At Top-K=5, the complete measured localization query, including retrieval, candidate matching, and robust geometric verification, takes 67.9 ms end-to-end: 1.8 times faster than the strongest separate sparse-matching baseline and over 40 times faster than RoMa, while achieving comparable re-ranking accuracy. These results establish an efficient and deployable pipeline for UAV global visual localization in GNSS-challenged environments.

AI.tldr: Cross-domain UAV global localization using a two-stage SALAD fine-tuning and Retrieval-In-Matching (RIM) to achieve fast, robust 6-DoF pose estimation against remote-sensing maps, evaluated zero-shot on Urbanscape and Park with strong improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: Cross-domain appearance and viewpoint shifts between UAV imagery and reference maps hinder robust 6-DoF localization; need an efficient, deployable pipeline that handles GNSS-challenged environments.
AI.method: Construct UAV-viewpoint reference views from Google 3D Tiles; apply a two-stage cross-domain fine-tuning of SALAD using pose-near positives and geographically distant hard negatives; re-rank candidates with local geometric consistency. Propose Retrieval-In-Matching (RIM): freeze the adapted DINOv2-B retriever and distill a local-descriptor decoder that reuses the retriever's token field alongside a shallow VGG19 detail stream; a single query forward serves both retrieval and local description, avoiding a second backbone.
AI.result: RIM outperforms ten recent retrieval baselines in zero-shot evaluation on Urbanscape and Park datasets; achieves higher Recall at given 3D distance thresholds (e.g., 25/50 m), and end-to-end localization at Top-K=5 runs in 67.9 ms, faster than strong sparse-matching baselines and RoMa, with comparable re-ranking accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline delivers an efficient, scalable, and robust UAV global localization framework for GNSS-challenged environments by combining cross-domain fine-tuning, a distillation-based local descriptor within RIM, and fast geometric verification.

title: The World Model Remembers, the Actor Forgets: Dream Rehearsal for Continual Model-Based RL
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures. Code, pre-registration trail, and run data: https://github.com/gurpnijjer/dream-rehearsal
summary: Model-based reinforcement-learning agents of the DreamerV3 family forget catastrophically when trained on task sequences, even when an unbounded replay buffer preserves every earlier experience. We ask a question the continual-RL literature has assumed an answer to but never measured: which component forgets? Under never-clear replay, pre-registered component-level probes (n=3 seeds throughout) show that the world model retains essentially everything measurable about old tasks -- reward discrimination (retention ratio ~1.0), value estimates, and termination structure -- while the actor's behavior collapses. Forgetting in this regime is a channel problem, not a memory problem. We demonstrate this by intervention: with the world model frozen and identical imagined rollouts, reinforcement learning in imagination fails to recover a lost skill (0/3 seeds), while supervised self-imitation on the world model's own graded dreams recovers it on 3/3 seeds with zero environment interaction. Interleaved during training, this graded dream rehearsal yields a task-label-free, parameter-constant continual learner: 3/3 four-task chains retained where plain replay passes 0/3, 3/3 eight-task chains, and consistent gains over matched real-episode cloning (paired difference +0.13, bootstrap 95% CI [0.07, 0.24], complete seed separation). The dream-grading step is load-bearing: we characterize two scoring failure modes, provide an offline selection gauge that caught both before they contaminated results, and give a realized-first grading rule that closes them. All experiments were pre-registered with committed protocols; every refuted hypothesis is reported.

AI.tldr: DreamerV3 agents forget due to a channel/policy failure, not memory loss: the world model retains old-task information under continuous replay, while the actor catastrophically forgets. Interventions show imagined-rollout RL fails when the world model is frozen, but supervised self-imitation on the model’s dreams recovers skills. Interleaved graded dream rehearsal yields a parameter-constant continual learner capable of preserving multiple task chains; plain replay fails. Dream-grading is essential to avoid scoring failures. All work is pre-registered.
AI.motivation: Identify which component of model-based continual RL forgets during task sequences and whether forgetting is due to memory loss or other factors, addressing a gap in continual RL literature.
AI.method: Component-level probes with never-clear replay, fixed-world-model interventions, imagined rollouts, and task sequences; pre-registered protocols across seeds (n=3); compare imagination-based RL versus supervised self-imitation on model dreams; interleave graded dream rehearsal; offline grading checks to detect scoring failures; evaluate multiple task chains (four-task and eight-task sequences).
AI.result: World model retains essentially all measurable old-task information (reward discrimination ~1.0 retention; value estimates; termination structure); the actor’s behavior collapses, indicating a channel-p vs memory issue. Imagined-rollout RL with a frozen world model fails to regain lost skills; however, supervised self-imitation on the world-model dreams recovers skills with zero environment interaction. Graded dream rehearsal enables a parameter-constant continual learner: 3/3 four-task chains retained; 3/3 eight-task chains; gains over real-episode cloning (paired difference +0.13, 95% CI [0.07, 0.24]); robust across seeds with explicit seed separation. Dream-grading is critical, with identified scoring failure modes and an offline gauge and rule to avoid contamination. All experiments pre-registered; all refuted hypotheses reported.
AI.conclusion: Memory in the world model persists across task sequences, but the forgetting originates in the actor/policy channel. Graded dream rehearsal is an effective, parameter-stable mechanism for continual learning in DreamerV3-like agents, enabling robust retention of multiple task chains without additional environment data. Proper grading and pre-registered protocols are essential for reliable conclusions.

title: HeadCast: Casting Attention Heads for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation
summary: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models have become a promising paradigm for long and streaming video synthesis, but the continuously growing Key-Value (KV) cache makes attention the dominant inference cost, especially at high resolution where each frame contributes many tokens. Existing remedies either evict the cache with coarse heuristics that cause inter-frame flickering, or require model re-training. We propose HeadCast, a training-free, plug-and-play acceleration framework built on the observation that a pre-trained AR model's attention heads exhibit stable, heterogeneous behaviors. After a short warm-up, HeadCast performs a one-time classification at the maximum-noise step that sorts every head into one of four archetypes: Sink, Dummy, Spatial, and Global, and restructures the monolithic KV cache into head-specific pathways. Crucially, it retains the Global heads that preserve the long-range temporal consistency aggressive eviction destroys. Because the Spatial pathway operates on a fixed-size grid, its savings grow with resolution: across state-of-the-art AR models, HeadCast accelerates inference by up to 1.62x at 720P and 1.95x at 1080P, while keeping VBench quality on par with full attention and largely flicker-free. Code is available at https://github.com/sjlgaga/HeadCast .

AI.tldr: HeadCast is a training-free acceleration framework for AR video diffusion that personalizes per-head KV caching by classifying attention heads into Sink, Dummy, Spatial, Global, providing up to 1.95x speed-up at 1080p while maintaining quality and reducing flicker.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive video diffusion models incur growing KV cache and attention costs; existing evictions degrades temporal coherence and retraining is costly. A training-free method to accelerate inference without sacrificing long-range temporal consistency is sought.
AI.method: After a short warm-up, perform a one-time classification at the maximum-noise step to categorize each attention head into four archetypes (Sink, Dummy, Spatial, Global); restructure the monolithic KV cache into head-specific pathways, retaining Global heads to preserve temporal coherence; the Spatial pathway uses a fixed-size grid; implement as a plug-in that does not require re-training.
AI.result: Across state-of-the-art AR models, HeadCast achieves up to 1.62x speed-up at 720p and 1.95x at 1080p; preserves VBench quality comparable to full attention and reduces inter-frame flicker.
AI.conclusion: HeadCast provides a training-free, plug-in acceleration for AR video diffusion that preserves temporal coherence and scales with resolution, offering substantial inference speedups without retraining; code is publicly available.

title: Convergence-Latency-Aware Adaptive Modulation and Resource Allocation in RIS-Assisted Wireless Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning (FL) over wireless networks suffers from significant training latency and degraded convergence due to unreliable wireless transmission, especially under blocked propagation environments. Although reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) can improve communication reliability, existing wireless FL studies rarely characterize the trade-off between learning convergence and communication delay under modulation-dependent transmission errors. In this paper, we consider a wireless FL system operating under RIS-assisted blocked-link propagation scenarios, and focus on adaptive modulation and sub-channel allocation for convergence-latency aware communication design. By characterizing the effect of symbol errors on uploaded local gradients, we derive a convergence-related upper bound that reveals the impact of symbol error rate (SER) on FL loss decay. Based on this result, we formulate a joint convergence-latency optimization problem, which is cast as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, and solve it using a low-complexity hybrid alternating optimization framework. Extensive experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Speech Commands show that the proposed scheme consistently achieves faster convergence and higher test accuracy than existing adaptive communication schemes, especially in complex tasks and challenging wireless scenarios.

AI.tldr: RIS-assisted wireless FL with blocked links; adaptive modulation and sub-channel allocation to balance convergence and latency; derives a SER-dependent convergence bound; solves a joint MINLP via a hybrid alternating optimization; experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Speech Commands show faster convergence and higher accuracy than existing adaptive schemes.
AI.motivation: Wireless federated learning suffers from latency and convergence degradation due to unreliable transmissions, especially in blocked propagation environments. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) can improve reliability, but there is a need to quantify and optimize the trade-off between symbol-error-rate (SER)-induced learning degradation and communication delay.
AI.method: Model the impact of symbol errors on uploaded local gradients to derive a convergence-related upper bound that links SER to FL loss decay. Formulate a joint convergence-latency optimization problem for modulation and sub-channel allocation (with RIS considerations) as a mixed-integer nonlinear program (MINLP). Solve with a low-complexity hybrid alternating optimization framework.
AI.result: The convergence bound shows SER directly affects FL loss decay. The proposed hybrid optimization framework achieves faster convergence and higher test accuracy than existing adaptive communication schemes, particularly in complex tasks and challenging wireless scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive modulation and sub-channel allocation in RIS-assisted wireless FL effectively improves convergence-latency performance under blocked links. The proposed MINLP formulation with a hybrid solver provides a practical design with demonstrated empirical gains on standard benchmarks; potential extensions include broader RIS configurations, energy efficiency, and robustness to channel estimation errors.

title: Real-Time EEG Cap Electrode Detection for Guided Point-of-Care Placement
summary: We present a two-stage vision system that detects EEG cap electrodes in a live webcam stream and validates their anatomical placement in real time. A single-class YOLO detector localises electrodes; a geometric stage assigns each detection to a named 10-20 role from facial landmarks. Evaluating under subject-disjoint leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation across five subjects wearing the clinically-validated Small/Medium/Large caps, the detector attains mAP@.5 = 0.94 +/- 0.07 across five held-out folds (0.96 pooled). A dedicated leave-one-cap-out axis, holding out every frame of a cap regardless of subject, leaves Medium and Large mAP@.5 within 0.01 of LOSO (0.97, 0.97) while Small drops to 0.72 +/- 0.28, a gap confounded with subject familiarity rather than cap style. Geometric augmentation (rotation, perspective, mixup) improves in-plane-roll robustness and temporal-electrode recall at no inference cost, and a landmark-driven head crop extends the usable distance range, lifting mAP@.5 from 0.23 to 0.45 at 0.6 x apparent scale. A compact mobile-candidate backbone (YOLOv10n) keeps the detector at real-time throughput (19 FPS) on a commodity CPU at 640 px.

AI.tldr: A two-stage, real-time system detects EEG cap electrodes in a live webcam stream and assigns them to 10-20 montage positions. A single-class YOLO detector localizes electrodes; a geometric stage maps detections to named locations. Evaluated with subject-disjoint LOSO across five subjects and cap sizes, achieving mAP@0.5 ~0.94–0.97; small-cap performance lags due to subject familiarity. Geometric augmentation and landmark-driven crops improve robustness and range. A lightweight backbone (YOLOv10n) maintains 19 FPS on CPU.
AI.motivation: Enable automatic, real-time verification of EEG electrode placement across subjects and cap sizes in consumer video settings, reducing manual electrode verification and ensuring correct 10-20 montage labeling.
AI.method: Two-stage pipeline: (1) single-class YOLO detector localizes electrode appearances; (2) a geometric stage assigns each detection to a named 10-20 electrode position using facial-landmark-derived framing. Evaluations include subject-disjoint LOSO cross-validation across five subjects with Small/Medium/Large caps, and leave-one-cap-out analyses. Augmentations (rotation, perspective, mixup) improve in-plane roll robustness and temporal electrode recall; landmark-driven head crops extend usable distance. A compact backbone (YOLOv10n) enables real-time CPU performance.
AI.result: mAP@0.5 = 0.94 ± 0.07 (LOSO across five folds); pooled mAP@0.5 = 0.96. Leave-one-cap-out: Medium 0.97, Large 0.97; Small 0.72 ± 0.28 (gap due to subject familiarity). Geometric augmentation improves in-plane robustness and recall; head-crop extends usable distance from mAP 0.23 to 0.45 at 0.6x scale. Inference runs at 19 FPS on commodity CPU.
AI.conclusion: A practical, real-time EEG-cap electrode detection and 10-20 mapping system. The two-stage approach yields strong cross-subject/generalization performance, with geometry-based augmentation and landmark-guided cropping boosting robustness and usable range; small-cap performance remains the main challenge, likely tied to subject familiarity rather than cap style. YOLOv10n enables mobile deployment.

title: AlphaRoute: Large Language Models as Semantic Optimizers for Multi-Objective Routing
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in the IEEE International Conference on LLM-Aided Design, 2026, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA. Code available at https://github.com/Kcbir/AlphaRoute
summary: Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) global routing is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem requiring signal net assignment across capacity-constrained 3D grids while minimizing congestion, wirelength, and via transitions. Because traditional heuristics rely on static penalty schedules that fail on complex congestion topologies, we present AlphaRoute: a multi-objective adaptive search framework reformulating rip-up and reroute (R&R) into a dynamic optimization system. We introduce SHAP-based overflow decomposition to isolate per-net congestion, driving targeted subgraph extraction via 3D Dijkstra maze routing and an adaptive PathFinder policy. Crucially, AlphaRoute employs Large Language Models (LLMs) as semantic policy optimizers. Bounded by a deterministic knowledge graph, the LLMs interpret congestion metrics to dynamically adjust penalty parameters. Evaluated on ISPD 2025 benchmarks, AlphaRoute reduces overflow by 98.6% on MEMPOOL. On the constrained ARIANE design, we achieve an overflow of 146,109 (a 29.8x reduction in overflow over the state of the art), yielding a penalized score of S_orig = 0.0538 versus the State-of-the-art (SOTA) 1.780. These results demonstrate that superior algorithmic search geometry can overcome the latency of interpreted Python implementations.

AI.tldr: AlphaRoute reframes VLSI global routing as a multi-objective adaptive search, integrating SHAP-based congestion decomposition, 3D Dijkstra routing, adaptive PathFinder, and LLM-driven policy optimization to dynamically adjust penalties. It achieves substantial congestion overflow reductions on MEMPOOL and ARIANE benchmarks, surpassing SOTA.
AI.motivation: Conventional static-penalty heuristics fail to manage complex congestion topologies in NP-hard VLSI routing; there is a need for adaptive, data-driven optimization that can dynamically reweight objectives during routing.
AI.method: Propose AlphaRoute: (1) SHAP-based overflow decomposition to assign per-net congestion, (2) targeted subgraph extraction via 3D Dijkstra maze routing, (3) adaptive PathFinder policy, (4) LLMs as semantic policy optimizers bounded by a deterministic knowledge graph to adjust penalty parameters based on congestion metrics.
AI.result: On ISPD 2025 MEMPOOL: overflow reduced by 98.6%. On ARIANE: overflow 146,109, a 29.8x reduction vs SOTA; penalized score S_orig = 0.0538 vs SOTA 1.780.
AI.conclusion: The integration of adaptive search with LLM-guided policy optimization yields substantial routing quality gains, indicating that algorithmic search geometry can offset interpretation latency and offer robust improvements over traditional heuristics.

title: SHFormer: Dynamic Spectral Filtering Convolutional Neural Network and High-pass Kernel Generation Transformer for Adaptive MRI Reconstruction
comment: Published in Neural Networks (Elsevier), Vol. 187, Article 107334, July 2025. DOI: 10.1016/j.neunet.2025.107334
summary: Attention Mechanism (AM) selectively focuses on essential information for imaging tasks and captures relationships between distant pixel neighborhoods to compute feature representations. Accelerated MRI reconstruction benefits from AM, as the imaging process involves Fourier domain measurements that influence image representation non-locally. However, AM-based models are more adept at capturing low-frequency information with limited capacity for high-frequency representations, restricting models to smooth reconstruction. Additionally, AM-based models need mode-specific retraining for multimodal MRI data, as their knowledge is restricted to local contextual variations that may be inadequate to capture transferable features across heterogeneous domains. To address these challenges, we propose a neuromodulation-based discriminative multi-spectral AM for scalable MRI reconstruction that can (i) propagate context-aware high-frequency details for high-quality reconstruction, and (ii) capture features reusable across deviated unseen domains in multimodal MRI. The proposed network consists of a spectral filtering CNN to capture mode-specific transferable features and a dynamic high-pass kernel generation transformer focusing on high-frequency details. We evaluate our model on comparative studies in supervised and self-supervised learning, diffusion model-based training, closed-set and open-set generalization under heterogeneous MRI data, and interpretation-based analysis. Our method offers scalable, high-quality reconstruction with best improvement margins of ~1 dB in PSNR and ~0.01 in SSIM under unseen scenarios. Code: https://github.com/sriprabhar/SHFormer

AI.tldr: Introduces SHFormer: a neuromodulated multi-spectral attention framework for scalable MRI reconstruction using a spectral filtering CNN and a dynamic high-pass kernel generation transformer to propagate high-frequency details and enable cross-domain transfer in multimodal MRI; achieves ~1 dB PSNR and ~0.01 SSIM gains on unseen data; code available.
AI.motivation: Address attention mechanisms' bias toward low-frequency information and limited high-frequency representation; and poor cross-domain transfer in multimodal MRI requiring mode-specific retraining.
AI.method: A two-branch architecture: spectral filtering CNN for mode-specific transferable features; dynamic high-pass kernel generation transformer (neuromodulated) to emphasize high-frequency content; integrates with a discriminative multi-spectral AM.
AI.result: Assessed in supervised and self-supervised learning, diffusion-model-based training, closed/open-set generalization across heterogeneous MRI data, plus interpretation-based analyses; shows best improvement margins (~1 dB PSNR, ~0.01 SSIM) under unseen scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Offers scalable, high-quality MRI reconstruction with transferable features across modalities; code release provided.

title: An Isotropy-Preserving Spectral Cap for Muon: Theory and Three Case Studies
comment: Preliminary Report; Larger scale experiments ongoing; Comments are welcome
summary: Muon and related matrix-sign optimizers are increasingly used to pre-train large language models, but their effect on the internal geometry of individual weight matrices is not well understood. This preliminary report proposes a unified framework built on a single idealizing assumption -- exact scale invariance of the loss under weight rescaling, which holds approximately in normalization-heavy networks. Under this assumption, plain SGD carries a built-in 1/||W|| brake on its update size, whereas Muon's matrix-sign step removes that brake, so both the Frobenius and spectral norms drift outward faster (t^{1/2} versus t^{1/4}). We further observe that the spectral-norm perturbation has a non-negative second-order term. This implies that a lightweight "spectral cap" -- which projects out only the first-order growth of the single top singular direction from each update -- can control the output covariance W K_X W^T without freezing training: the weight keeps learning through non-top directions, top-direction rotation, and top switching. We relate this cap to the min-entropy (H-infinity) of the singular-value spectrum. We then study three systems trained with Muon: a nanoGPT feed-forward projection, a 64-expert mixture-of-experts router, and the query/key projections of a bf16 FlashAttention block. In each case the cap increases isotropy and, at the margins -- a router collapsing to a single expert, and the near-divergence of one attention head -- prevents a concrete failure, while leaving validation loss essentially unchanged. We emphasize that the scale-invariance assumption is strong and that these small-scale results are preliminary; comments are welcome.

AI.tldr: Under a scale-invariance assumption, Muon's matrix-sign optimizer drives weight-norms outward faster than SGD; a lightweight spectral cap can preserve isotropy and learning without significant loss in validation, demonstrated on three Muon-trained systems; results are preliminary due to the strong assumption.
AI.motivation: Characterize how scale invariance interacts with matrix-sign updates and how to stabilize the resulting dynamics via spectral caps; provide a unified theoretical framework and preliminary empirical evidence.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis assuming exact loss scale invariance under weight rescaling; derive update scaling (SGD braking term 1/||W|| vs Muon's removal); analyze first- and second-order perturbations of spectral norm; propose spectral cap projecting first-order growth of top singular direction; connect to singular-value spectrum entropy; test on nanoGPT FF, MoE router, and bf16 FlashAttention projections.
AI.result: Spectral cap increases isotropy; in certain edge cases (router collapse to single expert; one attention head near-diverging) training persists with little change to validation loss; no clear failure; results are preliminary and rely on the strong assumption.
AI.conclusion: Spectral-cap approach is a lightweight stabilization that can coexist with ongoing learning; further validation needed; larger-scale experiments and relaxation of the scale-invariance assumption recommended.

title: StreamHOI: Interaction-aware Temporal Memory Adaptation for Streaming HOI Video Generation
comment: Code and models are available at https://github.com/KlingAIResearch/StreamHOI
summary: Existing human--object interaction (HOI) video generation methods are largely limited to offline short-video generation with complex driving conditions, making them unsuitable for real-time interactive applications. We present \emph{StreamHOI}, a low-latency streaming framework for long-duration HOI video generation. Instead of converting heavily conditioned HOI pipelines into streaming systems, we study how an image-to-video streaming generator should organize historical memory to preserve interactions under bounded latency. We find that the standard sink-local memory design faces a trade-off in streaming HOI generation, and different transformer blocks show different historical-memory preferences for HOI regions and surrounding regions. To match memory composition with block behavior, StreamHOI performs offline HOI-aware block profiling and applies bias-guided memory-specialized training to adapt the generator to block-specific memory layouts. We further introduce a memory distance scaling module to strengthen long-range access to early interaction states. Extensive comparisons with both long-video baselines and recent HOI generation methods demonstrate that StreamHOI achieves strong interaction plausibility, object fidelity, human quality and efficiency, reaching 17.6 FPS with 0.75s first-chunk latency.

AI.tldr: A streaming, low-latency HOI video generator called StreamHOI enables long-duration interactive HOI synthesis by profiling transformer blocks and customizing memory layouts with bias-guided training and a memory distance scaling module, achieving real-time performance (17.6 FPS) with 0.75 s first-chunk latency.
AI.motivation: To enable real-time, long-duration human--object interaction video generation, addressing the limitations of existing offline, short-video HOI methods and the challenge of maintaining interactions under bounded latency in streaming settings.
AI.method: Introduce offline HOI-aware block profiling to understand how different transformer blocks rely on historical memory. Develop bias-guided memory-specialized training to align generator parameters with block-specific memory layouts. Propose a memory distance scaling module to enhance long-range access to early interaction states. Replace or augment standard sink-local memory with a streaming memory design tailored to HOI regions and surrounding areas.
AI.result: StreamHOI achieves 17.6 FPS with 0.75 s first-chunk latency, while maintaining strong interaction plausibility, object fidelity, and human quality, outperforming long-video baselines and recent HOI generation methods in efficiency and quality.
AI.conclusion: By aligning memory organization with transformer block behavior and introducing memory-aware training plus a distance-scaling mechanism, StreamHOI enables low-latency, long-duration HOI video generation suitable for interactive streaming applications.

title: OPIUM: Mitigating Steering Externalities and Over-Refusal via Dual Objective Latent Optimization
comment: Accepted to the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Activation steering provides a lightweight mechanism for controlling large language models at inference time, but steering vectors can have unintended externalities: utility vectors may weaken safety behavior, while refusal vectors may induce over-refusal on benign prompts. We introduce OPIUM (Optimizing Protected Injections via Utility Manifolds), a training-free method for sanitizing steering vectors through representation matching. Given reference behaviors on two prompt sets, OPIUM optimizes a new steering vector that preserves the downstream representations induced by the desired intervention while matching a safer reference behavior on prompts where the original vector fails. Across steering-externality and over-refusal settings, OPIUM improves the safety--utility tradeoff relative to vanilla steering and directional ablation, suggesting that harmful side effects of activation steering can often be mitigated directly in activation space.

AI.tldr: OPIUM is a training-free method that sanitizes activation steering vectors by representation matching, improving the safety–utility tradeoff and reducing externalities without retraining.
AI.motivation: Activation steering can control large language models at inference but introduces externalities: safety degradation from utility vectors and over-refusal from refusal vectors. A lightweight, training-free sanitization method is needed to mitigate these harms while preserving desired behavior.
AI.method: OPIUM constructs a new steering vector by optimizing for preserved downstream representations induced by the desired intervention while aligning (matching) the representations on prompts where the original vector caused unsafe behavior to a safer reference behavior. This is done via representation matching across two prompt sets, enabling sanitization without retraining.
AI.result: Across both steering-externality and over-refusal scenarios, OPIUM yields a better safety–utility balance compared to vanilla steering and directional ablation, indicating that activation-steering harms can be mitigated directly in activation space.
AI.conclusion: Activation steering harms can be mitigated in activation space without training by optimizing steering vectors to match safe representations while preserving target interventions, providing a lightweight, training-free path to safer LLM control.

title: PerceptDrive: Perception Prior World-Action Modeling with Adaptive Expert Routing for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Frozen perception foundation models encode rich geometric, semantic, and dynamic knowledge. Yet narrow conditioning interfaces may attenuate task-relevant cues, while static fusion cannot adjust expert contributions to each scene. We cast this challenge as the prior-to-plan transfer problem and introduce PerceptDrive, a perception prior world-action modeling framework with adaptive expert routing. PerceptDrive feeds teacher-distilled priors from a frozen, driving-adapted provider and dense observation latents from a frozen self-supervised video encoder into a trainable expert-routed world-action model. Expert-specific query branches process these signals, while a prior-retention objective anchors each branch to its prior. A router predicts soft gates from a shared scene representation and combines the expert conditions before trajectory generation. During training, privileged rule-based sub-metric estimates for branch-specific trajectory drafts provide soft-gate distillation targets. The predicted action-free future latent conditions a flow-matching actor. At inference, privileged components are absent; with one front-facing camera, PerceptDrive generates one trajectory per planning step without test-time scoring, reranking, or search. Experiments show that PerceptDrive achieves state-of-the-art performance with 90.4 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.2 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, outperforming existing methods. Ablations confirm complementary gains from prior retention and scene-conditioned routing, alongside differential reliance on the three priors. These results demonstrate that preserving and adaptively routing perception priors improves direct planning without test-time candidate selection.

AI.tldr: PerceptDrive uses adaptive routing of frozen perception priors to guide a world-action model for driving; achieves state-of-the-art planning with no test-time search.
AI.motivation: Narrow conditioning interfaces and static fusion in perception-based planning limit task cues; a prior-to-plan transfer enables leveraging rich geometric, semantic, and dynamic priors from frozen perception models for planning.
AI.method: Teacher-distilled priors from a frozen provider plus dense latent encodings feed specialized expert branches; a router computes soft gates to combine expert conditions; a prior-retention objective anchors each branch; privileged rule-based sub-metric estimates provide soft-gate distillation targets; during training, privileged components used to guide routing; at inference, privileged components are absent; one front-facing camera yields one trajectory per planning step with no test-time scoring or reranking; a flow-matching actor handles the future latent.
AI.result: State-of-the-art NAVSIM results: PDMS 90.4 on v1 and EPDMS 90.2 on v2; ablations show complementary gains from prior retention and scene-conditioned routing; demonstrates benefits of preserving and routing priors without test-time candidate selection.
AI.conclusion: Preserving and adaptively routing perception priors improves direct planning in driving tasks.

title: Auto-Fill: Learning to Predict Missing Values Accurately with Specialist Language Models
summary:
Predicting missing cell values in tabular data is a fundamental problem in data cleaning. While state-of-the-art reasoning models show great promise in predicting missing values in tables, by reasoning holistically across rows and columns, they are costly to deploy at scale and tend to be overconfident, often generating hallucinated or false-positive predictions.
  In this paper, we observe that achieving high-precision missing-value prediction in tables requires a distinct combination of three capabilities: (1) world knowledge, (2) text-based reasoning, and (3) code-based reasoning. We systematically explore design choices for combining these capabilities, and propose an Auto-Fill approach that post-trains three specialist small language models (SLMs), each optimized for one capability. We develop a calibrated ensemble mechanism that either dynamically selects the most confident specialist or abstains, ensuring high accuracy.
  Extensive experiments on 11 benchmarks with 2200 real tables drawn from diverse domains show that Auto-Fill achieves superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art reasoning models (e.g., o3-pro, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek R1), while operating at a fraction (less than 1%) of the cost of these frontier models. Our results highlight the effectiveness of specialization and calibrated abstention in the important domain of tabular data. Auto-Fill is publicly available at https://github.com/lyrain2001/auto-fill.

AI.tldr: Auto-Fill post-trains three specialist small language models (world knowledge, text-based reasoning, code-based reasoning) for high-precision missing-value prediction in tabular data, using a calibrated ensemble with abstention.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art reasoning models for missing-value prediction in tables are costly and prone to overconfidence/hallucinations; high-precision prediction requires a mix of world knowledge, language reasoning, and code-based reasoning.
AI.method: Post-train three specialist SLMs, each optimized for one capability; develop a calibrated ensemble that dynamically selects the most confident specialist or abstains, enabling high accuracy at low cost.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 11 benchmarks with 2200 real tables show Auto-Fill achieves superior accuracy compared to models like o3-pro, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek R1, at less than 1% of their cost.
AI.conclusion: Specialization and calibrated abstention effectively improve missing-value prediction in tabular data; Auto-Fill demonstrates strong performance and cost efficiency and is publicly available.

title: RS-RIE-Bench: Benchmarking Reasoning-Guided Remote Sensing Image Editing
summary: Remote sensing image editing aims to modify remote sensing images according to natural language instructions while preserving geographic rules and sensor observation characteristics. Existing benchmarks mainly target natural images or general visual scenes, and thus may not fully capture the reasoning, regional control, and sensor-consistency abilities required in remote sensing editing. To fill this gap, we introduce RS-RIE-Bench, the first benchmark for reasoning-guided remote sensing image editing. RS-RIE-Bench organizes tasks into three categories: temporal reasoning, causal reasoning, and spatial reasoning. These categories capture temporal evolution, causal consequence, and spatial imaging consistency in remote sensing scenes. The evaluation protocol covers three dimensions: target region plausibility, non-target region preservation, and image quality consistency. We further demonstrate the feasibility of MLLM-based evaluation through cross-judge consistency analysis and stratified expert review. Systematic evaluation on eight open-source and closed-source image editing models shows that current models still have clear limitations in reasoning-guided remote sensing editing. Even the strongest model achieves only 24.28\% overall accuracy under the strict joint-satisfaction criterion, while the mean relaxed joint-4 success rate across all eight models is 32.23\%. Causal reasoning and spatial reasoning remain especially challenging, and several open-source models are close to zero in some categories. These results show that RS-RIE-Bench can effectively reveal the limitations of current models in geographic reasoning, regional control, and sensor-consistent generation. It also provides a standardized benchmark and a clear research direction for future remote sensing intelligent editing models.

AI.tldr: New RS-RIE-Bench benchmark for reasoning-guided remote sensing image editing, with three reasoning axes (temporal, causal, spatial) and tripartite evaluation (target plausibility, non-target preservation, image quality). Eight models show strong gaps; strongest at 24.28% strict joint-satisfaction, mean relaxed joint-4 32.23%. Highlights limitations in geographic reasoning and sensor-consistent generation, and provides a research direction.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on natural images or general scenes and do not capture the specific demands of remote sensing editing, such as geographic constraints and sensor observation characteristics. There is a need for a benchmark that measures reasoning capabilities and regional control in remote sensing contexts.
AI.method: Propose RS-RIE-Bench with three reasoning categories: temporal, causal, and spatial. Develop an evaluation protocol across three dimensions: target region plausibility, non-target region preservation, and image quality consistency. Validate the feasibility of MLLM-based evaluation via cross-judge consistency and stratified expert review. Systematically evaluate eight image editing models (open-source and closed-source).
AI.result: Current models show clear limitations in reasoning-guided remote sensing editing. The top-performing model achieves 24.28% overall accuracy under strict joint-satisfaction; mean relaxed joint-4 success rate across all models is 32.23%. Causal and spatial reasoning are especially challenging; several open-source models approach zero in some categories.
AI.conclusion: RS-RIE-Bench effectively reveals limitations in geographic reasoning, regional control, and sensor-consistent generation, offering a standardized benchmark and clear directions for future remote sensing intelligent editing research.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Regret for Reinforcement Learning without Horizon Dependence
summary:
We study horizon-free regret minimization for finite-horizon time-homogeneous tabular Markov decision processes with $S$ states, $A$ actions, horizon $H$, and per-trajectory total reward bounded by $1$.
  We propose a new algorithm and prove a regret upper bound \[\tilde O(\sqrt{SAK}+S^8A^3)\] with failure probability $δ$, where $K$ is the number of episodes and $\tilde O(\cdot)$ hides $\mathsf{poly}\log(S,A,K,1/δ)$.
  Thus, the regret is $H$-free and asymptotically optimal, matching the contextual-bandit lower bound $Ω(\sqrt{SAK})$ up to logarithmic factors. This completely removes the $\log H$ dependence from the previous $\tilde O(\sqrt{SAK\log H}+S^2A\log H)$ guarantee of Zhang et al. (2021), and drastically improves the prior best horizon-free regret $\tilde O(\sqrt{S^9A^3K})$ of Zhang et al. (2022) asymptotically.
  The main technical difficulty is that the optimal value functions $\{V_h^*\}_{h=1}^H$ are time-inhomogeneous even though the transition kernel is time-homogeneous. A direct union bound over all value functions typically incurs an additional $\min\{\log H,S\}$ factor. We avoid this factor by (i) exploiting the monotonicity of $V_h^*$ in $h$ and (ii) non-trivially projecting the value functions onto an $S$-dimensional grid.
  Our analysis relies on three additional ingredients. First, we introduce a horizon-truncation argument that enables reward-based exploration and removes the cost of a separate reward-free exploration phase. Second, we design a cutting bonus that preserves both optimism and the monotonicity needed for planning. Third, we prove a new bound on total deviation for time-homogeneous MDPs, which controls the clipped variance terms in the cutting bonus with adjustable polynomial dependence on $S$ and without any dependence on $H$. Together, these tools yield an asymptotically optimal horizon-free regret guarantee.

AI.tldr: Introduces horizon-free regret minimization for finite-horizon time-homogeneous tabular MDPs; achieves tilde O(sqrt{SAK} + S^8 A^3) regret, independent of H, via horizon truncation, a cutting bonus, monotone value-function projections, and a new total-deviation bound; improves on Zhang et al. (2021, 2022).
AI.motivation: Eliminate the log-H factor in horizon-based MDP regret bounds and reach a near-optimal rate akin to contextual-bandits. The work highlights the challenge that optimal value functions V_h^* are time-inhomogeneous under time-homogeneous dynamics, and aims to close the gap with the best lower bounds.
AI.method: Proposes an algorithm with (i) horizon truncation for reward-based exploration, (ii) a cutting bonus that preserves optimism and monotonicity for planning, (iii) projection of the time-varying value functions {V_h^*} onto an S-dimensional grid to control a union bound. Additionally, introduces a total-deviation bound for time-homogeneous MDPs to bound clipped variance terms in the cutting bonus with polynomial dependence on S and no dependence on H.
AI.result: Regret bound tilde O(sqrt{SAK} + S^8 A^3) with failure probability ; horizon-free and asymptotically optimal, matching the contextual-bandit lower bound aOmega(sqrt{SAK}) up to logarithmic factors; removes log H from previous bounds and improves prior horizon-free rates.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers the first asymptotically optimal horizon-free regret guarantee for finite-horizon, time-homogeneous tabular MDPs by combining horizon truncation, a cutting bonus, value-function projections, and a new total-deviation bound, offering techniques potentially applicable to broader settings.

title: Not All Patches are Equal: Sampling Matters for Visible-Infrared Pre-Training
summary: Visible-infrared (VIS-IR) alignment is a key pre-training task for robust multi-sensor perception. Most existing methods use uniform patch-wise contrastive learning, but this can be unreliable in VIS-IR data because imaging-physics differences make some spatially paired regions inherently less comparable, and aligning them with equal strength hinders representation learning and downstream transfer. In this paper, we revisit VIS-IR pre-training from a sampling perspective and propose Importance-Aware Sampling (IAS), which adjusts training emphasis based on patch reliability. Specifically, IAS (i) derives patch weights from infrared structural cues and uses them to reweight the contrastive objective; (ii) learns a soft importance mask with a lightweight sampler, optionally warm-started from the hand-crafted prior; and (iii) employs a patch curriculum learning strategy that gradually expands from high-reliability regions to harder patches. It is worth noting that IAS is plug-and-play and works with both patch-/correlation-level alignment (e.g., UNIV-style) and image-level contrastive baselines (e.g., ImageBind-style). Extensive experiments on multiple VIS-IR benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, including for IR semantic segmentation, IR object detection and VIS semantic segmentation and cross-modal retrieval task. Code will be released on https://github.com/KlayMa527/IAS.

AI.tldr: IAS reweights patch-level VIS-IR pretraining using patch reliability estimates to focus learning on trustworthy regions, with a soft importance mask and a patch curriculum, yielding consistent gains across VIS-IR tasks.
AI.motivation: Uniform patch-wise contrastive learning can be unreliable for VIS-IR data due to imaging-physics differences that make some spatial regions inherently less comparable; improving sampling emphasis on reliable patches can enhance cross-modal alignment and downstream transfer.
AI.method: 1) Compute patch weights from infrared structural cues and reweight the contrastive objective accordingly. 2) Learn a soft importance mask with a lightweight sampler, potentially warm-started from a hand-crafted prior. 3) Apply a patch curriculum that expands from high-reliability patches to harder ones. IAS is plug-and-play for both patch-/correlation-level alignment (e.g., UNIV-style) and image-level baselines (e.g., ImageBind-style).
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple VIS-IR benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines, including IR semantic segmentation, IR object detection, VIS semantic segmentation, and cross-modal retrieval.
AI.conclusion: IAS is an effective, plug-and-play sampling-based enhancement for VIS-IR pre-training that improves cross-modal alignment and downstream tasks by focusing learning on reliable regions and gradually incorporating harder patches; code will be released.

title: Adversarial Frontiers: Minimum-Norm Attack Ensembles for Robustness Evaluation
summary: Adversarial robustness is commonly evaluated with predefined attack ensembles, such as AutoAttack, at a single perturbation budget $\varepsilon$ and on a selective choice of perturbation norms. We argue this formulation is fundamentally limited. First, robustness--perturbation curves may intersect or decay at different rates across models, making single-$\varepsilon$ rankings unstable. Second, current ensembles provide no evidence of optimality, leaving an unknown gap to worst-case performance. Third, fixed attack configurations provide no systematic control over the trade-off between attack strength and evaluation cost. To address these limitations, we introduce a unified evaluation framework based on a comprehensive pool of minimum-norm attacks and robustness--perturbation curves across $\ell_0$, $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$ and $\ell_\infty$ norms. We define the attack frontier as the worst-case robustness estimate the attack pool produces against a model. We then formalize evaluation as a frontier-approximation problem, constructing minimum-norm attack ensembles, optimized subsets of the comprehensive pool, that approach the frontier under a controllable query budget, with larger budgets monotonically tightening the estimate. Furthermore, we define the defense frontier as the maximum robustness across the model set at each perturbation size. We finally propose the Defense Optimality Index to rank defenses by their gap to the defense frontier, providing a ranking without selecting a reference $\varepsilon$. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, our ensembles match or exceed AutoAttack on most defenses at every budget tier, at fixed and controllable query cost, offering practitioners a query-controlled, curve-based alternative to fixed-$\varepsilon$ evaluation.

AI.tldr: Proposes a unified, curve-based evaluation framework for adversarial robustness using a broad pool of minimum-norm attacks across L0, L1, L2, L∞, defines attack/defense frontiers and a Defense Optimality Index to rank defenses without fixed epsilon.
AI.motivation: Current adversarial robustness evaluations rely on predefined attack ensembles at a single perturbation budget epsilon, leading to unstable rankings, unknown optimality gaps, and uncontrolled evaluation cost.
AI.method: Introduce an attack frontier as the worst-case robustness from the attack pool; formulate frontier-approximation by constructing minimum-norm attack ensembles and optimal subsets under a query budget, with budget-driven tightening. Define the defense frontier as the maximum robustness across models per perturbation size; propose Defense Optimality Index to rank defenses by gap to frontier without choosing a reference epsilon.
AI.result: Empirical results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show ensembles match or exceed AutoAttack on most defenses at every budget tier under fixed or controllable query cost, offering a query-controlled, curve-based alternative to fixed-epsilon evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables controlled, comprehensive robustness evaluation that captures curve behavior and optimality gaps, providing practitioners with a practical, curve-based alternative to fixed-epsilon assessment.

title: Vera: Identity-Faithful Human Subject-to-Video Generation
summary: Subject-to-video (S2V) generation has made substantial progress in preserving reference subjects across diverse categories, yet generic subject consistency remains insufficient for human-centric generation. A video may appear globally consistent while identity-critical human details still drift across frames, poses, and interactions. This issue becomes more severe in multi-person scenarios, where incorrect identity-role binding leads to subject confusion, attribute swapping, and excessive copying of reference-specific appearance cues. We propose Vera, a unified human-centric S2V framework for single- and multi-person generation. We first construct a million-pair identity-aligned human image-video dataset through person-level cross-clip retrieval, providing explicit identity correspondence and diverse references. Built on this dataset, Vera introduces two complementary designs. Identity-Focal Masked Supervision (IFMS) strengthens identity-aware learning with spatially focused supervision while reducing interference from irrelevant artifacts. Reference-Aware Layer-wise Attention (RALA) regulates how video tokens interact with reference identity cues in the DiT backbone, preserving stable identity anchors and enhancing layer-aware identity readout. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Vera improves human identity consistency, multi-person subject binding, and motion naturalness, while reducing identity confusion and excessive reference-image copying.

AI.tldr: Vera is a unified human-centric S2V framework that improves identity consistency and multi-person binding using Identity-Focal Masked Supervision and Reference-Aware Layer-wise Attention, supported by a large identity-aligned dataset.
AI.motivation: Current S2V methods struggle with identity drift and misbinding across frames, especially in multi-person settings, leading to subject-confusion and over-copying of reference cues.
AI.method: Construct a million-pair identity-aligned human image-video dataset via cross-clip retrieval. Propose two designs: (1) Identity-Focal Masked Supervision (IFMS) for spatially focused, identity-aware supervision; (2) Reference-Aware Layer-wise Attention (RALA) to regulate how video tokens attend to reference identity cues within the DiT backbone.
AI.result: Experiments show improved identity consistency, enhanced multi-person subject binding, improved motion naturalness, and reduced identity confusion and excessive copying of reference appearance cues.
AI.conclusion: Vera advances human-centric S2V by combining IFMS and RALA with a large identity-aligned dataset, yielding more stable identity anchors and better per-frame identity preservation in single- and multi-person generation.

title: Local Causal Structure Learning in the Presence of Latent Variables and Selection Bias
summary: Discovering the direct causes and effects of a target variable from observational data is a fundamental problem in causal discovery, with broad applications in domains such as gene regulatory analysis and biomedical research. Existing causal discovery methods either learn a global causal structure, which incurs substantial computational cost, or assume the absence of latent variables and selection bias, assumptions that are often violated in real-world settings. Motivated by these challenges, we study local causal structure learning in the presence of latent variables and selection bias. Specifically, we first characterize a local region that enables target-specific causal discovery without recovering the entire global structure. We then establish a theoretical bridge between causal information learned from the observed distribution induced on this local region and the corresponding information in the global causal structure. Building on these foundations, we propose LoCaLS, a local causal structure learning algorithm that is sound and complete under standard assumptions and identifies the same direct causes and effects of a target variable as those identifiable by global causal discovery methods, while allowing for latent variables and selection bias. Extensive experiments on random and real-world structures demonstrate that the proposed method consistently achieves higher structural accuracy than existing local methods while requiring substantially less computational effort than state-of-the-art global methods. Furthermore, applications to two real-world gene expression datasets reveal biologically plausible target-specific causal structures, demonstrating its practical applicability in large-scale biological data analysis.

AI.tldr: LoCaLS pursues local causal structure learning around a target in the presence of latent confounders and selection bias. It characterizes a local region that suffices for target-specific discovery, builds a bridge between local and global causal information, and yields a sound and complete algorithm that matches the direct causes/effects identified by global methods while reducing computational cost. Empirical results show superior structural accuracy over other local methods and lower cost than global methods, with real gene-expression applications yielding plausible, target-specific causal structures.
AI.motivation: Global causal discovery is computationally expensive and brittle under latent confounding and selection bias. There is a need for efficient, target-oriented causal discovery that can operate under hidden variables and bias.
AI.method: Introduce a local region around the target whose causal information suffices for identifying direct causes and effects without recovering the full global structure. Establish a theoretical link between the local observed distribution and the global causal structure. Propose LoCaLS, a local causal structure learning algorithm that is sound and complete under standard assumptions, identifying the same direct causes/effects as global methods despite latent variables and selection bias.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on random and real-world networks show LoCaLS achieves higher structural accuracy than existing local methods and substantially lower computational cost than state-of-the-art global methods. Real gene-expression datasets demonstrate biologically plausible target-specific causal structures.
AI.conclusion: LoCaLS enables accurate, efficient target-specific causal discovery in settings with latent confounders and selection bias, aligning with global-method identifiability while offering practical scalability for large-scale biological data analysis.

title: How Does Urban Context Relate to Residential Building Health? A Vision-POI Fusion Framework for Building-Level Housing Inspection
summary: Housing-level urban physical examination is essential for identifying residential building problems and supporting targeted urban renewal. Existing automated inspection studies primarily rely on individual images and rarely examine whether surrounding urban functional context can provide supplementary information for building-level assessment. This study proposes a vision-POI fusion framework that combines multi-view visual inspection with POI-derived neighborhood context for residential building health assessment. The empirical dataset covers 92 old residential communities, 3,237 residential buildings, and 25,608 field-acquired inspection images in Qingdao, China, encompassing seven categories of housing-related issues. First, multiple object detection models are evaluated to extract issue locations, categories, and confidence scores from individual images. The image-level outputs are subsequently aggregated across multiple views to construct interpretable building-level representations. Second, POI features are extracted within 500m, 1,000m, and 1,500m neighborhood buffers to characterize surrounding functional environments. Pearson and Spearman correlation analyses, combined with false discovery rate correction, are used to identify candidate contextual features. Finally, visual and POI features are integrated using a cost-sensitive Random Forest classifier under community-isolated spatial cross-validation. The results show that multi-view aggregation provides the main performance improvement, increasing the building-level Macro-F1 from 60.84% under Direct Detection to 74.95%. Incorporating POI context further increases Macro-F1 to 76.79%, although the additional gain is modest and category-dependent. POI information therefore functions as a supplementary contextual prior rather than a substitute for direct visual evidence or a causal determinant of building condition.

AI.tldr: A vision-POI fusion framework for building-level residential health assessment; multi-view image aggregation yields sizable Macro-F1 gains; POI-derived neighborhood context provides an additional modest improvement; POI acts as a contextual prior, not a substitute for visual evidence.
AI.motivation: Existing automated inspections rely on single images and largely ignore surrounding urban functional context. Incorporating POI-based neighborhood context may enhance building health assessment and better inform targeted urban renewal.
AI.method: 1) Evaluate multiple object detectors to locate and categorize issues in individual images (locations, categories, confidences). 2) Aggregate image-level detections across multiple views to form building-level representations. 3) Extract POI features within 500 m, 1,000 m, and 1,500 m buffers to characterize surrounding environments. 4) Use Pearson/Spearman correlations with false discovery rate correction to identify candidate contextual features. 5) Fuse visual and POI features with a cost-sensitive Random Forest under community-isolated spatial cross-validation.
AI.result: Macro-F1 rises from 60.84% (Direct Detection) to 74.95% with multi-view aggregation; including POI context further increases Macro-F1 to 76.79%. Gains are modest and vary by category, indicating POI provides supplementary contextual priors rather than replacing visual evidence or causally determining building condition.
AI.conclusion: Multi-view visual evidence is the primary driver of performance; POI context offers a supplementary, context-driven boost. The approach is effective for building-level health assessment and could inform urban renewal planning, with potential for generalization and enhanced contextual signals in future work.

title: Nonlinear Bias-Compensated Adaptive Filter and Its Application for Time-Series Prediction
summary: Most existing nonlinear adaptive filtering algorithms only account for output noise, neglecting the fact that input noise is also prevalent in practice. Although the recently proposed bias-compensated kernel least mean square (BCKLMS) algorithm addresses input noise in the nonlinear errors-in-variables (EIV) model, it still suffers from two major limitations. First, the use of a fixed-size dictionary restricts network growth but also prevents it from fully capturing the characteristics of the input signal. Second, as an least mean square (LMS) based algorithm, it exhibits poor robustness in the presence of non-Gaussian noise in the output signal. To overcome these issues, this paper proposes the random Fourier bias-compensated filter under general adaptive function (RFFBCGA) algorithm. Within the random Fourier feature based bias-compensated (RFFBC) framework, the proposed algorithm not only maintains a fixed network structure and effectively mitigates input noise interference through the BC term, but also achieves improved characterization of the input signal. Moreover, by leveraging the flexible form of the general adaptive (GA) function, the algorithm's robustness across various noise scenarios is further enhanced. Extensive simulations, including real-world time series prediction tasks, demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: Proposes a random Fourier bias-compensated filter under a general adaptive function (RFFBCGA) to address input noise and fixed network growth in nonlinear adaptive filtering. It combines random Fourier features with bias compensation and a flexible GA output form to improve robustness to non-Gaussian noise and better signal characterization, validated by extensive simulations including real-world time-series tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing nonlinear adaptive filters typically ignore input noise or suffer from fixed dictionary size and poor robustness to non-Gaussian output noise (e.g., BCKLMS). There is a need for a fixed-structure, robust nonlinear adaptive filter that can model input noise effectively while capturing input signal characteristics.
AI.method: Develop the RFFBCGA algorithm within a random Fourier feature–based bias-compensated (RFFBC) framework. Maintain a fixed network structure, mitigate input-noise through a bias-compensation (BC) term, utilize random Fourier features to better characterize the input, and employ a general adaptive (GA) function for robust, flexible output modeling.
AI.result: Extensive simulations, including real-world time-series predictions, demonstrate that RFFBCGA outperforms existing approaches by providing improved noise robustness (especially non-Gaussian output noise), better input signal representation, and a fixed, efficient network structure.
AI.conclusion: RFFBCGA offers a robust, fixed-structure nonlinear adaptive filtering solution that effectively combats input noise through BC and leverages random Fourier features and a GA form to enhance signal characterization and robustness across diverse noise conditions.

title: Self-supervision drives representational convergence in medical foundation models more than clinical supervision
summary: Medical image encoders from different groups are increasingly treated as interchangeable, on the assumption that scale and clinical supervision concentrate their representations onto a shared structure. Whether this convergence is real, what produces it, and whether it is clinically usable are untested, and the similarity measures behind such claims are fragile. We present a controlled dissection across 18 image and 7 text encoders, all open-weight and run locally, spanning 7M to 27B parameters and five imaging modalities, including 650,982 chest radiographs from six datasets. To isolate cause, we train encoders that vary only the objective under fixed data, architecture, and scale, and reproduce the effect in a synthetic model. Convergence is modest but above a random floor, driven by the self-supervised objective, not clinical supervision: matched self-supervised encoders aligned most (40.4% on chest radiography), with label-supervised (21.1%) and image-text (3.3%) far lower, and did not grow with size (Spearman 0.302, p=0.223) or capability. It is within-modality, does not reach clinical language, and does not reproduce how radiologists judge case similarity. Yet a linear classifier transfers across encoders and to five held-out hospitals, retaining about 85% of within-encoder performance. Convergence in medical imaging is therefore set by the pretraining objective, not inherited from scale or clinical supervision. Interoperability is accordingly something to design for through that objective, and to validate where the shared geometry is weakest, across patient subgroups and against clinical judgment.

AI.tldr: Medical image encoders from diverse groups only modestly converge in representation; convergence is driven by self-supervised pretraining, not data scale or clinical supervision, and does not reach radiologist-style alignment. Linear transferability exists across encoders but full interoperability must be engineered around the pretraining objective and validated across subgroups and clinical judgment.
AI.motivation: To test whether encoders trained with different objectives and from different groups produce interchangeable representations, addressing claims of shared structure under scale and clinical supervision.
AI.method: Systematic, controlled dissection across 18 image and 7 text open-weight encoders (7M–27B params) across five imaging modalities, including 650k chest radiographs from six datasets. For cause isolation, vary only the objective while fixing data, architecture, and scale; reproduce effects in a synthetic model. Assess convergence within-modality; evaluate cross-encoder transfer with linear classifiers across held-out hospitals.
AI.result: Convergence is modest but above random; self-supervised encoders align most (40.4% on chest radiography); label-supervised (21.1%) and image-text (3.3%) much lower and do not scale with size (Spearman 0.302, p=0.223).
