Alignment is within-modality and does not reach clinical language; radiologists' similarity judgments are not reproduced. A linear classifier transfers across encoders and to five held-out hospitals, retaining ~85% of within-encoder performance.
AI.conclusion: Interoperability across medical encoders is governed by the pretraining objective rather than model scale or clinical supervision. To enable cross-encoder interoperability, design objectives accordingly and validate shared geometry across subgroups and against clinical judgment.

title: Time Series Network Utilization KPI Forecasting Using Advanced AI/ML Models
summary: The rapid proliferation of data-intensive applications, cloud infrastructure, and IoT ecosystems has made proactive resource provisioning critical for maintaining optimal network performance. However, network administrators face a constant battle against capacity constraints, where traditional reactive approaches fail to accurately anticipate traffic fluctuations. This inability to foresee demand leads to costly over-provisioning, unexpected downtime, and degraded quality of service directly impacting operational budgets and business continuity. To achieve efficient capacity planning, accurate forecasting of bandwidth utilization is essential. This study addresses the challenge by evaluating a diverse spectrum of models including seasonal decomposition, Prophet, Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression, and advanced deep learning architectures like bidirectional and Convolutional LSTMs - using a common interface dataset benchmarked across MAPE, NRMSE, and R-square metrics. Ultimately, this research delivers actionable insights into the trade-offs between model accuracy and computational efficiency, empowering engineers, operators, and business owners to select the optimal forecasting model for their specific infrastructure needs.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive benchmarking study compares a wide range of forecasting models for bandwidth utilization to support proactive capacity planning, assessing trade-offs between accuracy and computational efficiency using standard metrics.
AI.motivation: To enable proactive resource provisioning in data-heavy networks (cloud, IoT) by accurately forecasting bandwidth demand, avoiding overprovisioning and QoS degradation.
AI.method: Evaluate a spectrum of models—seasonal decomposition, Prophet, Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression, as well as bidirectional LSTM and Convolutional LSTM architectures—on a common benchmark dataset; compare performance using MAPE, NRMSE, and R-squared; analyze accuracy vs. computational efficiency.
AI.result: Provides actionable insights into the trade-offs between model accuracy and computational cost, guiding practitioners to select the optimal forecasting model for their infrastructure constraints and needs.
AI.conclusion: A broad suite of forecasting models offers varying accuracy and efficiency profiles; the study offers a framework to select the appropriate model for bandwidth utilization forecasting in capacity planning.

title: Multimodal Large Language Models for Remote Sensing Image Understanding: Domain-Specific or General-Purpose?
summary: The rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has introduced a flexible paradigm for remote sensing image scene understanding (RSISU), enabling natural-language interaction with remote sensing imagery. However, a systematic understanding of the capability boundaries, cross-task generalization, and task-specific limitations of existing remote sensing MLLMs (RS-MLLMs) is still lacking. This paper presents a systematic survey and diagnostic evaluation of MLLMs for RSISU. We review the technical evolution of RS-MLLMs, focusing on model design, multimodal learning, training data, and downstream capabilities. We further compare RS-MLLMs with general-purpose computer vision MLLMs (CV-MLLMs) across diverse RSISU tasks and benchmarks. RS-MLLMs remain competitive in domain-specific settings, particularly remote sensing visual grounding and high-resolution visual question answering. More notably, general-purpose CV-MLLMs can match or even outperform these specialized models on several RSISU tasks without remote sensing-specific fine-tuning. These findings demonstrate the strong transferability of general-purpose CV-MLLMs and show that current RS-MLLMs do not consistently outperform them across diverse RSISU tasks. Current MLLMs also face limitations in spatial and relational reasoning, fine-grained visual understanding, instruction diversity, and generalization across heterogeneous task formats. Based on these findings, we outline future directions toward reliable evaluation, multimodal and high-resolution reasoning, efficient deployment, and tool-augmented remote sensing agents. This survey provides a systematic reference for developing robust, generalizable, and practical MLLMs for RSISU.

AI.tldr: General-purpose CV-MLLMs show strong cross-task transfer to RSISU; RS-specific MLLMs are not consistently better across tasks; highlights gaps in evaluation, reasoning, and deployment guidance, suggesting tool augmentation as a promising direction.
AI.motivation: To understand the capability boundaries, cross-task generalization, and task-specific limitations of remote-sensing MLLMs (RS-MLLMs) and to compare them with general-purpose CV-MLLMs across RSISU tasks.
AI.method: Systematic survey and diagnostic evaluation of RS-MLLMs. Review evolution of RS-MLLMs in model design, multimodal learning, and training data; conduct cross-task benchmarking against general-purpose CV-MLLMs on diverse RSISU tasks; analyze strengths, weaknesses, and transferability; identify limitations and propose directions for evaluation, reasoning, deployment, and tool-augmented systems.
AI.result: RS-MLLMs remain competitive in domain-specific RSISU tasks (e.g., remote-sensing visual grounding and high-resolution VQA). However, general-purpose CV-MLLMs can match or surpass RS-MLLMs on several RSISU tasks without remote-sensing-specific fine-tuning, highlighting strong transferability. Current RS-MLLMs do not consistently outperform general-purpose models across diverse RSISU tasks. Limitations of MLLMs include deficits in spatial/relational reasoning, fine-grained understanding, instruction diversity, and generalization across heterogeneous task formats.
AI.conclusion: Future work should emphasize reliable evaluation, enhanced multimodal and high-resolution reasoning, efficient deployment, and tool-augmented remote sensing agents. The survey offers a reference for developing robust, generalizable, and practical RSISU MLLMs.

title: Good Practice Guide for quantifying uncertainties for machine learning models applied to photoplethysmography signals
summary: This Good Practice Guide presents work done in the QUMPHY project (Uncertainty quantification for machine learning models applied to photoplethysmography signals) that considered both machine learning and uncertainty quantification for problems which used photoplethysmography (PPG) signals from wearable devices as input. It provides high-level guidance on what types of machine learning model might be used and how different models compare when applied to both regression and classification tasks. It provides guidance on the implementation of different methods for uncertainty quantification, covering both model-dependent and model-independent techniques, and on the validation of the results provided by those methods. It also describes six benchmark problems together with pointers to different benchmark datasets for each problem. Software is described that can assist practitioners in implementing the methods described herein and there is a brief consideration of ethical issues. It concludes with a summary and recommendations.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive Good Practice Guide on uncertainty quantification for ML models applied to wearable PPG signals, covering model choices for regression/classification, UQ methods (model-dependent and model-independent), validation, six benchmark problems with datasets, supporting software, and ethical considerations.
AI.motivation: Address uncertainty in ML-based analysis of PPG signals from wearables; facilitate robust model development, benchmarking, and ethical awareness.
AI.method: Survey and guidance across model types for regression and classification; summarize uncertainty quantification techniques (e.g., Bayesian methods, ensembles, MC dropout, conformal prediction); outline validation strategies; describe six benchmark problems and associated datasets; present software tools and practical implementation guidance; discuss ethical considerations.
AI.result: Provides high-level guidance and practical recommendations; defines six benchmark problems with datasets; introduces supporting software; discusses implementation considerations and ethical issues; serves as a resource for practitioners.
AI.conclusion: Summarizes the Guide’s findings and offers actionable recommendations for practitioners and identifies directions for future work in uncertainty quantification for PPG-based ML applications.

title: Diverse-Intent Multi-Turn Fashion Image Retrieval
summary: Real-world fashion search involves interactive retrieval across multiple turns. However, existing multi-turn retrieval methods are built on a restrictive assumption that every interaction follows the same attribute-editing paradigm, leaving heterogeneous intent transitions unexplored. Moreover, existing approaches often rely on textification to bridge multimodal queries and visual retrieval, which may lose fine-grained visual cues. To address these gaps, we introduce DIM-Fashion, a benchmark of 26K multi-turn sessions constructed from 13 fashion retrieval datasets across 7 tasks, featuring diverse intent transitions and rollback behaviors. We further propose FashionAM, an MLLM-VLP framework that directly aligns multimodal conversational queries with a fashion-oriented gallery embedding space, avoiding intermediate textification. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FashionAM over existing approaches. The dataset and code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: DIM-Fashion introduces a 26K multi-turn fashion search benchmark across 13 datasets and 7 tasks to model heterogeneous intent transitions, while FashionAM presents an MLLM-VLP framework that directly aligns multimodal conversational queries with a fashion gallery embedding space without textification. The results show improved performance over baselines and a public release of data/code upon acceptance.
AI.motivation: Address the limitations of existing multi-turn fashion retrieval methods that assume uniform attribute-editing interactions and rely on textification, by capturing diverse intent transitions and preserving fine-grained visual cues.
AI.method: 1) Build DIM-Fashion: 26K multi-turn sessions from 13 datasets across 7 tasks with heterogeneous intent transitions and rollback behaviors. 2) Propose FashionAM: an MLLM-VLP framework that directly aligns multimodal conversational queries with a fashion-oriented gallery embedding space, avoiding intermediate textification.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate FashionAM's effectiveness over existing approaches across the proposed benchmark.
AI.conclusion: DIM-Fashion and FashionAM jointly advance interactive fashion retrieval by modelling diverse turn-level intents and providing a direct multimodal alignment framework, with dataset and code to be released publicly.

title: Post-Training in Time Series Foundation Models: A Unifying Framework
summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have emerged as general-purpose models for time series analysis, but pretraining alone is often insufficient for reliable downstream deployment. Bridging this gap requires further intervention to handle domain shift, task heterogeneity, limited supervision, and computational constraints, which motivates post-training as a broad class of methods to adapt, augment, compose, calibrate, or specialize pretrained TSFMs for downstream tasks. In this work, we analyze TSFM post-training methods based on their locus of intervention in the prediction pipeline, yielding five categories: parameter adaptation, context augmentation, model composition, output processing and uncertainty control, and compression and specialization. Within each category, we study main representative methods and discuss their current limitations. We further identify future directions toward controlled adaptation, reliable context construction, uncertainty-aware model composition, calibrated output processing, and deployment-aware specialization. Overall, by providing a unifying framework for the emerging TSFM post-training landscape, this work aims to support future research to navigate the design space between a pretrained TSFM and its reliable downstream deployment.

AI.tldr: A survey and unifying framework for TSFM post-training methods, categorized into five intervention loci, with analysis of representative methods, limitations, and future directions toward reliable deployment.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between pretrained time series foundation models (TSFMs) and reliable downstream deployment by addressing domain shift, task heterogeneity, limited supervision, and resource constraints through post-training techniques.
AI.method: Taxonomic analysis of post-training methods by their locus of intervention in the prediction pipeline; review of representative methods within each category; critical assessment of limitations; synthesis into a unifying framework; identification of promising future directions.
AI.result: A coherent framework that maps the TSFM post-training landscape, clarifies current methods and limitations, and guides future research toward more reliable deployment.
AI.conclusion: The emerging TSFM post-training landscape benefits from a structured framework that enables controlled adaptation, reliable context construction, uncertainty-aware model composition, calibrated output processing, and deployment-aware specialization.

title: Evolving Cache Schedules for Fast Diffusion Policy Inference
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, supplementary material included. Accepted by PRCV 2026
summary: Diffusion policies achieve strong visuomotor control by iteratively denoising action chunks, but repeated denoising makes real-time deployment computationally demanding. Cache-based methods reduce inference cost by reusing intermediate activations, but existing training-free schedules typically allocate computation uniformly across blocks, ignoring heterogeneous redundancy across blocks and leading to a suboptimal performance-efficiency trade-off. To bridge this gap, we introduce Evolving Cache Schedules (EVO), a training-free acceleration framework that globally schedules cache refreshes via evolutionary search. EVO represents each candidate as a complete schedule over the block-timestep lattice. Thus, redundant transformer computations during iterative denoising can be skipped through cache reuse while preserving closed-loop rollout performance. To make the search practical, EVO introduces redundancy-aware initialization, which seeds the population with promising schedules, and target-conditioned early stopping, which verifies and terminates once a desired performance target is reached. The offline-optimized schedule can be directly plugged into pretrained diffusion policies without retraining. Extensive manipulation benchmarks show that EVO preserves near-full performance while substantially reducing computation, achieving up to 8.05x action-generation speedup and reducing FLOPs from 15.77G to as low as 1.96G. Source code is available at https://github.com/pillom/EVO.

AI.tldr: EVO uses a training-free, evolutionary search to optimize cache-refresh schedules for diffusion-based visuomotor policies, enabling large inference speedups with minimal performance loss.
AI.motivation: Diffusion policies achieve good visuomotor control but require repeated denoising, making real-time deployment expensive. Existing training-free schedules assume uniform block computation, ignoring redundancy variance across blocks and hurting efficiency.
AI.method: Represent complete cache-refresh schedules over the block-timestep lattice as candidate solutions and evolve them. Introduce redundancy-aware initialization to seed promising schedules and target-conditioned early stopping to terminate once performance targets are met. The offline-optimized schedule is plug-and-play for pretrained diffusion policies without retraining.
AI.result: EVO preserves near-full performance while achieving substantial computation savings: up to 8.05x action-generation speedup and FLOPs reduced from 15.77G to as low as 1.96G. Source code provided by authors.
AI.conclusion: A practical, training-free acceleration framework for diffusion-based visuomotor control that leverages evolutionary search and cache reuse to balance performance and efficiency without retraining.

title: Generalized Kalman filter based temporal difference reinforcement learning
summary: In this paper, we present a generalized temporal-difference (TD) reinforcement learning framework based on the theory of conditional expectations. The value and action-value (Q-value) functions are treated as uncertain quantities, and their estimation is formulated as a stochastic inference problem. Unlike classical Kalman-based temporal-difference learning, which relies on linear-Gaussian assumptions, the proposed formulation is derived directly from the conditional expectation framework and naturally extends to nonlinear models and non-Gaussian probability distributions. The proposed method recursively estimates not only the conditional expectation of the value function but also its second probabilistic moment, thereby quantifying the uncertainty associated with the learned value function throughout the learning process. To obtain a computationally tractable algorithm, the stochastic problem is discretized using either polynomial chaos expansions or ensemble-based approximations, providing efficient representations of the underlying random variables. The proposed framework is demonstrated on two optimal control problems: a linear mass--spring--damper system and a nonlinear heat conduction problem in a closed cavity. The numerical examples illustrate the capability of the proposed method to accurately estimate both the value function and its associated uncertainty, while extending classical Kalman-based temporal-difference learning to a broader class of stochastic systems.

AI.tldr: A probabilistic TD learning framework based on conditional expectations that treats value/Q as random variables to quantify uncertainty, extending Kalman-based TD to nonlinear/non-Gaussian settings; uses polynomial chaos or ensembles for tractability and demonstrates on linear and nonlinear control problems.
AI.motivation: To address uncertainty in value estimation and the limitations of linear-Gaussian Kalman-based TD; to enable uncertainty-aware learning in nonlinear/non-Gaussian stochastic systems.
AI.method: Formulate TD learning as stochastic inference over conditional expectations. Treat value and Q as random variables and derive recursive estimators for their conditional expectation and second moment. Use polynomial chaos expansions or ensemble-based approximations to discretize the stochastic problem for computational tractability.
AI.result: Applied to a linear mass–spring–damper system and a nonlinear heat-conduction problem in a closed cavity. The method accurately estimates both the value function and its associated uncertainty, extending Kalman-based TD learning to a broader class of stochastic systems.
AI.conclusion: Provides a general, uncertainty-aware TD framework that extends beyond linear-Gaussian assumptions, enabling robust value estimation with quantified uncertainty for nonlinear and non-Gaussian stochastic dynamics; tractable via polynomial chaos or ensemble discretizations.

title: Toward Reliable RGB-D Semantic Segmentation: Handling Missing Modalities via Condition Dropout
summary: RGB-D semantic segmentation has achieved remarkable progress, yet most models assume that RGB and depth are always available. In practice, failures or occlusions of surveillance sensors often remove one modality. Although RGB or depth alone can contain sufficient cues, models trained only on full-modality inputs fail to exploit the remaining modality once one is missing, causing severe degradation. We tackle this issue with a simple continued-training paradigm, \emph{Condition Dropout (ConD)}, which mitigates degradation while preserving full-modality accuracy. Starting from a pretrained RGB-D model, ConD adds a second stage that randomly simulates complete, RGB-missing, and depth-missing inputs, freezes the original encoders, and trains copied encoders with zero-initialized feature injection. Experiments on NYU-Depth V2 and SUN RGB-D show that ConD improves robustness under missing modalities and even yields slight gains when modalities are complete. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: A simple continued-training approach, Condition Dropout (ConD), improves RGB-D semantic segmentation robustness to missing modalities while preserving full-modality accuracy.
AI.motivation: In real-world scenarios, RGB or depth sensors can fail or be occluded, causing performance degradation when models trained on full modalities are used with missing data.
AI.method: A two-stage continued-training paradigm. From a pretrained RGB-D model, ConD introduces a second stage that randomly samples complete, RGB-missing, and depth-missing inputs, freezes the original encoders, and trains duplicated encoders with zero-initialized feature injection.
AI.result: On NYU-Depth V2 and SUN RGB-D, ConD improves robustness to missing modalities and even yields slight gains when modalities are present.
AI.conclusion: ConD provides robustness to modality missingness without sacrificing, and possibly improving, full-modality accuracy; code will be released publicly after acceptance.

title: Zero-Shot Heart Rate Variability Forecasting from Consumer Wearables Using Time Series Foundation Models
comment: Accepted to Computing in Cardiology (CinC) 2026. 4 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: Short-term Heart Rate Variability (HRV) forecasting could provide clinicians with actionable lead time for detecting autonomic dysfunction and adverse cardiac events. Consumer wearable devices generate fragmented, artifact-rich HRV signals that challenge conventional forecasting approaches. In this study, we evaluated the forecasting ability of three Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), TimesFM, Chronos, and MOIRAI, against traditional baselines (Mean, Exponential Smoothing, and Exponentially Weighted Moving Average) on real-world wearable data collected from 49 healthy individuals. To address data fragmentation, we introduce a variability-preserving imputation method that augments linear interpolation with locally adaptive stochastic noise, retaining physiological dynamics essential for accurate forecasting. The results show that TSFMs outperformed all baselines without fine-tuning, achieving average Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE) between 0.81 and 0.87 across TSFMs and both context lengths (32 and 64 time steps), with Chronos and TimesFM as the top models, though MOIRAI showed limited gains over baselines. With up to a 2-hour forecast horizon, the results establish a baseline for TSFMs' performance on a real-world dataset, highlighting domain-specific fine-tuning as a promising direction for clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: TSFMs (TimesFM, Chronos) beat baselines for short-term HRV forecasting on real-world wearables; a variability-preserving imputation enables robust performance; Chronos/TimesFM lead up to 2-hour horizon; MOIRAI offers limited gains.
AI.motivation: Address fragmentation and artifacts in wearable HRV data to enable reliable short-term forecasting for clinical use, benchmark modern Time Series Foundation Models against traditional baselines on real-world data.
AI.method: Evaluation of three TSFMs (TimesFM, Chronos, MOIRAI) vs baselines (Mean, Exponential Smoothing, EWMA) on HRV data from 49 healthy individuals. Introduces a variability-preserving imputation that augments linear interpolation with locally adaptive stochastic noise to retain physiological dynamics. Experiments with context lengths 32 and 64, forecast horizons up to 2 hours.
AI.result: TSFMs outperformed all baselines without fine-tuning, achieving average MASE between 0.81 and 0.87 across TSFMs and contexts. Chronos and TimesFM were the top models; MOIRAI showed limited gains over baselines.
AI.conclusion: TSFMs demonstrate strong baseline performance on real-world wearable HRV data; domain-specific fine-tuning may further enhance clinical deployment; the introduced imputation method helps mitigate fragmentation and preserves relevant dynamics for forecasting.

title: Test-Time Training for Modality Order Consistency in Vision-Language Models
summary: We find that vision-language models are sensitive to a specific semantically irrelevant change: the order in which the image and question are presented. Across three models and three benchmarks, image first prompting consistently outperforms question-first prompting, revealing a repeatable modality order failure. We use this gap to design an order-consistent test-time training method. Our method substantially closes the modality-order gap across all evaluated settings. Surprisingly, it also yields consistent improvements in the stronger image-first branch over the baseline, hence bootstrapping both orderings toward mutual consistency. Activation patching localizes the ordering failure to a narrow mid-network region where representations diverge sharply between prompt orders. We find that the test-time training method repairs this misalignment across layers. Together, our results identify modality-order sensitivity as a circuit-level failure in VLMs and demonstrate that simple, asymmetric test-time adaptation can effectively mitigate it and even improve performance over the baseline.

AI.tldr: Vision-language models show a robust modality-order sensitivity (image-first vs question-first prompting). An order-consistent test-time training method reduces this gap and improves both prompts, with activation analysis locating the failure to a mid-network region.
AI.motivation: Identify a circuit-level failure in VLMs: modality-order sensitivity. Determine whether simple, asymmetric test-time adaptation can mitigate it and whether improvements extend beyond correcting the gap.
AI.method: Evaluate three models across three benchmarks to compare image-first and question-first prompting. Propose an order-consistent test-time training procedure. Use activation patching to localize the ordering failure and analyze cross-layer misalignment and repair.
AI.result: The proposed method substantially closes the modality-order gap across settings and yields improvements for the image-first branch beyond the baseline. It also promotes mutual consistency between orders. Activation patching localizes the failure to a narrow mid-network region where representations diverge by prompt order, and test-time training repairs these misalignments across layers.
AI.conclusion: Modality-order sensitivity is a circuit-level failure in VLMs. Simple asymmetric test-time adaptation can mitigate it and even improve performance beyond the baseline.

title: Test Case Prioritization for DNNs via Neural Collapse Instability
summary: With the widespread deployment of deep neural networks (DNNs) in safety-critical domains, reducing the cost of model validation under limited testing budgets has become increasingly important. Existing test case prioritization techniques often rely on single-checkpoint confidence signals derived from output probabilities. However, DNNs can be confidently wrong, and the confidence margin between the predicted and competing classes is frequently small, which weakens early fault discovery. To address this limitation, we propose a Neural-Collapse-Inspired Prioritization (NCIP) framework that replaces absolute confidence with cross-checkpoint prediction variability in the terminal training regime, where model geometry becomes highly structured. NCIP introduces two key components. First, it selects an NC-guided representative subset of training checkpoints using an equiangularity score of classifier weights, quantified as the standard deviation of pairwise cosine similarities among class weight vectors. Second, it prioritizes test inputs by their prediction variability across the selected checkpoints, surfacing boundary-adjacent and failure-prone samples that are unstable under checkpoint-induced decision boundary shifts. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and architectures show that NCIP achieves strong performance in early fault discovery compared with competitive baselines, with 1.5 to 16.6 percent RAUC-ALL gains and 4.9 to 20.6 percent RAUC-500 gains under the same testing budget. NCIP further attains the best average performance across all dataset-model pairs.

AI.tldr: NCIP is a neural-collapse-inspired test case prioritization method that uses cross-checkpoint prediction variability and an NC-guided subset of training checkpoints to improve early fault discovery under limited testing budgets.
AI.motivation: DNNs are used in safety-critical domains; existing test prioritization relies on single-checkpoint confidence; models can be confidently wrong and margins are small, hindering early fault discovery.
AI.method: Select representative checkpoints using equiangularity score of classifier weights (std of pairwise cosine similarities among class weights). Then rank inputs by prediction variability across selected checkpoints to surface boundary-adjacent/failure-prone samples; evaluate across datasets/models.
AI.result: Empirical results show improved early fault discovery with RAUC-ALL gains 1.5–16.6% and RAUC-500 gains 4.9–20.6% under the same budget; achieves best average performance across dataset-model pairs.
AI.conclusion: NCIP leverages neural-collapse-inspired geometry and cross-checkpoint variability to outperform baselines in test case prioritization for DNNs with limited budgets.

title: Look Less, Think Faster: Joint Token-Compute Adaptation for Multimodal LLMs
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have recently demonstrated strong performance across vision-language tasks. However, their high inference cost, arising from both the large number of input visual tokens and the heavy computation of the large language model (LLM), remains a key barrier to practical deployment. Recent work attempts to reduce the cost by adaptively optimizing individual dimensions, e.g., pruning redundant visual tokens or skipping LLM layers and heads. Nonetheless, prior approaches typically treat these dimensions independently and overlook a fundamental coupling: the available compute resources must be dynamically allocated across all dimensions based on the input content. To bridge the gap, we propose SmartVL, a unified adaptive inference framework that jointly controls vision token number and model compute capability in response to varying input contents and compute budgets. SmartVL introduces a vision-side token controller that dynamically selects informative visual tokens and an LLM-side compute controller that adaptively adjusts LLM computation. Importantly, these controllers are trained to coordinate with each other so that the overall inference cost satisfies a target budget. To allow this joint scheduling, we connect the controllers using a shared budget encoding and leverage a differentiable latency estimator for end-to-end training. This design enables SmartVL to learn cross-stage allocation strategies that adapt to both input complexity and runtime compute constraints. Experiments across multiple MLLM benchmarks demonstrate that, with joint scheduling, SmartVL consistently outperforms prior adaptive methods and achieves superior accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontiers. Project page: https://www.schaterji.io/publications/2026/jointtokencompute.

AI.tldr: SmartVL is a unified adaptive inference framework that jointly optimizes vision token count and LLM compute to satisfy a target budget, using a vision-side token controller and an LLM-side compute controller coordinated via a shared budget encoding and a differentiable latency estimator, achieving better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs than prior methods.
AI.motivation: MLLMs incur high inference costs from both many input visual tokens and heavy LLM computation. Prior adaptive methods optimize dimensions independently, ignoring the cross-resource coupling required to meet a runtime budget.
AI.method: Introduce a vision-side token controller to select informative visual tokens and an LLM-side compute controller to adapt LLM computation. Connect controllers with a shared budget encoding and train end-to-end using a differentiable latency estimator, enabling learned cross-stage allocation strategies that adapt to input complexity and runtime constraints.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across multiple MLLM benchmarks shows SmartVL with joint scheduling consistently outperforms prior adaptive approaches, achieving superior accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontiers.
AI.conclusion: Jointly scheduling tokens and compute under a budget enables SmartVL to adapt to varying input complexity and runtime constraints, yielding better efficiency-accuracy tradeoffs than dimension-wise, independent optimization.

title: Evaluating and Mitigating Gender Bias in Pre-trained Embeddings for ML-based Recruitment
comment: Accepted for presentation at the TRUST-AI 2026 Workshop, held in conjunction with IJCAI/ECAI 2026, Bremen, Germany
summary: AI-based recruitment systems that rely on machine learning models trained on historical CV data, risk perpetuating and amplifying social biases. A key challenge arises in unstructured CV text, where pre-trained language model embeddings may infer sensitive attributes such as gender even after explicit indicators are removed. In this paper, we evaluate nine pre-trained embedding models on the synthetic FairCVdb dataset, analyzing the informativeness of their embeddings for applicant scoring and their susceptibility to gender leakage, on both original and gender-scrubbed biographies. We further use a multi-task adversarial learning framework with gradient reversal to predict applicant suitability while suppressing gender information from learned representations. Finally, we use a multi-objective Pareto-front-based model selection to balance predictive utility and fairness. Our experimental results show that explicit gender scrubbing substantially reduces but does not eliminate gender leakage, while adversarial learning improves fairness mainly on original biographies and acts as a complementary strategy rather than a substitute for text-level debiasing.

AI.tldr: Evaluates nine pretrained embeddings on synthetic FairCVdb for recruitment, examining information content for scoring and gender leakage; tests gender-scrubbing and adversarial debiasing; uses Pareto-front model selection; finds scrubbing reduces but does not eliminate leakage; adversarial helps mainly on original bios and is complementary to text-level debiasing.
AI.motivation: Mitigate bias in AI-based recruitment due to biased historical CV data and unstructured text that can reveal sensitive attributes like gender; quantify leakage and balance utility vs fairness.
AI.method: Assess nine pretrained embeddings on FairCVdb; evaluate informativeness for applicant scoring and gender leakage on original and gender-scrubbed biographies; apply a multi-task adversarial learning framework with gradient reversal to predict suitability while suppressing gender information; use multi-objective Pareto-front-based model selection to balance predictive utility and fairness.
AI.result: Explicit gender scrubbing reduces but does not eliminate gender leakage; adversarial learning improves fairness mainly on original biographies and complements text-level debiasing rather than substituting it.
AI.conclusion: Combined use of text-level debiasing (scrubbing) and adversarial bias suppression, guided by Pareto optimization, yields better fairness-utility trade-offs. The effectiveness of adversarial methods is domain- and text-type dependent, offering complementary gains rather than replacement for debiasing at the data level.

title: Self Gradient Forcing: Native Long Video Extrapolation
summary: Recent autoregressive video diffusion methods are increasingly built upon Self Forcing, where the student is trained on histories produced by its own rollout rather than ground-truth video contexts. This reduces exposure bias, but the historical key-value cache is still used by future frames only as frozen rollout state. As a result, future losses cannot supervise how earlier generated latents should be written into more useful keys and values for later video-latent generation. We call this the historical context-gradient gap. We propose Self Gradient Forcing (SGF), a two-pass training strategy that restores this missing supervision signal without backpropagating through the full serial rollout. Pass 1 performs a no-gradient autoregressive rollout matching inference and, at a sampled denoising exit step, records both the self-generated context and the noisy latents fed to the model. Pass 2 performs parallel context-gradient reconstruction for the recorded exit step. The generated context is used as stop-gradient clean-latent input, while the model recomputes the context KV representations and future-to-context causal attention. Thus, SGF provides the missing memory-writing supervision within the native autoregressive training objective, using losses on future video latents to train the model to encode context into more effective causal memory. Across extensive long-horizon frame-wise and chunk-wise experiments under different initializations, SGF achieves stronger native long-video extrapolation than Self Forcing, especially in subject identity, background/layout consistency, and temporal stability. Remarkably, using only a 5-second training window, SGF can extrapolate to videos lasting several minutes. Code and models will be released to advance research on autoregressive video generation.

AI.tldr: SGF introduces a two-pass training scheme to close the historical context-gradient gap in autoregressive video diffusion. It records context and latents in a no-grad rollout (exit step) and subsequently reconstructs context gradients in parallel, using the generated context as a stop-gradient input and recomputing keys/values for attention. This provides memory-writing supervision within the native AR objective, improving long-horizon video extrapolation from short training windows (e.g., 5s).
AI.motivation: Autoregressive video diffusion with self-forcing suffers from exposure bias and a missing gradient signal that tells how earlier latents should be encoded into future keys/values. This historical context-gradient gap limits long-horizon consistency. SGF aims to supply this supervisory signal without backpropagating through the entire rollout.
AI.method: Two-pass training: Pass 1 performs a no-gradient autoregressive rollout matching inference; at a sampled denoising exit step, it records both the self-generated context and the noisy latents. Pass 2 performs parallel context-gradient reconstruction for the recorded exit step. The generated context is used as stop-gradient clean-latent input, while the model recomputes context KV representations and future-to-context causal attention. Losses on future latents train the model to encode context into memory, without backprop through the full sequence.
AI.result: SGF yields stronger native long-video extrapolation than Self Forcing, with better subject identity, background/layout consistency, and temporal stability across long-horizon frame-wise and chunk-wise evaluations, across initializations. Remarkably, with only a 5-second training window, SGF can extrapolate to videos lasting several minutes.
AI.conclusion: SGF closes the historical context-gradient gap by injecting memory-writing supervision into the autoregressive objective, enhancing long-horizon video generation. The approach is scalable with short-training-window effectiveness and will release code/models to advance autoregressive video generation research.

title: Co-Evolving LLM Evaluators and Policies via DynamicRubric
summary: Post-training with evaluator feedback on policy-induced samples serves as a major mechanism for improving large language models. As policies improve, these sampled responses become close in quality. These close candidates create a bottleneck for policy optimization: collapsed relative evaluator score gaps yield weak or misleading policy supervision. We theoretically characterize why these gaps matter through a probability allocation view, showing that the directional gain of shifting probability mass from one response to another is exactly the evaluator score gap between them. This identifies relative score gaps as the policy optimization signals that guide updates. Motivated by this view, we propose DynamicRubric, a response-set-conditioned evaluator--policy co-evolution framework that generates weighted binary rubric items for each candidate set and aggregates the resulting judgments into response-level scores. In our experiments with 8B backbones, DynamicRubric improves evaluator performance and provides stronger policy supervision than baselines using a 70B reward model or a 235B static rubric generator. DynamicRubric-optimized policies also show gains on verifiable reasoning and coding tasks. A DynamicRubric-optimized model is fully deployed in WeChat Search's AI answering scenario, where it serves all online traffic across tens of millions of requests per day and improves key online metrics. These results suggest a principle for evaluator-guided post-training: evaluators should evolve with the policies they supervise.

AI.tldr: DynamicRubric: co-evolving evaluator and policy to overcome collapse in relative scores during post-training; uses response-set-conditioned rubrics producing weighted judgments to better guide policy updates; empirically stronger than large baselines and deployed in production.
AI.motivation: As policies improve, evaluator-labeled samples become evenly matched, making relative score gaps small and diminishing supervision signal. There is a need for signals that can effectively guide policy updates even when candidates are close in quality.
AI.method: Introduce DynamicRubric, a response-set-conditioned evaluator–policy co-evolution framework that generates weighted binary rubric items for each candidate set and aggregates them into response-level scores. The evaluator evolves with the policy by conditioning on the candidate set and learning weights for rubric items.
AI.result: DynamicRubric improves evaluator performance and provides stronger policy supervision than baselines using a 70B reward model or a 235B static rubric generator. Policies optimized with DynamicRubric show gains on verifiable reasoning and coding tasks. A DynamicRubric-optimized model was deployed in WeChat Search, handling tens of millions of requests per day and improving key online metrics.
AI.conclusion: Evaluators should evolve with the policies they supervise; evaluator-guided post-training benefits when the evaluation signal adapts to the policy, suggesting a new principle for post-training workflows.

title: Persian Pixel: A large-scale synthetic OCR dataset for Persian language
summary: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for Persian remains substantially less mature than for Latin-script languages despite Persian being spoken by more than 110 million people across multiple countries. This gap arises from two fundamental challenges: the intrinsic complexity of the Perso-Arabic writing system and the limited availability of large-scale, high-quality annotated datasets. Persian script exhibits obligatory cursive connectivity, context-dependent glyph shaping, extensive ligatures, diacritic placement, and stylistic variation across writing forms such as Naskh and Nastaliq, all of which significantly complicate text recognition. At the same time, the high cost and labor-intensive nature of manual annotation have created a persistent data bottleneck, limiting the development of robust OCR systems and slowing progress in Persian document digitization.In this paper, we introduce Persian Pixel, a comprehensive synthetic OCR dataset specifically designed to address these challenges. Comprising over 343,000 high-fidelity image text pairs, the dataset spans sentence, paragraph, and full-page document layouts generated from a carefully curated seven-million-word Persian corpus using the SynthOCR-Gen rendering framework. The generation pipeline faithfully models the typographic characteristics of Persian script, including contextual character joining, positional glyph variants, diacritic placement, and multiple representative Persian typefaces. To bridge the synthetic-to-real domain gap, the rendered images are further enriched with more than twenty-five stochastic degradation models that emulate realistic document acquisition artifacts, including ink bleed, paper aging, blur, illumination variation, scanner imperfections, compression artifacts, and multiple noise processes.By overcoming the long-standing scarcity of annotated Persian OCR data, Persian Pixel provides a scalable and openly available resource for training and fine-tuning modern OCR architectures, including transformer-based models such as TrOCR and Donut. The dataset establishes a strong foundation for research in Persian document analysis, historical manuscript digitization, and end-to-end document understanding, while demonstrating that programmatic synthetic data generation offers a practical, cost-effective, and scalable alternative to manual annotation for advancing OCR in low-resource and typographically complex scripts.

AI.tldr: Persian Pixel is a large synthetic OCR dataset (343k image–text pairs) for Persian, addressing script complexity and data scarcity by rendering from a 7M-word corpus with realistic degradation to close the synthetic–real gap, enabling training of modern OCR models (e.g., TrOCR, Donut).
AI.motivation: Persian OCR lags Latin-script OCR due to (i) the complex Perso-Arabic writing system with contextual joining, ligatures, diacritics, and multiple styles; (ii) the high cost of manual annotation and limited high-quality labeled data. A scalable synthetic dataset can accelerate OCR development for Persian.
AI.method: Generate 343k high-fidelity image–text pairs from a 7M-word Persian corpus using the SynthOCR-Gen rendering framework. The pipeline models contextual joining, positional glyph variants, diacritics, and multiple Persian typefaces (Naskh, Nastaliq, etc.). It further applies 25+ stochastic degradations to simulate real-world document capture, including blur, ink bleed, illumination variation, scanner noise, and compression artifacts.
AI.result: A publicly available, scalable Persian OCR dataset that narrows the synthetic–real domain gap and supports training of transformer-based OCR systems (e.g., TrOCR, Donut), enabling robust Persian document analysis and digitization research.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that programmatic synthetic data generation is a practical, cost-effective route to advance OCR for low-resource, typographically complex scripts and can catalyze Persian document analysis and end-to-end document understanding.

title: Autonomous Collaborative Learning Among an Ensemble of Tsetlin Machines with Consensus-Based Inference
summary: Tsetlin Machine (TM) is a rule-based machine-learning algorithm comprising collectives of two-action Tsetlin Automata (TAs) that cooperatively form conjunctive logical clauses from Boolean inputs through stochastic feedback. Although few recent studies have examined TM Federated Learning, the broader area of distributed and decentralized TM learning has not received much attention in the existing literature and warrants further exploration. In this work, we propose a paradigm for decentralized collaborative learning under a vertical feature-partitioning setting among an ensemble of Tsetlin Machines using consensus-based inference. Within this decentralized paradigm, each agent maintains its own private TM model, and there is no exchange of raw data among agents. Inference combines individual agents model predictions into a global consensus. The paradigm accommodates heterogeneous TM-based agents with differing data acquisition means, local data distributions, or computational resources, thereby facilitating the integration and fusion of information in settings such as multi-modal sensing environments. Experiments conducted using two-dimensional grid and connected graph network topologies demonstrate that the classification accuracies achieved are comparable to those of centralized models.

AI.tldr: Decentralized, privacy-preserving TM learning with vertical feature partitioning using consensus-based inference; multiple private TM agents collaboratively classify without sharing raw data, achieving centralized-like accuracy on grid and graph topologies.
AI.motivation: Extend TM applicability to distributed/decentralized settings where data cannot be pooled, emphasizing privacy, heterogeneity, and multi-modal sensing through vertical partitioning.
AI.method: Each agent maintains its own private Tsetlin Machine. No raw data exchange; predictions are fused via a consensus-based inference mechanism. The framework supports heterogeneous agents (different data acquisition, distributions, compute) and uses vertical feature partitioning to combine information from multiple modalities.
AI.result: Experimental results on 2D grid and connected graph topologies show classification accuracies comparable to centralized models, validating the feasibility of decentralized TM learning.
AI.conclusion: A viable decentralized paradigm for TM under vertical feature partitioning that preserves data privacy while achieving centralized-like performance; it accommodates heterogeneous agents and paves the way for more flexible, multi-modal collaborative learning.

title: PercepCap: Video Captioner with Structured Spatio-Temporal Perception
summary: Video captioning requires fine-grained spatio-temporal understanding of videos, including spatial perception of where objects are located and temporal perception of when events occur. Existing MLLMs usually generate captions directly from video inputs without exposing the perceptual evidence behind descriptions. As a result, mistakes in spatiotemporal perception are only observed in the final caption, making it difficult to identify the underlying perceptual errors directly. To address these issues, we present PercepCap, a perception-aware video captioning framework that makes perceptual evidence explicit before producing the final caption. Specifically, PercepCap follows a perceive-describe generation chain, where the model first produces a spatiotemporal perception trace comprising object trajectories and temporal events, and then generates the final caption conditioned on the perceived evidence. To support this, we design a two-stage training strategy. Perceive-then-Describe Supervised Fine-tuning adapts the model from caption-only generation to the proposed perceive-describe chain, while Perception-Grounded Reinforcement Learning optimizes perception trace and caption quality with joint rewards over perception chain and the final caption. To support our two-stage training, we introduce Caption-Anchored Perception Data Construction. This pipeline builds the SFT and RL training data by first generating a caption-only description, extracting the objects and events it mentions, and grounding them back in the video with boxes and timestamps. This yields caption-aligned perception data that provides solid training ground truth, ensuring that the explicit perception trace and final caption refer to the same objects and events. Across direct caption and caption-to-QA evaluation, PercepCap consistently improves upon the Qwen3-VL baseline and demonstrates leading caption quality.

AI.tldr: PercepCap introduces a perception-aware video captioning framework that first extracts spatiotemporal perception traces (object trajectories and events) and then generates captions conditioned on this explicit evidence, using a two-stage training (Perceive-then-Describe SFT and Perception-Grounded RL) and Caption-Anchored data construction; it improves Qwen3-VL on caption and caption-QA tasks.
AI.motivation: Resolve the lack of perceptual evidence in existing MLLMs, which makes perceptual errors hard to diagnose, by exposing explicit perception traces to guide captioning and improve interpretability and quality.
AI.method: Propose PercepCap with a perceive-describe chain. Two-stage training: (1) Perceive-then-Describe Supervised Fine-tuning to adapt to the chain; (2) Perception-Grounded Reinforcement Learning with joint rewards over perception chain and final caption. Data construction: Caption-Anchored Perception Data Construction by generating caption and grounding mentioned objects/events back to video to produce caption-aligned perception data.
AI.result: Across direct caption and caption-to-QA evaluation, PercepCap outperforms the Qwen3-VL baseline and yields leading caption quality.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling and grounding spatiotemporal perception improves video captioning performance and interpretability; the proposed training strategy and data construction effectively align perception traces with the final captions.

title: CURED: Creating, Understanding, and Repairing Errors Demonstrator
summary: Detecting and cleaning errors in tabular data is a prerequisite for data intense software applications. Recent research at the intersection of Machine Learning (ML) and Database Management Systems (DBMS) highlights the potential of statistical learning algorithms for error detection and cleaning. This paper combines our recent work on ML-based data cleaning and error models in a unified demonstrator. The web application allows users to upload tabular data, perturb the data with realistic data dependent errors and use modern ML methods to clean and understand error mechanisms in data. Our demonstrator helps to bridge the gap between theoretical advancements and intuitive practical insights in the context of error models and data cleaning algorithms for tabular data. The demonstrator is available at https://cured.demo.calgo-lab.de/

AI.tldr: A web-based demonstrator that integrates ML-based data cleaning with error models for tabular data, enabling users to upload data, inject realistic data-dependent errors, and apply ML cleaning methods to study error mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Bridge the gap between theoretical ML-based data cleaning and practical application; improve data quality for data-intensive software by enabling interactive exploration of error models and cleaning algorithms.
AI.method: Develop a unified web demonstrator that combines ML-based data cleaning and error models; supports user data upload, perturbation with realistic errors, and application of modern ML cleaning methods to analyze and understand error mechanisms in tabular data.
AI.result: A functional prototype demonstrator accessible via a web application; showcases the integration of error models and ML-based cleaning, providing an interactive platform to explore data perturbations and cleaning strategies (no formal empirical results reported).
AI.conclusion: The demonstrator serves as a bridge between theory and practice in tabular data cleaning, enabling intuitive understanding of error mechanisms and cleaning algorithms; available at the provided URL.

title: ATSplat: Compact Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Adaptive Token Expansion
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high-quality novel-view synthesis by optimizing freely placed primitives in 3D and adaptively densifying them in under-reconstructed regions. However, this scene-adaptive capacity allocation is largely lost in existing feed-forward 3DGS methods, which commonly regress Gaussians at input pixels and lift them along camera rays. Such pixel-aligned formulations make the number and placement of primitives depend on image resolution and input viewpoints rather than scene complexity, resulting in dense and often redundant Gaussian sets. We present ATSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework that restores the adaptive allocation capability of 3DGS optimization through Adaptive 3D Tokens. ATSplat first lifts coarse patch-level depth and camera cues into sparse 3D anchor tokens, forming a compact scaffold of the scene. Each token is then regressed into local Gaussians with learnable 3D offsets, decoupling primitive placement from input image grids. An Adaptive Token Expansion module predicts a token-level uncertainty score, supervised by rendering error maps, and selectively expands high-uncertainty tokens through learnable expansion layers. This sparse-to-adaptive formulation enables ATSplat to concentrate primitives in challenging regions while maintaining a compact representation. Experiments on two representative datasets, RealEstate10K and DL3DV, show that ATSplat achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality while reducing the number of Gaussians by more than $5.7\times$ compared with dense feed-forward 3DGS methods. From 12 input images at $512 \times 960$ resolution, ATSplat completes reconstruction in less than a second using a single commercial GPU, and renders high-quality novel views at 1136 FPS ($512 \times 960$) with only 311K Gaussians.

AI.tldr: ATSplat introduces Adaptive 3D Tokens to perform sparse-to-adaptive 3D Gaussian Splatting in a feed-forward framework, achieving state-of-the-art rendering quality with significantly fewer Gaussians and real-time performance.
AI.motivation: Pixel-aligned 3DGS methods regress Gaussians at input pixels, leading to dense, redundant primitives and allocation that depends on image resolution rather than scene complexity. There is a need for scene-aware, adaptive primitive allocation.
AI.method: The approach lifts coarse patch-level depth and camera cues into sparse 3D anchor tokens, regresses each token into local Gaussians with learnable 3D offsets, and uses an Adaptive Token Expansion module to predict token uncertainty (via rendering error maps) and expand high-uncertainty tokens with learnable expansion layers. This sparse-to-adaptive pipeline decouples primitive placement from input image grids and enables focused allocation where needed.
AI.result: On RealEstate10K and DL3DV datasets, ATSplat achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality while reducing the number of Gaussians by over 5.7× compared with dense feed-forward 3DGS methods. From 12 input images at 512×960, reconstruction completes in under 1 second on a single consumer GPU, and novel views render at 1136 FPS (512×960) using ~311k Gaussians.
AI.conclusion: ATSplat demonstrates effective adaptive allocation of Gaussians through a token-based sparse-to-adaptive framework, enabling high-quality rendering with far fewer primitives and enabling real-time-style performance.

title: Active Inference as a Convex Markov Decision Process
summary: Active Inference (AIF) frames adaptive behavior as the minimization of expected free energy (EFE), combining epistemic and pragmatic objectives within a single variational principle. We frame AIF as policy optimization and show that, for closed-loop control policies, EFE minimization can be formulated as a convex Markov decision process (MDP). In this formulation, the pragmatic terms are linear in the predictive state marginals and therefore equivalent to reward maximization in a latent MDP, while the epistemic value introduces a nonlinear component that distinguishes EFE minimization from standard reinforcement learning. This perspective further reveals the epistemic drive of active inference as a policy-dependent (performative) reward. We analyze finite-horizon, discounted, and average-reward formulations of EFE and derive a mirror descent (MD) algorithm that locally linearizes the objective around the current state marginals, yielding a policy-dependent reward that is compatible with actor-critic methods and dynamic programming. Finally, we argue that coupling world-model learning with policy optimization gives active inference the structure of performative reinforcement learning, providing a route toward grounding active inference within modern reinforcement learning and optimization theory, including convergence analysis and principled policy improvement guarantees.

AI.tldr: Active Inference can be reformulated as a policy-optimization problem that yields a convex MDP in predictive marginals; epistemic value adds a nonlinear term, making EFE minimization differ from standard RL. A mirror-descent algorithm yields a policy-dependent reward compatible with actor-critic and DP, and coupling world-model learning yields performative RL with convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: To unify Active Inference with modern reinforcement learning/optimization by (i) casting EFE minimization as a convex MDP, (ii) clarifying the epistemic term as a policy-dependent reward, and (iii) establishing algorithms with convergence guarantees across finite-horizon, discounted, and average-reward settings.
AI.method: Frame AIF as policy optimization; show EFE minimization for closed-loop policies forms a convex MDP in predictive state marginals; decompose EFE into a linear pragmatic reward and a nonlinear epistemic term; interpret epistemic drive as a policy-dependent (performative) reward; derive a mirror descent algorithm that linearizes the objective around current marginals; discuss compatibility with actor-critic methods and dynamic programming; argue for coupling world-model learning with policy optimization to realize performative reinforcement learning with convergence guarantees.
AI.result: Pragmatic terms reduce to reward maximization in a latent MDP due to linear dependence on predictive marginals, while the epistemic term introduces nonlinearity distinguishing EFE from standard RL; the epistemic drive is framed as a policy-dependent reward; a mirror-descent update yields a locally linearized objective suitable for actor-critic and DP; the framework provides a pathway to ground AIF in RL theory with potential convergence guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Coupling world-model learning with policy optimization places Active Inference within performative reinforcement learning, offering a principled route to theoretical grounding, convergence analysis, and provable policy improvement within modern RL and optimization frameworks.

title: Local Stability and Gaussian Smoothing of Quantized Neural Networks
comment: Accepted at the 23rd IFAC World Congress (IFAC WC 2026), Busan, Republic of Korea, 2026; 6 pages, 2 figures
summary: We study Gaussian averaging as a smooth surrogate for quantized neural models. Under bounded local oscillation, we derive a local dimension-dependent bound on |f-g|, linking Gaussian smoothing to the stability analysis of discontinuous networks. We compute closed-form Gaussian averages of the rectified linear unit (ReLU) and sign activation functions, and illustrate the mechanism on a high-dimensional binary perceptron, where layer-preactivation aggregation under an explicit quantization-noise surrogate yields the Gaussian envelope used in inference-side smoothing and training-side smooth surrogate gradients.

AI.tldr: Gaussian smoothing serves as a smooth surrogate for quantized neural models, with a dimension-aware stability bound and closed-form averages for ReLU and sign, demonstrated on a high-dimensional binary perceptron to enable smoothing and smooth surrogate gradients.
AI.motivation: Quantized neural networks introduce discontinuities; Gaussian averaging can provide a smooth surrogate to analyze, train, and deploy these models, and to quantify how close the smoothed proxy is to the original under bounded local oscillation.
AI.method: 1) Derive a local, dimension-dependent bound on |f-g| under bounded local oscillation, linking Gaussian smoothing to stability of discontinuous networks. 2) Compute closed-form Gaussian averages for ReLU and sign activations. 3) Demonstrate the mechanism on a high-dimensional binary perceptron using a quantization-noise surrogate to induce a Gaussian envelope for inference smoothing and for training-time surrogate gradients.
AI.result: A local dimension-dependent bound on the difference between the original and smoothed functions is established. Closed-form expressions for Gaussian-averaged ReLU and sign activations are derived. In a high-dimensional binary perceptron, layer-preactivation aggregation with an explicit quantization-noise surrogate yields the Gaussian envelope used for inference-time smoothing and for smooth surrogate gradients during training.
AI.conclusion: Gaussian smoothing provides a principled, dimension-aware surrogate for quantized neural models, linking smoothing to stability analysis, and enabling practical inference smoothing and differentiable surrogate gradients during training.

title: Self-organizing Architecture of Receptron Units: a Hardware-Aware Framework for Edge Intelligence
comment: This work has been submitted to NeuroPHY 2026
summary: The growing demand for intelligent processing at the edge of IoT networks is constrained by the severe computational and memory limitations of microcontroller units, which render impractical conventional deep learning approaches. We propose a neuromorphicinspired classifier based on the Receptron model, a single-unit architecture capable of implementing non-linearly separable decision boundaries, without resorting to multi-layer networks. The model is designed for direct deployment on mid-range MCUs, while supporting continuous on-device adaptation. Experimental evaluation on basic dataset benchmarks yields cross-validated accuracies compatible with standard machine learning method baselines. These results position the Receptron as a viable and interpretable alternative for resource-constrained neuromorphic edge systems operating in dynamic, non-stationary environments.

AI.tldr: A neuromorphic-inspired single-neuron classifier (Receptron) enables non-linear decision boundaries on microcontroller units without deep networks, with on-device adaptation and competitive accuracy; suitable for resource-constrained, dynamic edge environments.
AI.motivation: Address the computational/memory constraints of MCUs in IoT edge scenarios, requiring lightweight, interpretable models capable of on-device adaptation and non-linear decision boundaries.
AI.method: Introduce the Receptron, a neuromorphic-inspired single-unit classifier that can implement non-linearly separable boundaries without multi-layer networks; designed for direct deployment on mid-range MCUs and supports continuous on-device learning/adaptation.
AI.result: Cross-validated accuracies on basic dataset benchmarks comparable to standard ML baselines, indicating viable performance for edge deployment.
AI.conclusion: Receptron offers a viable, interpretable alternative for resource-constrained neuromorphic edge systems operating in dynamic, non-stationary environments.

title: Instance Hardness-Based Relevance for Imbalanced Regression
summary: Imbalanced regression problems arise when the target variable has an asymmetric distribution, resulting in underrepresented value ranges in the dataset. Traditional approaches for identifying rare instances rely on a relevance function that assigns higher importance to specific regions of the target distribution. However, the effectiveness of imbalance-aware learning methods depends strongly on how relevance is defined. In more complex scenarios, such as bimodal distributions, traditional relevance functions struggle to capture rarity, as they assign fixed relevance values based solely on target values, thereby compromising the distinction between truly rare and normal instances. To address these limitations, this study proposes an Instance Hardness-based relevance function (InHaR) for identifying rare instances in regression problems. Unlike traditional relevance functions, the proposed approach incorporates learning difficulty, allowing rarity to be inferred not only from the target distribution but also from the difficulty of instances for the learning algorithm. This property is particularly important in bimodal scenarios, where rarity cannot be accurately inferred from target values alone. Experimental results demonstrate that the InHaR correctly identifies rare regions under bimodal distributions and, when used to guide resampling strategies such as Random Oversampling (RO) and Gaussian Noise (GN), leads to significant improvements in predictive performance compared to traditional relevance-based approaches. The code, dataset, and further details about the proposed method are publicly available at https://github.com/VitorLeitao/instance-hardness-Imbalanced-regression.

AI.tldr: Proposes InHaR for imbalanced regression; uses instance hardness to identify rare instances; improves resampling-based performance, especially in bimodal distributions; code available.
AI.motivation: Imbalanced regression with asymmetric distributions; traditional relevance functions fail to capture rarity in complex distributions; need to leverage learning difficulty.
AI.method: Introduce InHaR: an instance hardness-based relevance function; compute rarity from model's learning difficulty; use to guide resampling (RO, GN); compare against traditional relevance-based methods; evaluate on bimodal targets; public repo.
AI.result: InHaR accurately identifies rare regions in bimodal distributions; improves predictive performance when used with resampling; outperforms traditional relevance-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: InHaR effectively identifies rare instances in imbalanced regression; robust to bimodal distributions; addresses shortcomings of target-value-based relevance; reproducible via provided code.

title: On Optimization Complexity of Second-Order Certified Unlearning
summary: We study machine unlearning: the removal of memorized training data from a trained model. Specifically, we investigate the algorithmic complexity of certified unlearning from an optimization perspective. We formalize the goal of an unlearning algorithm as simultaneously achieving certified unlearning and optimization accuracy. Utilizing the notion of uniformly convex regularizers, we prove new bounds on the distance between initial and unlearned models using a novel substitute for generalization error. Thus we theoretically demonstrate that if the removed data is well-predicted by the unlearned model, the corresponding optimization problem is simple. Furthermore, we develop a new second-order unlearning algorithm with an anisotropic Gaussian mechanism and state-of-the-art global convergence. We prove fast rates for our method in achieving certified unlearning for linear models with quasi-self-concordant losses. As a direct application, our theory covers unlearning for logistic and exponential regressions and shows a provable benefit of utilizing second-order information compared to first-order unlearning methods.

AI.tldr: The paper studies certified machine unlearning under an optimization lens, deriving bounds on model drift when data is removed using uniformly convex regularizers, and introduces a second-order unlearning algorithm with an anisotropic Gaussian mechanism, achieving fast convergence for linear models with quasi-self-concordant losses, and applying to logistic/exponential regression.
AI.motivation: To formalize and quantify the complexity of unlearning, connect it to optimization accuracy and generalization, and to develop provable, efficient unlearning algorithms that outperform first-order methods.
AI.method: Analytical framework using uniformly convex regularizers; derive distance bounds between original and unlearned models; design a second-order unlearning algorithm with anisotropic Gaussian noise; prove convergence rates for linear models with quasi-self-concordant losses; specialize to logistic and exponential regressions.
AI.result: New theoretical bounds on model distance after unlearning; a substitute bound for generalization error; fast certified unlearning rates for linear/quasi-self-concordant losses; empirical or theoretical demonstration of superiority of second-order over first-order methods; applies to logistic and exponential regressions.
AI.conclusion: Certified unlearning can be efficient when the removed data are well-predicted by the unlearned model; second-order information under anisotropic Gaussian mechanism yields provable performance gains; the framework provides concrete guarantees for logistic and exponential regression tasks.

title: OLEDLM: A Unified Language Model for OLED Molecular Design
summary: The development of organic light-emitting diode (OLED) materials faces the compounded challenges of an astronomically large chemical space, stringent quantum-chemical constraints, and a scarcity of labeled data. Although the question of OLED generation is important, few models have been trained effectively for this specific domain. We propose an inverse molecular design framework based on causal language models: given target optoelectronic properties (e.g., excitation energy, oscillator strength), our model directly generates OLED SMILES sequences satisfying the specified constraints. We employ a multi-stage strategy: first, we establish a foundational chemical language model using a LLaMA-style transformer architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first successful adaptation of LLMs specifically for the OLED domain, bridging the gap between generic molecular generation and the stringent structural requirements of optoelectronic materials. Second, we fine-tune property predictors based on a BERT model pre-trained on our large-scale OLED dataset. Then, we perform Reinforcement Learning on our fine-tuned model, leveraging our property predictor, for better SMILES generation. Finally, through DFT verification, we demonstrate that our framework can efficiently navigate the OLED chemical space, generating novel candidates with high structural validity and optimized optoelectronic properties.

AI.tldr: A causal-language-model-based inverse design framework for OLEDs that generates SMILES conditioned on target optoelectronic properties, using a multi-stage pipeline (LLaMA-style foundation model, BERT-based property predictors, RL), with DFT verification to validate novelty and property optimization.
AI.motivation: OLED design faces enormous chemical space, strict quantum-chemical constraints, and limited labeled data. Efficient, controllable generation of valid OLED candidates conditioned on specific properties is required.
AI.method: Multi-stage pipeline: (1) train a LLaMA-style transformer as a foundational chemical language model tailored to OLEDs; (2) fine-tune BERT-based property predictors on a large OLED dataset; (3) apply Reinforcement Learning to the generative model using the property predictor as a reward signal; (4) validate generated candidates with DFT to ensure structural validity and property optimization.
AI.result: The framework can efficiently navigate the OLED chemical space, generating novel candidates with high structural validity and optimized optoelectronic properties, demonstrated via DFT verification.
AI.conclusion: An effective, data-efficient design framework that bridges generic language models and domain-specific OLED constraints, enabling targeted generation conditioned on desired properties.

title: The Quadrilateral Loss: Additivity as a Measurable Behavior of Dense Neural Networks
summary: Additive models buy interpretability by forbidding feature interactions, a constraint that neural instantiations enforce architecturally. We introduce the quadrilateral loss, a differentiable penalty that treats additivity as a measurable behavior instead: a second-order mixed difference on pairs of training points swapping one coordinate, which vanishes if and only if the coordinate carries no interaction, remains informative for piecewise-linear networks, and equals in expectation the per-coordinate interaction mass of the interventional Shapley-GAM. The loss turns additivity into a dial - most learned interactions prove removable almost for free, and on small datasets a moderate penalty improves accuracy and additivity simultaneously - and into an online observable: its per-feature surrender curves show, across seeds and datasets, that pre-regularization interaction magnitude barely predicts what a regularized model retains, undermining post-hoc interaction rankings. Against this instrument we compare routes to exact additivity, spanning structural masks, behavioral penalties (optionally crystallized into exact structure), weight decay, backfitting, the shared-section model, and bagged boosted stumps: constraining behavior before structure dominates weight-space constraints, rankings reverse between data regimes, and converging routes agree on the shape functions themselves. Three silent failure modes we document share one anatomy: guarantees imported into settings that quietly void their preconditions.

AI.tldr: Quadrilateral loss provides a differentiable measure of additivity for neural nets and serves as a tunable dial for interaction control, enabling pre-regularization behavioral constraints to dominate over weight-space constraints; it enables both improved additivity and modest accuracy gains on small data, while exposing limitations of post-hoc interaction rankings.
AI.motivation: To quantify and regulate feature additivity (interaction absence) directly during training, rather than relying on post-hoc explanations or architectural constraints alone.
AI.method: Introduce a second-order mixed-difference penalty across training points that vanishes when a feature does not interact with others; relate the expected penalty to per-coordinate interaction mass of interventional Shapley-GAM; apply to piecewise-linear networks; compare various exact additivity routes (masks, penalties, decay, backfitting, shared-section, bagged stumps).
AI.result: Moderate penalty improves accuracy and additivity on small datasets; pre-regularization interaction magnitude poorly predicts post-regularization rankings; different routes to additivity converge on the same shape functions; rankings reverse across data regimes; three silent failure modes tied to broken preconditions.
AI.conclusion: Controlling behavior before structure is more effective than weight-space constraints for achieving additivity; guarantees must be checked against their preconditions to avoid silent failures.

title: ELSAA: Efficient Low-Rank and Sparse Attention Approximation for Training Transformers
summary: The quadratic $N\times N$ attention score matrix remains a central obstacle to extending Transformers to longer input lengths.
