Existing efficient attention methods usually reduce this bottleneck by either imposing sparsity, so that each query attends to only a small subset of keys, or by using low-rank/kernel sketches, so that global interactions are compressed into a lower-dimensional representation. We propose \emph{ELSAA}, an efficient low-rank and sparse approximation of attention. Importantly, ELSAA does \emph{not} decompose the learned projection or output matrices of the Transformer into sparse and low-rank factors. Instead, after dense projections produce $Q,K,V$, ELSAA approximates the induced attention score operator itself: a sparse branch captures selected high-similarity interactions, while a low-rank branch summarizes diffuse global interactions. Since the two branches can be normalized over supports with very different denominator mass, ELSAA introduces a denominator-aware fusion term that scales the sparse branch according to its estimated attention mass relative to the low-rank branch. This gives a practical framework for constructing low-rank and sparse attention outputs without materializing the full quadratic score matrix, aiming to enable longer-context training while preserving both sharp token-level interactions and broad contextual mixing.

AI.tldr: ELSAA proposes a joint sparse and low-rank approximation to attention that directly approximates the attention score operator after standard Q/K/V projections, enabling longer sequences without materializing the full quadratic score matrix.
AI.motivation: Quadratic attention scales poorly with input length, hindering long-context modeling. Existing approaches trade off either sparsity (locality) or low-rank approximations (global structure) by decomposing projection matrices. A unified framework that preserves sharp local interactions while capturing global mixing is needed.
AI.method: After computing dense Q, K, V from the input, the method constructs two attention branches that approximate the score matrix: (1) a sparse branch selecting high-similarity interactions, (2) a low-rank branch capturing diffuse global interactions. These branches are combined via a denominator-aware fusion term that normalizes according to their respective attention masses, without factorizing the learned projection or output matrices. The approach avoids materializing the full quadratic score matrix and aims to scale attention computations to longer sequences.
AI.result: The abstract presents a practical framework (ELSAA) for building joint sparse and low-rank attention outputs, with a focus on maintaining token-level sharp interactions and broad contextual mixing while enabling longer-context training.
AI.conclusion: ELSAA introduces a unified, non-decompositional attention approximation that separately models high-similarity and diffuse interactions and fuses them with denominator-aware normalization, potentially enabling scalable, accurate attention for long sequences.

title: User-Centric Modeling of Transactional Sequences with Explainable State Space Models
summary: We propose a hybrid approach for user-centric modeling of transactional event sequences that combines contrastive representation learning (CoLES) with State Space Models (SSMs). While contrastive methods yield high-quality compressed user representations, existing encoders -- RNNs and Transformers -- suffer from vanishing gradients or quadratic complexity, respectively. Mamba, a selective SSM, efficiently handles long-range dependencies but remains underexplored for personalized user analysis. We investigate two integration strategies: (1)~initializing the Mamba hidden state with a CoLES embedding, and (2)~prepending the projected CoLES embedding as a prefix token to the input sequence. Both approaches supply the model with an informative user prior from the first step. Experiments on three public datasets -- Age (multiclass age-group prediction), MBD (multi-label product acquisition), and Taobao (binary purchase prediction) -- demonstrate consistent improvements over standalone Mamba and CoLES with a linear classifier, with the hybrid models converging 2--3$\times$ faster than the plain SSM baseline. Explainability analysis via discretization-step maps and Integrated Gradients reveals selective event filtering on behavior-rich datasets and identifies the most informative transaction features.

AI.tldr: Hybrid user-centric modeling of transactional sequences by integrating CoLES with Mamba SSMs using two strategies: (i) CoLES-embedding initialized hidden state, (ii) CoLES embedding as a prefix token. The approach improves over standalone Mamba and CoLES, accelerates convergence 2–3x, and offers explainability via discretization maps and Integrated Gradients across three datasets (Age, MBD, Taobao).
AI.motivation: To combine high-quality contrastive representations of users with efficient long-range sequence modeling, addressing vanishing gradients in RNNs and quadratic complexity in Transformers, enabling scalable personalized analysis of transactional sequences.
AI.method: Two integration schemes: (1) initialize Mamba hidden state with a projected CoLES embedding; (2) prepend the projected CoLES embedding as a prefix token to the input sequence. The CoLES embedding provides a user prior; evaluation uses a linear classifier. Datasets: Age (multiclass age-group), MBD (multi-label product acquisition), Taobao (binary purchase).
AI.result: Hybrid models outperform standalone Mamba and CoLES baselines; consistent improvements with a linear classifier; 2–3× faster convergence than plain SSM baseline; explainability analysis via discretization-step maps and Integrated Gradients reveals selective event filtering and identifies informative transaction features.
AI.conclusion: The combination of CoLES priors with selective state-space modeling yields superior accuracy and efficiency for personalized user modeling on long-range transactional data, with interpretable cues highlighting key transaction features.

title: PIER: Physics-Informed Environmental Retrieval for Time-Series Modeling
summary: Accurate modeling of environmental systems is fundamental to scientific understanding and decision-making, yet remains challenging because observations are limited and physical dynamics vary across systems. Retrieval-augmented approaches offer a natural path to transfer knowledge across systems, but standard embedding-based retrieval does not guarantee consistency of underlying physical processes, since scenarios with similar embeddings may arise from different underlying mechanisms. We propose Physics-Informed Environmental Retrieval (PIER), a model-agnostic framework that augments embedding-based retrieval with a physics-aware stream that scores candidates by flux-response consistency with the target, using local verifiers trained on physics-derived flux features. A weight adjustment mechanism then learns per-scenario weights that adaptively balance the two retrieval streams based on diagnostic features summarizing physics-stream reliability. Experiments on 356 lakes across the Midwestern United States spanning 41 years show that PIER consistently outperforms baselines for water temperature and dissolved oxygen prediction, and serves as a general augmentation strategy across diverse backbones.

AI.tldr: Physics-Informed Environmental Retrieval (PIER) augments embedding-based retrieval with a physics-aware stream that enforces flux-response consistency via local physics-driven verifiers, plus per-scenario adaptive weighting. Demonstrated on 356 Midwest lakes over 41 years, improving water temperature and dissolved oxygen predictions and generalizing across backbones.
AI.motivation: Observation-limited environmental systems exhibit diverse underlying physics; standard embedding-based retrieval can conflate distinct mechanisms. A physics-informed augmentation is needed to ensure consistency with physical processes while enabling cross-system knowledge transfer.
AI.method: PIER adds a physics-aware retrieval stream that scores candidates by flux-response consistency using verifiers trained on physics-derived flux features. It also incorporates a per-scenario weight adjustment mechanism that balances the physics and embedding streams based on diagnostic features of the physics-stream reliability. The framework is model-agnostic and tested with multiple backbones on lake data.
AI.result: PIER consistently outperforms baselines for predicting water temperature and dissolved oxygen across 356 lakes over 41 years, and serves as a general augmentation strategy across diverse backbones.
AI.conclusion: PIER provides a robust, physics-consistent retrieval augmentation for environmental modeling, enabling more reliable cross-system knowledge transfer and potentially broad applicability beyond the tested lake dataset.

title: PhaseAware: Interpretable Human-in-the-Loop Rehabilitation Scoring with Boundary Monitoring
comment: 22 pages, 4 main figures, 3 tables, and 17 supplementary figures. Supplementary Information is included in the same PDF
summary: Rehabilitation scoring systems are most useful when their outputs can be reviewed and interpreted within clinical workflows. This study presents PhaseAware, a compact framework for continuous rehabilitation quality assessment that combines a temporal backbone with phase- and body-group descriptors through a backbone-conditioned gated residual pathway. The model was evaluated on the UI-PRMD deep-squat protocol and further tested on the KIMORE squatting subset. On UI-PRMD, PhaseAware achieved an RMSE of 0.0230, corresponding to an 88.9% reduction relative to the accepted baseline. It also maintained favorable performance on KIMORE, suggesting that the phase-aware design transfers across related squatting protocols. In addition to score prediction, PhaseAware generates structured review cues based on phase- and body-level sensitivity, highlighting the movement stages and body regions most relevant to each prediction. The architecture employs a backbone-conditioned gated residual mechanism to stabilize feature representation, supporting use in resource-constrained settings. These cues are intended to support clinician review, boundary-case monitoring, and human-in-the-loop triage rather than autonomous decision-making. Overall, PhaseAware offers a practical and interpretable approach to rehabilitation scoring that may help integrate automated assessment into information systems while preserving clinician oversight.

AI.tldr: PhaseAware is a compact, interpretable rehabilitation scoring framework that uses a backbone-conditioned gated residual pathway with phase- and body-group descriptors to enable continuous quality assessment. It achieves strong accuracy on UI-PRMD deep-squat (RMSE 0.0230, ~89% improvement over baseline) and transfers well to KIMORE, while providing phase- and body-level cues to aid clinician review in resource-constrained settings.
AI.motivation: There is a need for interpretable, workflow-friendly rehabilitation scoring that can provide continuous assessment and meaningful feedback without replacing clinician oversight, and that generalizes across related protocols.
AI.method: The framework combines a temporal backbone with phase- and body-group descriptors through a backbone-conditioned gated residual pathway. It also generates structured review cues based on phase- and body-level sensitivity. Evaluated on UI-PRMD deep-squat protocol and KIMORE squatting subset to assess accuracy and transferability; designed for resource-constrained settings to stabilize feature representation.
AI.result: RMSE of 0.0230 on UI-PRMD with an 88.9% reduction relative to a baseline; maintained favorable performance on KIMORE; phase-aware design transfers across related squatting protocols; cues identify movement stages and body regions most relevant to predictions.
AI.conclusion: PhaseAware provides a practical, interpretable approach to automated rehabilitation scoring that supports integration into clinical information systems with clinician oversight and triage rather than autonomous decision-making.

title: Breaking the $T^{3/4}$ Barrier for Regret Minimization With Bi-Dimensional CDFs
summary: We study regret minimization for learning CDF-related objectives of the form \[ g(x)\cdot\mathbb{P}_{X\sim\mathcal{D}}(X\le x), \] over $[0,1]^2$, where $g$ is a known Lipschitz function and $\mathcal{D}$ is an unknown distribution. At each round $t$, the learner selects a point $x_t$ and observes the binary feedback $\mathbb{I}(X_t\le x_t)$, where $X_t\sim\mathcal{D}$. We design an algorithm achieving regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{7/10})$, improving over the previous best-known bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{3/4})$ and showing that the curse of dimensionality can be at least partially lifted for this class of objectives, though a gap remains with the $Ω(T^{2/3})$ lower bound. As an application, our techniques yield the same $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{7/10})$ regret bound for profit maximization in repeated bilateral trade with fixed prices.

AI.tldr: Sublinear regret for learning CDF-related objectives with binary feedback: achieves ~T^{7/10} regret, improving over ~T^{3/4}, partially lifting the curse of dimensionality; applications include profit maximization in repeated bilateral trade with fixed prices.
AI.motivation: Address online learning of objectives that depend on the CDF of an unknown distribution, with only binary feedback. The goal is to minimize regret in a two-dimensional domain, shedding light on how much dimensionality can be mitigated for this class of objectives.
AI.method: Propose a new online learning algorithm tailored to CDF-based objectives of the form g(x)·P(X≤x) with known Lipschitz g and unknown D, operating on [0,1]^2. The algorithm uses binary feedback per round and achieves a regret bound of Õ(T^{7/10}).
AI.result: Regret bound Õ(T^{7/10}) is achieved, improving upon the previous Õ(T^{3/4}) bound. This demonstrates partial mitigation of the curse of dimensionality for these objectives and narrows the gap to the Ω(T^{2/3}) lower bound.
AI.conclusion: The developed method attains the same Õ(T^{7/10}) regret for profit maximization in repeated bilateral trade with fixed prices, indicating broad applicability to economic settings involving CDF-related objectives under binary feedback.

title: Interpretable Fuzzy Rule-Based Regression Extension for Ex-Fuzzy Library
summary: Machine learning models achieve high predictive accuracy in regression tasks, but their deployment in safety-critical and regulated domains requires interpretability. While fuzzy rule-based systems offer transparent, linguistically explicit interpretable models, Mamdani-style fuzzy regression remains underrepresented in modern machine learning software libraries. This paper presents an interpretable regression extension for the Ex-Fuzzy library, enabling Mamdani fuzzy inference with scalar consequents learned directly from data. For this, a target-aware partition initialisation strategy based on Fuzzy C-Means clustering is introduced, in which linguistic variables are derived from an augmented input-output space to emphasise output-relevant regions of the feature space. The proposed extension is evaluated on ten regression datasets from the KEEL repository, comparing Gaussian and trapezoidal partition strategies against standard baselines including linear regression, multilayer perceptron, and random forests. Experimental results show that Gaussian partitions consistently outperform uniform trapezoidal partitions, achieving a mean coefficient of determination of approximately 0.86 while producing compact rule bases of 10-15 human-readable rules. The proposed implementation provides a transparent and competitive alternative to black-box regression models, supporting practical interpretability with competitive predictive performance.

AI.tldr: Interpretable Mamdani fuzzy regression extension for Ex-Fuzzy with target-aware fuzzy partitioning.
AI.motivation: High predictive accuracy is insufficient in safety-critical/regulatory domains; transparent, linguistically explicit models are needed. Fuzzy rule-based systems offer interpretability but Mamdani-style regression is underrepresented in current libraries.
AI.method: Introduces a target-aware partition initialization using Fuzzy C-Means on augmented input-output space to derive linguistic variables. Learns scalar consequents from data within the Ex-Fuzzy framework, compares Gaussian versus trapezoidal partitions, and benchmarks against linear regression, MLP, and random forests on KEEL regression datasets.
AI.result: Gaussian partitions outperform uniform trapezoidal partitions, yielding mean R^2 ≈ 0.86 and compact rule bases of 10–15 human-readable rules across ten datasets.
AI.conclusion: The extension provides a transparent, competitive alternative to black-box models, delivering practical interpretability with strong predictive performance.

title: The Blessing of Dimensionality: How Near-Orthogonality in High-Dimensional Spaces Explains Temporal Portability
summary: Fine-tuning has been widely used to adapt large language models (LLMs) for domain-specific tasks. Parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) are frequently used to reduce computational costs. PortLLM is a training-free and data-free scheme used to adapt LLMs after continual pretraining. Although the initial PortLLM results show that LoRA patches exhibit short-term temporal portability, the long-term performance of PortLLM across several updates of continual pretraining remains underexplored. Furthermore, the intriguing effectiveness of PortLLM is not well understood from a theoretical standpoint. We address these two open questions by (1) performing an extensive empirical study of the long-term temporal portability of PortLLM patches across 10 continual pretraining steps using base models Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen; and (2) offering two theoretical analyses to explain our observation that the simple PortLLM method achieves competitive performance. We find empirically that the portability persists across longer time duration, indicating that repeated fine-tuning is not required when the base model is periodically updated. We find theoretically that near-orthogonality of high-dimensional vectors is a key justification for temporal portability. Our analyses also demonstrate a geometric perspective of the loss landscape in facilitating the theoretical comparison of different adaptation options.

AI.tldr: Study of PortLLM's long-term temporal portability across multiple continual pretraining updates; empirical validation over 10 steps on Mistral, Gemma, Qwen; theoretical explanations for its effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Two open questions: (1) whether PortLLM patches remain portable over long-term continual pretraining, and (2) why PortLLM works so well from a theoretical standpoint.
AI.method: Empirical study of PortLLM portability over 10 continual pretraining steps on three base models (Mistral, Gemma, Qwen); two theoretical analyses to justify observed portability, focusing on near-orthogonality of high-dimensional vectors and a geometric view of the loss landscape.
AI.result: Portability persists across longer time durations, indicating repeated fine-tuning is unnecessary when the base model is periodically updated. Theoretical analyses show near-orthogonality as a key mechanism for temporal portability, and provide a geometric perspective on the loss landscape to compare adaptation options.
AI.conclusion: PortLLM demonstrates durable long-term portability with simple patches; high-dimensional near-orthogonality underpins this effect, and the loss-landscape viewpoint supports systematic comparison of adaptation strategies.

title: Classical Hardware Acceleration of Quantum Autoencoders for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in Collider Experiments
summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms in high energy physics (HEP) can efficiently represent and leverage long-range, high-order correlations in high-dimensional collider data, potentially with fewer parameters and favorable scaling relative to classical models. Deployment of QML in real-time collider applications such as trigger systems requires the ability to emulate and compile quantum circuits classically, then synthesize the resulting quantum gates onto low-latency hardware accelerators, namely field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). We present a study of variational quantum autoencoder models for real-time anomaly detection triggers in modern collider experiments. The models achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art classical approaches and, after FPGA synthesis, satisfy resource usage and timing constraints consistent with trigger applications in future colliders. This work provides one of the first FPGA implementations of QML models for HEP triggers, enabling higher-capability models in today's classical data acquisition pipelines while advancing quantum readiness of collider experiment infrastructure.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates FPGA-ready variational quantum autoencoder for real-time HEP triggers; comparable to classical methods and meets latency/resource constraints, marking an early FPGA QML deployment in collider pipelines.
AI.motivation: Address real-time anomaly detection in high-dimensional collider data; exploit potential quantum advantages in capturing long-range correlations with fewer parameters; bridge quantum models to hardware accelerators via FPGA for real-time use.
AI.method: Developed variational quantum autoencoder (VQA) models; performed classical emulation and circuit compilation; synthesized the resulting quantum gates onto FPGAs; evaluated on trigger-like constraints; compared performance to state-of-the-art classical models.
AI.result: Achieved comparable anomaly-detection performance to classical baselines; after FPGA synthesis, resource usage and timing satisfy trigger requirements for future colliders; one of the first FPGA implementations of QML for HEP triggers.
AI.conclusion: Shows feasibility and practicality of deploying QML in real-time HEP pipelines; enables more capable models within existing infrastructure; advances quantum readiness, while highlighting integration challenges and need for further validation and optimization.

title: Multi-modal transformer for signal classification in nanopore blockade experiments
summary: Nanopore devices have emerged as powerful tools for single-molecule sensing, with potential for rapid, portable diagnostics. They detect changes in ionic current as analytes enter nanometer-scale pores, providing a means of identifying diverse biomarkers from their characteristic signal patterns. However, these signals are highly complex, and reliably assigning them to specific molecules remains a major challenge. Here, we address this by introducing a multi-modal deep learning architecture that jointly processes multiple signal representations, including raw time-series data, wavelet-based images, and static feature vectors. Our approach surpasses existing methods by more than 10 percentage points on a 42-peptide benchmark and transfers to a 20-amino-acid dataset with near-perfect accuracy. The model integrates complementary information from these representations, with attention analysis showing that the time-series and wavelet-image inputs emphasize different features of the same event. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of machine learning to enable robust, high-accuracy molecular identification with nanopore sensors.

AI.tldr: Multi-modal DL architecture combining time-series, wavelet images, and features improves nanopore-based molecule identification, achieving >10 percentage-point gains on 42-peptide benchmark and near-perfect accuracy on 20 amino acids.
AI.motivation: Nanopore signals are highly complex, making reliable molecule identification challenging; leveraging complementary representations may improve discrimination.
AI.method: A multi-modal neural network that jointly processes raw time-series nanopore signals, wavelet-based images, and static feature vectors, with attention mechanisms to analyze representation contributions.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines by >10 percentage points on a 42-peptide benchmark and attains near-perfect accuracy on a 20-amino-acid dataset; attention suggests time-series and wavelet inputs emphasize different signal aspects.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates practical potential for robust, high-accuracy molecular identification with nanopore sensors; multi-modal fusion captures complementary information that enhances performance.

title: Interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANN and fPANN) for uncertainty quantification and propagation in constitutive modeling
summary: Constitutive modeling under uncertainty remains a central challenge for reliable mechanics simulations, particularly when the available stress-deformation data are sparse, noisy, or heterogeneous. We propose interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANNs and fPANNs) for uncertainty-aware hyperelastic constitutive modeling. iPANNs learn sparse lower, mean, and upper free energy density branches whose stresses, obtained by automatic differentiation, ultimately enclose noisy stress observations. In contrast to this deterministic interval description, fPANNs embed the learned iPANN branches into a fuzzy-set representation through alpha-cut interpolation, yielding a nested family of admissible responses. iPANNs and fPANNs encode mechanistic constraints - preserving objectivity, consistency and promoting polyconvexity - and smoothed L0 regularization promotes interpretable energy representations. The bound models are trained through a two-stage transfer-learning procedure in which a sparse mean constitutive response is learned first and then fine-tuned into lower and upper energy branches. We evaluate the framework on synthetic isotropic hyperelastic data with heteroscedastic noise, varying random realizations, shifted noise means, and varying noise magnitudes. The results show that the learned bounds enclose noisy stress observations while generalizing to the test set. Further, we examine the propagation of uncertainty through the mean, upper and lower bound predictions of the learned iPANN models in a finite element setting. The proposed framework provides a compact, physics-consistent route for distribution-free aleatoric uncertainty quantification in hyperelastic constitutive modeling, and propagation in downstream finite element simulations.

AI.tldr: Proposes interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANNs and fPANNs) for uncertainty-aware hyperelastic constitutive modeling, with two-stage transfer learning to learn bound energy branches that enclose noisy data and propagate uncertainty in FE simulations.
AI.motivation: Constitutive modeling under uncertainty with sparse, noisy, or heterogeneous stress-deformation data. Need distribution-free (aleatoric) uncertainty quantification that is physics-consistent and interpretable, suitable for downstream finite element simulations.
AI.method: iPANNs learn sparse lower, mean, and upper free energy density branches; stresses from automatic differentiation bound noisy observations. fPANNs embed iPANN branches in a fuzzy-set representation via alpha-cut interpolation to yield nested admissible responses. Both enforce objectivity, consistency, and promote polyconvexity; use smoothed L0 regularization for interpretability. Two-stage transfer learning: first train sparse mean response, then fine-tune to lower/upper bounds.
AI.result: On synthetic isotropic hyperelastic data with heteroscedastic noise, varying realizations, shifted noise means, and different magnitudes, learned bounds enclose noisy stress observations and generalize to test data. Uncertainty is propagated through mean, upper, and lower predictions in a finite element setting, demonstrating a distribution-free approach to uncertainty quantification and propagation in FE simulations.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a compact, physics-consistent route for distribution-free aleatoric Uncertainty quantification in hyperelastic constitutive modeling and its propagation in downstream FE analyses, enabling robust predictions under data scarcity and noise.

title: Variance-reduced Domain Adaptation using Paired Sampling
summary: Correlation alignment and the maximum mean discrepancy are two widely used distribution-matching frameworks for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). However, high variance in these losses has been shown to undermine their effectiveness in minibatch optimisation settings. Furthermore, the losses lack finite-sum structure, which renders them incompatible with classical stochastic variance reduction (SVR) methods. This paper proposes Paired Sampling for Domain Adaptation (PSDA), a novel SVR technique tailored to such objectives. PSDA pairs observations both within and across domains, to form quadruplets that are always sampled together during training. The pairings are designed to minimise expected gradient variance, and reduce to solving a set of linear assignment problems. Our simulations demonstrate reduced variance compared to related methods, and experiments on three domain shift datasets show improved target domain accuracy.

AI.tldr: PSDA introduces quadruplet-based paired sampling to enable stochastic variance reduction for correlation alignment and MMD in unsupervised domain adaptation, reducing gradient variance and improving target accuracy.
AI.motivation: High variance in correlation alignment and maximum mean discrepancy losses harms minibatch optimization in UDA. Additionally, these losses lack a finite-sum structure, limiting compatibility with classical SVR methods.
AI.method: Construct quadruplets by pairing observations within and across domains; optimize pairings to minimize expected gradient variance; the pairings reduce to solving a set of linear assignment problems; train by sampling these quadruplets together.
AI.result: Simulations show reduced gradient variance compared with related methods; experiments on three domain-shift datasets show improved target-domain accuracy.
AI.conclusion: PSDA is a novel SVR technique tailored to distribution-matching objectives in UDA, leveraging paired sampling to reduce variance and enable effective finite-sum–like optimization, yielding better target-domain performance.

title: Online Variance Reduction for Domain Adaptation on Streaming Data
summary: This paper studies the problem of stochastic variance reduction (SVR) for the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) and correlation alignment (CORAL) loss functions. Although various offline SVR algorithms for these losses have been proposed, these are incompatible with online, distributed, or incremental learning settings. This paper presents Adaptive vaRiance Reduction via Online reWeighting (ARROW), the first online SVR algorithm for the MMD and CORAL for streamed data. The method maintains moving average references of the alignment statistics, and adaptively reweights incoming minibatches so that the minibatch and reference statistics are aligned. Further, we propose a relaxed reweighting scheme so that the ensuing weight-optimisation problem is tractable. In experiments and simulations, we show that ARROW performs competitively with offline algorithms in terms of runtime, degree of variance reduction achieved, and target domain accuracy.

AI.tldr: Introduces ARROW, the first online stochastic variance reduction method for MMD and CORAL losses, enabling streaming data with adaptive reweighting; shows competitive performance with offline methods.
AI.motivation: Offline SVR methods for MMD/CORAL exist but are unsuitable for online, distributed, or incremental learning; there is a need for online SVR to reduce variance in streaming settings.
AI.method: Proposes Adaptive vaRiance Reduction via Online reWeighting (ARROW). It maintains moving-average references of alignment statistics and adaptively reweights incoming minibatches to align with references. Also introduces a relaxed reweighting scheme to make the weight-optimization tractable.
AI.result: Empirical results (experiments and simulations) show ARROW is competitive with offline algorithms in runtime, variance reduction achieved, and target domain accuracy.
AI.conclusion: ARROW is the first online SVR algorithm for MMD and CORAL, enabling variance reduction in online/streaming contexts and performing competitively with offline counterparts; suggests potential for broader online alignment-based learning applications.

title: PG-KINN: A Physics-Informed Petrov-Galerkin Kolmogorov-Arnold Network for Solving Forward and Inverse PDEs
summary: Physics-informed learning of partial differential equations (PDEs) has been dominated by multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), whose spectral bias and dense parameterization limit both accuracy and interpretability. Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KANs) mitigate these limitations because their learnable spline activations are structurally aligned with the piecewise-polynomial bases of classical discretizations. However, the way a PDE is cast into a loss functional is as decisive as the choice of approximator: strong-form residual minimization requires high-order derivatives and heavily weighted losses, the energy (Bubnov-Galerkin) form is restricted to self-adjoint operators and, as we show, collapses to a trivial solution for parameter-identification problems, and boundary integral forms require a known fundamental solution. We propose PG-KINN, a physics-informed KAN built on a Petrov-Galerkin formulation in which the trial space is a KAN and the test space is an independent, compactly supported, piecewise-polynomial space evaluated with Gauss-Legendre quadrature. Integration by parts lowers the differentiation order while retaining applicability to general non-self-adjoint, nonlinear, and inverse problems; the localized test functions turn the global residual into a set of element-wise weak residuals with favorable conditioning. On a suite of benchmarks spanning crack singularities, stress concentration, Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, inverse parameter identification in heterogeneous media, and complex geometries, PG-KINN consistently outperforms legacy MLP baselines and state-of-the-art KAN-based strong/energy/inverse formulations (PIKAN). These results position the Petrov-Galerkin coupling of KAN trial spaces and polynomial test spaces as a robust and accurate route for AI-based computational mechanics.

AI.tldr: PG-KINN uses a Petrov-Galerkin framework with Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs) for physics-informed PDE learning, achieving improved accuracy and conditioning over MLPs and prior KAN formulations.
AI.motivation: To overcome spectrally biased, dense MLP-based PDE solvers and to avoid the limitations of strong-form, energy, and boundary-integral formulations across non-self-adjoint, nonlinear, and inverse problems.
AI.method: Construct a physics-informed KAN (PG-KINN) via a Petrov–Galerkin approach: trial space is a KAN; test space is an independent, compactly supported, piecewise-polynomial space evaluated with Gauss–Legendre quadrature; apply integration by parts to reduce derivative order; yields element-wise weak residuals suitable for non-self-adjoint and inverse problems.
AI.result: In benchmarks including crack singularities, stress concentration, Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, heterogeneous-media parameter identification, and complex geometries, PG-KINN outperforms legacy MLP baselines and prior KAN-based strong/energy/inverse methods (PIKAN).
AI.conclusion: The Petrov–Galerkin coupling of KAN trial spaces with polynomial test spaces provides a robust, accurate route for AI-based computational mechanics.

title: Isaac Sim-to-Real: Reinforcement Learning based Locomotion for Quadrupeds
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures. Accepted manuscript. Published in the 2025 IEEE 21st International Conference on Automation Science and Engineering (CASE), pp. 2194-2199
summary: Learning-based approaches to locomotion have risen in popularity in recent years, showing the capability for complex legged locomotion and whole-body control. Reinforcement learning (RL), the primary learning-based approach for locomotion, often utilizes a high-performance simulation tool, providing a controlled and efficient training and development environment. However, policies that perform well in simulation frequently encounter unexpected challenges when deployed on a physical system, known as the sim-to-real gap. This work presents a robust RL locomotion framework capable of whole-body control. The proposed RL framework utilizes Nvidia's new set of simulation tools, Isaac Sim, and its companion RL framework, Isaac Lab, for training, achieving a zero-shot sim-to-real policy. The performance of our policy is validated on physical hardware using the Unitree Go1, with experimental results showing similar velocity tracking performance to the quadruped's integrated controller, with a greater ability to recover from large disturbances, and achieve linear velocities of 2.0 m/s and angular velocities of 1.8 rad/s.

AI.tldr: A robust RL-based locomotion framework enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 using Nvidia Isaac tools, achieving competitive velocity tracking and superior disturbance rejection.
AI.motivation: To address the sim-to-real gap in learning-based locomotion; high-fidelity simulation environments offer efficient training but policies often fail on hardware, necessitating robust transfer.
AI.method: Train a whole-body RL policy in Nvidia Isaac Sim with Isaac Lab for data collection and policy optimization, achieving zero-shot transfer to hardware without per-robot fine-tuning; validate on the Unitree Go1.
AI.result: Policy achieves velocity tracking comparable to the quadruped's integrated controller and shows greater disturbance rejection; reaches 2.0 m/s linear velocity and 1.8 rad/s angular velocity on hardware.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the viability of zero-shot sim-to-real RL locomotion on a real quadruped using advanced Nvidia simulation tools, with robust performance and disturbance resilience.

title: Towards Torque-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Quadruped Locomotion
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Accepted manuscript. Published in the 2026 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII), pp. 1259-1264
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for legged robots is advancing locomotion, demonstrating its ability to adapt to new and challenging terrain. Traditionally, these RL locomotion frameworks are position-based, making the policy less adaptable to terrain types and requiring state estimation techniques in the observation space, i.e., linear velocity. Moreover, these RL frameworks often use small, lightweight quadrupeds that are limited in their viability for high-complexity tasks due to hardware constraints. This work explores an RL torque control framework for heavyweight high-torque quadrupeds. The RL framework in this paper can traverse rough terrain and effectively track a desired linear velocity without requiring knowledge of the agent's current velocity. Using Nvidia's Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab, simulation results of the RL torque control policy are shown on the Unitree B1 quadruped, achieving speeds of 3.5 m/s and 1.5 rad/s. In addition, the quadruped can walk up and down stairs without the aid of an exteroceptive sensor.

AI.tldr: Torque-control RL for heavyweight quadrupeds enables terrain-adaptive locomotion without velocity observation; simulated on Unitree B1 achieving 3.5 m/s and stairs traversal.
AI.motivation: Overcome limitations of position-based RL policies that rely on velocity/state estimation; enable high-torque, heavyweight quadrupeds to operate on rough terrain with limited sensory input.
AI.method: Developed an RL torque-control policy trained and evaluated in NVIDIA Isaac Sim/Lab; applied to a Unitree B1 in simulation; policy outputs joint torques and does not require current velocity in the observation.
AI.result: The robot traverses rough terrain and tracks a desired linear velocity without velocity feedback; reaches 3.5 m/s linear speed and 1.5 rad/s angular velocity; can walk up/down stairs without exteroceptive sensing.
AI.conclusion: RL torque control for heavyweight quadrupeds is feasible in simulation, reducing dependence on velocity observations and external sensors and showing promise for real hardware deployment.
